1.title: Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice

metadata.tagline: A time-traveling, double-crossing, ass-kicking comedy.

1.rich_text: Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice A time-traveling, double-crossing, ass-kicking comedy. Comedy Science Fiction Crime BenDavid Grabinski James Marsden Vince Vaughn Eiza González Keith David Jimmy Tatro Stephen Root Lewis Tan Ben Schwartz Emily Hampshire Arturo Castro Two gangsters and the woman they love try to survive the most dangerous night of their lives. As if that wasn’t enough, there’s one wild ingredient added to the mix: a time machine. Yes I am friends with the writer/director yes I am biased no I don't care because I'm not being paid for this review. Often felt like BenDavid made this movie specifically for me. There's an action scene set to Andrew WK (something I've been waiting forever to see). There's a scene involving one of my favorite songs ever that turns into one of the more moving moments I've seen in a movie this year. It has Jimmy Tatro onscreen doing… As a major Oliver & Company fan, that opening needle drop was like activating a sleeper agent within me. UR IN DANGER GIRL!!!!!! ok but Jess IS the best Rory boyfriend Ok, I’m a little embarrassed that I didn’t pick up on the connection right off the bat, but midway through a little light went off in my brain saying “something about this feels like Mikey and Nicky ” (which is one of my favorite movies). After that it all became kinda obvious…don’t judge me. Guys, I fucking loved this. James Marsden? Eiza Gonzalez being (standardly) super hot? Vince Vaughn (who’s dramatically grown on me over the years)? Jimmy Tatro (who I… Maybe the last time I’ll see it in a theater. Tonight at Vidiots was one of the best nights of my life. Ugh. The stuff I enjoyed the most was the use of time travel as a means to have Vince Vaughn tell himself he needs to get his head out of his ass; reminded me of ’90s Schwarzenegger movies like Last Action Hero or Total Recall where big sci-fi or fantasy conceits are a conduit to star deconstruction and self-reflection. The action recalls that period too; really jarring and visceral hits and falls. Fun! Fun merging of quirky time travel buddy comedy and violent gangster-hitman actioner. Marsden, Gonzalez and Vaughn are all quite charming doing what plays like 2000s rom-com banter while navigating their way through hyperviolent 90s action, both of the Hollywood and Hong Kong variety. Not every joke/reference landed for me but I respect that BenDavid didn't remotely compromise on his specific sense of humor or bleeding heart, which snuck up on me by the end. Wish I had been able to… It’s like someone made a movie just for me. So many funny specific moments wrapped up in kick ass action buddy movie with a A+ cast and a great surprise. Oh and also it’s got TimeTravel. Especially Great For Fans of Alf’s Christmas Special Time Cop & Oliver and Company Man I wish this was like a normal theatrical movie and not straight to hulu cuz it’s a pretty fun time and I would’ve loved to see the action on the big screen

WHY IS THERE PONY PLAY IN WUTHERING HEIGHTS WHY IS MARGOT ROBBIE DRESSED AS A SCANDINAVIAN MILKMAID WHY IS HEATHCLIFFE A SEXUAL SADIST NOT A VICTIM OF RACISM WHAT THE FUCK IS GOING ONNNNNNNNNN I really enjoyed that one part of this movie where Heathcliff looks right at the camera and says, "It's Wuthering time." this is what happens when you let people who were born to make aesthetic pinterest boards direct movies I’m not a purist about adaptations. Change things. Reinterpret. Go wild. But this version of Wuthering Heights feels less like an adaptation and more like someone skim read the blurb, vibesed for a bit, then decided Emily Brontë was simply being too intense and needed calming down. The big problem is tone. Or rather, the complete lack of the one Brontë actually wrote. This is a novel powered by spite, obsession, cruelty, class rage, and emotional violence. It is feral.… This all could’ve been prevented if Ao3 was made in Fennell’s youth. Realizing that Emerald Fennell so wildly misread this novel as a swoony teenager and that it then became a core artistic touchstone for her really unlocks her whole deal. Jettisoning the text's intrinsic racialism, classism, and story of abuse as love in favor of recasting Cathy and Heathcliff as doomed lovers locked in mutual acrimonious kink is certainly an eminently memeable take, and fealty to source is no barometer for success in adaptation, but this movie isn't even momentarily discomfiting to compensate.

I'd never had to resort to watching a movie using the 1.5x playback speed, but it was the only way I could finish this tedious mess that just doesn't seem to go anywhere. 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple worked better for me than the previous film. Not because it is necessarily bigger or more impressive in every way, but because this time many of its ideas feel more fully in place and the story finds a stronger shape. Watching it, you can tell that the third film will be needed to judge the whole picture properly, but this second chapter already works very well on its own.What makes it stand out is that it does not simply repeat the previous film’s structure or live off the prestige of the saga. It has more internal logic, more dramatic weight, and a story that moves forward with conviction. There is still violence, tension, and real ugliness, of course, but this time those elements are better integrated into something that wants to do more than just show a fight for survival. It feels more ambitious and, above all, **** cast is also excellent. Alfie Williams is outstanding again and confirms that he has a rare kind of screen presence. Ralph Fiennes is superb, bringing that distinctive mix of authority, strangeness, and humanity, while Jack O’Connell and Erin Kellyman are both terrific as well. The film gains a lot from the fact that its characters are not just figures thrown into a bloodbath, but real presences with weight, tension, and a very defined way of occupying the screen.I also liked the tone a lot. There is something darker, more reflective, and at the same time more emotional than in the previous film. It never abandons the genre, far from it, but it does not settle for shock, brutality, or chaos alone. There is a very strong story underneath, and that is what makes several scenes stay with you. Even when it gets savage, it never feels like empty **** then there is the music, which I thought was wonderful. Not just because of the pieces that are used, but because of how they are used. They are not there as decoration or as obvious emphasis, but to give the film identity, rhythm, and at times even a strange kind of beauty. In a film like this, that makes a huge difference, because it turns several sequences into something more powerful and more memorable.That is why, for me, this is a stronger entry than the previous one and a very good continuation within this new trilogy. We will have to see how everything fits once the third film arrives, but The Bone Temple already gives the feeling that there is more here than just a well-made genre sequel. The dialogue is packed with forced jokes, cheap quips, and one-liners that constantly interrupt the pacing, even stopping chase scenes just to deliver them. It completely kills the momentum.

Rosamund Pike’s South African accent is extremely distracting, and she isn’t a compelling villain at all. There’s no real presence, threat, or intelligence behind her character, which removes any sense of tension from the story.

The action scenes are just as frustrating. Once again, Hollywood leans into ridiculous fight choreography where a much smaller female character is shown effortlessly beating up multiple full-grown men. It looks completely unrealistic and breaks immersion. This isn’t about gender — it’s about basic physics and believability.

The film also relies heavily on lazy nostalgia, awkwardly reintroducing old characters with forced callbacks instead of letting moments happen naturally. It feels cheap, repetitive, and uninspired.

Overall, this is a lazy, poorly written sequel that fails to capture the cleverness and style of the original. Easily one of the most frustrating movie experiences I’ve had in a long time.

First of all - "Dunkirk" (2017) is not the best war film ever made in my opinion. By far. I don't think that there ever will be a better war movies then "Apocalypse Now" (1979) or even "Saving Private Ryan" (1998), "Platoon" (1986) or "The Thin Red Line" (1998). It is not even the best Christopher Nolan movie at the moment (the crown goes to "Interstellar (2014)). That said, "Dunkirk" is something absolutely unique, stunning, kinda mesmerizing movie going experience. It is not perfect, sometimes even a bit confusing (because of the time lines, but its not "overdone") movie, but the one which absolutely has to be seen in a movie theater.
The best thing about "Dunkirk" is the craftsmanship and the biggest star of "Dunkirk" is without a doubt Christopher Nolan. The script in here is not a great one, and like i said i was a bit confused at some moments, but the storytelling here is so powerful itself that it tells everything. Music is simply astonishing. Hans Zimmer (again) does something absolutely unique with Nolan movie - it transcendence the whole experience. Cinematography by Hoyte Van Hoytema is a masterpiece. So here are the 4 Oscar nominations for sure - best director, music, cinematography (probably a winner) and sounds (sure winners). Acting was good given the roles, but nothing very memorable except for a great Mark Rylance and Fionn Whitehead which i really liked in this role.
Overall, "Dunkirk" is not a bloody or gore war movie. Its "horror" is terror. This is not an "easy" movie going experience because you have to pay attention during a whole movie and it doesn't have sharp characters to which you can relate - its about a situation at the moment - right here right now. There are "time line" sections / intersections that makes you think about what you are seeing. And it is done so unique, so ambitious that i probably haven't witnessed this kinda movie before. "Dunkirk" is not a mainstream "war movie", basically it is a thriller set in a WW2. But its crafted so uniquely that it can not be missed. A sure classic, if not for everyone. I especially like the kind of quick and straight progress which generates and undertow and atmosphere till the last credit of the film is running over the screen. 10/10 One of the better war time films made in recent years, which looks and sounds incredible. Impressive budget and effects, but beyond that not much new or interesting. The terror of a quiet solitude, exposed on an endangered French beach and desperately awaiting evacuation at the height of World War II. Abandoning the more experimental themes he toyed with in Inception and Interstellar, Christopher Nolan has set out to make a mostly-straight war picture, shining his spotlight on a major test (and ultimate turning point) for the British armed forces. Told from three entangled perspectives - one each from land, sea and air - we see heroes, victims, cowards and lunatics emerge from what might have otherwise seemed a nondescript group of frightened young men.

Dunkirk is far less bombastic than the standard combat film, with a soft, observant character and distinct lack of extraneous dialogue. That reticence, paired with an emphasis on beautifully-composed photography, reminded me more of an art film than an action epic. The battlefield's thick tension is inescapable, though, always drawing us back to the moment, with the wary skyward eyes and skittish, shell-shocked nature of nearby soldiers proving a constant reminder that arbitrary death could be mere moments away. It’s also the rare positive example of a recent tendency toward uneven sound mixes: a barrage of gunfire or sudden, screaming airborne bombing run can pack a mighty punch.

Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets Something evil has returned to Hogwarts! Adventure Fantasy Chris Columbus Daniel Radcliffe Rupert Grint Emma Watson Kenneth Branagh Toby Jones Robbie Coltrane Richard Harris Alan Rickman Tom Felton Jason Isaacs Cars fly, trees fight back, and a mysterious house-elf comes to warn Harry Potter at the start of his second year at Hogwarts. Adventure and danger await when bloody writing on a wall announces: The Chamber Of Secrets Has Been Opened. To save Hogwarts will require all of Harry, Ron and Hermione's magical abilities and courage. One of the most mature works of the saga.

When I was a kid, I watched ‘Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets’ many times, but it never fascinated me as much as the other installments. Back then, I wanted more action, more duels between students, and a greater display of visual magic. However, revisiting it years later with a more mature perspective, I’ve come to realize that what once seemed like a flaw —its focus on plot and mystery— is now one of its greatest strengths.

This second entry stands out for its narrative solidity. Chris Columbus manages to adapt J.K. Rowling’s second book with remarkable fidelity and coherence, without losing rhythm or clarity in the storytelling. Despite being one of the most information-dense chapters in the saga, the plot is easy to follow. Every question raised finds its answer in due time, and the screenplay strikes an admirable balance between exposition and emotion.

From a technical standpoint, the special effects deserve special recognition. Beyond the digital visuals, the practical effects —now almost nostalgic— truly stand out. The giant spider Aragog, brought to life through animatronics, is impressive in its realism and physical presence. The same goes for the petrified characters, recreated with mannequins of astonishing detail. These effects, though evidently handcrafted, blend seamlessly into the magical world.

Harry’s protagonism feels more defined than in the first film, and the main trio continues to shine with charisma, even when one of them is absent for much of the runtime. John Williams’ score remains an essential element: majestic, immersive, and capable of stirring emotion even after countless listens.

Visually, the film is a delight. The sets of Hogwarts and its surroundings are so carefully designed that they convey a tangible sense of reality. Everything feels so natural that one can’t help but wish to be there. Moreover, the atmosphere achieves a darker, more mysterious tone, foreshadowing the saga’s evolution toward more mature and complex storylines.

Ultimately, ‘Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets’ is one of the most balanced and engaging entries in the series. It may feature less overt magic than others, but it compensates with a story that is rich, coherent, and deeply immersive. It’s a film that grows with time —and with the viewer’s own maturity—, a true example of how fantasy cinema can evolve without losing its sense of wonder. It's weird how this movie has so many fewer reviews than the first one.  I smell Metacritic shenanigans to bump the score up higher than the first one.  Dune 1 established the style which is the most striking accomplishment of the series.  Yes the narrative feels unfinished but that's to be expected; it's the first half of a single novel.  Dune 2 carries all of that forward while having the benefit of resolution which adds to the satisfaction factor.  However this film rewrites the novel in ways that are unforgivable.  In an attempt to modernize the narrative (or whatever, I just see it as feminist propaganda) they completely ruin Channi's arc in an attempt to make her seem less dependent and more strong and independent.  In chasing trends it actually makes the character seem petty.  There's real strength in the novel and a sense of yearning in Chani's decision to accept her role as Paul's crypto love interest playing second fiddle to a union that is overall better for the power structure.  These decisions at the stake of this narrative feel more real than a love interest attempting to call the shots with a god-king.  It's like Dune was rewritten as a YA novel.  Really disappointing stuff, although I'm sure the producers insisted the changes be made like they always do. To me DUNE part one and two are one film, but if I had to pick a favorite of the two, it'd be this one. DUNE part two is full of action, and most of the setup from the first unfolds here, but then leaves a lot of directions forward from the answers. DUNE part two is fantastic, complicated film that doesn't follow the modern way of making movies, and in that way already, I love it. Again - gorgeous cinematography and epic visionary display but the horrendous "creative" changes just ruined any love I have for this version.  Come on!?!  I just can't rate this any higher and I had held out so much hope that someone maybe, somewhere, would smack the production team and director and go back to the source material and stay true but in classic Hollywood fashion . . . they f***ed it up! It is a perfect Movie i Like the Charakters and the Story is Peak .Dune Part two is one of my favorite Movies of all time. The Soundtrack is also 10/10 Es una secuela monumental, una experiencia visual y narrativa que confirma el genio de Denis Villeneuve. Cada plano es arte, cada diálogo, una pieza de un universo político y místico que se siente tan real como soñado. Es cine épico en su máxima expresión, donde la ciencia ficción se funde con la fantasía para recordarnos por qué aún vale la pena maravillarse en una sala oscura. As I said before, the first part was just a prologue to a big something in the making and here we go! This is a well-crafted movie. It goes without saying that the narrative is intersecting with a lot of islamic beliefs in a suspicious way; Lisan Al-Gaib, Muad’Dib, Mahdi, Fedaykin, the way of Sujud, women chadors and even the Atreides & Arrakis has something to do with the Maturidis & Iraq. If Edward Said still with us, he would have a lot to say! I found that very unpleasant and that's why the rating. My only flaw for Villeneuve's masterpiece sequel is pacing/runtime. And even then, I don't think I would really throw a fit if the movie was 15 minutes longer. Dune: Part Two demands your attention and will make any humble movie theatre feel like an IMAX. Gorgeous visuals, dynamic performances, and turns out Austin Butler is a better Stellan Skarsgard than Stellan Skarsgard. It will never be Dune as it's just an adaption and in how it has strayed far from the books. So I will enjoy it for what it is a thing of it's own like fan fiction.

Lots of motion and you can tell it is optimized for 3D.

The issue is the script can be pretty dumb ("unobtanium"?) & unoriginal, and characters do things because the movie needs for them to happen, not because they make sense or are possible. And the passage of time isn't really explained -- Jake leaves his avatar for hours (days?) on end, but when he comes back, he jumps right back into the mix.

A big time event movie that should be seen in the theater, and then not really ever again. (ENG) Avatar strikes me as a film ahead of its time, though not without debatable aspects. Its greatest strength lies in the visual impact: Pandora remains one of the most breathtaking worlds ever portrayed on screen, with a use of 3D, color, and special effects that feels truly immersive and seamlessly integrated into the narrative. The setting, the fauna, the flora, and the Na’vi culture are crafted with a level of detail that reflects a clear and ambitious vision. I also value the central message about colonialism, resource exploitation, and the connection with nature, which, while not particularly subtle, is effective and easy to grasp. On the negative side, the story itself is fairly predictable; the protagonist’s arc and the overall structure echo familiar tales, making the narrative less surprising. Some human characters come across as flat or stereotypical, and the moral conflict is presented in a very straightforward way, without much nuance. Even so, the balance between spectacle, emotion, and internal coherence works well. It is neither perfect nor revolutionary in terms of script, but as a cinematic experience it is powerful, memorable, and visually extraordinary, allowing its narrative weaknesses to fade into the background compared to everything it does right.____________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

This first part of one of cinema’s greatest sagas began, for me, with very modest expectations. My experience with the book was negative, which made me fear that the film would be overwhelming and tedious due to its density. However, the surprise is overwhelmingly positive from the very beginning.

The film stands out for its remarkable production values. The performances are solid, the cinematography is extremely crafted, detailed, and impressive, with effects that still hold up remarkably well today. The set design is equally strong, adding depth and character to the world. The soundtrack may not linger in memory, but it works perfectly for this kind of film. Overall, the result is enjoyable both visually and aurally.

I greatly appreciate Peter Jackson’s narrative clarity. The book can be overwhelming with its abundance of names, places, and concepts, but Jackson translates all that into a visual language that is both clear and accessible. The information is presented intelligently, allowing the viewer to follow the story without feeling lost or overwhelmed.

The differences between the book and the film are undeniable, but far from detrimental. On the contrary, they enhance the experience. Nothing feels sacrificed; the story gains cohesion and rhythm. I had feared the film’s runtime—not because it lasts nearly four hours, but due to the potential density of the plot—but the pacing dispels that concern. The nearly four-hour length never becomes an obstacle, especially when the final half-hour is credits.

I wouldn’t say the film completely captivates me, but this first installment leaves a positive impression. It is a grand welcome to Tolkien’s universe, demonstrating that adaptations can honor the source material while improving the cinematic experience by understanding potential pitfalls and avoiding them. Peter Jackson’s The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is a masterclass in epic storytelling, seamlessly blending breathtaking visuals, meticulously crafted world-building, and deeply human emotion. The film introduces audiences to Middle-earth with a perfect balance of wonder, danger, and intimate character moments, making even its extended three-hour runtime feel purposeful and engaging. The Fellowship’s journey is imbued with courage, friendship, and moral complexity, anchored by performances that feel timeless and sincere. Howard Shore’s sweeping score elevates every scene, while Jackson’s direction ensures that spectacle never overshadows heart. For newcomers and longtime fans alike, this film is not just a fantasy adventure—it is an immersive, emotionally resonant cinematic experience that stands as a benchmark for the genre. With the first installment of “The Lord of the Rings” trilogy, Peter Jackson did the almost impossible: He brought J.R.R. Tolkien’s Middle-earth to life in the hills of New Zealand, appealing to longtime fans and newcomers who might be wary of the jargon about elves and orcs. The film set a new bar for fantasy blockbusters with makeup and effects that still hold up, and set pieces that are immersive and occasionally terrifying. As soon as Howard Shore’s score kicks in, it’s hard not to feel transported. All three movies are masterpieces; this one is just best of the best. Lower scope fantasy here is like playing an RPG game.

68.rich_text:
Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die Time is running out. Are you ready to join the revolution? Science Fiction Action Comedy Gore Verbinski Sam Rockwell Juno Temple Haley Lu Richardson Michael Peña Zazie Beetz Asim Chaudhry Tom Taylor Georgia Goodman Daniel Barnett Artie Wilkinson-Hunt A 'Man from the Future' arrives at an LA diner where he must recruit the precise combination of disgruntled patrons to join him on a one-night quest to save the world from the terminal threat of a rogue artificial intelligence. A little too 'lol so random' for my taste. I do think there is a decent story at the center of it and I enjoyed the anti AI sentiment and some of the modern satire. Dark, humorous, and thought-provoking; Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die lives up to its title by maintaining a lighthearted, self-deprecating tone while delving into social themes with more depth than one might expect. It's rejected black mirror episodes hung on a time travel thread. 
The longer it goes on the less I liked it. 
It's entertaining, in parts - but thinks it's smarter than it is.
thinks it has weigh and meaning, it doesn't. 
It's 30 minutes too long. 
With little mcguffins that appear in periods, then you think --- yeah but what didn;t that happen scenes ago.
A poor man's time travel of Sean of the dead and Brazil. Without its brilliance.

But all in all - I don't know why someone would have greenlit this. There’s no preamble to this plot: Sam Rockwell stomps straight through the doors of a busy diner at the one minute mark, loaded for bear in the most crackpot homemade science fiction maniac costume one can imagine, and lays it all out for us. Hey gang, I’m from the future and I’m here to recruit a squad of nobodies to help save the world. Oh, and also, I’ve made this speech, to this room, more than a hundred times already. We haven’t managed to get it right just yet. Cue the police sirens and the first of many frantic escape sequences. 

It’s a goofy premise that acknowledges as much. Perhaps too much, if I’m being completely honest... there’s a *lot* of conspicuous winking going on. And while the narrative toys with all sorts of pointed, valid, high-tech phobias en route to its explosive finale - AI, VR, engagement algorithms, school shootings, drones, clones, pervasive gamification - for me, that inauthentic weirdness calls its intent into question. Is this just a cheap effort to use our societal disarray for fake depth, or does it actually have something to say? The first act seems to imply one answer, but the balance flips as we wade deeper into the conceptual weeds. By the climax, I was beginning to feel annoyed. Are we going to crap here, or are we just going to hang around on the pot for a couple hours? 

As the journey proceeds, we cut away to document each supporting character’s immediate origins. How their day was going before they entered the restaurant. In each case, not so good. Without exception, these play like a procession of sugared-up Black Mirror episodes. In a few cases, I think their concepts are actually lifted directly from the show, watered down and over-saturated in the name of broader entertainment value, then plugged back into the machine. The first example, a treatise on inattentive teens and shell-shocked teachers, is amusing but light, and the returns diminish from there. These sidetracks offer a lot of color and wacky ideas, but never resolve. Even as their subjects are summarily killed off. 

On a strictly superficial level, Good Luck is abstract fun in the same vein as Everything Everywhere All at Once, but it lacks that film’s conviction and often gets hung up on proving it’s half as clever as it thinks it is. Loudly insecure, I think, is the right way to put it. A big, erratic caper with wild ideas and eccentric performances, but it’s so focused on gaining our approval that it forgets to follow through on its promises. 可以认为是《黑镜》超长同人作品，杂糅了很多集的点子。这片的网飞味儿太正了，但却是环球的作品……
有好几位熟脸都在影片中出演，所以倒是看的还挺乐呵。至于故事，融合了目前短视频泛滥、娱乐至死、注意力分散、对AI飞速发展未来的担忧等。实际成片效果嘛，个人觉得不如看3集《黑镜》。不过依然值得一看。 Verbinski’s first movie since 2016, and it’s an ambitious one. It stars Sam Rockwell as a man who goes into a Norm’s Diner claiming to be from the future, and says he needs to take some people with him to stop an evil AI from taking over the world.

And from that point on, we get a bizarre unpredictable action-comedy. Complete with three long segments of backstory for many of its main characters that seem a lot like episodes of Black Mirror. At the beginning it appears that we are in the modern times, but these stories suggest that the dystopian future may already be upon the people in that diner. The first one is easily the weakest and feels like a boomer lecturing about “them kids and they’re blasted phones.” The second one surprisingly deals with the school shooting epidemic, and it is dark comedy with emphasis on the dark. One high point would not be out of place in a Yorgos Lanthimos film. The last one is a sort of slower romance thing, and despite not having as much ridiculous **** happening, it still stays consistently interesting.

In fact, the whole movie stays consistently interesting. It’s two hours and fourteen minutes long, but there is enough plot and backstory to justify that length and make it still perfectly paced. And it’s a great meshing of several genres, including comedy, action, a bit of horror, a little drama. Much of the comedy is great. Sam Rockwell gives an energetic performance, that’s dripping with charisma.

The story is always unpredictable. And not only because of how many people don’t make it out alive. Even if you were to somehow know which of Rockwell’s assistants make it to the end, there’s no real point where it is clear where the movie is headed next.

This is Verbinski’s Everything Everywhere All At Once. They threw in so many ideas that are so out weird and out there, and make it all mostly work they way they intended in one wildly entertaining fever dream.

It deals with a lot of issues mostly involving technology and AI. But also other problems of todays world, like that aforementioned school shooter story. It is a tale of everything wrong with the digital age.

But unfortunately not all of it is as deep as it wants to be. Once again there are parts that just feel like an old man yelling at a cloud. And a bunch of half-baked stuff about how “oooh, your phone is actually a prison!”

But its intentions are good: pointing out the absurdity of today’s modern hellscape. In one weird, entertaining, unpredictable ride. Verbinski comes back strong with this one. Good luck trying to create something like this with AI. This movie is something you will have fun watching. And not die. And… good luck?

****/@jaythemovieguy7751 This movie exceeded my expectations coming in. It was a very entertaining and fun movie that blew me away. It really is a one of a kind movie that is wild and fearless in crossing the boundaries of the human imagination. I look forward for the sequel and more movies like this. A bit of a bait and switch. If like me you thought this was just a time travel comedy about saving the world from phone addiction and VR, then you'll be disappointed. It's really a black mirror episode in disguise. The film even takes short breaks to tell smaller subplot stories about some of the side characters. The first half of the film is ok, but it starts huffing its own farts in the second half with scenes that are over the top and that don't really make much sense even at the end when you're told what happened (although many people will likely figure out what happened on their own). I think this is one of those films that are best streamed at home, since you can turn it off without loosing any money. It's annoying since the early commentary on phone addiction, VR, school shootings and how people have become so psychologically weak made for an interesting comedy and was much more interesting film. Movie showed the fans how life has changed I loved the message about how phones and computers have took over our daily lives. It's a funny and thought-provoking B-Movie in the best sense of the term.  Rockwell, Juno, and Haley Lu (as well as Michael Pena in a smaller role) are all uniformly terrific.

The Devil Wears Prada es de esas películas donde siempre queda la duda abierta: quién es realmente el villano, hasta dónde llegan los límites del trabajo y los derechos laborales. Todo eso ya se ha discutido mil veces, y aun así la película sigue funcionando perfecto. Es un 10/10. Y solo agregaría esto: si de verdad te encanta el cine, tienes que verla. Más allá de la moda y los diálogos, la película sabe contar con imágenes. Definitivamente: es cine The title doesn't lie – Miranda Priestly is the devil. But I'd watch the film again sometime just for the dialogue. It's a sharply written film with great performances, memorable characters, and a story that fully earns its impact, i truly love The Devil Wears Prada. I am here reviewing this movie because I want to see the sequel.

"The Devil Wears Prada" is a smart, stylish film that blends humor with a touch of drama, set against the backdrop of the high-pressure fashion industry. Meryl Streep is magnetic as the commanding Miranda Priestly, delivering a performance that's both intimidating and captivating, while Anne Hathaway shines as the relatable protagonist navigating the chaos of her new role. The movie's greatest strength lies in its ability to make you reflect on the sacrifices we make in pursuit of success and whether they're truly worth it.

The pacing is well-done, keeping you invested without dragging, and the supporting cast, especially Emily Blunt, adds layers of wit and charm. What stands out is the film's subtle commentary on personal growth, ambition, and staying true to what really matters, all wrapped in sharp dialogue and stunning visuals. It never feels preachy but leaves you thinking about how much of yourself you're willing to compromise to fit into someone else's definition of success.

While it doesn't dive too deeply into its themes and follows some predictable beats, the movie more than makes up for it with its entertainment value and heartfelt moments. It's a fun, engaging watch with enough substance to leave a lasting impression. Perfect for when you want something light yet meaningful. The Devil Wears Prada teaches an important lesson, but in the end makes it seem an easier decision than it really is.

​Borscht was officially recognized by UNESCO in 2022 as part of Ukrainian Intangible Cultural Heritage. Titanic Titanic Nothing on earth could come between them. Drama Romance James Cameron Leonardo DiCaprio Kate Winslet Billy Zane Kathy Bates Frances Fisher Gloria Stuart Bill Paxton Bernard Hill David Warner Victor Garber 101-year-old Rose DeWitt Bukater tells the story of her life aboard the Titanic, 84 years later. A young Rose boards the ship with her mother and fiancé. Meanwhile, Jack Dawson and Fabrizio De Rossi win third-class tickets aboard the ship. Rose tells the whole story from Titanic's departure through to its death—on its first and last voyage—on April 15, 1912. Titanic remains one of the most immersive and emotionally devastating films ever made. From its sweeping scale to its intimate character work, the film fully earns its legendary status. James Cameron crafts a world that feels authentic and lived-in, making the tragedy not just spectacular but also deeply personal and credible.

Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio are extraordinary, especially considering how young they were at the time. Their performances are natural, sincere, and emotionally grounded, giving the love story a timeless quality that never feels forced or overly sentimental. Their chemistry anchors the film and makes the heartbreak inevitable—and unforgettable.

What sets Titanic apart is its ability to balance epic filmmaking with raw human emotion. It is visually breathtaking, meticulously detailed, and profoundly heart-wrenching. No matter how many times it’s watched, the emotional impact never dulls. Titanic isn’t just a film—it’s an experience, and one that continues to resonate decades later. Frankenstein Frankenstein Only monsters play God. Drama Fantasy Horror Guillermo del Toro Oscar Isaac Jacob Elordi Christoph Waltz Mia Goth Felix Kammerer Charles Dance David Bradley Lars Mikkelsen Christian Convery Nikolaj Lie Kaas Dr. Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant but egotistical scientist, brings a creature to life in a monstrous experiment that ultimately leads to the undoing of both the creator and his tragic creation. This is really good, it still holds up today and is very engaging with great characters. There are issues with the production around the limitations of filmmaking at the time but none of that really bothered me. The film looks beautiful and the sound quality is certainly better than Dracula (1931). The story is a bit different to the book but it’s a great story nonetheless and a sad one too. This film defines so many tropes in the genre like villagers with burning torches and Frankenstein’s monster being a gentle soul even though his brain was from a deranged criminal. I think you could really dig deep and analyse so much of this film. It’s probably my favourite Universal monsters movie. Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein is exactly what you’d expect from him — visually stunning, deeply romantic, and dripping with atmosphere. It’s a gothic fever dream full of haunting sets, lavish lighting, and moments of real emotional beauty.

That said, it can be a bit too much **** thing. The theatrical tone sometimes overwhelms the story, turning scenes that should feel intimate into grand performances. Mia Goth, usually magnetic, pushes so hard here that her intensity starts to feel like overacting — fascinating to watch, but occasionally distracting. And while Jacob Elordi makes a strong impression as the Creature, I wasn’t sold on the makeup design; it’s elegant and painterly, but it lacks the raw, unsettling quality I wanted.

Still, there’s no denying the craft on display. Even when it stumbles, Frankenstein is ambitious and heartfelt — a lush, tragic fable about creation and loneliness that only del Toro could make. Beautiful, flawed, and worth seeing. I didn't expect the story to be this dark, this was my very first introduction to the Frankenstein story, and what a fascinating experience it was, even though the film runs for only about 70 minutes, it still feels like there's more to explore in the story, more layers to the themes of creation, humanity, and morality that made Mary Shelley's original tale so timeless.

The acting is solid overall, with Colin Clive delivering an intense performance as Dr. Frankenstein, perfectly capturing the obsession and madness behind his character, some other performances aren't as strong, but they don’t take away from the film's power, Boris Karloff as the Monster is absolutely iconic, his presence, expressions, and movements make the creature both terrifying and sympathetic.

I was completely drawn in by the film's atmosphere, legacy, and the eerie yet beautiful vibe that defines early horror cinema, it's easy to see why Frankenstein remains such an important part of film history, personally, i enjoyed this much more than Béla Lugosi's Dracula, both the story and the film itself just felt far more engaging, in my opinion. Incredible production design and sets. Obviously a template and inspiration for a million things to come. Фильм можно посмотреть, но чисто для ознакомления, с чего началась история монстра Франкенштейна. Слишком уж коряво и наивно всё смотрится на текущий день. Un clásico, de eso no hay duda, pero en general no me termina de convencer la película en su totalidad. Es decir, la primera parte es bastante lenta sin demasiada gracia, pero la segunda mitad mejora mucho ya con el "monstruo" vivo. Me pasa lo mismo que con Nosferatu, la película como tal es normal sin demasiadas cosas buenas, pero la estética del ser de fantasía realmente es excelente y esta película es igual: cuando lo ves vivo y cómo se comporta es genial. Queda la duda de si con el cerebro de alguien normal, podría comportarse diferente y no hacer algunas cosas que hizo, ya que para mí no lo puedo juzgar; es decir, nunca se lo intentó tratar con paciencia, siempre se lo trató mal, por lo que matar a su creador para mí fue justicia. En conclusión, es buena película, pero hasta ahí. This rather loose interpretation of Mary Shelley's classic novel picks the bones of the source material before spinning off into something very different. Both involve discredited scientists, experimenting while in isolation, and their successful attempts to create one new life from the broken remnants of several others. That's where the similarities end.

The movie is certainly less intellectual, less challenging, with a tendency towards a kitschy, garish side. Doctor Frankenstein is more comically unhinged, recklessly dashing about the screen or pantomiming the shapes produced by his personal Tesla coil in a fit of exhilaration. The monster also differs from his printed counterpart, trading eloquence and ambition for a taste of raw, base humanity. In this case, I prefer the film's version: an articulate quarry with existential objections is less compelling than an impulsive toddler in a looming seven-foot frame. Or maybe it's just because this version is so incredible well-realized. Boris Karloff is a showstopper, and not just for the timeless, genre-defining makeup that's weighing him down. There's a sad, quiet pathos to his take on the creature, beneath the fiery temper and blunt physical presence. Even when he's at fault, he draws us in. We wish he were more present as the screen veers back to his tormentors, over and over again. But then again, maybe a larger bite would spoil the flavor.

A risky take for its time, one that ran afoul of censors across the globe, Frankenstein is surprisingly well-realized, considering its age, and its morals remain both simple and profound. This movie is the classic game changing horror film.  Compelling and well performed throughout.  I liked the Expressionistic set design, the iconic monster makeup, and the now iconic creation sequence, and the fiery windmill scene. I watched it this Halloween season (**** it's still a good movie.
Short, beautiful black and white glory, a classic.
Better than Dracula in my opinion There have been complaints that Frankenstein is dated. Personally I don't find that, it isn't the most sumptuous of all films, but it is still a wonderful film, that is still shocking and enthralling to me. The Gothic set design is very imaginative, helped by the beautiful cinematography with suitably bizarre camera angles, and the music score is haunting, melancholy and atmospheric. James Whale's direction is also very impressive, it is very focused and innovative. The story is without a doubt a classic, tense, moody and melancholic, and the Monster itself is just a masterful creation. The cast are superb, Colin Clive is very good as the eccentric Henry Frankenstein, while Mae Clarke is an alluring and sympathetic Elizabeth. There is no doubt in my mind though that Boris Karloff gave the best performance, not only that but the definitive portrayal of the monster. He is almost unrecognisable and scary with his make up, and while he was scary with the towering presence and the frightening look in his eyes, his monster is also somewhat touching, particularly when he reaches up to grasp a ray of sunlight. Overall, shocking, enthralling and just wonderful. "It's Alive!" 10/10 Bethany Cox

I had seen an old special edition DVD of this film a long time, it had a haunting standoffish and dream-like quality that resulted in all three of us falling asleep. And I never revisited it, mostly because of the butchery this film underwent, I rarely had a fancy to go back and indulge in an unfinished and adulterated vision.

But a chance to see it at a packed house, with a pal who loves it, at the Prince Charles I couldn't pass up and I was greatfully surprised at the film and slightly surprised at how much of a campy, guffawing audience we had; it's a silly movie, it's cheesy and it is camp, but it's not that bad.

I think the first half of the film won me over. As a fan of the book it's a remarkably faithful translation and shares many hallmarks with Villeneuve's modern duology. The first half has remarkable physical effects, sets and design, digital effects ahead of its time, very strong directing, edgy creative choices, a really mature and ugly visual style that now feels like a modern video game, a spectacular soundtrack and a really very strong cast.

The middle sags and I did feel the familiar pang that dreamlike science-fantasy delivers as it tried to pull me to sleep, but the final third is so mired in montage, desperate to cram everything that the book held (and missing much of the satire and commentary) and also so full of bonkers ideas and imagery that I couldn't help be repulsed and engaged by. This is where the camp lies and the film is a comical, rushed jumble until the end.

But overall I really love campy, cheesy sci-fi-fantasy that really tries something weird and po-faced and bold, and this film hits all of that. Also I love their tan uniforms and non-binary Military. Есть мысли, что эта экранизация наиболее близка к книге, так как участвовал непосредственно автор, но это разбивается об то, что тут подобавляли то, чего не было, и вообще меняет отношение к этому, те же голосовые модули как по мне лишнее. Потом, по сравнению с фильмом «Дюна 2» Вильнёва, концовка незакончена что ли, а между тем у Вильнёва мне этот момент очень понравился. И всё-таки подход 2000-го года сериала был лучше, тут же в середине фильма сократили некую часть событий, пересказав события последних 2 лет.Итог: в каждой экранизации, есть свои сильные стороны, и смотря другую экранизацию я узнаю что то новое, а что знал мне не сказали, но зная это я все понимаю ибо видел это в пред. фильмах.Смотрел в озвучке: СТС Même après toutes ces années, on est encore surpris de la qualité du scénario (entièrement écrit par le réalisateur lui-même) d’une grande fidélité au livre d’Herbert, plus fidèle sur nombre d’aspects que les films de Villeneuve, c’est dire ! en deux heures et quart, il a tout résumé, tout plié, extrait la substantifique moëlle de Dune, ses affabulations, son mysticisme de pacotille et j’en passe (oui, je parle du livre, résolument perfectible et… baroque !).

David Lynch délivre une réalisation classique et solide, insistant sur les côtés décadents (et kitschs) de l’oeuvre d’origine. Les effets spéciaux sont tout aussi kitschs, une façon élégante de dire qu’ils sentent vraiment le poisson… d’ailleurs, pour moins les ‘voir’, pour moins être ‘choqué’ , il vaut mieux visionner le dévédé un peu pourravenaze, histoire de noyer ce fatras d’effets suspects sous une bonne couche de flou (on ne conseillera pas la VHS, ça deviendrait insupportable -encore pire que la « boîte »‘ !).

Cela étant, on apprécie tout de même des décors intéressants et créatifs et certains accoutrements (qui peuvent faire sourire !) ainsi qu’une certaine ironie… et bien entendu une excellente distribution : on a -pour cette époque- que des pointures ou presque, non pas des ‘triple A’ certes, mais des comédiens et comédiennes toujours judicieusement choisis, y compris parmi les figurants, ce qui tranche très agréablement de la distribution discutable des Dune de Villeneuve, les ‘Dune : Woke Edition’ !

En définitive, avec ce Dune 1984, on est en présence d’un nanar plus ou moins haut de gamme et pourtant toujours aussi fascinant malgré son allure de navet fatigué ! il y a dans ce film quelque chose de plus, de supérieur à la somme de toutes les parties qui le composent, c’est ce ‘quelque chose’ qui lui confère un statut à part, celui de ‘classique’ en somme, envers et contre tous ! It's more cartoonish, colorful, surreal an grotesque take on Dune, but Lynch did his best to pack as many plot points into his film in limited run time. I have good memories despite the departure from the source. Still very watchable! I recommend it. This is where it's at; there was never a need for a remake. This isn't something David would have normally created, but it's such a bizarre science fiction anyhow, one that can easily bore most people.  

When you add the amount of color and craziness that Lynch brings, it makes for a better experience! Um längen besser als die langweilige neuverfilmung. Klar sind die Effekte veraltet aber der rest dafür eindeutig besser.

78.title: Marty Supreme

metadata.tagline: Dream big.

78.rich_text:
Marty Supreme Marty Supreme Dream big. Drama Thriller Josh Safdie Timothée Chalamet Gwyneth Paltrow Odessa A'zion Kevin O'Leary Tyler, The Creator Fran Drescher Abel Ferrara Emory Cohen Géza Röhrig Koto Kawaguchi Marty Mauser, a young man with a dream no one respects, goes to hell and back in pursuit of greatness. What a joke. This movie isn't even a 89/100. It's 60/100 at best. I don't even know why you would want to watch this movie, and skip out on good ones like god father and similar movies of high caliber. This movie of 89/100 rating makes it sound like it is as good as Glenn Gary Ross, or almost as good. This whole movie is like a nothing burger; you expect to learn something interesting, you expect to explore something new or a new idea but the overwhelming disappointment that veers on you the moment you find out that there's absolutely nothing interesting that happens in this movie and the ending is boring.

The main character's back story IS /kind/ of interesting, but that also is boring. It's like watching an anti climatic Frankenstein. A well made picture, great cast and acting from everyone. Chalamet’s performance is excellent and the cinematography looks  artistic, lightning is very efficient in magnifying Marty’s tragic and suspenseful torments. Nonetheless , the story about a selfish man who doesn’t care about anyone but him, turns the audience like him, starting losing interest about the protagonist about 45mn-1h in the movie. It might not be for everyone. I went in without any expectations, but the movie has pacing issue and is way too long, director could have shelved 20mn without losing -if any- much of its story and depiction of Marty’s challenge. This is not a hero’s journey nor a story about a charming underdog who’ll overcome is own issues. Josh Safdie strikes again with a raw, cacophonous, and chaotic work, while Timothée Chalamet, much like the Marty he portrays, once more demonstrates his extraordinary ambition and acting prowess. Marty Mauser is a piece of ****, and the attempt to redeem him in the final act looks absolutely pathetic. Not worth more than the required 75 characters. What a disappointment…wondering what rave reviewers saw. A movie about Timothée Chalamet running from one place to another.

For weeks I had been dying to see 'Marty Supreme'. The anticipation bordered on impatience. When the critical consensus is that unanimous—when even the harshest take is “it might be a little overrated, but it’s still good”—I get suspicious. Weeks after its release, I still hadn’t heard anyone truly tear it apart.That made me nervous. I was already placing it on a pedestal before watching it, which is always dangerous. I usually approach films neutrally, but this time I let myself believe I was about to see something special. And while it isn’t flawless, it’s so good that its weaknesses are hard to pinpoint.

This is my first film by Josh Safdie that I can recall, and it’s enough to recognize his talent. It’s not about flashy cinematography or poster-ready shots. It’s about rhythm. Safdie directs pulses. Every cut and transition builds tension, leaving little room to breathe. The film feels immersive and relentless.

Co-written with Ronald Bronstein, the screenplay embraces unpredictability. It wanders without losing purpose, building obsession piece by piece. At two and a half hours, I checked the time once. It never feels empty—only escalating.

Certain scenes linger vividly: the honey sequence, the bathtub moment. Intimate, uncomfortable, bold. When Timothée Chalamet shares the screen with Gwyneth Paltrow or Odessa A'Zion, the film ignites. Especially with A’Zion—their chemistry is volatile.

My main frustration lies with the ping pong. It functions more symbolically than viscerally. I wanted longer rallies, sharper psychological warfare, more competitive intensity. I understand the focus is obsession, not sport—but I still craved more raw tension at the table.

Chalamet’s performance is commanding. He builds Marty as brilliant yet unsettling—cold, egocentric, obsessive, magnetic. It’s not a performance that asks to be liked; it demands attention. His presence recalibrates every scene. It feels bold and fully controlled.Paltrow is solid, providing balance, though her character feels more structural than disruptive. The real surprise is A’Zion. Her presence reshapes scenes, giving Marty emotional resistance rather than mere support. I’m genuinely excited to see where her career goes next.

'Marty Supreme' isn’t about sport. It’s about ambition mutating into obsession. Marty wants transcendence, not just victory. The film doesn’t judge him—it observes, forcing us to ask how much we would sacrifice for greatness.

It isn’t visually revolutionary, but its atmosphere is gripping. Not perfect—but one of the strongest recent biopics, even if its historical fidelity remains uncertain. challenging watch.  Very different than expected
Marty is very abrasive, not easy to like and more difficult to root for.  But he has a dream and nothing is going to stop him from achieving it.  No matter who he has to step on, mis-treat, harm, etc...

But the payoff is worth it.  Doesn't hit you over the head and isn't going to leave you second guessing the rest of the movie.  Things just click into place in a subtle and natural way.  

Great movie if you can sit through watching a complete a$$-#0LE... Certainly not what I was expecting. This film is more about a terrible person conning his way through life, similar to the director’s previous work, Uncut Gems. Ping-pong is very secondary and barely featured in the film. It's hard to root for Marty, as he isn’t a great person, but Timothée Chalamet brings enough charm to make the character at least ****’s a two-hour, anxiety-inducing ride as we watch every bad decision unfold. However, in the last 20 minutes, it suddenly decides it wants to be a sports film, delivering a "Rocky" style final act. The tonal shift feels a bit strange, but it makes for an exciting **** you’re looking for an entertaining sports film, this isn’t it. If you want a stressful, high-kinetic rollercoaster ride, though, it’s definitely worth a watch. Josh Saffdie continues his excellent run of movies by maintaining his trademark suffocating atmosphere in which a series of interwoven plotlines build into a never ending anxiety attack. Chalamet is a tour de force as Marty, playing his narcissism perfectly where you end up routing for him despite making bad and self centered decisions at all every turn. The anachronistic 80s synth pop/rock soundtrack is sensational and the film lets you know it's willing to get weird from the outset with two standout scenes (sperm and honey). SCHWAB, indeed, Marty Supreme is electric, i'm telling you, if Timothée Chalamet doesn't win an Oscar for this, it's only a matter of time, he's on an unbelievable run right now, easily one of the strongest breakout actors of the 2010s, and he just keeps getting better.

Interestingly, both Josh and his brother Benny Safdie have delivered two of the year best films, with Benny behind The Smashing Machine, both films feel connected in a way, they're centered around sports and share the same tense, fast-moving style, The Smashing Machine is really good, but this time the older Safdie brother takes the crown.

Marty Supreme is a wild ride, the film throws you into the chaotic world of Marty Mauser, a man who claws his way toward success, crashes hard, and gets back up again, it s frustrating, sometimes intense, but always fascinating, there's so much happening, yet it never feels messy, the writing is sharp, the structure is tight, and the direction keeps everything moving with purpose.

I also have to talk about Kevin O'Leary, as a longtime fan of Shark Tank and Dragon's Den, seeing Mr. Wonderful make his feature film debut was surreal in the best way, and he doesn't just pop in for a cameo, he actually plays a major role, basically portraying a 10-times meaner version of himself, and he absolutely nails it, confident, ruthless, and weirdly entertaining, i was genuinely impressed.

The rest of the cast is just as strong, every performance feels locked in, that's what makes the film work so well, the acting, the writing, and Safdie's direction that works perfectly.

Marty Supreme is chaotic, gripping, and really entertaining film, the movie pulls you into one man messy journey and makes you feel every win and every loss, it's just that good.

79.title: The Ruins

metadata.tagline: Terror has evolved.

79.rich_text:
The Ruins The Ruins Terror has evolved. Horror Carter Smith Jonathan Tucker Jena Malone Shawn Ashmore Laura Ramsey Joe Anderson Sergio Calderón Jesse Ramirez Balder Moreno Dimitri Baveas Patricio Almeida Rodriguez Americans Amy, Stacy, Jeff and Eric look for fun during a sunny holiday in Mexico, but they get much more than that after visiting an archaeological dig in the jungle. The Ruins (2008) is a screenplay that Scott B. Smith adapted from his 2006 novel of the same name, a novel that is usually referenced in a bunch of horror lists as a must-read—but that this review won't consider, of course. Director Carter Smith, unrelated to Scott B. Smith, directs this adaptation as his debut feature-length film, he himself in 2025 managing a modest career in filmography. That modesty is different than Scott B. Smith's prominent career in writing and his often endeavors in screenwriting.

The story follows a group of young adults on their vacations in Mexico, a bit cooked with their time there already, when they stumble upon this guy that suggests they go on this expedition trip to meet his brother on this ancient ruins in the middle of the jungle. A change of pace, you know, from sunny beaches and parties to a wet, enclosed jungle and ruins as old as the place itself. Little did they know that these ruins hide horrors from centuries old.

Supported by great acting, the character development is decent and well-done. Each arc, and the overarching narrative and intersections as the plot thickens, explore interesting lines of traits for each of the characters in our group, thus culminating on their closures, all pleasing according to the story premise.

The plot alone is also good. The curveballs are interesting, keeping us hooked to what could happen next. You never know, and that keeps you going on and on until the end; which is where things go south a bit.

The existence of an alternate ending is a clear indication that something was amiss. The original ending is too open and lacks closure, that putrid taste you feel when you bite something that looks fresh but happens to be stale. After all we and the characters endure, we wanted closure, goddamit. The alternative is to watch something that tries to wrap everything up but still… A bit unsatisfying.

Another thing that might throw people off a bit is the genre: limited-space horror and body horror. Yup, you read it right. The story is good, but we are enclosed to the ruins, and maybe that is a bit stale after a while—for some people. You need to enjoy horror and a good mystery to keep going.

The pacing, though, is solid. You get hooked fast and the hook keeps you throughout the whole length of the movie. Never will you bore or want to move faster.

Of course, the FXs are superb for 2008. I always wonder what happened to CGI after the early 2000s, something got wrong. Nowadays, with all tech we have, it feels like the old still delivers solid graphics rather than the new.

The Ruins is a good film for its genre, so good it got 7 nominations accordingly. You won't see it in scariest movies of all time lists, but you should stumble upon it on lists like movies to watch before you die or specialized lists. The reality is that The Ruins appeals to a niche, and little would you know that, if you like horror, than that niche might be something you enjoy too. Not nearly as bad as the critics made it out to be. An enjoyable horror B movie with decent acting and impressive for 2008 CGI. Only real downside is that the "HD" version of the film isn't mastered very well. Un groupe de jeunes cons partent explorer une pyramide maya… mais ça ne se passe pas comme prévu ! le paranormal et des indigènes peu accueillants se montrent bien peu hospitaliers…

Le film semble typique du genre a priori, celui du vague thriller horrifique (à pop-corn bien sûr) plus ou moins brutal et sanguinolent… sauf que même à cet égard, on reste engore sur sa faim ! il faut attendre la fin… une fin qui ****, alors que le machin ne dure même pas une heure et demi.

C’est dire si ça se traîne assez lamentablement… quasiment du début à la fin et en plus, c’est carrément sans queue ni tête, finalement. Rien ne va là-dedans, ça pue le nanar total, définitivement à côté de ses pompes. Je mets 1 quand même pour la blonde, fort bonnasse, ma foi. Même le metteur en scène s’en est aperçu. C’est un début, à défaut d’un film, pauvre tocard ! - college kids that are likable - you can feel the heat - awesome practical effects, good cg work
- very cool location (especially for a nerd like me)
- no superfluous scenes in this film, IT'S 80 MINUTES
- shirtless Dimitri very original and refreshing kind of horror movie and the sense of dread and uneasiness is prominent throughout the movie with shocking scenes and the fight for survival adds to the drama and tension in an already terrific setting while facing an abominable enemy It looked nice. The blacks were crushed and the whites too hot but that seems the style now and it looks fine. I would have rather seen it in high-def due to the lovely landscapes but I'm not that arsed. I liked the sounds actually. The sound effects were convincing and the music was unnoticeable (so it must have done its job). It has the slowest pacing. The most shocking scene is where the guy is shot but that takes place early on and is soon forgotten amongst rather boring plant attacks. To be fair there are some gross bits but it is not enough to stop is being boring. The characters are too annoying and you want them to die. There is no emotional attachment. It reminded me of Hostel (2005) in structure. For a horror film it is not scary. It's not even that gory or anything. It is boring though! No fue mucho como lo esperaba, los personajes estuvieron OK, la violencia gráfica estuvo a la altura pero no logró sorprenderme y la idea principal no estuvo bien desarrollada. O longa tem altos e baixos, porém minha imersão foi tamanha que eu não consigo ser tão chato quanto a isso.

A principio, os personagens são apresentados e seus arquétipos são postos em ação, porém, o mais interessante aqui é que o roteiro sabe muito bem como trabalhar com cada um deles. Para um filme de terror, eles estão longe de serem unidimensionais. Apesar de gostar bastante do personagem, o aspirante a medico era talvez... racional demais pra ser verdade, porém o longa dá indícios de que ele tem um olhar indiferente a sentimentos, como o fato dele obviamente saber e não fazer nada quanto a traição da namorada dele.

O maior ponto do filme é a tensão. O suspense aqui é feito de diversas formas, em diversos momentos e ele sempre funciona bem. Em diversos momentos me encontrei tenso e com medo do que havia por vir pelos personagens. Era como se eu estivesse lá com eles - ou pelo menos com muita pena dos mesmos. Isso é indicio de uma boa construção de personagem. O suspense envolvendo o "mal maior" do filme funciona bem. Tudo faz sentido uma hora - antes mesmo dos personagens explicarem. Uma cena especifica no meio do filme pode caracterizá-la como uma das mais agonizantes que já vi. Minha empatia já é deveras alta, então imagina-se como reagi a ela.

No que se diz respeito ao aspectos técnicos, o filme tem um gore incrivelmente fidedigno, sem exageros nem nada. A edição de vídeo lida muito bem com o suspense, e é claro que há um grande mérito na direção por parte disso. A cenografia é boa e indica muitas coisas, acrescentando na narrativa instantânea e progressivamente. Para um terror de 2008, até que há poucos clichês e momentos previsíveis. Eles, ao meu ver, me impedem de dar uma nota mais positiva, porém, não me incomodaram tanto quanto eu achei que aconteceria.  A trama me prendeu tanto que eu nem queria saber deles. Exceto no final, que me deixou com um "sério mesmo?", na cabeça. A good adventure/horror movie. Not a lot of action but it is interesting and original. I recommend it. The movie started with a cliche idea.A group of friends in vacancy the they **** and then the get ****,the visuals were amazing the script was unpredictable and the acting was great.Sure,some ideas were stupid like the plant who can scream like a cell phone but the movie was enjoyable.

80.title: Pulp Fiction

metadata.tagline: You won’t know the facts until you’ve seen the fiction.

80.rich_text: Pulp Fiction Pulp Fiction You won’t know the facts until you’ve seen the fiction. Thriller Crime Comedy Quentin Tarantino John Travolta Samuel L. Jackson Uma Thurman Bruce Willis Ving Rhames Harvey Keitel Eric Stoltz Tim Roth Amanda Plummer Maria de Medeiros A burger-loving hit man, his philosophical partner, a drug-addled gangster's moll and a washed-up boxer converge in this sprawling, comedic crime caper. Their adventures unfurl in three stories that ingeniously trip back and forth in time. Tarantino expertly blends pulp crime fiction with snappy dialog and situational humor. While some scenes drag on too long, the overall result is an outrageous and original vision of the criminal underworld in Los Angeles. No doubt about it, it's a Quentin Tarantino movie. Probably his best movie, to be fair. If you're a big Tarantino fan, I suppose it could easily be worthy of a 10/10. É ok. Não entendi o porquê esse filme é tão amado. Vi reviews que "explicaram", mas apenas foi uma prova que o filme é coerente, oque deveria ser o mínimo. Devo não ter entendido o filme, mas se o objetivo foi me fazer pensar sobre ele ou me marcar, falhou bastante. Me entreteu, mas não tenho motivos para ver de novo. La claque Même si j'avais vu quelques bouts de scène et les mêmes du film, je ne savais pas à quoi m'attendre. Le film a mis des bases d'un film de gangster assez classique pour encore mieux nous prendre à contrepied. Le film se savoure pendant 2h30 sans nous laisser un moment de répit pour faire ce qu'il fait de mieux. La musique du film, c'est tellement des classiques que ça m'a fait plaisir de les entendre comme si j'étais nostalgique. Cela aide aussi à me faire aimer cette esthétique digne des années 90 qui est assez particulière. Le découpage assez particulier du film le rend encore plus particulier et c'est cette chose qui me fait regretter de ne pas avoir pu le voir en 94 au cinéma (ça et le fait que je n'étais pas né). é um filme muito bom, não acho incrível como grande parte da crítica diz ser, mas sim, é um filme muito bom e extremamente memorável, 9/10! a trilha sonora, os personagens, as falas, é tudo muito icónico, até a capa do filme. Pulp Fiction. There are seven narrative sequences. The film "Pulp Fiction" is a true work of art that leaves a lasting impression. Director Quentin Tarantino created a unique picture that combines black humor, vivid dialogues and memorable characters. Each scene is filled with meaning and unexpected turns, which keeps you in suspense from the first to the last minute. Stylish direction, excellent acting and an unpredictable plot make this film a true masterpiece of cinema. It makes you think about morality, fate and the randomness of life. "Pulp Fiction" is a movie that is worth watching again and again, because it deserves a rating of 10 out of 10 for its originality and depth. a genuinely great movie though when I first started it I expected a bit more scenes from Samual Jackson and wish we saw more of his character Um bom passatempo com personagens carismaticos, mas a história não é tão profunda e nem tão engraçada Pulp Fiction isn’t just a movie—it’s a cinematic grenade lobbed into the gut of '90s Hollywood. Tarantino’s dialogue is razor-sharp, every scene dripping with swagger, tension, or sheer absurdity. The nonlinear storytelling flips convention the bird and makes you pay attention. Travolta and Jackson are electric—equal parts philosophical hitmen and dark comedy icons. Uma Thurman’s cool detachment, Bruce Willis’s desperate grit—it all clicks. The soundtrack? Untouchable. Every needle drop feels surgically chosen. It’s violent, stylish, weirdly profound, and unapologetically cool. Sure, it’s not for everyone—some will whine about the pacing or excessive talking. Let them. Pulp Fiction didn’t come to hold your hand. It came to redefine cinema. And it did. This is genre-breaking, endlessly quotable, bloody brilliance. Accept no substitutes. such a great movie lmao. watched this three times and i understand it so much better every time and understands the hidden details in it

81.title: Deadpool & Wolverine

metadata.tagline: Come together.

81.rich_text:
Deadpool & Wolverine Deadpool & Wolverine Come together. Action Comedy Science Fiction Shawn Levy Ryan Reynolds Hugh Jackman Emma Corrin Matthew Macfadyen Dafne Keen Jon Favreau Morena Baccarin Rob Delaney Leslie Uggams Jennifer Garner A listless Wade Wilson toils away in civilian life with his days as the morally flexible mercenary, Deadpool, behind him. But when his homeworld faces an existential threat, Wade must reluctantly suit-up again with an even more reluctant Wolverine. "I guess I'm the one who saves people after all." Welcome to the MCU, Marvel Jesus.241209 (4.0)"I guess I'm the one who saves people after all." Deadpool, who always insisted he wasn't a hero, finally finds his place as the "Marvel Jesus" of the MCU. This film is a chaotic, meta-heavy celebration that drags Wolverine back into the spotlight—not by ruining the perfect ending of *Logan*, but by digging up his skeleton (literally) and throwing him into a multiverse-spanning adventure. It’s a love letter to the Fox era, filled with the kind of R-rated humor and fanservice that only Ryan Reynolds can pull **** story kicks off with Deadpool attempting to join the Avengers of Earth-616, only to be rejected by Happy Hogan. Six years later, working as a used-car salesman, he’s recruited by Mr. Paradox of the TVA. Paradox reveals that Earth-10005 is dying because its "anchor being"—Logan—has died. To save his world and his friends, including Vanessa, Deadpool hunts through the multiverse for a replacement Wolverine, eventually settling on the "worst Wolverine," a version who failed his X-Men and lives in a drunken **** two are pruned into the Void, a *Mad Max*-style wasteland where "Fox" characters go to die. Here, the cameos are legendary: Chris Evans returns not as Captain America, but as a foul-mouthed Johnny Storm; Wesley Snipes is back as Blade; Jennifer Garner as Elektra; and even Channing Tatum finally gets his shot as Gambit. They face off against Cassandra Nova, Charles Xavier’s powerful and sadistic twin sister, who rules the Void from the skull **** Ant-Man. The action is brutal and stylish, especially the opening fight choreographed to *Bye Bye Bye* and the final showdown against an entire "Deadpool Corps" (featuring Ladypool—voiced by Blake Lively—and their children as Kidpool and Babypool).Ultimately, the film is about choice and redemption. "We must decide for ourselves who we are," echoes through the chaos as Deadpool and Wolverine sacrifice themselves to destroy the Time Ripper, only to survive thanks to their shared healing factors. It’s a massive win for the MCU, proving that the multiverse can work when it’s handled with this much passion and irreverence. From the "Cavill-rine" cameo to the touching tribute to Fox’s history in the credits, this movie is a top-tier healing factor for the entire franchise. "**** it, Fox—I’m going to Disneyland!" I'm very conflicted with this movie. On one hand, it's a pretty fun enjoyable buddy cop movie with some pretty good action sequences as well as spectacles. Some of the jokes were pretty funny. And that intro was chef kiss perfection. 

But I felt like the jokes were a little bit too much this time around. Mostly because the movie doesn't leave much breathing room between the jokes. So, Deadpool just kept shooting out one joke after another to the point it became tiresome. I never really felt annoyed by Deadpool in the previous two movies but wow.. this movie really open my eyes on why some truly dislike Deadpool.

I also felt like sometimes they prioritize jokes more than the story. In the first two movies, the story was still the main focus. But in here, sometimes they kinda move away from the plot a bit for jokes that doesn't really play much role into the story. The main case for this is Nicepool and Dogpool because I feel like they don't really add much value to the story other than being fun gimmicky characters. 

The story also feels a bit weak and doesn't make much sense if you think really deeply into it. The second act also felt like they were meandering a bit. Lastly, the direction and the treatment of the main villain felt a bit weird for some reason to me especially near the end. 

Still.. I did enjoy it somewhat. It wasn't too bad. I just wished it has a stronger plot and more breathing room between the jokes just so it doesn't feel too tiresome overtime. Disney did it again.  Takes all your favorite things and just ruins them with that Disney-ickyness that just makes you feel like you can't scour the schlock off no matter how many times you wash!

What should have been another grand slam felt like Reynolds meets Jackman in all the worst ways.  Cameos were absolutely a bonus that didn't disappoint, but what did was watching them all die or get left behind - again.  Yet again another Disney property where the plot only makes sense if you have watched every other Disney property - probably against your will.

Best parts were the comic cover accurate snapshots and Lady Deadpool's fat ass! Deadpool & Wolverine — A Wild Ride of Chaos and LaughsThe pace of this short is incredible — it moves so quickly that you’re constantly laughing, cringing, and marveling at what comes next. The fight scenes, while a little too bloody at times, are hilariously over-the-top, perfectly capturing the chaotic energy you expect from Deadpool.What really makes it shine is how it blends the unbelievable action with Deadpool’s signature fourth-wall-breaking humor. Every absurd stunt, every ridiculous punch, and every meta joke lands with the perfect timing, making it feel like the short was crafted for fans who just get the Deadpool ****’s a short, wild, and unapologetically insane ride — messy, bloody, and absolutely hilarious.Score: 8.5/10 — chaotic fun, laugh-out-loud violence, and perfect meta mayhem. Deadpool & Wolverine is pure fan service with a great cast and nothing else.

The writing has a lot of exposition, unnatural dialogues, too much telling and not enough showing. The story doesn't make sense, lot of the character decisions are inconsistent. On the other hand, there's a lot of fun service and that's a positive for me here, because it was certainly the main goal to service the fans. Should I be harsh on the movie because of that? Sure, but I won't be. There's a lot of fun to be had.

The cinematography offers a few awesome camera movements and dull lighting. The editing is okay. It doesn't offer anything special, but it also never gets too boring. The legendary genesis of a digital revolution: A timeless masterpiece that redefined reality and my love for cinema.260312 (5.0)I revisited this 1999 masterpiece in 2011, though it’s a film I’ve seen at least three times. This particular viewing was special because I gathered my younger siblings around a laptop to act as their personal guide to the Matrix. I remember passionately lecturing them about the film's "terribly brilliant" imagination while they listened (or endured!). It remains the perfect foundation of the trilogy, earning a definitive 5.0 for the way it changed how we see the world—and for the fun memory of sharing it with family. Saying that 'The Matrix' is a dystopia is to prove it right.

'The Matrix' was not just a revolution within the science fiction genre: it was a breaking point in the history of cinema. A clear before and after that forced the industry to rethink how digital effects and practical effects could be integrated into a single visual language. The film introduced unprecedented systems of digitally choreographed action, new ways of manipulating cinematic time, and a completely different relationship between the body and space.

The Wachowski sisters construct a world that anyone would label as dystopian or unreal. However, stopping at that surface is paradoxical. To say that 'The Matrix' is unreal or merely science fiction is, in a way, to prove the film right. Just as you yourself take refuge in the certainty that the world is real, 'The Matrix' poses that very assumption—and Morpheus himself explains why you are mistaken. One could say that we adopt the role of Neo, except that some never question the reality around them, while others sometimes feel closer to Descartes. And that leads us to think that the film was not just a film: it was—and still is—a kind of analogy of Cartesian philosophy.

The possibility that reality is a construction, a perfect illusion. A simulation we do not control. We trust what we see, hear, and touch because we have no other choice. We believe because we need to believe. And that everyday, often unconscious faith is precisely what the film calls into question. But 'The Matrix' does not stop at philosophical doubt alone. It is also an abstract reflection on destiny: everything is written, even when we are choosing. It is a matter of accepting risks and consequences. Freedom, then, becomes a question rather than a certainty.

Hope, the need to believe in something or someone, and the role of machines in human society—an idea that, seen today, is even more unsettling than at the time of its release—are all key elements of the story it presents.

Of course, the Wachowskis left us with images burned into our memory: moments tied to camera movement, slow motion, gravity, gunfire, and frozen time. Action cinema—and yes, science fiction—was redefined. Pure iconography, replicated to exhaustion, yet never surpassed in its original impact. The use of multiple cameras firing simultaneously to capture movement around Neo as he dodges bullets; the combination of 3D and live action; the use of wires to alter gravity… A true turning point, one that even had its own origins in production techniques.

Decades later, it remains a masterpiece—not only for what it tells, but for how it tells it. Iconic, influential, and unforgettable.
