Given the influence of rose-tinted nostalgia and the remarkable staying power of the original, Tom Cruise and company could be forgiven for just running everything back and cashing it in for the Top Gun sequel. And, as far as the plot is concerned, that’s pretty much what they’ve done. Sure, we’ll see a few mild distinctions, plus a shift in perspective (Cruise certainly isn’t going to play a student pilot, nor is he apt to give up that top billing), but the bones are essentially the same. Cocky kids in an elite dogfight academy are ordered to set aside their differences and accomplish an impossible mission in hostile airspace. Adrenaline, testosterone and pheromones run wild. Where Maverick really soars (if you’ll pardon the awful pun) is in a technical sense. All that work to embed an array of super-resolution cameras into the pilot’s seat has paid off: this is a major level-up moment, on par with the very best IMAX showpieces. Paired with a persistent soundtrack of strained grunts and rapid breathing, the footage does a fantastic job of conveying the intense physical effort that’s required to maintain control of a fighter jet, while also portraying the stunning vistas and dizzying speeds of afterburner combat. More than just special effects for a film, Maverick’s vision of airborne cinema borders on a true life experience. As a film, it’s a light-hearted flex of the bicep, designed to pluck memory threads and evoke warm feelings established by the original. Worthwhile, especially for long-term fans, but not particularly special. The cockpit scenes, though, especially that blood-rushing one-cut takeoff from the aircraft carrier, will stick with me for a long while.

Spider-Man is a character that really benefits from a smaller stage anyway, so the timing is appropriate, but he's quickly pulled out of that comfort zone and never totally settles into the new one. Zootopia is one of those films that works on every level. As pure entertainment, it is incredibly funny, fast-paced, and filled with visual details that don’t wear out after a single viewing. But it also offers something more: an intelligent message disguised as a colorful fable. And that, when seen with perspective, is what elevates **** first watch, what stands out is its rhythm and the chemistry between Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde. The buddy-movie structure is perfectly measured: personality clashes, constant humor, and an investigation that unfolds naturally. The jokes work for both children and adults, and some gags —like the sloth scene— are already part of animation history.Visually, it is stunning. The city is built with astonishing attention to detail, each district follows its own climatic logic, and the world feels alive. It’s not just a pretty setting; it’s a coherent universe. There is a clear ambition to create something more sophisticated than a typical animal comedy.What truly makes it stand out is its social reading. Beneath its friendly surface, the film speaks about prejudice, collective fear, and manipulation. And it does so without becoming solemn. It has the intelligence to raise complex issues without overwhelming the viewer with obvious moral lessons. That makes it far more mature than it initially **** is also one of those films that becomes tied to family memories, to specific stages of life, to that moment when the talking toy of the protagonist had to be found because the fascination was absolute. And that is when cinema stops being just cinema.Zootopia is funny, sophisticated, and emotionally generous. Disney at its peak. It's a whip-smart, gorgeously animated crowd-pleaser that pairs sharp social commentary with heartfelt character growth and rapid-fire humour, delivering one of Disney’s most clever and emotionally satisfying modern animated triumphs Peak 3D Disney Animation.

Another thing was that In the movie, predators are discriminated against because of their biology, I think it tries to teach you that you should not discriminate against groups because they may be different to you. A história é simples: um cara ambicioso descobre como manipular a Bolsa e, com uma turma de amigos, constrói uma montanha de dinheiro à base de fraude, drogas e festas épicas. O que funciona é a energia descontrolada. O filme não te julga; ele te coloca no meio da loucura. Você sente a atração perigosa da riqueza e do excesso. Leonardo DiCaprio está genial, totalmente insano, e consegue fazer você se divertir mesmo sabendo que ele é um canalha. Para quem gosta de uma história forte, com ritmo e que te faz pensar sobre até onde a ganância pode ir, é imperdível. Che film di Scorsese, un capolavoro dall'inizio alla fine...   Interpretazioni irraggiungibili e formidabili buona sceneggiatura e **** principali scritti benissimo. Non perfetto ma quasi Decent story although it really becomes something extremely cringe. Better movies out there frankly overrated. The qualudes scene is very funny, but overall the actors try way too hard to be funny, and the movie lionises an awful person. Oh. My. Goodness. Where do I even begin with this. First of all I must say, Leonardo DiCaprio did such a good job acting in this movie it still 11 years later baffles me. The humor is unmatched whilst still containing an element of realism and sadism. As a billionaire playboy myself I see myself in Jordan Belfords reckless nature.
10/10 this is a CLASSIC! An unapologetic celebration of mean-spirited excess and the depths of human greed. The Wolf of Wall Street is entertaining as hell, wildly indulgent and more off-the-wall than the craziest Jackass movie, but at the end of the day there really isn't much more to it than that. Leo DiCaprio is effective as the drug-powered, decadent master of ceremonies, even showing us a glimmer of internal conflict behind the hazy fog of those unfocused eyes, but his rare moments of shame are quickly washed away with all manner of intoxicants.

The film's purpose is puzzling. Are we to pull for this loathsome figure, the very embodiment of the ugly American 1-percent stereotype? Shall we root for his comeuppance at the hands of the law? Merely observe, jealous but just, as he squanders our relatives' retirement funds on a perpetual hunt for fleeting ecstasy? In any case, we're in for disappointment. After an hour, the novelty of this lewd dash of A-list voyeurism begins to wear thin. At two, it's long overstayed its welcome. Thirty minutes later, it begins to deal with repercussions, but those too are impermanent and flimsy. I'm torn. On the one hand, it's a savory ride, looking over the shoulder of giants as they splurge on a **** life of luxury. On the other... did we really do more than spin our wheels?

A glittery, contemplative experience that misses its shot at excellence, I've decided, and one that really doesn't need to be half as long as it is. I generally love this movie. It has comedy, story, drama, etc, but the plot does get dragged out a bit. Don’t get me wrong, the whole thing was amazing, but I feel like a few parts could have been skipped, like, do we really need another slow mo sex scene? Or when the movie goes completely off plot, how did this guy Jordan Belford, end in a flooding ship with drugs in his system watching his private plane go down. Overall, a very good movie. 9/10. While it may be interesting to see how rotten and corrupt the Wall Street environment (and for that matter, major Consultancy firms) from someone who was part of it, the constant immodesty and swearing make the movie deserve a round O. Pretty enjoyable movie, but wild when you remember this is based on real life events. DiCaprio is very charismatic as Jordan Belfort and the rest of the cast is great, like Margot Robbie and Jonah Hill. Some scenes are a bit too cartoony, where you can tell they took major creative liberties to punch up the laughs. Still, a fun movie that makes you feel only a bit dirty.

Some films don’t need big ambitions to work, and Ready or Not is one of them. It’s pure, bloody fun wrapped in dark humor — a mix between a wild slasher and a social comedy drenched in gore. Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man quickly establishes Peter Parker’s transformation after being bitten by a radioactive spider, granting him enhanced strength, agility, and wall-crawling abilities. The film balances Raimi’s dynamic visual style with Peter’s personal growth, from selfishly exploiting his powers to facing the tragedy of Uncle Ben’s death. Ben Stiller and Owen Wilson are back on the runway as male models Derek Zoolander and Hansel, perhaps sporting a few extra wrinkles around the eyes. The original Zoolander was a sleeper hit, pulling a shocking number of laughs from what seemed like a very thin concept, and its delayed sequel, unfortunately, pales in comparison.

Like many folllow-up efforts from the same genre (Austin Powers and The Hangover, I'm looking at you here), Zoolander 2 falls into the trap of constantly re-hashing the gags that worked the first time. Why innovate when the well's right there waiting for you, after all? What new material it does bring to the screen is often good for a chuckle, but not deep enough to mine for richer material. Benedict Cumberbatch's gender-bending role as a competing supermodel is a great example. We get about three minutes of big laughs from the character, but then he's spent and is summarily cast aside. Even the returning faces seem lighter and less interesting, particularly Will Ferrell's big-haired fashion mogul, Mugatu. They're propped up with sight gags and cheap one-liners, but there's no masking the lack of inspiration in their writing and performance.

Humor arrives in sprinkles throughout this film, like a series of not-quite-ready pitches for an upcoming episode of SNL, but that's not good enough to make up for a bland, obvious storyline and an aimless, meandering pair of central character arcs. Pointless and under-cooked, or maybe over-cooked, considering how long it was left to incubate. Whatever the cause, it's a swing and a miss. It was a sequel made 15 years later, need say more?

True masterpiece The film is a ruthless, intoxicating ride — one that feels alive in its depiction of a world that’s glamorous on the surface and rotting underneath. With electric energy, the narrative sweeps you along into a realm where power, money, loyalty and fear intermingle so completely you barely know where one ends and the other begins. Every detail — from the slick suits and shiny shoes to the lingering stares and sudden violence — adds up to a world that looks alluring and feels poisonous at the same time.What impresses most is how you end up *rooting* for these characters despite knowing they operate in a moral void. They crack jokes, swagger, win, lose, betray — and you still find yourself drawn into their orbit. That tension between attraction and revulsion is precisely what makes the picture work. The direction never lets you settle comfortably: the tracking shots, the kinetic editing, the music cues all conspire to keep you on edge. A sequence that glides effortlessly through the back entrance of a nightclub becomes a statement of power, and in the same breath a harbinger of **** this isn’t simply a style show. Beneath the surface fun and bravado lies a sharp illumination of emptiness — of what happens when the rush ends and the cost comes due. A life lived chasing status, thrills and money eventually collapses, not in a grand moral reckoning, but simply by wearing itself out. It’s not preachy. It doesn’t offer redemption. It leaves you somewhere uneasy, aware of how seductive and dangerous this kind of life can **** the minus side, the sheer ferocity of the violence and the constant barrage of profanity keep the film from being comfortable in any sense — even for seasoned viewers. Some might find the pace overwhelming or feel the characters are so immersed in their own world that connecting emotionally becomes tougher. It demands a viewer willing to ride the chaos and absorb the **** the end, this is more than a gangster movie: it’s an examination of myth and reality, of glamour and consequence. It shows how the “good life” built on crime, loyalty and adrenaline eventually reveals itself as hollow. And that, in its way, is the film’s power. I had a weird experience with Primate, the first half actually felt promising, and i kept hoping the film would carry that energy through to the end, and i thought the first half was fine, but at the same time, it's not the part where they should be good at, it supposed to be the part where Ben starts losing control because of the rabies, but instead, by that point, Primate turns into another generic B-movie slasher that feels like Jason Blum produced, where the characters are unlikeable and i simply don't care, a string of stupid, unrealistic moments, the worst part is, it's not even a Blumhouse film, which somehow makes it feel like an even bigger waste.

Following Shrek, a grouchy yet lovable ogre, on his quest to save Princess Fiona, the story pokes fun at classic fairytales while delivering its own heartfelt message about love and acceptance.Iconic Characters: The cast of characters is unforgettable. Shrek (voiced by Mike Myers) is a relatable and endearing protagonist, while Eddie Murphy's Donkey provides nonstop laughs with his energetic and witty performance. Princess Fiona (Cameron Diaz) breaks the mold of the typical damsel in distress, bringing depth and charm to her character. Even Lord Farquaad (John Lithgow) stands out as a hilarious, over-the-top villain.Sharp Humor: Shrek strikes a perfect balance between slapstick comedy for kids and clever satire for adults. Its witty dialogue, pop culture references, and playful jabs at traditional fairytales make it a joy to watch for all ages.Timeless Themes: Beneath its humor, the film carries powerful messages about self-acceptance, friendship, and looking beyond appearances. These themes resonate deeply, making the movie as meaningful as it is entertaining.Groundbreaking Animation: For its time, Shrek boasted impressive CGI animation. The vibrant, detailed world of Duloc and the swamp are beautifully rendered, creating an immersive experience that still holds up well today.Memorable Soundtrack: The film's music, including Smash Mouth's "All Star" and the heartfelt "Hallelujah," perfectly complements its tone and adds to its charm. The soundtrack has become iconic in its own right.Cons: Some Dated References: While the pop culture jokes were fresh and funny in 2001, a few of them feel a bit outdated now. However, the core humor and heart of the film remain timeless.Pacing Issues in the Middle: The film's pacing occasionally slows down in the middle, particularly during the travel scenes. However, the humor and character interactions help keep things engaging.Simplistic Villain: Lord Farquaad, while funny, lacks depth as an antagonist. He serves his purpose in the story, but he doesn't have the complexity of other animated villains.Conclusion: Shrek is a hilarious and heartfelt film that redefined animated storytelling. With its clever humor, endearing characters, and timeless messages, it remains a must-watch for audiences of all ages. While some elements show their age, the film's charm and originality make it a true classic. 8/10. This is one of those terrible terrible movies that has absolutely no idea what a movie is. However, It does have a tender little spot with the father and son relationships that gives this movie just a little bit of a pass. The dynamic between Kevin James and Alan Ritchson in Playdate, coupled with a ridiculous plot, is silly enough to generate a few laughs, even if the film feels like a rinse and repeat of other comedy films. Sometimes you sit down to watch a movie that clearly isn’t going to change your life… and somehow you end up laughing more than you thought you would. That’s exactly what happened to me with Playdate. It’s not smart, it’s not original, and it’s definitely not aiming high, but there’s something in its clumsy charm that ends up being genuinely fun. Maybe it’s the mix of goofy action, ridiculous situations, and a cast that looks like they’re just having a good time.I mainly watched it because Alan Ritchson is in it, and honestly, he surprised me. He has a natural comedic timing that doesn’t feel forced. That big-kid energy he has —half brute, half puppy— works surprisingly well here. The movie relies on that vibe more than anything else: when he’s on screen, things flow; when he’s not, the weaknesses show more **** humor is simple. Very simple. The kind that makes you ask yourself, “Why am I laughing at this?”… right before you laugh again. But hey, in a comedy like this, getting real laughs already counts as a win. It never pretends to be clever or groundbreaking; it just wants to entertain for a while, and that honesty helps.Technically, it’s nothing to brag about. The script is bare bones, the action scenes run on autopilot, and some moments feel so out of nowhere that they might as well have been improvised. But because the film never asks you to take it seriously, you end up forgiving a lot. There are comedies that try so hard to be sharp that they become painful —this one at least knows exactly what lane it’s in.I won’t remember it next week, and I doubt anyone will. But during its runtime, it gave me a handful of genuine laughs, and that’s more than what many “bigger” comedies manage nowadays. Sometimes a silly movie is all you need. Look, this is a fun, fast-paced actioner that you'll want to enjoy with popcorn and soda or "Psycho Juice" if you have that on-hand (wink). 114.title: A Minecraft Movie

metadata.tagline: Be there and be square.

114.rich_text:
A Minecraft Movie A Minecraft Movie Be there and be square. Family Fantasy Comedy Adventure Jared Hess Jason Momoa Jack Black Sebastian Eugene Hansen Emma Myers Danielle Brooks Jennifer Coolidge Rachel House Allan Henry Bram Scott-Breheny Moana Williams Four misfits find themselves struggling with ordinary problems when they are suddenly pulled through a mysterious portal into the Overworld: a bizarre, cubic wonderland that thrives on imagination. To get back home, they'll have to master this world while embarking on a magical quest with an unexpected, expert crafter, Steve. Is a really good movie for towatch in family, connect much with de game andthe representation from the caught soilder in youtube in the movie was a special admiration, 10/10 A Fast-Paced Adventure Lacking the Magic of Creative Inspiration250514 (2.1)"Being an adult is really no fun at all"—especially when it feels like I’ve lost the ability to fully immerse myself in a movie like this. While the film maintains the brisk, energetic tempo typical of a children's adventure movie, it lacked the "creativity" needed to fill the gaps in its frantic pacing. I couldn't help but feel that if I had actually played the original game properly, I would have found the experience much more enjoyable and engaging. There were clearly nods and elements intended for fans that didn't quite land for me as a casual viewer. However, the performance of Alex from the sequel caught my interest, making me curious enough to want to check out the second installment. Ultimately, it’s a film that serves its target audience well, but for someone looking for a bit more narrative depth or inventive world-building, it felt somewhat hollow. It’s a reminder that some adventures are best enjoyed through the eyes of a child—or at least someone with a controller in their hand. I watched the Minecraft movie last weekend with two friends at my place, and the whole thing ended up feeling really relaxed and funny. We had snacks, joked around, and honestly expected it to be terrible. It wasn’t amazing, but it was colorful, entertaining, and way better than we imagined.
The movie itself was adventurous and surprisingly emotional in scenes. The characters felt more relatable than I expected, and the world looked bright and detailed. Some moments were rushed, but most parts were fun. I thought the action was exciting, the monsters looked awesome, and the ending wrapped everything well. Avoid this movie like a plague.  It is offensive to your intelligence.  It tries too hard for cheap jokes that I actually lost respect for the actors.  It was so hard for me to keep watching.  I just gave up at mid point and I have zero interest to ever finish watching this movie. Video-game movies always walk a weird tightrope: either they try to please everyone and satisfy no one, or they become so specific that only the hardcore fans understand what’s going on. Minecraft lands right in the middle. It’s peculiar, a bit chaotic, clearly aimed at kids… and yet it has moments that work much better than I **** first thing that stands out is the tone. It’s loud, colorful and never tries to take itself seriously. For children, that’s already enough: big creatures, silly gags, impossible chases, and that “improvised adventure” feeling that actually resembles how people play the game. For adults, well… it depends on your tolerance that day. Sometimes it’s tiring, sometimes it slips down easily, but it isn’t the pain some other adaptations have been.Emma Myers is easily the highlight. She’s got a natural glow, a charisma that lifts even the most basic scenes, and she’s becoming one of those actors who improve anything they’re in. Jack Black does his usual over-the-top chaos (fun but familiar), and Momoa brings more comedy than expected, even if the script doesn’t always help **** biggest issue is the lack of imagination. Minecraft —the game— lives off total creativity, of building whatever you want from nothing. The movie, instead, plays it safe: a predictable adventure, familiar jokes, and set pieces we’ve all seen before. It works, but it doesn’t leave a mark. There are moments where you feel all the energy is going into noise, not spark.Even so, it delivers on its basic mission: entertain without overthinking, give kids a fun time, and offer a tiny bit of nostalgia to anyone who spent hours mining and building. It won’t be remembered forever, but it doesn’t need to be. And, somehow, within its imperfections, it ends up being kind of likable. Pour moi c'est un bon film car il respecte globalement le monde de Minecraft même si il y à des incohérences par rapport au jeux.
Il y a des référence pop culture comme la légende Technoblade, Dream (je crois) ... 
Le film est vraiment beau (je trouve) la 3D est super :)
POUR moi ce film mérite la note de 8/10 :) The Movie is one of those rare cases where the fanbase around the game ends up being more entertaining than the movie itself. The film tries to build its own story instead of focusing on what made Minecraft special; creativity, exploration, and freedom. Unfortunately, that decision backfires. The movie feels so disconnected from the actual game, with barely any real nods to the world fans know so well.

What saves it from complete failure though is Jack Black. His performance carries the film with the kind of energy and charm. Can't imagine anyone else in Steve's role. 

But let’s be honest. The true reason this movie became memorable isn’t because of its script or direction. It’s because of the hype, the memes, and the fanbase that rallied around it. Without that wave of community energy, the movie would’ve sunk into obscurity as another lazy video game adaptation.

In the end, it’s not good, but it’s not entirely worthless either. Thanks to the fans, we at least got some legendary moments — just not the ones the filmmakers probably intended. 

Based on the movie alone, it doesn’t deserve more than a 6. Let’s just hope the sequel does it better. This isn't just any movie. This is A Minecraft Movie! With Steve! Honestly, this film is really fun and a good time. It is not to be taken too seriously, and it is just incredibly ridiculous. I am sure many young people are going to love it, but if you just need a movie to let go with, this is the one. Many memes will come out of this. Crazy to think this is the biggest box office movie of 2025. This movie is one of the most entertaining films I have ever seen. Some people call this movie cringe due to the fanbase or age range, but I think you could enjoy this movie at any age. The actors did amazing, especially Jack Black (a household favorite). The animation for the Minecraft world was absolutely incredible compared to what people were saying about the trailer. A Minecraft Movie was actually better than I thought. Sure it's a dumb movie, but it has some good and hilarious moments. And even though I might think it's sort of a ripoff of The Lego Movie, it's actually not that bad.

Nuremberg Nuremberg Judgment is coming. History Drama James Vanderbilt Russell Crowe Rami Malek Michael Shannon Leo Woodall John Slattery Richard E. Grant Colin Hanks Mark O'Brien Lotte Verbeek Wrenn Schmidt In postwar Germany, an American psychiatrist must determine whether Nazi prisoners are fit to go on trial for war crimes, and finds himself in a complex battle of intellect and ethics with Hermann Göring, Hitler's right-hand man. Stella cast( even though I have an issue with Crowe)… brilliant acting and cinematography. I never new how intense the trial was , but the director does an amazing job of showing different points of view… 9/10 A film that trades the power of the trial for an analysis that doesn’t hold up.Nuremberg had everything it needed to be a great courtroom drama… but instead turns into a psychological study that never goes as deep as it thinks it **** idea of a showdown between Rami Malek and Russell Crowe is good on paper, but in practice it devolves into an exchange of dialogue that doesn’t develop as much as it promises. And the more the film tries to “understand” evil, the closer it gets to a somewhat uncomfortable humanization that undermines the whole thing.Interestingly, once it gets to the courtroom, the film finally clicks… but by then it’s too **** the end, it works more because of the weight of the true story than because of what it builds. It was a great legal film waiting to happen, but it fell short. Anyone familiar with 20th century history will recognize this film’s title as the place where the world-changing cases against **** leaders took place. Instead of staging a grand trial drama, this film focuses on a psychiatrist who’s sent to evaluate the leaders before the trials (Rami Malek). His interviews with Hermann Göring turn into an obsessive bond, as he strives to understand the evil behind the man (played with subtle bravura by Russell Crowe). Meanwhile, the prosecuting lawyers (led by Michael Shannon) strive to determine the best way to approach this controversial new case. The character dynamics are emboldened by the captivating performances from every member of the cast, which also includes Leo Woodall and Richard E. Grant. Director James Vanderbilt has crafted a tightly gripping narrative that brings humanity to the horrors, while never excusing their actions. Despite it’s 2:28 length, every minute was compelling, sometimes disturbing. It’s a significant historical drama that packs a powerful dramatic wallop. 'Nuremberg' is the typical Oscar-bait. The greatest strength of this portrayal of the famous trials of high-ranking **** officials is Russell Crowe, who prevents the depiction of Hermann Göring from descending into caricature. Rami Malek, on the other hand, succumbs to melodrama. A historical legal drama that embraces every cliché of its subgenre to deliver an outdated history lesson instead of a deeper exploration of the origins of evil within the individual. It's a good movie, i wouldn't call it masterpiece, but it's a solid performance by Crowe and Malek and definitely worth your time. Der Film war ziemlich schwer, aber er hat mir gefallen. Ehrlich gesagt, habe ich mehr erwartet, aber insgesamt war er gut. Ich würde ihm sieben von zehn Punkten geben. Completely underrated film. Crowe is really fantastic. This movie deserves more attention and word of mouth. Superbly written and there is really no weak spot in this glowing cast list. Film lento e in vari punti prevedibile, in complesso abbastanza buono.
Ottimo lavoro da parte del cast, vari pezzi esageratamente lunghi e altri corti.
Non più di 7/10 You would think this is just a standard throwback drama. But it features modern editing (bad) and inconsistent characters. The "Welcome to Nuremberg!" delivery was so stupid. They had a chance to do something compelling here, but the writing really drags down a fantastic cast.  The exposition is so ham-fisted you’ll be rolling your eyes as characters try to mangle Wikipedia sections into normal conversation as though the audience can’t be trusted to have intelligence.  It also viciously rips you out of the experience of a period drama when the people of the 1940s all speak like snarky teenagers from the 2010s and Marvel-esque attempts at humour like the cutaway explaining Rudolf Hess’ role in the war.

The 2000 Nuremberg mini-series with Brian Cox as Goering is vastly superior and the better option if you’re only going to choose one.

A relação abusiva é interessante sim, mas não acho que isso carregue um filme sozinho nas costas, algo que poderia ser feito em 40-60 minutos demora quase 2 horas "Whiplash" is the powerful and intense portrayal of pressure and perfectionism from debut filmmaker, Damien Chazelle, whose film marks what may be the most exciting debut feature years. There is phenomenal filmmaking on display, as well as phenomenal acting from J.K. Simmons and Miles Teller. A drum solo might not ever be so tense or intimate on film again.

Chazelle who made a small independent student film about a jazz couple called "Guy and Madeline on a Park Bench" explores ideas of characters struggling through creativity. Chazelle's greatest talent may be in creating extremely tight and hypnotic scenes out of very little story. Sequences of pure drumming or of bands playing turns into something entirely different, much more personal, and spellbindingly close. He uses a shallow focus lens and a variety of shots including extreme close-ups that channel through masterfully structured editing to create scenes of pure tension that transcend the pages. Even in sequences of mostly dialogue, many of the same techniques are used that work in getting the audience lost in the moment with the excellent writing and delivery from the actors. It's an extremely absorbing watch.

J.K. Simmons may have the best supporting performance of the year. He's instantly unrecognizable from the very first scene. He understands himself and how to manipulate and test those around him by putting on a persona, yet appears so inhumanly unsympathetic at times. And when he gets pissed he's ferocious, sometimes even hilarious. Miles Teller just about matches Simmons, proving once again to be a master of subtlety and realism, creating a character who wants nothing but to be great. Both actors give their characters such humanity, and yet have serious detachment from others. They are given plenty of moments to develop so that we see all sides of their selves until they become so real that they might be like people we know in some way or another. What they create when they're both together on screen, the looks they give each other, show the serious conflict between them, but at times reveal what it is they share.

What makes "Whiplash" great is that it's not a movie about art or consequences, or about people who learn something. It's about Neyman and Fletcher the way that they are, the nature of their beings. We see that sometimes people don't get lessons, they just do what they feel is their nature to do, to succeed at whatever price. It's a feverish experience. Mel Gibson directed this one to perfection and it shows in the cinematography. Great cast too, and the plot an visual are amazing There are war films that focus on strategy, sides, or victories. This one goes in a different direction. From the very beginning, it’s clear that the core of the story isn’t the battlefield itself, but the moral stubbornness of a man who refuses to carry a weapon, even when everything around him collapses. That choice, simple yet radical, is what holds the film together and sets it apart within such a well-worn **** premise is powerful: a conscientious objector who wants to serve in World War II as a medic, saving lives without firing a single shot. The film doesn’t mock that position or soften it; it presents it head-on, with all its contradictions and with a very strong religious foundation. Mel Gibson’s hand is unmistakable here, along with his beliefs and his extreme way of understanding faith. It may be uncomfortable for some viewers, but it’s also part of the film’s raw strength.When the war truly begins, the film shifts gears. The combat scenes are brutal, physical, and exhausting. There’s no clean heroism or polished epic imagery — only mud, blood, **** bodies, and a constant sense of horror. Gibson has no interest in subtlety, but he undeniably captures the chaos and violence of the front line with overwhelming intensity.Andrew Garfield carries the weight of the main character with conviction. His performance blends faith, innocence, and resilience in a way that feels grounded rather than sanctified. The supporting characters mainly serve as reflections of the moral conflict rather than fully developed arcs, but they work within that **** film’s central paradox is unavoidable: a pacifist message delivered through extreme violence. Gibson condemns war while filming it as a visceral, almost hypnotic hell. That contradiction may clash for some, but it also prevents the film from feeling safe or complacent. It doesn’t tell you what to think — it forces you to sit with the ****’s not a perfectly balanced film, but it is powerful, unsettling, and deeply impactful. 'jurassic world: fallen kingdom' starts with an interesting opening, though it doesn’t quite reach the brilliance of the first installment. the film presents a plot that, within the saga’s universe, offers a more original approach by moving away from the repetitive formula of reopening the park, bringing a breath of fresh air to the narrative.

the introduction is clear and direct, avoiding over-explanations, although it feels more emotionally contained compared to its predecessor. the connection with the original trilogy is maintained through characters and visual elements that fans will recognize and appreciate.

narratively, the story may not fully engage every viewer, but it preserves the subtle humor characteristic of the franchise, keeping the essence that defines it despite changes in its main focus.

in the acting department, chris pratt continues to be the strong point thanks to his charisma and presence. from a technical standpoint, although it doesn’t surprise as much as the previous entry, it maintains a very high visual level, with realistic dinosaurs and an outstanding cinematography that plays with light, color, and framing to create fascinating images — in my opinion, the strongest aspect.

bayona’s direction is generally solid, with a smooth flow between scenes, dialogue, and narrative pacing that avoids moments of fatigue, making the film entertaining and a good option for family audiences. one of its strengths is the careful rhythm construction, which keeps interest without tiring, and the inclusion of scenes that appeal to emotions without going overboard.

thematically, the film revisits ideas present in the saga about the relationship between humans and nature, among others. although it shares the elements of action and adventure with its predecessor, it feels like a different product — less impactful but equally enjoyable.

the ending, while not as memorable as the first film’s, is intense and satisfying, leaving the door open for future installments with a promising storyline.

in summary, 'fallen kingdom' ends up being less interesting than its predecessor, but it’s still a good film if you genuinely enjoy the saga. My favorite thing about this one in the series, and one of my only gripes in the series, is that we don't get more magic like Dumbledore and Voldemort's duel. The boy with the lightning-bolt scar and his magical playmates return to Hogwarts for a fifth term, having sprouted almost overnight into young adults. Daniel Radcliffe has undergone the most striking change, filling out his robes with broad shoulders and a strong jawline, which ties in well with his character's pubescent bouts of temper and gloom.

As the kids have matured, so has the filmmaking. This entry continues the franchise's trend towards the serious, both in plot and technique. Harry learns more about his parents' personalities, realizes they may not have been the virtuous angels he once believed, launches a private rebellion against a strict new professor and investigates members of the opposite sex. The school grounds feel more ancient and formidable, the dialogue less fluttering and whimsical, the action scenes far better realized. That last note has been a trouble spot for the series so far, as it's struggled to master believable special effects for years now. They've finally managed it this time: the large-scale wizarding battle at the end of the film is head and shoulders above anything we've seen so far.

Some knowledge of the books is a prerequisite - the opening scenes abruptly leap right into the action with little preamble, and the rush of new faces could be dizzying without some sort of primer - but that's nothing new, and I suppose one of the benefits of running such a lengthy series is that eventually we can do away with formalities and get right to the meat. Whittling down a nearly-900-page tome into roughly two hours of film does result in some exclusions: Ron and Hermione once again have very little to do, relegated to the background in many scenes, and several surviving subplots find themselves combined or streamlined for pacing reasons. That's understandable, something of a necessary evil for what's still, certainly, among the best efforts in the series. Things are starting to get interesting. In the fifth installment of the series, Harry faces various obstacles, from a difficult relationship with the Ministry of Magic, battling his inner demons and building a resistance against Lord Voldemort. Despite disappointments and betrayals, Harry finds support in his friends and proves his will to win. Director David Yates brings the world of JK Rowling's book to life in a visually stunning way, using dazzling special effects and a rich palette. The performances from the actors, especially Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint, are striking in their maturity and emotional depth. The film also raises important questions about friendship, loyalty and fighting for what you believe in. It makes you think about the meaning of honor and self-sacrifice. "Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix" is not just a film about magic, but also about growing up, being and honor. After months of hype, trailers and endless discussion, I expected Barbie to at least be a clever or original film. Instead, it’s a bright pink mess that can’t decide what it wants to be. The movie tries to cram in satire, comedy, social commentary and nostalgia, but ends up shallow, confused and at times outright irritating.

What really drags it down is how it handles its themes. Rather than telling a strong story or creating believable characters, Barbie leans on exaggerated stereotypes: men as clueless or selfish, women as flawless leaders or helpless victims. By the end, the Barbies literally trick and manipulate the Kens to regain control — a plot point that feels mean-spirited and cartoonish rather than clever. Instead of nuance, the film offers slogans and cheap shots.

Another big problem is the direction. Greta Gerwig seems to be repeating the same formula across her projects — heavy-handed, one-note “feminist” messaging presented as art — and here it’s at its weakest. Rather than crafting a smart, inclusive story, the film pushes the same tired narrative that pits genders against each other. This isn’t daring or subversive; it’s lazy and predictable, and it’s exactly why these kinds of films keep failing to resonate beyond their hype.

The script is riddled with contradictions. There are tiny hints of something interesting — like early nods to insecurities and social pressures — but those moments are buried under one-note lectures and over-the-top set pieces. Characters don’t develop, jokes rarely land, and whole scenes feel more like skits than part of a coherent movie.

Technically, it’s just as underwhelming. The humor feels forced and cringey, with endless self-aware winks that stop being funny almost immediately. The plot is disjointed, bouncing between Barbieland and the “real world” with cardboard cut-out transitions that look cheap rather than charming. Margot Robbie’s Barbie is bland and underwritten, and even Ryan Gosling’s Ken — easily the best part of the movie — can’t save it from collapsing under its own weight.

Even the production design, which so many people praised, is overrated. Yes, it’s colorful and resembles Barbie dream houses — but copying toy houses at a big scale is more novelty than artistry. Without strong storytelling to back it up, it feels like an empty Instagram set rather than a world you want to spend time in.

By the last act, I stopped caring about the characters or their journey. The film feels less like a major event and more like a chaotic, cynical parody of itself. Whatever message it was trying to send gets lost in the noise, leaving only bright colors and a hollow lecture.

Overall, Barbie is one of the most disappointing films I’ve seen in years. It promised something big, bold and unforgettable; what it delivered was confused, condescending and exhausting. Barbie (2023): Corporate Gender Engineering Disguised as "Fun"Greta Gerwig’s Barbie is not a film—it’s a psychological operation, a Severance, a $150 million exercise in social reprogramming wrapped in the aesthetic of a Mattel commercial. Its mission? To accelerate the collapse of sexual difference, pathologize masculinity, and condition audiences to accept a future where identity is dictated, not discovered. This is activism masquerading as art, a candy-colored dystopia where men are either imbeciles or oppressors, and women’s "liberation" means trading one set of plastic constraints for another.

The Kens are not characters; they are cautionary tales. Their crime? Existing as men. They are allowed no dignity, no complexity—only humiliation, infantilization, or villainy. The film’s idea of "equality" is not balance but inversion: a world where Barbies reign supreme while Kens grovel for scraps of validation. This isn’t feminism; it’s sexual revenge fantasy repackaged as empowerment.

And then there’s the ending—a grotesque parody of self-actualization where Barbie’s ultimate act of "freedom" is submitting to the sterile, state-enforced androgyny of the real world. The message? Gender is a construct, biology is a lie, and the only happy ending is one where everyone is equally neutered. It’s not subversive; it’s corporate-approved radicalism, a billion-dollar brand selling the illusion of rebellion while prepping the masses for a future where male and female are relics.

Why the single star? Because Ryan Gosling’s Ken, in his absurd, doomed crusade for relevance, is the only honest thing in this film—a walking metaphor for modern manhood, laughed at by the narrative even as he accidentally exposes the movie’s own emptiness. That, and Margot Robbie’s delivery of "I’m not Stereotypical Barbie anymore!" is so unintentionally tragic it loops back into comedy.

In my previous reviews of the Hobbit trilogy, I said that as we go further into the trilogy, the quality of movies decreases; and it's right; The Battle of Five Armies has the lowest rating in my opinion among the movies. Why? I can think of a couple of reasons. But the most obvious would be that in BOFA, it's really clear that they stretched what easily should have been a two parts story into a third one. I mean, Desolation of Smaug obviously had padding too, but I really felt it in BOFA. Another thing would be the pacing. The pacing in BOFA is rather slow until almost halfway into the movie. There is one or two exciting sequences (one of which is my highlight of this movie), but in terms of the main plot (Durin’s quest), it progresses rather slow up until the halfway point. As for CGI, yes, unfortunately BOFA is the most CGI fest of the trilogy (CGI’d dwarves, elves, etc.) and in some cases it really shows! But overall, I really can't say I hated it. In fact, it is one of my guilty pleasures rewatching this trilogy alongside the LOTR. Look, we all know the Hobbit will always be inferior to LOTR, in terms of storytelling and overall production. More importantly, Jackson is a good storyteller, even though he was forced to stretch this story more than it should have been and that he certainly can entertain the audience. But above all and with another set of trilogy under his belt, Jackson really and truly left his mark on Middle Earth. There’s no trick here: the film knows exactly what it is and doesn’t try to hide it. Straightforward action, gunfire, chases, a clearly juvenile tone, and a story that moves forward without stopping too much to think about whether everything makes sense or not. And, oddly enough, that honesty works in its favor. It doesn’t aspire to be smarter than it is, nor to disguise its seams.Everything revolves around Dave Bautista, who once again delivers sheer physical presence. It’s not the most complex role of his career, and it doesn’t need to be. His charisma and the way he fills the screen carry much of the runtime, even when the script starts repeating ideas or leaning heavily on well-worn clichés of action cinema involving cartels, special forces, and young people in over their **** pacing is one of its strongest points. It doesn’t linger, it doesn’t turn solemn, and it doesn’t get lost in unnecessary subplots. It goes straight to the point most of the time, which makes many of its implausibilities easy to accept. When there’s no time to think, there’s also no time to question too much of what you’re **** problem arises when it tries to mix tones. At times it feels like it wants to be a carefree teenage adventure, and at others it turns serious, violent, even dark. That combination doesn’t always fit, leaving the sense that the film never fully decides what kind of story it wants to tell. It doesn’t break it, but it does make it somewhat uneven.Narratively, it’s very basic. There are no real surprises or twists that change the game. Everything works through the accumulation of action scenes and the energy of its lead. If you’re looking for depth, nuance, or something that lingers afterward, you won’t find it here. This is fast consumption, almost late-night video-store fare.Overall, it’s an entertaining, occasionally effective, and clearly forgettable film. It works as uncomplicated action filler, goes down easily, and little more. It doesn’t deceive, it doesn’t promise anything it won’t deliver, and it leans on its star to get by. Sometimes, that’s enough. "Trap House" is a fun enough time worth watching, but it traps its star and doesn't let him out. Amazingly, very little of this film is played for laughs, except of the unintentional variety.

It's the third installment of Harry Potter and already the child actors have done a lot of growing up. Visually and dramatically, they've grown into their roles, and director Alphonso Cuarón lets them flaunt that newfound independence in his only take on the series. The school feels more lived-in and tangible, as opposed to the amusement park it seemed in the first two movies, and its residents (particularly the three central Hogwarts kids) are less buttoned-up and disciplined, more comfortable with their surroundings. It's also darker and more foreboding, foreshadowing the idea that this series was headed into stormy waters.

Adding Gary Oldman to the mix seems a good choice, though he does little more than snarl and growl menacingly. Elsewhere, Michael Gambon plays a more vibrant Dumbledore in relief of the late Richard Harris, and the returning cast all continue to perform well in their established roles. The plot flitters around for quite a while, however, obsessing over excessive amounts of day-in-the-life snapshots and unrelated asides. Inside Out Inside Out Meet the little voices inside your head. Animation Family Adventure Drama Comedy Pete Docter Amy Poehler Phyllis Smith Richard Kind Bill Hader Lewis Black Mindy Kaling Kaitlyn Dias Diane Lane Kyle MacLachlan Paula Poundstone When 11-year-old Riley moves to a new city, her Emotions team up to help her through the transition. Joy, Fear, Anger, Disgust and Sadness work together, but when Joy and Sadness get lost, they must journey through unfamiliar places to get back home. Desde su apariencia amable, entretenida e infantil, Inside Out se despliega a través de un desarrollo que va mucho más allá de su carácter de coming-of-age pasado por la licuadora de un thriller contra reloj, adentrándose a través de su discurso en territorios profundamente humanos, allí donde las impresiones esenciales y puras gobiernan, en latitudes propias de la psique emocional alejadas del imperio de la racionalidad, regidas por aquellas estructuras mentales que realmente definen la identidad individual de cada sujeto. El conflicto permanente de nuestros estados de ánimo, de manera diaria y masiva, se resuelve aquí gracias a un maravilloso guion que plantea la inequívoca necesidad de todas las emociones como células anímicas que nos promueven el acto y la interacción social, determinando nuestro lugar en el mundo.

No obstante, toda esa seria riqueza narrativa no supone un relato complejo o adulto, sino que se desarrolla dentro de unos parámetros artísticos sencillos, a partir de un lenguaje inteligible y un atractivo estético superior, mediante un tratamiento del color diferencial y radiante, acompañado en todo momento de tiernas melodías que se adaptan a los distintos estados de ánimo representados. En todo momento logro empatizar con la turbación espiritual de la joven protagonista Riley Andersen, la versión externa del conflicto emocional entre la Alegría y la Tristeza, con la Ira, el Miedo y el Asco como elementos subsidiarios.

Quizás el drama infantil más potente tras la pérdida sea la sensación de desarraigo forzoso, de alteración de unos ejes vitales aún frágiles y en construcción, y ese es, en este caso, el detonante del conflicto, el germen de esa potente mezcla sensitiva desconocida. La continua turbación del estado de templanza puede devenir en desordenes impactantes, en decisiones irreflexivas que acaban resquebrajando los débiles cimientos de una personalidad aún tierna. En todo caso, la súbita pérdida de la inocencia, la fugacidad de la infancia debido a experiencias traumáticas pueden suponer también el nacimiento de cosas maravillosas, dar a luz una constitución de la personalidad más amplia y sólida, reforzando a la vez los lazos sociales como puntos de apoyo vitales.

Arriesgada e imaginativa, Inside Out logra sortear el sentimentalismo barato a través de su propia franqueza, de su revalorización de la diversidad y la cooperación en tiempos de disputas y polarización, aportando suficientes elementos y valores para una amplia franja de potencial público. Además, consigue divertir y emocionar de principio a fin, y eso para un producto de animación ya es un logro mayor. Clásico mayúsculo, genuino y sincero simbolismo sobre la inocencia humana. Спасибо

In this unusual mesh of fantasy, romance and science fiction, a mute woman working as a lab custodian in the late '60s falls for an abused, captive sea monster. The Shape of Water dons many hats, several at the same time, which distract and compete for attention: that central relationship, the military's plans for the creature, a neighbor's quest to reclaim his job with an ad agency, a coworker's marriage, a supervisor's frustrated home life. Each adds a layer to the onion skin, and color to the world, but ultimately they feel like light diversions from the main course.

On a technical level, it's exceptional. Guillermo del Toro's work has never been short on conceptual know-how, and The Shape of Water merely continues his habit of one-upping the preceding film. The beast itself, heavily influenced by The Creature from the Black Lagoon with a hint or two of Abe Sapien from del Toro's Hellboy, looks fantastic. Lifelike and expressive, it's easy to buy into as a thinking, feeling participant in the story. Sally Hawkins is equally wonderful as the human lead, drawing inspiration from dozens of classic silent films in her flourishing role as a mousey, passionate, eloquent young woman. Set designs, too, are distinct and remarkable, from the slimy, clinical confines of the military science lab to her crusty, crumbling apartment right above a busy movie theater.

But within that formula, Bloodlines works surprisingly well.Right from the start, with an opening sequence that’s already among the best in the franchise, the film makes it clear it’s going all in. There’s tension, spectacle, and a pace that rarely drops. Directors Adam Stein and Zach Lipovsky take their job seriously, even knowing they’re staging a twisted joke. And it shows in the precision of many set **** of this installment’s strengths is not taking itself too seriously, while avoiding full-on parody. There are nods for longtime fans, visual cues referencing earlier films, and a sense that—for once—the characters aren’t entirely clueless about what it means to be trapped in this curse. The family tree concept adds an intriguing layer, though it could’ve been explored more deeply.Visually, the movie is solid. Shot with large screens in mind, it offers wide shots, more polished cinematography than usual, and staging that aims for impact without losing clarity. The kills are brutal, yes, but also creative, with that playful sadism that has always defined the franchise.Does it have flaws? Of course. Some dialogues are flat, the characters stick to cliché roles, and the film occasionally flirts with unintentional parody. But overall, the balance between dark comedy, suspense, tension, and gore makes it a surprisingly enjoyable chapter—even for those who thought the saga had nothing left to **** reinvents nothing, but it does prove that with a bit of genre love, you can still make entertaining entries in a franchise that seemed spent. An absurd film isn't a flaw in itself: once past a certain threshold, you enter experimental cinema even unintentionally. In this sequel, Stalberg reaches heights of narrative fragmentation and cluttered editing that go beyond Malick, who nonetheless follows an underlying logic. Anything but a revenge movie, it reaches an extreme level of hallucinated and hallucinating unpredictability, as if we were inside the PTSD of a protagonist yet still compelled to make the right moral choices. Pleasantly unsettling and, incredible but true, even devoid of protagonists with postpartum depression. "Muzzle: City of Wolves" is an uninspired, clunky and bland revenge thriller that's just as underwhelming as its predecessor.

Don't Look Up is a scathing satire of modern society so spot-on that it is painful to watch. On the surface, the movie's premise is reminiscent of one of today's more polarizing debates: the politicized struggle between those whom claim to believe science to be a viable solution to society's ills, and those who denounce and accuse science of unnatural and underhanded intentions.

Dig a little deeper though, and Don't Look Up's brilliance lies in the more subtle yet relevant themes it weaves into its narrative. There is a constant underlying message about the distracting and numbing effects modern media formats have on the human psyche, so powerful that even the destruction of the entire world is not enough to shock it into action.

Problems are not struggles that are meant to be solved lest they cause suffering. They are a product to be packaged and marketed and commented on, a child's toy that is not played with but instead kept shrink-wrapped in its original packaging for display on a shelf. Commercial media outlets use the comet to justify endless punditry and special event programming. Social media personalities and everyday people use it as an issue to position themselves against and demonstrate virtue to their cliques of choice. In turn, society feeds off of its own social disfunction and inadvertently spins a narrative for the comet that becomes entirely disconnected from the real issue at hand. Some who at first meant well are soon swept up in the calamity, corrupted by the allure of fame and social status over survival.

There is no sense of urgency to deal with the comet, no worldwide mobilization of minds and resources. People go about their normal lives, the impending doom too great a challenge for most to even consider approaching. Only a few truly attempt to save the world from destruction, but even they are caught in the throngs of human nature, beholden to a wealthy and powerful few who are over-eager to capitalize on the tragedy for the sake of their own egos.

It's one of my favorite movies of the last decade, even if it can be so hard to watch. When a pair of low-level university astronomers (Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence) discover a massive comet on an impact trajectory with the Earth, they're dumbfounded by the lack of immediate government action or media interest. Nobody's anxious to address the elephant in the room because it's more immediately gratifying, and familiar, to focus on the latest celebrity breakup or political hot potato. Besides, these things always blow over in the end. Except this one doesn't, and as an extinction event draws near, the world grows increasingly frantic when their usual array of deflection tactics, age group demographics and strategic business partnerships have no effect.

The metaphor is awfully tough to miss. I tend to agree that this particular moment, in the midst of an extended pandemic that's been mishandled, politicized and exploited, is probably the right one for such an overwhelmingly cynical take. There's a certain level of personal catharsis in seeing these concerned, composed scientists pushed to an on-air emotional breakdown by the obstinacy of an aloof, absurd world that refuses to process such grave news. Their frustration mirrors my own; their swift, crushing loss of faith rings familiar. Sometimes I wish I could also drop a few f-bombs on a cable news show, even if the act of doing so would make a meme of me.

That said, this still feels like way too much. There's a forty-minute stretch in the middle, after the silliest lampoons have fired but before we approach the inevitable climax, where the story lags and everyone goes numb from the relentless hammering. Multiple characters endure the same desperate arc to, ultimately, prove the same point. The proverbial horse has rigor mortis by this point, but still the beatings continue. It's possible that this is just a limitation of the unusual genre pairing. The realms of goofball humor and sharp social satire don't always overlap, and in trying to pursue a grander point, director Adam McKay has stretched those boundaries.

Don't Look Up does have vision, plus a unique voice that excels when focused on the enormity of the situation. It would be easy to zero in on the American perspective, or maybe even the human one, but McKay takes care to remind us that this event would affect everything on the face of the globe. His frequent cutaways - to ignorant animals, happy babies, pensive families on the other side of the planet - reinforce important points and strive to make this something more than just a concept-heavy comedy. It wants to be all that and more, but does it succeed? Not exactly. This is more like Mars Attacks! with an agenda. The commentary in this movie gets called out for being "too on the nose" but I think it actually captures a lot of different interesting aspects of the human condition. I'm not a fan of Jennifer Lawrence's performance here, it's definitely the most confused presence in the film, but overall, the cast is fun and the humor is enjoyable. horrible, they tried to educate the viewers and is a blatant atempt to frame trump on everything evenf hurricanes or whatever "Don't Look Up" is an ambitious and divisive film. It's a dark comedy that sticks with you, for better or worse, and it was directed by Adam McKay, who is recognized for his sarcastic take on social and political themes.

In addition to Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, the picture features a slew of other well-known actors. Their acting is excellent, and they really make you care about their characters and what happens to them.

"Don't Look Up" isn't hesitant to poke fun at the ridiculousness of modern life and politics. It's a metaphorical story about how we treat existential dangers with apathy. This is a much-needed wake-up call couched in biting humor.

Climate change, media sensationalism, and government denial are all topics that are critically examined in the film. It provokes thought about the seriousness of ignoring actual crises and their repercussions.

The film's satire is sharp, yet there are times when it becomes too didactic. At times, the message seems like it's trying too hard to make a point that we already get.

Sometimes, "Don't Look Up" can be a bit slow. The second half, in particular, drags and could need some trimming from the film's overall runtime of over two hours.

Many of the supporting characters, including President Orlean (Meryl Streep), come across as flat. Their occasional cartoonishness distracts from the film's otherwise nuanced and profound message.

Both its power and its weakness lie in the lasting impression that "Don't Look Up" creates. However, not everyone will appreciate the film's occasionally heavy-handed style and inconsistent pacing, despite the fact that its message about the world's indifference to approaching disasters is topical and thought-provoking.

Watch "Don't Look Up" if you enjoy sarcastic social commentary and value films that make you think. It's a captivating experience because to the stellar work of DiCaprio and Lawrence, and it will get people talking about the status of the world. However, this film may not be for you if you like more nuanced storytelling. In the end, it's a divisive film that will have you thinking about it long after the lights go out.

The Dark Knight Rises (2012), the final installment of Christopher Nolan’s Batman trilogy, serves as a powerful and emotionally charged conclusion to Bruce Wayne’s journey. The film begins with Gotham enjoying a false sense of peace after the events of The Dark Knight, but Bruce, now physically and emotionally broken, is forced to rise once more when a new, formidable foe, Bane, threatens the city.

Tom Hardy’s portrayal of Bane is imposing and memorable, with a unique blend of intelligence and brute strength. His voice, though initially criticized, becomes a chilling trademark of the character. The plot is ambitious, with Bane taking control of Gotham, causing widespread chaos, and pushing Bruce to his limits. The stakes feel higher than ever, and Nolan successfully balances large-scale action with personal stakes for Bruce, who must overcome his physical limitations and confront his past.

Anne Hathaway’s Catwoman, aka Selina Kyle, brings a fresh dynamic to the film, combining wit and mystery. While she may not have the same narrative weight as other characters, her role is essential in Bruce’s transformation.

The themes of redemption, sacrifice, and hope dominate the film. Bruce's arc is one of renewal, moving from despair to heroism once again. The film also tackles larger social issues, like inequality and revolution, while still maintaining a focus on Gotham’s survival and Bruce’s personal evolution.

The action sequences are thrilling, with the film’s scale being massive, including explosive confrontations and large set pieces, all culminating in a satisfying, albeit controversial, conclusion. The emotional resonance of Bruce's final choice and the fate of Gotham provides a bittersweet end to the trilogy.

The Dark Knight Rises may not quite reach the heights of its predecessor, The Dark Knight, but it is a fitting and satisfying conclusion to a legendary trilogy, offering both spectacle and emotional depth.

A perfect fit alongside Christopher Nolan's preceding Batman films, with no single chapter standing clearly above the others. Where The Dark Knight played with the conundrum of Bruce Wayne as a public mask for Batman, this installment flips the script and focuses more intently on a well-rounded civilian identity at the expense of Wayne's more notorious alter-ego. That shift in focus fits snugly alongside the presence of a more grounded, topical-tinged foil in Bane, whose grand plans aren't all that different from those of his two predecessors, but reverberate in the modern social atmosphere. The strict black-and-white nature of the very real debate at the core of Bane's scheme is my sole disappointment, really, as the shades of gray I so appreciated in the first two episodes have been subtly brushed aside.

Tom Hardy performs admirably in full pantomime as the big bad, with Anne Hathaway playing a fine Catwoman (though the role seems inessential for the majority of the film), but it's Michael Caine who steals the show in a very brief, emotional final turn as Wayne's famous butler Alfred. Although he enjoys only five minutes of screen time, when the curtain falls it's his vivid performance you'll most remember. A brilliant, daring, explosive climax that expertly slams the lid on one of modern film's finest action/adventure trilogies, it surprised and impressed me from the very first word.

Additional thoughts from 2013: A Blu-Ray rewatch, which already hasn't aged as gracefully as its predecessors. I loved it on my initial viewing back on opening day, but removed from the initial "wow" factor, its plot holes really start to catch the light.

Anne Hathaway was an inspired choice as Catwoman, but the character doesn't really seem important or even necessary... just fluff and padding for a nigh-three-hour flick that already had enough going on. And, after thriving under the spotlight for the first two acts, Bane's sudden dismissal and the associated bait-and-switch doesn't sit particularly well with me either.

Not to sound all doom and gloom, because it's still a perfectly enjoyable film and a decent enough way to wrap up the trilogy, but it does feel quite scattered and I think a lot of what I enjoyed was just leftover fumes from Batman Begins and The Dark Knight. A very great Batman movie. Maybe not as good as The Darl Knight but nevertheless still a masterpiece in its own way! Perfect end to the trilogy….

100 out 100 star Captain America: Civil War. The End of the Avengers? "Captain America: Civil War" is a gripping film that masterfully combines action and deep emotional conflicts. The plot revolves around disagreements between Tony Stark and Captain America over the registration of superheroes, which leads to a split among the Avengers. Directors Anthony and Joe Russo create a tense atmosphere, where each character has their own motives and beliefs. The fights are staged at the highest level, and the appearance of Spider-Man and Black Panther adds freshness. The film makes you think about morality and responsibility, making it not only spectacular but also philosophical. A true masterpiece of the Marvel Cinematic Universe! An impassioned disagreement splits Earth's greatest superteam in half and ultimately drives them to fight with more than just words. Captain America 3 is basically The Avengers 2.5, but you already knew that. And like the two preceding, star-studded chapters, most of what makes it work is the thrill of seeing all the big names geared up together, slinging zingers and blowing dollars through the VFX budget like t-shirts from a cannon.

Civil War represents a more serious take for the series, sober and steely outside of a few great jabs from the new guys (Ant-Man and Spider-Man steal the show on this front). Which is fine, it adds a necessary level of gravitas to the subject and it wouldn't seem proper for Iron Man to be going all tongue-in-cheek while he's trying to punch his buddy's eyebrows off. That heavy-duty weight can make the film feel long and overstuffed, though, and all told I was feeling a bit weary by the time it got around to wrapping itself up.

There's a whole lot of action, as you'd have to expect, but this time it feels less grounded than in the past. It's as comic book as the MCU has ever been, really, with loads of Kool Aid-colored lights flashing around the room, bodies careening through walls and one ridiculous chase scene in which our heroes sprint through traffic at highway speeds. And that's the focus, no doubt about it: action with a side of Bucky, whose quest for answers and redemption seems far more important than the moral dilemmas and personality clashes that divided The Avengers. Personally, I was more interested in that lesser-explored gray area, but at the end of the day it's Cap on the marquee so I can understand the emphasis on his pet plot threads.

Civil War is a strong entry and a fine continuation of this cornerstone franchise, but at times it tries to pull off too much. Could've easily been broken into two films, and I'm almost never one to recommend trying something like that. this movie was very good. absolutely loved it. the finale was so awesome. can't wait for the next one Making the climax not about that stellar airport brawl, which was very tempting I'm sure, but instead about the very messy breakup of Cap and Iron Man, was a genius move that elevates everything else about the movie. With the cursory introduction period now behind us, the Avengers are finally able to shift into what's made them so appealing to readers for so many years: their personal relationships, both on and off the battlefield. Of course, with more characters than ever, it also runs the risk of crowding the screen, but that's not a problem at all: Joss Whedon manages to get everyone that much-desired moment in the sun in a simple, organic way.

Drama Science Fiction Mystery Denis Villeneuve Amy Adams Jeremy Renner Forest Whitaker Michael Stuhlbarg Mark O'Brien Tzi Ma Abigail Pniowsky Julia Scarlett Dan Jadyn Malone Frank Schorpion Taking place after alien crafts land around the world, an expert linguist is recruited by the military to determine whether they come in peace or are a threat. Definitely my flavor of sci-fi. Grounded in both fascinating concept and rich emotion. Grief and inspiration packaged together beautifully. Arrival presents a powerful and genuinely original premise: language as a force capable of reshaping human cognition and even the experience of time itself. The depiction of the aliens—radically non-anthropomorphic, non-verbal, and truly alien—is one of the film’s greatest strengths. However, once this idea is established, the film hesitates to fully engage with its human consequences. Instead of developing the emotional, ethical, and relational impact of knowing one’s future, the story fragments the human drama into brief, scattered flash-forwards, never allowing it to unfold in real time. What could have been a deeply unsettling exploration of choice, responsibility, and loss becomes a restrained, almost cautious treatment. The result is a film that feels intellectually promising but emotionally underdeveloped, as if it deliberately stepped back from the most difficult questions its own premise demanded. Yapımda ortalama ve altı seviyede bence. Matt Damon is left for dead during the rushed evacuation of a small-scale Martian expedition. This is like Apollo 13 on steroids, mixed with short dashes of 127 Hours, MacGyver and Survivorman. It's much less of a one-man show than I was expecting, which gives the film a little more spirit but also a more conventional structure. I think it would've made a far more interesting, daring picture if we'd seen more personal video journals from space and less debate around a round table at NASA, if just because we've seen the latter film several times already.

Damon is excellent, delivering an expert blend of hopeless desperation and punchy good humor that gives him credence as both a technical expert and a likable, relatable everyday guy. Still, the epic moments far outweigh the sub-standard ones, there's a strong sense of humor beneath all the suspense, and the visuals are downright incredible. Bonus points for getting so much of the science right, too. "Beauty and the Beast" is a testament to the power of storytelling, visual artistry, and remarkable performances. Regretting You es un drama que sabe jugar con las emociones sin sentirse exagerado. La historia se apoya en relaciones familiares complejas, decisiones que duelen y momentos que resuenan más por lo humanos que por lo melodramáticos. 'Regretting you' is one of those films that fails spectacularly in every single one of its aspects. It is not merely a bad and uninteresting story—though it certainly is—but rather a series of creative decisions throughout the production that make the experience extremely difficult to defend. The issue lies not only in what is being told, but in how it is told.

The screenplay is among the worst I have seen in a long time. Poorly justified narrative jumps, scenes forced to the point of nearly collapsing under their own weight, and dialogue lifted from simplistic, foolish teenage conversations. There is no sense of dramatic construction whatsoever, despite the film positioning itself squarely as a drama. Everything feels artificial; I am constantly aware that I am watching a scripted film—in other words, nothing feels natural, because it simply isn’t.

The direction could have helped soften or disguise the screenplay’s many flaws, but it does precisely the opposite. It highlights them with a fluorescent marker, repeatedly drawing attention to everything that doesn’t work. In fact, there are scenes that collapse under the sheer weight of their own disastrous construction. They don’t support one another; they actively undermine themselves. It gives the impression of a film determined to remind the audience of its own narrative limitations.

The cast features well-known names and charismatic figures. Dave Franco and Mason Thames stand out the most for me, yet the miserable roles they are given do no justice to how talented they truly are. Both have proven their abilities this very year in notable titles such as 'Black Phone 2' and 'Together'. They are capable actors with presence, which only makes it more frustrating to see them trapped in such poorly written characters. Dave Franco in particular is saddled with one of the worst roles I have ever seen in cinema. Mason Thames at least benefits from a minimal sense of narrative coherence, though he too cannot escape the overall superficiality. To be clear, these are not bad performances, but rather empty, poorly defined characters—despite the supposed narrative development they are given.

Allison Williams and McKenna Grace fare no better. They carry nearly all of the film’s emotional weight. Both deliver competent performances, but the material they are given simply does not allow them to stand out or create anything memorable.

There is hardly any need to mention the film’s predictability: from the very first scene, it is obvious how everything will unfold. There is no tension, no sense of surprise. The film takes no risks and shows no creative ambition. Despite You does not fail because of a single flaw, but because of the accumulation of many. It stands as one of the biggest disappointments of the year.
