194.title: The Hateful Eight

metadata.tagline: No one comes up here without a damn good reason.

194.rich_text:
The Hateful Eight The Hateful Eight No one comes up here without a damn good reason. Drama Mystery Western Quentin Tarantino Samuel L. Jackson Kurt Russell Jennifer Jason Leigh Walton Goggins Demián Bichir Tim Roth Michael Madsen Bruce Dern James Parks Dana Gourrier Bounty hunters seek shelter from a raging blizzard and get caught up in a plot of betrayal and deception. This movie was filmed on 65mm physical film, and released in Ultra Panavision 70mm format - which is the format I saw it on in theatres, which was cool - but the film itself is very much a Tarantino film, for what that's worth. If you're a big fan of his films, it's worth a watch, but it's not his best imho. The scenery is great, and the dialogue at the start is somewhat interesting, but it's still boring enough to where you need to power through. The movie starts picking up towards the end, and most people will probably become very interested at that point. The Hateful Eight is a well paced thriller and genre-slicing western. Tarantino manages to strike the delicate balance of keeping the intimacy of a stage while still infusing the material with enough cinematic flourishes to keep it from feeling too constrained. For a simple premise and multi-layered characters, Tarantino's expert style and execution makes his eighth film an enjoyable experience. Seeing this re-released in 70mm was great. Quentin Tarantino once again proves in The Hateful Eight that dialogue can be just as lethal as a gunshot. The film begins at a slow pace, with characters that feel like they’ve stepped out of a mystery play, gradually revealing their cards through conversations filled with venom, dark humor, and that unmistakable Tarantino flair. From the outset, it’s clear that what matters is not just what’s said, but how it’s delivered.What’s most striking is that much of the story takes place in a single setting: a cabin lost in the snow. This makes the experience feel almost like a stage play, where every gesture and every word weigh as heavily as bullets. Tarantino here recalls the essence of Reservoir Dogs: trapping a group of suspicious characters, letting the atmosphere grow thick with tension, and waiting for everything to **** cast is fully committed. Samuel L. Jackson and Kurt Russell dominate the screen with charisma and authority, but it’s Jennifer Jason Leigh who steals the show, turning each of her appearances into something both disturbing and magnetic. The script gives her room to shine, and she makes the most of it.Ennio Morricone’s music deserves its own mention. His Oscar-winning score adds both an epic and sinister tone, lifting the film above any recent western. Every note seems to foreshadow the violence to come, reminding us that we’re in the hands of a master capable of creating tension even in ****’s true that the running time might feel excessive for some, and Tarantino indulges in his own trademarks: endless dialogue, insults, and bursts of gore that flirt with self-parody. Yet this is exactly his essence: a filmmaker who never apologizes for his excesses and turns chaos into **** Hateful Eight is not just a western, but an exercise in style where words carry as much power as gunpowder. It may be uneven at times, but when it all comes together — dialogue, characters, music, and violence — it reminds us why Tarantino remains a unique voice in today’s cinema. What a disgusting and horrible movie; it was painful to watch. Easily the worst Tarrantino movie I have ever seen. The part where Tarrantino provides dialog about the scene is one of the most cringe things I have ever seen in a movie. The way they physically abuse the woman in this movie is sick and almost unwatchable. Only people who are depraved could get any enjoyment from this film. The basic story isn't even bad, but the development has an excessively slow pace for what it offers, an exaggerated duration and ends up boring at large stretches. The best thing I've ever seen! Yet another masterpiece from Quentin Tarantino and a score from Ennio Moricone which deserves every award it has gotten. One Academy Award is not enough for this perfect piece of cinema. I love this movie. The cinematography is fantastic, the score is majestic, the characters are fun and entertaining - it's just perfect to me. 

Part of what makes this 4-hour film so entertaining, apart from the fantastic dialogue, is the mystery. We don't know anything about these characters except what they tell us. For all we know, everyone could be lying.

Add in a crazy 3rd act, and this is one of my favorite movies that don't get nearly enough love. In the mid nineteenth century, a blinding snowstorm blows several crooked paths to one central location: a haberdashery in the middle of nowhere. Here, a motley gathering of bounty hunters, fugitives, lawmen and soldiers takes place, but nothing is quite as it seems. Eight may walk in, but far fewer will see the sunlight when this storm clears.

Structurally, The Hateful Eight is quite similar to Tarantino's first directorial effort, Reservoir Dogs. It features a wide variety of brash, violent, colorful characters, bouncing off the walls (not to mention each other) in an enclosed space while an unseen threat keeps them right where they are. Secrets abound, betrayals too, with the audience kept as much in the dark as the participants. Both are reminiscent of a one-set stage show, really, with the added benefit of cinematography.

The biggest stumbling block here is setup, specifically how much of it there is before the plot feels ready to proceed. I'm a proponent of establishing things, of not rushing in with guns blazing, but this may be an extreme example. The first act alone runs for longer than many feature films, and while there's some good character work in that space, it surely could've achieved the same purpose in half the time or less. The auteur’s infamously witty, cutting dialogue is absent for this portion of the film, too, which may have contributed to that lethargy.

Those who tough it out are rewarded when the pace finally quickens, leading to a typically Tarantino climax - grisly, shocking and wild - but that's awfully familiar territory. For now, this director can still deliver the goods with his back up against the wall, but the time feels nigh for an evolution. He can't answer every riddle with two barrels of lead and a wet, crimson explosion... can he? I was tore on watching it but I’m glad I watched it. It’s not as good as Django but it’s a masterpiece in its own right.

Story/plot could be better. Not enough climax suspense & thriller. Can be skipped. We’re on the fourth one already, and somehow the formula still works… more or less. Ride or Die doesn’t try to reinvent anything, but it knows exactly what it is: a dose of over-the-top action, buddy banter, and ridiculous chases that care little for logic and go all-in on spectacle. And if you’re on board with that, it’s a good time. Such a good movie that I never knew existed. If you like mega man and super hero movies you will love this film. And even if not,  it’s such a stand alone good movie, many reviews state it’s as good as a Pixar movie. The characters are funny and light hearted but the theme is dark and serious which gives novelty . Very good movie and I’m waiting for part 2 Big Hero 6 is... a weird movie for Disney to make. It's based off a Marvel Comic and its world feels cyberpunk-y at heart, neither of which Disney had animated at the time. And yet it's an incredible film, one of my favorite that has come out of this studio in the last 15 years and really hasn't been appreciated enough for the weight it carries.

The themes it incorporates make the film much like a kid-friendly Cyberpunk. couple examples are:
- Technological improvements and the positives/negatives it carries 
-Corporate Greed and Unsafe Practices
Not to mention, it goes unusually deep into loss and sadness. This combination of themes is quite unusual for a kid's movie, and I applaud the writers for conceiving them.

The world it's based in is phenomenally designed; this is simply one of the finest futuristic cities ever conceived. It reminds me of Night City from CP2077 or Oedo from Cyber City Oedo 808. The fancy buildings, high-tech transportation and gadgets, corporations controlling it all- fantastic work.

I simply cannot believe this film hasn't gotten more attention. The world is beautiful, the characters are well-written, its themes are brave to put in a kid's movie, I am amazed. Props to John Lasseter for directing yet another amazing film. Super impressive even getting here so late. A little bit predictable at times, but genuinely funny. Must watch. It's perfect, one of the greatest films that Disney has made in a long time.

This blows mid films like Moana and Frozen outta the water.

Baymax is a likable robot, and this animated film is one of the some animated films about superheroes, like "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse" and "The Incredibles". It features a white, inflatable robot named Baymax, who is one of the most beloved Disney robots, along with WALL-E and EVE. Probably the most Pixar a movie has ever felt without actually coming from Pixar. The direct involvement of many studio alumni surely has a lot to do with that, with John Lasseter and Ed Catmull now overseeing Disney's animation division, heavily involved with Big Hero's production. Their fingerprints are all over the screen, from the impressive ambition of the city of San Francisokyo, which is just as dazzling as it sounds, to the heart-on-the-sleeve sensibilities of the core cast.

Yet, despite the grand scale, admirable attention to detail, sweet tone and bright, diverse character designs, its story falls just short of the standard set by CGI's lead dog. In a word, it's formulaic, terribly so. Every shred of plot seems ripped straight from the beginner's guide to making a movie, to the point that any seasoned viewer could accurately predict the entire plot after maybe fifteen minutes.

Which doesn't mean it's without value - Baymax, the big, friendly, inflatable Stay-Puft robot who dominates the branding, is alone worth the price of admission - just that it's not quite as timeless as it may have hoped. The kids will love it, though, and their parents won't get bored. Just don't look for it to stick with you through the years like the genre's elite. As an aside, that post-credits scene was probably the biggest geek-out moment I've enjoyed in years.

Updated thoughts after a 2019 re-watch: Manga-influenced, team-based teen superhero antics with an emphasis on engineering over fantasy and mysticism. Nobody's struck by a meteor or experimented upon by the government, they're all just classmates at a prestigious technical school with a very specific set of passions and capabilities. That's refreshing, both for the way it keeps the story grounded and for the limitations it places on the cast. They're each decidedly human, even the cute inflatable robot whose personality is dictated by a memory card.

Paired with a bright, friendly sense of style and a spacious, unique world that's loaded with fun little surprises, Big Hero 6 is a visual and conceptual triumph. Unfortunately, the plot runs a bit generic, its well-worn twists and turns telegraphed a mile away, so those quirks and design touches are leaned on quite often. Well-made, good natured and unique in a very crowded crossroad of genres, but too complacent and vanilla with its storytelling. Given a little more ambition, a sequel could do really well. This is everything that movies shouldn't be in terms of storytelling. The most cliche filled story and moments, filled with the most cliche, boring and flat characters I've ever witnessed, combined with the most horrible and unnatural dialogue. A predictable movie and plot, but visually good looking.

200.title: Eternity

200.rich_text:
Eternity Eternity You can only choose one. Romance Comedy Drama David Freyne Elizabeth Olsen Miles Teller Callum Turner Da'Vine Joy Randolph John Early Barry Primus Betty Buckley Darryl Scheelar Danny Mac Damon Johnson In an afterlife where souls have one week to decide where to spend eternity, Joan is faced with the impossible choice between the man she spent her life with and her first love, who died young and has waited decades for her to arrive. A spiritual rom-com that balances absurdity and sincerity with impressive poise. Elizabeth Olsen shines as a woman caught between two great loves, with Miles Teller and Callum Turner delivering strong turns as her equally compelling suitors. Set in an afterlife that feels more grounded than fantastical,Freyne's Eternity is a rare original that invites laughter, reflection, and just the right amount of heartbreak-a warm, thoughtful journey through the emotional weight of love, memory, and what we choose to carry forward. While this is billed as a rom-com, the comedy elements of the film fall rather flat, as the subject-matter does not lend itself well to comedy.    As a result, it wobbles a bit early on, as it tries to find the right tone.  The last act, however, pulls it all together nicely and manages to stick more to the drama of the story.  The acting by the three leads is superb throughout. I’m giving this movie a 10, not necessarily because it genuinely deserves a solid 10 (my objective score would probably be around a 7.5-7.8), but because it really took me back to the feel of late-90s/early-2000s cinematography and we need that back! I also appreciated how much they managed to do with very simple **** acting is less deep and more comic, but it’s clear this isn’t due to any lack of skill or talent on the part of the main trio, it’s a deliberate creative choice. The Heaven shown here was hell, and the movie was not much better. I was actually excited to watch this, but it was horrible. Eternity es una película que no necesita prisas para conectar. Se toma su tiempo para hablar del amor, de las decisiones y de cómo los momentos pequeños pueden pesar más que los grandes. Tiene una vibra melancólica pero cálida, de esas que no te rompen, solo te acomodan las emociones. Funciona porque es honesta, sencilla y porque entiende que a veces el impacto no viene del drama exagerado, sino de lo cotidiano. Sales con el corazón tranquilo… y la cabeza llena de pensamientos. A different romance plot. Acting was good. Pace was good. Story was good. We'd say: "watch this movie for an enjoyable time." Eternally bland.

Miles Teller once again proves why he is one of the most compelling actors in cinema. After his remarkable work in 'Whiplash', he shines here with naturalness and charisma, giving his character a distinct identity of its own.

Unfortunately, I don’t get the same effect from Elizabeth Olsen or Callum Turner. Both are talented actors, but here they fail to connect with me. Olsen spends much of the runtime trapped in a monotonous expression of anguish and crying, which becomes exhausting. Turner lacks the presence that Teller brings: his character feels flat, just a face and a name rather than someone with personality. I suppose this is due to the limited character development.

The story doesn’t manage to sustain interest throughout its duration. The humor works occasionally, and some sequences are entertaining, but they cannot overcome the constant sense of repetition. The film feels long and heavy, spinning on itself like a top, with each turn offering only minimal changes to avoid complete repetition.

'Eternity' does have its strengths. The cinematography is striking and colorful, constantly reminding me of Wes Anderson—a detail I always appreciate in film. However, the set design of this particular utopia doesn’t fully convince me: visually impressive, yes, but not captivating. The script isn’t deficient either; I just didn’t connect with it.

Overall, it’s an uneven experience: mostly irregular performances, a story that increasingly loses interest, and visuals that don’t compensate for the lack of pacing. A24 continues to explore different styles of filmmaking, but here it doesn’t quite reach the heights it has in the past. 影片的设定颇为有趣，人死后会以生前最快乐时的容貌永生，还可以选择一个永生世界前往并永远待在那里。（虽然我坚定认为永生是惩罚）
但片子本质还是个爱情片，对设定并没挖掘太多。对我这种没谈过恋爱经历过爱情的人来看，难以共情。 Touching dramedy set in an "afterlife" scenario. The casting, production quality, soundtrack and screenplay are all excellent. I suppose the only issue is its just not as breathtaking or memorable as other examples in this genre (ghost, always).A decent outing overall. Has there ever been a movie so undermined by its catastrophic final minutes? The ending is poorly constructed that I was briefly convinced the credits would prove to be a gotcha before the real ending was revealed.

201.title: Wreck-It Ralph

metadata.tagline: When the game is over, the fun begins.

201.rich_text:
Wreck-It Ralph Wreck-It Ralph When the game is over, the fun begins. Family Animation Comedy Adventure Rich Moore John C. Reilly Sarah Silverman Jack McBrayer Jane Lynch Alan Tudyk Rich Moore Raymond S. Persi Mindy Kaling Jamie Elman Adam Carolla Wreck-It Ralph is the 9-foot-tall, 643-pound villain of an arcade video game named Fix-It Felix Jr., in which the game's titular hero fixes buildings that Ralph destroys. Wanting to prove he can be a good guy and not just a villain, Ralph escapes his game and lands in Hero's Duty, a first-person shooter where he helps the game's hero battle against alien invaders. He later enters Sugar Rush, a kart racing game set on tracks made of candies, cookies and other sweets. There, Ralph meets Vanellope von Schweetz who has learned that her game is faced with a dire threat that could affect the entire arcade, and one that Ralph may have inadvertently started. The genre of video game movies is a tough nut to crack but this movie manages it very well, I think because it looks at the concept as a whole and not at one particular game. Loads of call backs to arcade classics and newer games and an enjoyable story to boot. As a kid who was amazed by Tron this movie would be this generations version of it. 9/10 in isolation but 10/10 for being one of the few that have 'cracked' the code. Some films connect from a very simple place: the pure joy of discovering something new. Here, the initial idea is already a stroke of genius, but what truly stands out is how it develops without ever losing its sense of play. Everything is designed to draw the viewer in with a smile and keep them there for something deeper that doesn’t need to be spelled **** story moves forward at a steady, well-balanced pace. It doesn’t rely solely on references or winks to the audience, but builds a journey with clear rules, a strong personality, and a huge heart. The humor works, but it’s never just humor: every joke pushes the story forward and strengthens the characters instead of distracting from **** protagonist is a complete success. He’s not a typical hero, and he doesn’t try to be. His conflict is familiar and relatable: wanting to be seen, valued, and loved for who you are, even when you don’t quite fit in. That vulnerability is what makes the emotional journey so effective and impossible not to connect with.Visually, the film is a constant celebration. Each world has its own identity, color palette, and overflowing creativity, yet nothing feels chaotic. Everything serves the story. It manages the difficult balance of being spectacular without becoming exhausting, and fun without losing coherence.Beyond entertainment, there’s a clear and well-integrated message about identity, friendship, and our place in the world. It’s never overstated or explained too much; it simply exists and works naturally. That’s what makes it ****’s a bright, imaginative, and deeply comforting film. One of those stories that become tied to a happy memory and continue to work just as well over time. Cinema that proves emotion and fun can go hand in hand with intelligence. Más que increíble, la vi varias veces y no me aburrió, una trama compleja y bastante bastante completa (no es una historia tan sencilla y ya, tiene un trasfondo, desarrollo, y giro de eventos que resulta espectacular), engancha al espectador, se enfoca en la calidad a lo largo del tiempo (nunca decae, al menos no recuerdo que lo haga), recuerdo que desde el inicio hasta el final hace que valga la pena (cosa muy difícil de conseguir, porque debes pensar mucho en la trama, y muchos detalles que pulir y demás), tiene ese ambiente familiar, cálido y alegre que hace que me sienta en casa, es impresionante ver que hagan cosas así y me gustó en mi niñez (el hecho de que la viera y la pasara entretenido una y otra vez de niño me recuerda su calidad, no solo eso, es que la recuerdo así, siendo muy buena y notándose que la hicieron con cariño, para los niños). Tante ispirazioni da prodotti storici, uno sviluppo intrigante ed un cast piacevolissimo. Meraviglioso. Detona Ralph não é apenas um filme divertido sobre videogames, mas uma história com coração, camadas e personagens memoráveis. Ele combina nostalgia e inovação, criando um universo rico e cheio de detalhes para explorar. A mensagem de que o valor de alguém não é definido pelo papel que os outros impõem ressoa forte, tornando o longa uma obra-prima atemporal.Nota: 100/100 – Obra-Prima. Favori yapımlarımdan. Herkese tavsiye ederim. İzlemenizi öneririm. Vaktinizi böyle kaliteli yapımlarda harcayın. Cute, family-friendly adventures with a wealth of buried treasure scattered about for long-term arcade lurkers. Wreck-It Ralph provides a fun twist on the old, sentimental framework established by Toy Story, but when the sight gags, winks and grins run out it starts to feel a bit thin. The prologue hints at something really dense, vivid, expansive and bright, especially in the bad guys' support group scene that features in all the trailers, but the story never truly delivers on that potential. As a small-scale adventure, though, it's just fine, and I certainly appreciated the efforts it made to secure so many cameos from classic gaming characters.

Everything looks great, both in full 3D and pixelated 8-bit facsimile, and the voice acting is a series of loose, warm, top-notch efforts. The concept just never feels like it’s fully realized, and a long layover in one particular game world puts the brakes on what was, until then, a pretty snappy pace. I guess at the end of the day, the comparisons to recent Pixar and Disney epics are inevitable, and it's a clear step or two below that level of prestige. A good, safe effort that's worth a lazy watch, but not exactly what I was hoping for. I am blown away by how good this film was, having watched it for the first time today, in 2024, when I'm 51, 5 years after being diagnosed with autism.  I'm still processing the depths and complexity of this Disney film. Wreck-it Ralph is an absolute blast of a film. It is so much fun and it is super cute. I definitely recommend this movie and it will steal your heart. I don't understand how people think that the first movie is better than the second one. This is a atrocious. It's actually traumatic. Because Ralph is such an idiot. I just don't get it. It is so violent to achieve something. That doesn't make any sense at all.-

202.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past

metadata.tagline: To save the future, they must alter the past.

202.rich_text:
X-Men: Days of Future Past X-Men: Days of Future Past To save the future, they must alter the past. Action Adventure Science Fiction Bryan Singer Hugh Jackman James McAvoy Michael Fassbender Patrick Stewart Ian McKellen Jennifer Lawrence Halle Berry Nicholas Hoult Anna Paquin Elliot Page The ultimate X-Men ensemble fights a war for the survival of the species across two time periods as they join forces with their younger selves in an epic battle that must change the past – to save our future. This is the direction we have all been waiting for the studios to take and it does an excellent job on all fronts.  That's it.  Just go watch! I really enjoyed Days of Future Past and believe it's one of the better X-Men films. Blending both the original and new school casts together in a time travel scheme, the results are entertainingly good. It also retcons a lot of the previous films in a good way, which sets the slate clean for the franchise moving forward. X-Men: Days of the Future Past is probably my absolute favourite X-Men film.

Most of the characters are already established and they are very well-used. The new characters are also great. The enemies are not completely stupid or evil. There is at least some sense to what they are doing. Overall the stakes are very high, but they managed to balance the serious and funny moments really well. There are also great little twists that I love. At first I didn't like how it ended, but having sit on it for some time, I'm completely positive about it now.

The direction and the cinematography are the best they've ever been in the franchise. This is Bryan Singer's finest work I've seen. The editing is out of this world for a superhero movie. It doesn't have the right to be as good as it is. The visual parallels between the timelines are so cool. The visual effects are beyond amazing too. The stuff with Peter is mind-blowing. The cast is close to being as enormous as any Avengers movie. The performances are superb even though not many actors got enough time to shine. This time there wasn't a single performance I thought was cheesy or weird.

X-Men: Days of the Future Past has no right to be this good, although I don't get the post credit scene. It teases the next film, but after this film the audience can't connect it to anything. I really liked this film, I thought it was definitely the best in the series of x men films until that point. The future world was awesome and terrible. The action scenes in the future were great to watch.  I loved going back to the early 70s, and the amusement that could be had. I really liked the guy who could move super-quickly - some of the best scenes in the film had him in. Peter Dinklage was fantastic as the villain! The story was great! I'd definitely watch it again. What an interesting idea! I'm not a huge fan of time travelling, but the creators nailed it in this case. It has memorable scenes, a well-constructed story and awesome fights. Sadly, this is the last time the past timeline actually worked. So, the movie is a nice concept well executed. A film with a classic plot for its genre but well developed and which stands out for the excellent intensity that it maintains from beginning to end both for the plot content and for the action. The connection with the past differentiates it positively from the other films in the saga Does it resemble the same story arc from the comics?  Not in the slightest.  Does that matter for this film?  Absolutely not.  The pace and editing of the past and future timelines are top-notch and create great amounts of tension.  Centering the movie around Logan was a brilliant choice commercially and creatively, and, aside from his titular film later on, this might be the best Jackman performance we have, which is saying something considering how much he has to stand out among the large cast.  Everyone is great.  Fassbender is genially brutal, and the prison break-out scene is one of the best in the series.  This is the one movie where the J-Law Mystique clicked for me - she captures both her ferocity and her wounded spirit.  The scene where she limps away from a jeering crowd after being shot is heartbreaking.  The future stuff hits all the right notes.  This is a crackerjack movie and everything a superhero film should be.  It's not half-baked like some of the later entries - there's stakes, there's melodrama to spare, everything feels heightened and epic. Wolverine gallops through time and space to deflect an ugly outcome for all of humanity, pausing frequently to give old cast members the time to wink directly into the camera and strut off the stage. I'm somewhat ashamed to admit I thought it was a gigantic mess.

The story had a lot of potential, especially in the unusual settings of both timelines, but it somewhat predictably gets tangled in the tripwires often associated with a time travel flick and spends far too much time delivering fan service when it should've been examining character motivations and further world-building. Trask and his sentinels barely play a supporting role in the proceedings, patsies at best, and I'm still struggling to comprehend Magneto's decision-making in the third act. Days of Future Past retains all of the unease-inspiring puns and goofball moments that I'd hoped the series could shed, making it feel dated and slightly pandering... a significant backtrack from the progress made in First Class.

Even the built-in fireworks of two heavyweight casts, finally meeting face-to-face, doesn't really work as well as it should. Seeing the new guys (McAvoy and Fassbender) alongside the old guard (Stewart and McKellen) didn't result in a torch-passing or spotlight the nuanced efforts that so delighted me in the previous picture, it just made me yearn to see more of the older guys.

I mean, it's not all bad - the effects work is wonderful, it's a lot of fun spotting all the little love notes scattered about, and the action roars right along for a two-hour Candyland cruise - but I had trouble shutting off my brain when earlier chapters hadn't been nearly so demanding in that department. X-Men: Days of Future Past is one of the better time-travel movies that just happens to be a superhero movie as well. Another movie that I always rewatch at least once a year. It's not perfect, there are a few moments that could been better but you can easily overlook them due to the overall experience. X-Men: Days Of Future Past Makes Suffering through the previous Films worth it. Its a Genuinely good Film even with Its few downsides.

Monsters, Inc. Monsters, Inc. It's nothing personal. It's just their job. Animation Comedy Family Pete Docter John Goodman Billy Crystal Mary Gibbs Steve Buscemi James Coburn Jennifer Tilly Bob Peterson John Ratzenberger Frank Oz Daniel Gerson Lovable Sulley and his wisecracking sidekick Mike Wazowski are the top scare team at Monsters, Inc., the scream-processing factory in Monstropolis. When a little girl named Boo wanders into their world, it's the monsters who are scared silly, and it's up to Sulley and Mike to keep her out of sight and get her back home. Ne yazık ki eskimiş bir yapım artık. Hala izlenebilir ama aynı tadı ilk defa izleyenlere verebilir mi? Top 1 Pixar Movie, Whoever came up with a idea like this is a genius, I cant believe I was able to find a better Pixar movie than The Incredibles One of the best movies ever made, Monsters Inc still watchable today & just as enjoyable as the first time. Monstros S.A. é um clássico absoluto. O filme tem um roteiro excelente, personagens inesquecíveis, animação inovadora e uma história que mistura humor e emoção na medida certa. Além disso, traz uma mensagem poderosa e um final que emociona mesmo depois de várias **** dúvida, merece 100/100 – Obra-prima. Um dos melhores filmes já feitos pela Pixar e um marco na animação. When this movie was released in 2001 as I would of been coming up for 3 years old at the time looking at it now Pixar really set the bar high as I thought it was an absolute strong solid entertainment as I thought Pete Docter gives the audience an absolute Screaming & Scaring entertainment in a comedic stand up manner but with a solid vision. Tables turn as a charming young girl bursts through her own closet door and sends shivers through the monsters on the other side. Everything about Monsters, Inc. is wonderful, from the essentially Pixar concept to the warm, sentimental relationships at its core. Even the animation has held up quite well, which isn't always the case with these early CG efforts: humans look a bit wonky, but most of the cast seems drawn straight from the pages of a Caldecott winner and that kind of bright, absurd character works beautifully.

John Goodman and Billy Crystal carry most of the heavy-lifting as Mike and Sulley, blue collar creatures with an easy, free-flowing rapport, but three-year-old Mary Gibbs threatens to steal the scene every time she gets the chance with her adorable almost-words and penetrating good cheer.

Exceedingly well-balanced, with the kind of imagination that keeps mouths gaping and so much heart, even the boogeyman might have to fight back a tear or two. One of my favorites of the entire Pixar catalog, it swings hard and connects on every level. Sweet, sad, silly and stupendous, it's a timeless classic that I was glad to share with my kids. This movie is one of Pixar’s best really a truly emotional and complex movie from a creative perspective I really like this movie. I just think it's funny. I like the characters and yeah, 
just a banger overall. A true classic that never gets old despite being perhaps my most re-watched movie. The unique setting and characters are chock-filled with amusing little details that give "Monsters" that prime-Pixar charm that you can't quite get anywhere else.

The whole concept of the film itself is scarily creative. A world where monsters work a 9-5 scaring human children around the world in order the extract power from the children's screams is such a unique concept that it's a wonder Pixar took 12 years to make a sequel and another 7 after that to make a television series. Even the background characters in the original film are full of life and have unique traits to them.

The main characters, one-eyed green ball of charm Mike Wazowski and scaring superstar James P Sullivan are the best duo to ever come out of a Disney or Pixar film (yes, that includes Woody and Buzz). Incredible voice-acting performances by the iconic Billy Crystal and John Goodman bring a stunning amount of life and depth to these two characters that could easily come out flat in the wrong hands. This is Mike and Sully's story and the two characters carry the film as such, although curiously cute human "invader" Boo has more than her fair share of show-stealing moments.

Even after 22 years, "Monster's Inc" is still well worth a watch for its unique world and scarily relatable monsters. This is one that will continue to stand the test of time. Excellent movie. The story is so enjoyable, scoring is really great, visual is decent, and the voice is stunning

204.title: Iron Man 3

204.rich_text:
Iron Man 3 Iron Man 3 Unleash the power behind the armor. Action Adventure Science Fiction Shane Black Robert Downey Jr. Gwyneth Paltrow Don Cheadle Guy Pearce Rebecca Hall Jon Favreau Ben Kingsley James Badge Dale Stephanie Szostak Paul Bettany When Tony Stark's world is torn apart by a formidable terrorist called the Mandarin, he starts an odyssey of rebuilding and retribution. A polarized look at the man behind the gold-and-red mask, balancing anxiety with blockbuster spectacle.260312 (3.0)I watched this in the theater back in 2013. While it was interesting to see the protagonist grappling with his anxiety and human vulnerabilities, the overall execution felt a bit hit-or-miss for me. The major villain twist was polarizing, and although the action was polished, it didn't quite reach the heights of the first film or the earlier ensemble crossover. A solid 3.0 for an entertaining blockbuster that felt more like a personal epilogue than a groundbreaking superhero spectacle. The Mandarin is who? What?! Why?! You did so much disrespect to one of the greatest villains in the Marvel Comics and for what -  And you replaced Tony's alcoholism with self-doubt and depression?!  COME ON!!!!  Best part was seeing Pepper in the suit to save Iron Man!  Someone deserves to be fired for this one. 4Dmax特效公司的团队也参与了电影制作，通过扫描现场道具和设施进行数字化重建。为了实现雷达定位扫描，其使用了莱卡扫描测量系统工具集，该设备性能强大且稳定，可以轻松应对长时间持续工作。工作组还使用了基于4D动态尖端科技的投影灯光系统来捕捉镜头前的全部表演，几乎涉及到100多位演员。在扫描道具方面，工作团队使用了感知器构成的近景扫描激光系统。这些测量工具通常在高端汽车和航空电子产业中得到广泛应用 The best visual effects in Marvel movies. Good soundtrack, dynamics and acting. But a terrible villain and a bad script. I don't know, it's on a similar level for me as the second film. A film focused on the human Tony Stark is a good idea, however, it doesn't have many interesting parts. The worst part of it is that terrible "plot twist", it just pisses you off. Once again, I can only say that the idea was nice, but the execution was lacking, just like in the case of the previous part. All that invincible villian build up, to just get destroyed by one random bs right at the end. R u kidding me? Kid segments were also unnesessary. Could’ve been way better movie The finale of the Iron Man Trilogy perfectly and poetically shows the change of Tony Stark as a man. Contrasting to many scenes of his prior years, we can see the growth that has happened within him and the self actualization of what type of person he was and who he wants to become for the future. This movie says farewell to the loved character peacefully with amazing visuals and graphics as well. Iron Man 3 has very high stakes while managing to be hilarious at the same time.

The dialogues are as funny as ever even though they don't always make complete sense. I think the Mandarin has been the best villain in the Iron Man movies so far, one of the best in the MCU. I knew who was behind the curtain all along, but he felt like a real danger and he was menacing. I like that Hogan got a bigger role and I also like how Tony Stark is evolving throughout the story. Speaking of the story, it was less predictable the most MCU movies, it had a few great twists including both the protagonist and the villain.

The cinematography is good, the editing too, but it's a common theme with Marvel movies that most of them are a little too long or overstretched and this is no exception. The casting is amazing, the acting performances are good, Robert Downey Jr. is just absolutely perfect for this role. Guy Pearce is amazing as Aldrich Killian is amazing. The visual effects looked wonderful, I had no issues with it. The action sequences were outstanding.

Iron Man 3 is an amazing conclusion to the trilogy, which ends at a perfect point from the character's perspective. Badly in need of a spark after an underwhelming second installment, this series has swapped directors and imported a major villain from the comics for its third. Frankly, it doesn't fare any better for the effort.

That's partially due to the Tony Stark character hitting a wall (his arc has been stagnant for a while now) but I found more culpability in the icy set of cold feet developed around the plot's midway point. In the blink of an eye, the whole tone of the picture changes from a topical dash of political intrigue (and a pointed metaphor for the US approach to terrorism) to just another struggle between Stark and the latest in a long line of bland, suit-wearing, self-enhanced business rivals with an eye on one of his inventions.

That the Mandarin is downplayed doesn't necessarily bother me. Actually, I found Ben Kingsley wonderful in the role and enjoyed the sudden wheel-jerk of his course change (those upset about his blasphemous take on a sacred character need look no further than the short follow-up film, All Hail the King, for vindication). But that sudden, accompanying leap from a new path to a tired, over-familiar formula is a development sour enough to curl toes.

This character needed a blast of fresh air, some momentum to carry him through the next phase of Marvel's plans. Instead, he's simply planted his feet deeper in the same vat of quicksand. Despite all its intentions, this is really no better than Iron Man 2. Not as bad as I remembered, but still... The villain is such a waste of an opportunity, man.

However, the plane scene was cool.

205.title: The Substance

metadata.tagline: Have you ever dreamt of a better version of yourself?

205.rich_text:
The Substance The Substance Have you ever dreamt of a better version of yourself? Horror Science Fiction Thriller Coralie Fargeat Demi Moore Margaret Qualley Dennis Quaid Edward Hamilton-Clark Gore Abrams Oscar Lesage Christian Erickson Robin Greer Tom Morton Hugo Diego Garcia A fading celebrity decides to use a black market drug, a cell-replicating substance that temporarily creates a younger, better version of herself. This is the most pretentious and distasteful pile of garbage I have seen.  The film completely loses itself from the writer’s inability to compose a compelling ending and the beauty standards message is a substitute for a story progression or character development.  Hollywoods pretentious obsession with making a statement is on full display here where critics construe a pile of excrement as art. The Substance is a competently made film with an interesting concept, strong performances, and striking visuals, but its heavy reliance on body horror makes it an unpleasant experience for me. The narrative setup and character work are engaging, and I appreciate the film’s thematic ambitions, yet every time it leans into graphic physical transformation and grotesque imagery, my engagement collapses. I can recognize the craftsmanship behind its execution and understand why fans of the genre might enjoy it, but on a personal level, body horror does nothing for me beyond generating disgust. As a result, I acknowledge its quality while strongly disliking the experience of watching it. The Substance is the kind of film that crawls under your skin and dares you to look away. It is body horror as self-reflection, a grotesque mirror held up to beauty culture, celebrity, and the impossible expectations placed on women to stay perfect forever.

Directed by Coralie Fargeat, the film follows a fading actress who discovers a scientific serum that can create a younger, idealized version of herself. What begins as a miracle of reinvention quickly becomes a nightmare of identity and control. The result is bold, hypnotic, and deeply uncomfortable.

Demi Moore gives the performance of her career. She plays a woman dissected by the gaze of others, her every expression loaded with decades of real-world pressure. The film weaponizes her presence, turning the audience into complicit voyeurs. Margaret Qualley is equally unsettling as the younger self, embodying a flawless ideal that feels more alien than human. Together, they make the screen ache with tension.

The body horror is relentless but never empty. Every grotesque moment serves a purpose, revealing how perfection consumes the imperfect until both are destroyed. It is not the usual shock-for-shock’s-sake approach. Instead, the violence feels psychological, as if the film itself is peeling back the skin of vanity to expose what lies beneath.

Fargeat directs with precision and fury. The film’s neon aesthetic and glossy artificiality make every frame pulse with contradiction. It is beautiful and disgusting at once, much like the culture it critiques. Beneath the gore, there is tragedy. The horror is not in the blood but in the desperation to be seen, to matter, to stay visible in a world that discards women past their supposed prime.

The pacing is deliberate, allowing the discomfort to settle. It never feels rushed or apologetic. Even the moments of silence carry weight, as if the film knows it has already earned your unease. The sound design amplifies that dread, turning every whisper and breath into a reminder that transformation has a cost.

The Substance works because it understands that horror and satire are two sides of the same mirror. It laughs, it screams, and it dares you to recognize yourself in the reflection.

Verdict: Visceral, intelligent, and deeply personal. The Substance is not just a movie about transformation. It is a dissection of what we lose trying to become who we think we should be. I found the set design and screenplay fascinating. The decision to tackle the themes in such an exaggerated, almost grotesque style was powerful and refreshingly free of excessive sentimentality. I loved how it dug into ageism, the objectification of women, the cult of performance, and the inflation of ego, alongside total body control, the idea of a body that can be reshaped without limits, and the fleeting nature of fame, especially when it’s built on something as fragile and instant as physical beauty. Marca un nuevo comienzo para el body horror, una mezcla brillante de crudeza, belleza y reflexión. Es una obra que duele y fascina a la vez, con actuaciones que llevan el género a un nivel profundamente humano. Original, visceral y necesaria: así se reinventa el miedo en el cine moderno. If you truly listen to The Substance, what it’s saying is that the industries we rely on for many things – our entertainment, our wellbeing, our connection to other people – are corrupted by unfounded fears of female aging, loss of beauty, and the next generation. Sure, it’s an exaggerated and somewhat obvious film, but that doesn’t make director Coralie Fargeat’s point any less true – nor does it detract from the tremendously gory way in which she makes it. Elisabeth’s story is a tragedy because those who are allowed to age are actually the lucky ones. To deprive yourself of that grace – physically, mentally, or both – in order to fulfill someone else’s twisted goals is a fate which The Substance hopes no woman will ever have to suffer again. The Substance is incredibly interesting, and honestly really sad. Demi Moore does an incredible job portraying Elisabeth, the older and aging star losing her identity, and this was my first time seeing Margaret Qualley, as Sue, and she absolutely nailed it playing the young clone of her old self. The effects and the idea behind this movie are excellent, but the end of the movie goes off the rails and leans into the insanity of body horror. This is one of the artsy independent movies where you are waiting for something to happen that never really comes. The success of this film is going to be based more on the ending, on how they will tie up all the different plot devices. Unfortunately, they took the more over-the-top approach, and at least for me, this just didn't work. Une bonne claque dans la gueule, ca faisait longtemps que je ne m’étais pas caché devant un film. C’est gore à souhait mais si glamour à la fois c’est addictif. Le jeu d’acteur est exceptionnel bravoà demi Moore. After being booted from the lowest rung of the Hollywood ladder on the eve of her fiftieth birthday, a faded starlet gets desperate. Swayed by a shady viral marketing campaign, she injects herself with a goopy green mystery drug and cannonballs off the conceptual diving board. We know trouble’s brewing when she cracks open that slick little welcome kit to find a series of single-use injectors and two packs of intravenous food, then decides to proceed anyway. The ensuing chaos completely blew past my expectations.

The Substance is a wild and crazy, metaphor-rich body horror experiment that crashes through boundaries and stomps all over the presumed lines of decency. Explicit and uncompromisingly weird, with similar energy to Everything Everywhere All at Once, it hits dark notes with heavy hands and extends well beyond the most obvious analogies. Yes, there’s plenty of meta chatter about the uncomfortable consume-and-churn lifespan of a star actress. That’s a touchy subject which merits inspection, even if it takes a bonkers, high-concept horror movie to get our brains tuned in. I expected that; the rest of the commentary, including a smart parody of dumb public taste and several notes about our younger selves doing things we’ll regret when we’re older, caught me by surprise and gave me a whole lot more to chew on. It’s rare for something this loud and grotesque to also have more than one interesting thing to say.

Demi Moore’s lead casting is perfect, not to mention crucial. As a discarded hot ticket herself, she’s exactly the right kind of spokesperson to deliver these messages. Her credibility no doubt brought distribution power (and eyeballs) to the project that might have otherwise gone missing. Still bold and defiant, even at sixty-plus years of age, her name makes this something worth noticing, and her performance validates the extra attention. This production asks a lot of her and she’s often game to take it a step further. Her famous makeup scene in the mirror will be this film’s most resonant, lasting image, but it’s far from her only standout moment.

I do feel that, eventually, The Substance writes itself into a corner and can’t find a way out. The ending suits its identity as a horror picture - that’s where it does some of its nastiest work - but doesn’t match the thoughtful undercurrents that made the rest of it so intoxicating. I groaned and laughed, grossed out, but only for superficial reasons. Still, 90% of a home run is enough to score points with me. Potent stuff, even with the somewhat underwhelming climax.

The film answers this eternal question with a resounding "No!" while beautifully weaving a tale that feels like a modern, emotionally resonant successor to "Lilo & Stitch." The story follows Elio Solis, a lonely middle schooler who feels like a burden to his aunt Olga, a space program major who sacrificed her dreams to raise him. Elio's yearning to be abducted by aliens isn't just curiosity; it’s a desire to free his aunt from the weight of his existence. When he accidentally becomes the first human to contact the "Communiverse"—an intergalactic organization of highly intelligent beings—he is thrust into a world of vibrant alien ambassadors like Questa and the formidable yet misunderstood Lord **** film excels in its emotional depth, particularly through Elio’s bond with Glordon, Grigon's lonely son. The visual storytelling and character movements are exceptionally expressive, capturing the nuances of a child trying to act brave while feeling small. One of the most heartbreaking moments occurs when a clone of Elio acts "normal," and Olga’s relieved reaction inadvertently highlights the distance between them. However, through a series of cosmic negotiations and the help **** network of "HAM" radio enthusiasts, Elio realizes his own worth. The ending is bittersweet; despite reaching the Communiverse he longed for, he chooses to return to Earth, understanding that while being "special" can be lonely, he is no longer truly alone. With a new radio built with his friend Bryce to keep in touch with Glordon, Elio finally finds a sense of belonging both in the stars and at home. There’s something immediately pleasant about Elio. From the very first minutes, it feels colorful, lively, and welcoming, with Pixar’s craftsmanship evident in every frame. Everything works… and yet, there’s also a lingering sense that we’ve been here before. Not in this exact setting, but certainly in this structure, this emotional journey, and this careful way of moving forward without straying too far off **** story touches on meaningful themes — loneliness, feeling out of place, the need to be seen — and does so with sensitivity. The issue isn’t what it wants to say, but how it chooses to say it. Pixar seems to have internalized its own formula so thoroughly that it now executes it almost on autopilot. Emotional beats arrive right on cue, lessons are clearly signposted, and the adventure never truly risks spinning out of control. Everything is solid, even charming, but genuine surprise is rare.Visually, however, Elio is operating at a very high level. The universe design, colors, textures, and sheer imagination behind every creature and environment remind us why Pixar remains a benchmark in animation. Some sequences instantly captivate and deliver that sense of wonder the studio knows so well how to create, even when the story itself doesn’t fully take off.Where the film falls slightly short is in its emotional weight. It aims to move the audience, and at times it succeeds, but without the depth or boldness of Pixar’s strongest works. There’s a feeling that it avoids pushing too far, as if reluctant to challenge or unsettle viewers. The result is a warm, empathetic experience that nevertheless feels a bit lightweight by the studio’s own **** the end, Elio is an enjoyable, well-crafted film that’s easy to like. It’s far from a misstep, but it doesn’t redefine anything either. It works as family entertainment, delivers what it promises, and leaves a pleasant aftertaste. At the same time, it reinforces the sense that Pixar is currently in a phase where familiar structures feel safer than creative leaps into the unknown — and that may be its greatest limitation. The final version falls back on Pixar’s familiar trope of grief and parental death, a theme that feels underdeveloped and tacked on, weakening the emotional core and making Elio’s initial wish to leave Earth harder to grasp. While the film remains beautiful, adventurous, and fun enough for family viewing, even Pixar animators have admitted in interviews that much of its original poetry and uniqueness was lost in the process. A triumphant return to the reckless mayhem and guilt-free indulgence of the early '80s action/adventure bubble. Fury Road puts foot to floor right from the opening bell and never lets up, somehow topping itself over and over again, even when it seems like there's nowhere left to go. It's joyous anarchy, a world that thrives on all of society's dirty secrets; completely post-apocalyptic crazy but also a little more familiar than we'd care to admit.

Of course, it's a visual powerhouse - a glowing example of art direction, stunt driving, cinematography and character design that's damn near unrivaled in modern cinema - but it's also an audio behemoth. Like Inception's deep bellow or Terminator's ominous rumble, Mad Max 4 can convey a looming sense of dread through its frequent, effective use of bass. You feel that rumble? That's the ride starting back up again. Junkie XL's accompanying soundtrack is a perfect tonal match, the right blend of fuzzy, maxed-out guitar licks and incessant, pounding tribal drums.

Perhaps most impressively, the film doesn't feel obligated to dig up every last bit of backstory on its way to the finish line. If anything, it revels in leaving that to the viewer, whose imagination is bound to fill in the blanks for such a broad, wildly eccentric cast of characters far better anyway. It's a raucous success, a lethal dose of sensory overload that hits like a two-hour surge of adrenaline. I loved it, constantly shaking my head at the experience and laughing at myself like a little kid at his first R-rated movie. Loved every minute.

Revised thoughts after a 2016 re-watch: Technically and visually, there's really nothing that can compete with this. A continuously dazzling, picturesque visual marvel that's half Burning Man and half Clockwork Orange, I could sit back and just soak up the atmosphere for hours without complaint.

The opening forty minutes, almost exclusively an action/chase scene, are absolutely captivating and whip past in a heartbeat. It slows down momentarily after that, if just to offer the audience a fleeting lungful of air, but we're rarely more than five minutes from our next pulse-rocking orgasm of steel and violence.

The story is conveyed in bursts and shreds, often illuminating just enough of the world to force more questions, which probably bucked some viewers. If we look closely enough, though, many of those answers arrive via background action or subtle hints. That uber-minimal approach gives us extra time to linger in the visual splendor, while still feeling nourished by a story that's more than just skin and bones. Still one of my favorite films of the last ten years, and a must-have for any home Blu-Ray collection. A Genius Dissection of Violence and IdentityA History of Violence might seem like a crime thriller at first glance, but beneath its quiet surface lies a complex and disturbing work of art, one of director David Cronenberg's most significant achievements. Here, Cronenberg abandons the "body horror" he's famous for to delve into a different kind of terror: the psychological horror rooted in the depths of human **** story places us in an idyllic American town where an ordinary man lives a quiet life. But when fate forces him to commit a violent act to defend his diner, the doors to a past he thought he had sealed forever are thrown open. What distinguishes this film is its handling of violence; it's not for show. It's brutal, realistic, and has dire consequences that leave scars on the soul before the **** performances are the cornerstone here. Viggo Mortensen delivers an exceptional, multi-layered performance, brilliantly embodying the internal conflict between the man he is and the man he was. He's supported by Maria Bello with a powerful, emotional performance, while Ed Harris and William Hurt deliver short but terrifying and memorable supporting roles.Cronenberg's direction is cold, precise, and almost clinical, observing the horrific events with an unsettling calm that forces the viewer to think rather than just feel. This style, combined with a controversial score that at times seems deliberately mismatched with the scenes, can make the film a challenging experience for some.Ultimately, A History of Violence is not a film that aims to please you, but to challenge you. It's a profound cinematic work that poses philosophical questions about whether we can truly escape our past, and whether violence is an inseparable part of our nature. An unforgettable film, and an essential watch for any lover of serious **** Personal Rating: 7.5/10 A very average and slightly boring film! Acting is ok in parts, but the story is meh! There is no reason why i shouldn't like it with the story being good and the cast was excellent.  For some reason I just didnt like it. mannerism foliates its space and crowdedness equally..

A History Of Violence A History Of Violence is a character driven dramatic thriller about a guy whose hidden past haunts him back to his family after he leaves his street credit behind. The feature is surprisingly fast and utterly exhilarating to the core with its street ruggedness and raw brutality that grounds this stunning craft. The range of its narrative is fascinatingly wide and it excels on each peak moments that it dares to achieve. It is sharply calm with a jagged script behind the screen that is slowly ticking along with it which when hits its allotted frame, it explodes emotionally that leave an everlasting impact on you. The background score is decent, the sound effects are sharp and aptly loud, the art designing may not be in its A game, the cinematography is stunning and so is its fine editing. Despite of resonating tremendously with practicality, it glorifies its malleable mythological characters with such panache that leaves the audience in an awe of it. Mortensen is poised, reserved and profoundly calm in its horrifying portrayal with Harris supporting convincingly as always and Hurt giving some of his career's best work in here. Olsen's adaptation tells a compelling gritty tale whose mannerism foliates its space and crowdedness equally. And armed with a script as such Cronenberg executes the anticipated vision on screen with his finesse and a bit of pepper added in it, that makes it raunchy. The short screenplay enfolding characters and eye popping decisions which is also justifying to the core as much as entertaining it is, along with a stellar performances by a cast of such caliber are the high points of the feature. A History Of Violence has a plethora of emotional distress in here to keep the tense environment alive among the characters and the hook that binds them all. After reading all of the good reviews for this movie, I can not believe that I watched the same movie as all of these other people writing good reviews. The movie was just flat-out boring. There were maybe 3 events that happened in the entire movie, and the rest was just filler in order to make it a normal length for a film. It didn't help that the acting was terrible, which if had been good would've made the movie a little more bearable. In the beginning, I was willing to give the movie a chance, after reading the summary it seemed like it would be an alright movie. As I kept watching I kept waiting for something exciting to happen, and the only interesting parts of the movie were the fights and the killing. If you're thinking about watching this movie I have one message for you: Don't waste your time. Esta película me parece maravillosa. La presentación tanto de todos los personajes como de la trama y como hacen que todo encaje en un mismo punto es genial. Aunque cuando parece que la película se va a estancar y necesita un empujón, lo tiene con un espectacular giro de guión. A partir de ese momento parece que va a caer, pero se mantiene bien hasta el final. Y es que ese es otro de sus puntos fuertes, lo rápido que llega el final. Indicando que está bien escrita y muy BIEN montada, lo que hace que tenga un gran ritmo toda la película.

Los personajes están bien construidos y te crees que los protagonistas son una familia. Muy interesante el personaje de Viggo Mortensen e interpretado de manera sensacional. Mención aparte para la valentía de la mujer del protagonista. Ole.

Otro de los puntos fuertes de la película reside para mí, en la crudeza de las imágenes en la mayoría de las ocasiones. Una cámara que no rehuye de nada, ni de las consecuencias de la violencia ni se priva de mostrar las escenas de sexo, como si de una serie de la HBO se tratase.

En resumen, película fácil y rápido de ver pero no por ello menos buena. Todo lo contrario. Me ha dejado muy satisfecho y con un final muy 'agridulce' que la eleva más si cabe como una propuesta valiente. Genial. Un PEDAZO de 8.

219.rich_text:
Heat Heat A Los Angeles crime saga. Crime Drama Action Michael Mann Al Pacino Robert De Niro Val Kilmer Jon Voight Tom Sizemore Diane Venora Amy Brenneman Ashley Judd Mykelti Williamson Wes Studi Obsessive master thief Neil McCauley leads a top-notch crew on various daring heists throughout Los Angeles while determined detective Vincent Hanna pursues him without rest. Each man recognizes and respects the ability and the dedication of the other even though they are aware their cat-and-mouse game may end in violence. It’s a great film, and not just because of the De Niro–Pacino duel, which on its own would already be enough to make it special. What’s really impressive is the way Michael Mann turns a cops-and-robbers story into something much bigger, sadder, and more elegant. It isn’t only about heists, chases, or shootouts, but about men trapped inside their own way of understanding the **** my case it also carries something extra, because it is tied to an important memory from youth, the kind that stays attached to cinema forever. Maybe that is why I smile at the fact that the first time I saw it, I didn’t really give it the attention it deserved, and had to watch it again later with my head in the right place. And the truth is that the film rewards that second look, because it is full of details, silences, and glances that carry as much weight as the action.What makes Heat so strong is that it has the muscle of a thriller and the soul of a drama. The famous shootout is still astonishing, dry, brutal, and perfectly executed, but the film does not live on that alone. It also lives through its conversations, its codes, and that idea that hunter and hunted resemble each other far more than either of them would like to admit. That is one of its great strengths: understanding that the real center is not the clash between good and evil, but between two obsessions.Pacino is over the top, yes, but here it works. He has energy, eccentricity, and a wild presence. De Niro, by contrast, takes the opposite route: more restrained, colder, quieter. And that is exactly why the collision between the two has so much force. Mann knows he does not need to put them together twenty times; a few scenes are enough to make you feel you are watching something major.I also love the way it is shot. That nocturnal city, those cold interiors, that sense of emotional distance, of broken lives that keep moving even when they already know they are not going to end well. Heat has style, of course, but the right kind of style: the kind that does not decorate but defines the world of the film and the people living inside it.Overall, I think it is a massive film, one that ages beautifully and still commands respect. It may be long, yes, but when it ends you feel you have watched major cinema: an adult thriller, elegant, tense, and melancholy, with two giants in front of the camera and a director who knew exactly what he had in his hands. Aged poorly. I was old enough for Jurassic Park, but too young for this when it came out. Seeing the cast and the type of performance (over the top and soulless) makes me grateful for the diversity we now have on our screens and behind the cameras. Heat is a long film that earns its runtime through purposeful pacing and scenes that consistently justify their existence. It never feels like filler, instead building tension through patience and accumulation rather than forced twists. The plot is strong and controlled, and the film is elevated by magnetic performances from Robert De Niro and Al Pacino, whose presence gives even quieter dialogue real weight. The writing keeps conversations engaging and consequential, not merely stylized. Technically, it looks like a film of its era, but in a way that feels grounded and self-aware rather than embarrassed by limitations, avoiding cheap spectacle and focusing on what it can do well. The sound work is also a major strength, adding immersion throughout. Val Kilmer feels comparatively flatter next to the leads, but it is a minor weakness in an otherwise excellent experience. Heat feels iconic, epic even though it's a character-driven story.

It's pretty artistic despite the genre of heist-action. This is the story of two similar people living opposing lives. The editing is great, there was one transition during a car scene, where I just had to stop and watch again. The pacing is fantastic. The acting is spectacular too, with Al Pacino, Robert De Niro and Val Kilmer delivering career defining performances.

What can i say about this film, that hasn't been said before. I saw this film for about 7 times, i think. I love this film for a many reasons. Because it's so wonderfully acted and directed (the script is wonderful too). Because it's so epic. Because it's so beautifully sad. This isn't just a "cops and robbers" movie - NO. I don't know, maybe it's just my imagination, but in this movie i saw a fight not just between cops and robbers but a battle between good and evil. And it's a breathtaking experience, when in one, just one scene, two characters, who are representing good and evil (and two different worlds), just sit dawn and talk. How this film wasn't nominated for a best cinematography, editing and sound effects is beyond **** this films line A.Pacino will be remembered forever: "because she had a great xxx !!!" :). Two main characters talks not about films plot but about them self's, what they do, and how they are fitting in this world. Bank robbery scene i a very familiar to "The Dark Knight". And this goes for a real fans: don't know how much of You noticed, but at movies ("Heat") time 100 there is a shoot that goes for 6-8 seconds. This shot shows a car, with all the "bad guys" when they are going through the city. This is 99% identical shot that was used in "The Dark Knight", when Harvey Dent is being transported in a cop car through the city - view goes "from the sky", there is no music, no city sounds, just a night and this excellent tune.Watch this "Los Angeles crime saga" - this is a timeless art. Stylish melancholic neo-noir with excellent pace. 90's vibes. Al Pacino's acting is all over the place, though. I watched the 'Director's Definitive Edition', where Michael Mann took another look and deleted eight(!) words from the soundtrack. Now his 170-minute monster is finally perfect... or is it?If you like boredom, you've definitely found a masterpiece here. The film starts off really promisingly: the robbery of the armored car, the music by Elliot Goldenthal and the images from L.A. are really great. The idea of ​​developing a cat-and-mouse game between a gangster (De Niro) and a hardened investigator (Pacino) also sounds good on **** Mann quickly loses focus and indulges in endless banal dialogues full of clichéd characters and some really bad acting (+ some horrible green screen). I couldn't connect with the characters enough to be able to get involved in the multifaceted narrative. I have seen everything that is told here in a more focused, exciting and believable way elsewhere. Pacino chews up every scene, but still makes it entertaining; in contrast to De Niro, who plays his gangster so reservedly and coolly (his scenes in the house are very reminiscent of "Manhunter") that my eyes sometimes closed. The quality of the images also varies greatly: from beautiful to 90s TV movie level to ugly. The sound design in the action scenes is great, yes, but the sound quality and the mix as a whole are disappointing.Nevertheless, I would like to recommend the film - or at least parts of it - with reservations: When there is some movement in this boring parade, "Heat" is terrific. The bank robbery with shootout is rightly one of the best action scenes in American cinema, and the finale at the airport also manages to build up tension. And most of the time the film looks really fantastic, especially the **** here are the top 3 moments from "Heat":- Al Pacino talks about asses- Al Pacino beats up a TV and kicks it out of the car- the bank robbery

220.title: Karate Kid: Legends

Karate Kid: Legends Karate Kid: Legends When masters unite a new legacy begins. Action Adventure Drama Jonathan Entwistle Jackie Chan Ben Wang Joshua Jackson Sadie Stanley Ming-Na Wen Wyatt Oleff Aramis Knight Ralph Macchio Olivia Yang Avis Aaron Wang After a family tragedy, kung fu prodigy Li Fong is uprooted from his home in Beijing and forced to move to New York City with his mother. When a new friend needs his help, Li enters a karate competition – but his skills alone aren't enough. Li's kung fu teacher Mr. Han enlists original Karate Kid Daniel LaRusso for help, and Li learns a new way to fight, merging their two styles into one for the ultimate martial arts showdown. Jackie Chen did a great job as usual. He spoke like a native English speaker! LOL. Closing the circle of a saga like Karate Kid seemed almost impossible, but this new installment finds a way to do it without betraying its roots. The idea of bringing together two generations —the original from the 80s and the reboot in China— could have been a disaster, but the chemistry between Ralph Macchio and Jackie Chan carries the film from the very beginning. Seeing them together works as the perfect bridge between past and **** movie doesn’t hide that its structure is the same as always: naïve student, demanding mentor, tough training, and the final showdown. But that’s exactly where its strength lies. This formula, repeated endlessly, still works because it taps into a universal emotion: personal growth. You may see every step coming, but what matters is how it’s told and the energy it gives off.Macchio and Chan make for a curious and endearing duo. Each brings his own style and legacy, turning nostalgia from a burden into a driving force that pushes the story forward. The nod to Cobra Kai is there, but the film finds its own tone, closer to classic family cinema than to the twist-heavy drama of the **** new protagonist delivers, bringing freshness and emotion to a story that, while predictable, works thanks to its brisk pace and straightforward focus. It doesn’t try to reinvent anything, but it updates just enough to hook new generations without them needing to have seen everything that came before.Visually, it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but the staging is clean and effective. The fights carry the right intensity, avoiding excess and gimmicks, and the emotional side, even if a bit heavy-handed, keeps the heart of the story intact. There are no groundbreaking moments, but it doesn’t need them: the audience knows what they came for, and here they’ll find **** the end, Karate Kid: Legends doesn’t try to revolutionize the saga, but to celebrate it. It brings back the classic values, pairs two icons that work well together, and delivers a dose of simple, effective emotion. It’s a reminder that sometimes, sticking to the formula is the best thing you can do. I guess pretty much nothing worked for me here, the drab sets and performances really dragged this down. The lead shows some good physical action abilities but this story is just taped together. Le film n’a absolument rien d’original. Tout ce à quoi on s’attend dans un Karate Kid se produit, mais sans la moindre créativité. Tout est expédié à une vitesse folle, ce qui fait que l’on ne ressent jamais réellement la difficulté d’un entraînement ou d’un défi quelconque.Pour parler plus concrètement de l’aspect sport de combat, c’est un grand n’importe quoi. On a un pratiquant de kung-fu qui, à un moment donné, entraîne un gars censé être un ancien champion local de boxe anglaise… mais il le ridiculise sans effort, alors qu’il a deux fois moins d’années que lui. Finalement, notre personnage principal finit par pratiquer le karaté (il était temps, vu le titre du film), mais comme il est déjà “cheaté” de base et que tout est expédié, il passe d’une discipline à l’autre sans aucune difficulté. Oubliez l’époque où il fallait lustrer les palissades de Mr. Miyagi : désormais, il suffit de préparer quelques pizzas en faisant vaguement des mouvements de “karaté” pour devenir le combattant le plus fort du ****-delà de ça, la volonté de mélanger les arts martiaux et leurs valeurs avec un aspect “street” donne un résultat complètement ridicule. À aucun moment on n’est emballé par le pseudo tournoi urbain de karaté. On a même l’impression d’assister à un jeu de course récent avec ses festivals façon Motorfest ou Forza Horizon pour ceux qui ont la référence. Bien sûr, côté antagonistes, on a droit aux “racailles” clichés des années 80. Franchement, c’est du grand n’importe **** dialogues et les pseudo-citations sont plats et totalement bateau. Les combats, eux, ne sont ni intéressants, ni réalistes, ni spectaculaires. Comme je le disais, tout est expédié très vite, et on ne ressent jamais la douleur d’un combat, la difficulté ou la souffrance d’un entraînement (qui, eux aussi, sont complètement **** film n’apporte rien : ni émotion, ni motivation, ni **** bref, je ne vous conseille vraiment pas ce film. Si vous êtes amateur de films d’arts martiaux, il existe des milliers d’œuvres bien plus intéressantes à regarder, comme les anciens films de Jackie Chan, par exemple. Mais pas celui-là. A Fresh Roundhouse Kick of Nostalgia

Karate Kid Legends arrives with the weight of legacy but doesn’t quite aim for the heart the way its predecessors did. Unlike earlier entries that explored self-discovery and redemption with personal stakes, this film feels more like a spiritual side-quest than an emotional journey. What it lacks in depth, though, it tries to make up for in style.

The story is a mix of new and old — offering a fresh, urban visual palette while leaning heavily on nostalgia. Yet, it blends both elements smoothly, making the past feel present without being overbearing. However, the pacing becomes uneven. It begins steadily but starts to drag before lurching into a faster rhythm that unfortunately dilutes the emotional payoff of certain scenes.

The screenplay does manage to balance drama and emotion, even if the action choreography doesn’t quite punch at franchise standards. Where the film truly shines is in its characters. Jackie Chan and Ralph Macchio return naturally, serving more as guides than crutches. But it’s Ben Wang who impresses most — carrying the narrative with conviction and holding his own against legends. Among the supporting cast, Joshua Jackson delivers a standout performance that demands more attention than he’s given.

Visually, the film leans into a modern city vibe with crisp framing and contemporary tone. While the fight scenes are serviceable, they don’t leave lasting marks. Thematically, legacy is the beating heart — though it’s explored more externally than within.

Sum up - Karate Kid Legends leaves a mild imprint. It stays with you mostly for its fresh energy and respectful callbacks, not for any deep emotional punch. Still, it’s an enjoyable watch — especially for fans and newcomers alike looking for something familiar yet lightly reimagined. What The Next Karate Kid failed to achieve, it achieves here. A story about friendship, valor, courage, and some very good fights. Redemption, humanity, compassion, family, kindness, and doing the right thing—recurring themes in The Karate Kid—are beautifully realized here. A cute, lighthearted film for the whole family. It's reminiscent of the best films made in the '90s. If you like the Karate Kid saga and well-written scripts, you'll love this film. However, it's a new story. It's not about the characters seen so far (who appear as supporting characters); this is a new Karate Kid.Thank you so much to the entire cast! There are too many characters and various plot lines that all feel rushed. There are good parts here that were enjoyable, though. It kind of felt like they had two screenplays and decided to mash them together. It's like they filmed 5 hours of a film and then ripped it apart to fit into a 1h 30-minute advertisement for Tekken, Pizza and Rooftop fighting.
