Well, it’s more of a wandering journey than a structured story. Things happen, characters interact, but there isn’t much tying it all together in a traditional sense. That’s expected from Tarantino, he’s more about moments than narratives. The slow-paced intro sets the tone, but it doesn’t really pick up in a way that makes you feel a sense of urgency.

The directing is classic Tarantino, with his trademark long conversations, sudden bursts of energy, and, of course, his obsession with feet. The cinematography nails the late '60s aesthetic, from the lighting to the vintage sets, making Hollywood feel alive in every frame. Camera work is bold, sometimes chaotic, but never dull. I've been watching this film since 1999 and i will be rewatching it hopefully for years to come. But in case i don't see you - good afternoon, good evening and good night! In the summer of ’98, the idea of an absolute nobody becoming a celebrity, living his whole average life under a camera’s eye, seemed a little far-out and scary. Flash forward thirty years and the one-two punch of social media and influencer culture has made this a dream occupation. Of course, the difference is Truman didn’t realize he was under constant surveillance, his emotions mined and manipulated for maximum dramatic effect, but otherwise the parallels are pretty shocking. The difference in perception is also rather telling. When Truman discovers the truth, appalled at the idea of what he’s been subject to, he panics and bolts. Society (both in the viewing audience and in their twisted cinematic mirror image) cheers his escape; the orchestra swells; the vibes are good. The little man is resisting a truth that’s been imposed by external forces. I wonder how many modern viewers smile and switch off the television, then reach for their phone and check their favorite livestream without registering the irony. Peter Weir’s direction really emphasizes the uncanny and off-putting aspects of Truman’s existence. The brow-furrowing moments that threaten to shatter the illusion, like the best buddy who expertly positions a beer label before making a toast. The hip checks and shoulder blocks that physically redirect a too-polite nice guy away from his heart’s desire and into the arms of the woman producers have already cast as his designated love interest. These little beats are crucial in deconstructing the lie. He might not think much of them at the time - that was a little weird but whatever - but once he’s been given a legitimate reason to doubt the fantasy, they all come flooding back in a rush. In that leading role, Jim Carrey first exudes a great cheeseball suburban white guy attitude, then visibly cracks and spirals into conspiracy-induced mania. Everyone watching at home knows he’s in the right, but we also recognize how impossible it must have felt to earnestly believe one thing and hear something different from everyone who’s ever meant anything to him on a personal level. That’s good philosophy fodder, a debate about the meeting point of free-will and social expectation. What are the limits of the cage we compose around ourselves? The Truman Show doesn’t delve too terribly deep into these weeds - this is a big-budget summer movie, after all - but it gives its audience enough to get dirty if they’re so inclined. Parts of his head are shown splitting open.Main characters are gunned down with no warning or fanfare, often taking minutes to die as they are often shot in the stomach and die of blood loss.A man's ankle is badly sprained and bloody, he could no longer walk and is shot by an officer.A man is knocked off an tank and has his legs crushed, this happens fairly quickly without much detail.A boy's legs are run over by a halftrack. You see the gore pour out of his legs as they are crushed. In the background of the next shot, you can see the two halves of his legs, completely bisected.A father is murdered in front of his family after being dragged from his home.A man shoots himself in the head after he shoots and kills another man. There are copious, graphic amounts of blood spatter and lots of langauge but intressting story good ending good start bit boring in the middle and dragged on but still How’s that for a descriptive title? Every year, fifty boys line up on a desolate stretch of highway and commence marching until only one remains. Slow down or stop for too long, you’re dead. Leave the path, you’re dead. Outlast the others, though, and you’ll score wealth beyond your wildest dreams. Riches and the fulfillment of a personal favor. No matter where they finish, then, these young adults’ lives will be forever altered. Despite the simplistic premise, The Long Walk’s execution is shaky. As these games have been running for quite some time now, the participants should have no illusions about what they’re in for. And yet, each has plans for his future, win or lose. One kid plans to write a tell-all book about the experience. Another says he’s here to make friends. Are they expecting a different set of rules? As the road extends, we catch little peeks at the faded American flag behind all the misery - quick flashbacks that float ideas of civil unrest and fascist thought police - but these are thin and dopey. Tough guys bully artists. Kids are sent into the meat grinder for some sort of vague national entertainment, then saluted for their naïveté. The ideas seem pertinent, especially in the modern political climate, but they don’t yield much to closer inspection. Along the same lines, I didn’t really connect with any of the characters, because each can be boiled down to one or two basic traits. Here’s the native kid with a grumpy attitude. Here’s the kid with a Walkman (even the main characters struggle to remember his name). This kid might be too young for the competition. This kid chews gum. The actors do a good job of conveying their youthful optimism, and the eventual thousand-yard-stare of their attrition, but when it comes to meaningful development, there’s not much to go around. Even the more substantial backstories just feel like they’re checking boxes on a registration sheet. Apparently recognizing this, the editor lathers on an extra helping of weepy, drawn-out, emotionally manipulative music to help us understand what we should be feeling. It’s unbelievably heavy handed, like an after-school special. By the time we hit the home stretch, and its ridiculous string of final eliminations (essentially a back-to-back-to-back set of “I don’t deserve this as much as you guys, so I’m giving up”), my patience had reached its limit. The Long Walk has some good ideas. It features some memorable performances, particularly from Mark Hamill, who hams it up in his best Hank Williams Jr., all hat and aviator glasses and goateed accent. It’s well-produced and evenly paced. But it doesn’t make for good cinema.

Adventure Fantasy Action Peter Jackson Martin Freeman Ian McKellen Richard Armitage James Nesbitt Ken Stott Sylvester McCoy Barry Humphries Dean O'Gorman Aidan Turner Graham McTavish Bilbo Baggins, a hobbit enjoying his quiet life, is swept into an epic quest by Gandalf the Grey and thirteen dwarves who seek to reclaim their mountain home from Smaug, the dragon. When it comes to rewatching Middle Earth grand adventure movies made by Peter Jackson, I usually see them in this order: First, the LOTR trilogy then the Hobbit Then this year, I broke my habit and wanted to watch them in their proper chronological order, which was Hobbit first then ****, after watching the Hobbit trilogy (for the nth time), I wanted to share my thoughts on it. Okay. I don't know where to start. But let's just say that I think for me and a lot of people, the first Hobbit movie was the best among the trilogy. I know Jackson shot and made them back-to-back as he did for LOTR. But I think visually, in terms of storytelling, An Unexpected Journey was the better of the three, but overall, I love all three, flaws and all. Why? Well, I guess you could say, the focus of the story is more or less on the story and has one storyline. Its cast and characters are not that many (14 or 13). And in the case of most franchise films, the first one sets the stage. Therefore, its job is rather easier than the second and third, which are mostly escalation and presenting a satisfying conclusion. And one thing I like to say on Jackson's directing and storytelling (other than making the scenes a visual feast) is that he knows how to keep the flow of the story. Even in the quieter parts where it's mostly dialog between the actors, I was never bored or taken out of it during my rewatches; I was completely engrossed in the adventure and in the world of Middle Earth. Okay. Why am I emphasizing this? Because in today's Hollywood, rare is the director that can deliver this kind of storytelling. Yes, I know how Hobbit movies are vastly inferior to the cinematic masterpiece of LOTR trilogy. but rewatching the hOBBIT trilogy 9 years after its release makes me realize how the quality of Hollywood movies have worsened and how the Hobbit trilogy, which was criticized a lot at the time, is by far much better than 99% of the movies that Hollywood has produced in the recent years.TLDR: An Unexpectant Journey is the best in the trilogy. Rating: 8/7/10 . If only the genre wasn’t dead for 15 years. People don’t like it and it’s a very fair assessment, especially comparing to LOTR. Back in 2012 people were really spoiled with the quality and didn’t know where the whole film industry is moving (down to the drain). Which isn't necessarily a bad thing - that's how the source material reads and there's plenty of room in the genre - but it seems to be internally conflicted about its own identity. Director Peter Jackson constantly stretches for more serious, grandiose moments, which in turn seem out of place and extraneous. For the most part, this sorta-prequel strikes the right chords and delivers a jolly, magical adventure that's plenty of fun to tag along with... even if it does grow long-winded in spots.

As an audio-visual showcase, The Hobbit never stumbles. From sweeping landscapes to stunning vistas, breathtaking architectural relics to disgusting subterranean creatures, it runs a vast gamut and never ceases to amaze. For that reason alone, it's worth a long glimpse.

The plot does seem overstuffed and more than a little long, but it does feel like there's enough material here to justify three films, which was my main concern going in. This latest entry to the LOTR mythos adds nice depth to the original trilogy, while wisely making no effort to directly compete with them. There are plot lines and character changes that feel completely out of place here (I.e. Thorin and Gandalf are nothing like their book counterparts). Also the excessive use of CGI above practical effects was an odd and sometimes controversial choice that cheapens the film’s quality. But I’d be lying if I said I don’t enjoy every minute of this film and come back to it all the time. Also Martin Freeman does such a good job as Bilbo, how did he not win an Oscar!? I am typically very fussy in regards to the movies, but I can't tell of one thing I didn't like - it's perfect in every way. It’s ok. The characters are there, and the story is good when it uses the source material. Visually, it’s bad. It’s strange to see something produced a decade after the LOTR series look so bad by comparison. Obviously if you think that this is a LOTR prequel series it is a product, but inevitably, far inferior. In the end it is none other than The Hobbit. Exactly, The Hobbit. Peter Jackson has defined his career as the fantasy-epic guy, but what makes him special is his robust cinematic ingenuity. He has a range of directorial skills, not just as a visionary or a special effects pioneer, but as a storyteller, actor’s coach, showman. His Hobbit is fittingly family-friendly, wonderfully full of charm and humor.

299.title: Get Out

299.rich_text:
Get Out Get Out Just because you're invited, doesn't mean you're welcome. Mystery Thriller Horror Jordan Peele Daniel Kaluuya Allison Williams Catherine Keener Bradley Whitford Caleb Landry Jones Marcus Henderson Betty Gabriel LaKeith Stanfield Stephen Root Lil Rel Howery Chris and his girlfriend Rose go upstate to visit her parents for the weekend. At first, Chris reads the family's overly accommodating behavior as nervous attempts to deal with their daughter's interracial relationship, but as the weekend progresses, a series of increasingly disturbing discoveries lead him to a truth that he never could have imagined. Der Film hat mir gefallen aber insgesamt habe ich ein bisschen höhere Erwartungen gehabt von dem Film als wie es ist. Get Out’s whole journey, through every tense conversation, A-plus punchline and shocking act of violence, feels totally earned. And the conclusion is worth each uncomfortable chuckle and moment of doubt. Ultimately Get Out can’t help but ask the question: How would all these white people feel if they could walk in a black person’s shoes for a day? And that’s something worth considering. Sometimes a movie gets under your skin without you really knowing why. Get Out starts off calm, almost ordinary, and then something begins to feel off. That unease grows until it turns into pure tension. Jordan Peele takes something as simple as meeting your partner’s parents and turns it into an elegant nightmare full of irony and fear.What’s really disturbing isn’t the jump scares, but that feeling of being trapped, powerless. It’s a kind of terror that works from the inside. Daniel Kaluuya is outstanding — you can see the fear, the rage, the confusion in his eyes. Allison Williams, on the other hand, is that perfect smile hiding something you don’t want to find out.Peele directs with scary precision. Every look, every pause, every silence has a hidden meaning. And when the truth finally comes out, you realize the real horror isn’t the plot twist — it’s the society he’s showing us: one that calls itself tolerant but still carries deep, buried **** Out mixes horror with sharp intelligence. It makes you laugh sometimes, then immediately wipes the smile off your face. Peele proves you can talk about uncomfortable truths without preaching — just by holding up a mirror. And what that mirror shows is anything but **** the end, it’s a story about fear, about control, about manipulation wrapped in kindness. A bold, personal debut that feels completely unique. Get Out doesn’t just scare you — it lingers. Get Out is often praised as a groundbreaking thriller, but for me it was one of the most frustrating viewing experiences in recent years. While Jordan Peele's concept is undeniably bold, the execution leaves a lot to be desired. The film moves at a sluggish pace; much of the first half feels padded with drawn-out conversations and repetitive foreshadowing. Instead of building genuine tension, it drags, making it difficult to stay engaged. The writing itself feels heavy-handed and one-dimensional. Virtually every white character is portrayed as suspicious, predatory, or outright evil, leaving no real nuance or complexity. Rather than exploring racism through layered characters and situations, the film paints in broad strokes that feel more like caricature than commentary. This lack of balance undercuts the credibility of the story and makes it feel more like a polemic than a thriller. Even the symbolism - such as the cotton-picking scene - feels on-the-nose rather than clever. The social commentary could have been powerful, but instead it often comes across as preachy and simplistic. The result is a movie that seems more interested in making a statement than telling a gripping or believable story. While Get Out has moments of style and a few effective suspense sequences, its slow pacing, weak writing, and one-sided portrayal of characters made it a disappointment for me. What could have been a sharp, thought-provoking psychological thriller ended up feeling heavy-handed, overhyped, and far less nuanced than its reputation suggests Extraordinarily detailed psychological work. You understand more seemingly normal lines have a larger meaning. The ideas that inspired this film are horrifying and Peele exploits that into a thriller that puts this idea into the light. The dynamics in this movie are incredible. It is truly eerie and terrifying, sending chills down my spine, and haunting my brain with its psychological horror tension. Yet, it is also pretty hilarious at times, seeing as the director, Jordan Peele, has a comedy background. This film is beautiful and horrifying, and is nearly perfect. This is still my favorite of all Jordan Peele movies. Everyone’s calling it a masterpiece — I was checking my watch.I get it, not everyone is going to connect with this film, and I know the core idea is **** the execution? Completely predictable from start to **** moment we meet the parents, it’s obvious who’s playing what role in the story, and from there… nothing surprises. Get Out is a rare psychological slow-burn that creeps under your skin before you even realise what’s happening. As someone who loves the genre, it’s easy to be biased — but Jordan Peele’s directorial debut earns every bit of the praise it’s received. Clean, clever, and quietly unnerving, the film uses colour, silence, and space with the precision of a seasoned filmmaker.

While its social commentary on racism, identity, and performative allyship may feel a bit on the nose depending on your context, it never feels forced. The “Sunken Place” isn’t just a concept — it’s a visual metaphor that lands hard. Peele’s world is eerie, calm, and quietly hostile, where the threat hides behind polite smiles and curated conversations.

Daniel Kaluuya delivers a restrained yet powerful performance, carrying the film with a grounded sense of unease. And while not every creepy performance feels like a standout, the slow unraveling of personalities around him — especially Georgina and Walter — keeps you tense. Every sudden shift, every offbeat line delivery adds to the dread.

What elevates Get Out is its payoff. It doesn’t settle for a surface-level escape — it burns the whole house down, literally and metaphorically. It’s the rare horror film where the message is as sharp as the scares, and both cut deep.

Sum up - A smart, slow-burning thriller that weaponizes politeness and silence — Get Out stays with you long after the credits roll. To quote Bill Burr: How many more of those 'White people are evil' movies are they going to make? 

Full of cliches, it becomes hard to watch quickly. "Get Out" is a tight, edge of your seat, sophisticated, dark comedy, superbly written, acted, and directed.  It is one of the top 10 films of the 21st century.  It's better the second time.

Star studded cast put forth memorable performances, great direction and smooth screenplay. The worst part was the beginning. For about half an hour I wasn't really entertained or impressed and I thought it wouldn't be that great, but it gradually changed and after about an hour I was completely engrossed in it. I wasn't bored for a moment after that and I was on tenterhooks waiting to see how it would all turn out. I was hooked and towards the end I started to enjoy it a little more. In short, I wasn't really into it at first, but the further it went on, the more I was intrigued and that by a lot more. For me, an amazing movie that I would recommend to fans of I would say maybe the detective genre because it's all about watching two sides and especially the main character's side as he moves on and then rooting for him, at least I did. 313.title: Her

metadata.tagline: A Spike Jonze love story.

313.rich_text:
Her Her A Spike Jonze love story. Romance Science Fiction Drama Spike Jonze Joaquin Phoenix Scarlett Johansson Lynn Adrianna Lisa Renee Pitts Gabe Gomez Chris Pratt Artt Butler May Lindstrom Rooney Mara Bill Hader In the not so distant future, Theodore, a lonely writer, purchases a newly developed operating system designed to meet the user's every need. To Theodore's surprise, a romantic relationship develops between him and his operating system. This unconventional love story blends science fiction and romance in a sweet tale that explores the nature of love and the ways that technology isolates and connects us all. I tried to like this movie, and I think Joaquin Phoenix is a great actor, but I just didn't enjoy it for one reason or another. Her is a film that celebrates the universality of love. Love is not just a biological fact, it is an experience that can be reproduced on any platform capable of having mental experiences, even an ever-evolving artificial intelligence. Love is polytropos, many-sided. AI, moreover, is inherently scalable and this is something the protagonist must reckon with, enjoying its advantages while suffering its consequences. An intelligence that expands increases its abilities, but with that comes a growing number of tasks it can attend to at once and a shifting perception of time and space. The thinkers of today and tomorrow will have to confront the challenge of reconciling AI’s expandability with human limitation. Watching this movie in 2025, it feels amazingly prophetic.  It's more relevant now than ever.  I think this might be the saddest movie I've ever seen.  Joaquin Phoenix's performance is breathtaking as he depicts this heart breakingly lonely man whose only connection is with an AI. Wait, straight heat by Spike Jonze. The film takes place in the near future and is the story of Theodore Twombly and his troubled approach to romantic loss as he explores new relationships amidst a more and more depraved society.I think this movie does and says a lot. The script is meant to make you feel, but so is the setting and the space in which each scene takes place. The whole point of the disassociated society is to really make the viewer feel uneasy and uncomfortable before the emotional manipulation and self-destructive tendencies even come into play. The script is one of the most well-written ones I have experienced in a long time. Also, Joaquin plays his role to a T, like a holy cow. As a viewer, the emotions are real and that is hard to create. I will say, that the provocative nature of the movie was more than I thought it needed, but, the emotions are intense so it makes sense. Excellent cinematography and the sound was beautiful and fit each scene perfectly. Future foggy LA was beautiful to look at, the performances were great. Thought the humor worked better than the more serious moments.

Shout out to the little blue video game guy, extremely funny and unexpected. Es como crearte una novia imaginaria que te ayuda a llenar el vacío y soledad que te deja una persona que amaste tanto tiempo y se va, porque todo se va y necesitas soltarlo, incluso alguien que no es tangible. En cuestión de la trama es una comedia/romance/ciencia ficción que suele ser predecible y toca temas muy abstractos y complejos que lo hace interesante. Hay personajes muy complejos con tantas emociones, muy idealista, visualmente es atractivo más no lo mejor y sientes una gran conexión psique con todo. Además el recurso de la carta como algo personal e intimo frente a la tecnológico es mágico.
El final es algo que puede romper tanto a alguien con un duelo, y se siente como un abrazo hasta el alma. From the Screenplay over the acting to the score, this movie is the one closest to absolute perfection I've ever seen.

There is nothing quite like it! Randomly bought it because it was on sale and went into it without any expectations since I have never even heard about this movie prior. Could not have turned out to be any better of a surprise jewel find. About a half-hour in, I started thinking, "A man wrote this." Then of course I found out it was Spike Jonze. (I'd gone into it without reading too much about it first, obviously.) We've all heard about "the male gaze." This was that, plus the voice equivalent, depending on which female we're talking about: so stereotypically breathy and/or giggly etc. The blind date with Olivia Wilde was especially grating. Here's a silly women if ever there was one, supposedly longing for a deep relationship yet perfectly willing to play "if you were an animal, which one would you be." Of course he says "tiger" and she sexily meows. Oh please. Soon after we've got the virtual phone sex. Once again, I don't understand the critical acclaim. Once again we've got underdeveloped characters in a "cool" premise. Who IS this Theodore, beyond a guy with a broken heart? How many times have we seen that? I'm a big Joaquin Phoenix fan, by the way. Put him in a well-written film and he'll make you care, big-time. Here it all rang hollow, and even he couldn't pull it off. That's saying a lot. Man and artificial intelligence. A film so sensationally predictive, set in a dystopian future but at the same time so real and close to our present. This film, seen in 2022, is even more relevant. In a world governed by technological innovations, this film ages like good wine. Spike Jonze's direction is simply fantastic, the cinematography of a dystopian Los Angeles is equally wonderful and then ... What should I say about Arcade Fire's soundtrack? Superb. Joaquin Phoenix acts at his best levels here and Scarlett Johansson is also good at giving voice to the operating system.
A film that speaks of loneliness, of the degeneration of social relations to which technological innovation will lead. All through the great direction of Spike Jonze. Granted, 'Her' is not for everybody, likewise with Spike Jonze films in general, people may find the slow pacing a turn off and the premise while unlike any other premise is weird and may be ridiculous for many.

However, this reviewer was one of those who loved 'Her', while acknowledging that it has imperfections. 'Her' did feel longer than it needed to be, which meant that the pacing did drag a bit in the second half and lost tightness, it could easily have been 20-25 minutes shorter.

The ending is also very predictable and easy to figure out early on. While the cast are exemplary, Kristin Wiig felt a little out of place in her role.

Flaws aside, while polarising and a love it/hate it film, 'Her' this reviewer found to be magical film-making. For example, 'Her' is a gorgeous-looking film with the cinematography, with a lot of use of extreme close up, some of the most beautiful of any film in recent years and maybe ever (and there are a lot of films with beautiful cinematography) and the scenery and colours positively eye-popping.

Also present are one of the best music scores personally ever heard (and music in film and television is very important to me to look out for, as a classically trained singer and cellist myself), it has such a wonderful dream-like hypnotic quality and complements the film's mood perfectly. As well as a beautifully crafted screenplay, with a deft balance of the hilarious, the poignant, the charming and the thoughtful. The story's pacing is deliberate, but this was necessary, making the most of the premise, the weirdness slightly alienated at first but turned out fascinating when stuck with and there is genuine emotional impact and a well-done message that doesn't feel too heavy-handed.

Jonze's direction is superbly adept, while the characters are interesting and apart from Wiig the performances are exemplary. Particularly good are Joaquin Phoenix, in a towering performance that is almost on the same level as his spell-binding performance in Paul Thomas Anderson's 'The Master', and Scarlett Johansson, who voices Samantha with sultry sexiness. Amy Adams and Rooney Mara are charming and affecting in sympathetic female roles.

In conclusion, will divide and has divided viewers and has its flaws (especially the length) but a magical piece of film-making. 9/10 Bethany Cox

315.title: The Incredibles

315.rich_text:
The Incredibles The Incredibles Super strength can’t carry everything. Action Adventure Animation Family Brad Bird Craig T. Nelson Holly Hunter Sarah Vowell Spencer Fox Jason Lee Samuel L. Jackson Elizabeth Peña Eli Fucile Maeve Andrews Brad Bird Bob Parr has given up his superhero days to log in time as an insurance adjuster and raise his three children with his formerly heroic wife in suburbia. But when he receives a mysterious assignment, it's time to get back into costume. Watching The Incredibles in 2025 is a masterclass in classic nostalgia. It’s wild to think this came out over 20 years ago because it still manages to out-write and out-pace about 90% of the live-action superhero movies that have flooded theaters since. Brad Bird didn’t just make a "kids' movie"; he made a midlife-crisis drama that happens to have capes, and that grounded reality is why it’s a timeless masterpiece.From the jazzy, 60s-inspired score to the retro-futuristic aesthetic of Syndrome’s island, the film drips with style. The pacing is relentless, the stakes feel surprisingly heavy (the "Kronos" scene is still chilling), and the family dynamic—especially the relatable bickering between Dash and Violet—feels more human than most actual human **** we have to talk about the animation. While the tech has obviously evolved, the character designs remain iconic. However, let’s be real: the animators had absolutely no business going that crazy with Elastigirl. Her design is highkey "IYKYK" territory, and it’s become a permanent part of the internet’s collective consciousness for a reason. They really sat in the studio and decided to give Helen Parr the most distracting silhouette in Pixar history, and honestly? **** movie is a perfect 10. It’s the definition of "they don't make 'em like this anymore." Whether you’re here for the sharp social commentary on mediocrity or you’re just a fan of the... specialized character design, The Incredibles remains the gold standard for animation. It’s pure, unadulterated nostalgia that holds up better than any of us could have hoped. This is my 2nd favorite Pixar movie, and it's an amazing one! Pixar makes the best movies of all time, and me calling it the 2nd best must win an award! (Oh wait, it did.) 10/10. The Incredibles is no doubt incredible.

A film that parodies the superhero genre and yet takes it more seriously than almost any superhero movie of the modern age.

The film follows the Parrs, a family of superheroes and the father Bob wishing the return to the glory days before superheroes were illegal, however he bites off more than he can chew.

This film's two major strong suits are its characters and its tone.

The characters in this movie are incredibly well written.

-Bob Parr (Mr. Incredible): A washed up superhero forced underground who longs to return to his glory days. When he gets to be a hero again he forgets what he can lose in the process. He is well meaning but not very forward thinking.

-Helen Parr (Elastagirl): Unlike her husband, she is able to try and enjoy her retirement as a superhero. She is the rock of the family keeping not only Bob but their children in check. When Bob is captured she springs into action. She is cautious and careful. 

-Syndrome: One of the most cunning Disney villains of all time. A wannabe sidekick ousted by his favorite hero who turns into a villain who exterminates heroes in an attempt to become one himself. 

The kids, Frozone, even Edna Mode, everyone has something to bring to this film. Even the Syndrome guards or the police during the fire scene have their moments. No character is wasted in this film.

The tone of this film is what leaves it so iconic.

As cartoonish and the characters can be, the film does not hide the darkness in their world. Syndrome exterminated most heroes, there are scenes including suicide and murder. The guards in this movie hunt the Parrs, they want to kill them including the children. Helen even has a speech where she explains to the kids the bad guys are not like the ones you see in cartoons. This world takes itself seriously. The color grading and music help elevate this to give a very specific style of cartoonish whimsy with a touch of reality.

The Incredibles also uses its cartoon style to give the superpowers a more normal look. A film in 2004 with a superhero using stretch powers would not hold up graphically in the current day but when the whole film is animated it helps keep it timeless.

In the end this is one of the greatest superhero films of all time, and easily surpasses most modern superhero films through its use of dark storytelling and incredibly written characters. Pride & Prejudice Pride & Prejudice Sometimes the last person on earth you want to be with is the one person you can't be without. Drama Romance Joe Wright Keira Knightley Matthew Macfadyen Brenda Blethyn Rosamund Pike Carey Mulligan Jena Malone Talulah Riley Donald Sutherland Simon Woods Judi Dench A story of love and life among the landed English gentry during the Georgian era. Mr. Bennet is a gentleman living in Hertfordshire with his overbearing wife and five daughters, but if he dies their house will be inherited by a distant cousin whom they have never met, so the family's future happiness and security is dependent on the daughters making good marriages. Pride & Prejudice là phim tình cảm chuyển thể từ tiểu thuyết Jane Austen, nổi bật với diễn xuất tinh tế và phong cách hiện đại. The book by the wonderful Jane Austen is definitely better than the film, dealing with the consequences of love, and the social differences of the late 18th century. The film is certainly handsome looking, with some truly beautiful locations and costumes, with a nice script and some excellent performances from Keira Knightly as Lizzie and in particular Judi Dench as Lady Catherine. Donald Sutherland (yeah, you saw right) was quite charming as Mr Bennett if you put his awkward accent aside. I liked Matthew MacFadyen as Mr Darcy, with his handsome looks and all that, but I will say I do prefer Colin Firth's interpretation from the sublime 1995 mini-series, Firth seemed to adopt a more likable and sympathetic approach to the character. I liked the way the film dealt with the period look and the social differences, and while there was a lot of the pride I would have liked to have seen a little more of the prejudice. If anything, the film could have done with being twenty minutes longer, as I felt there wasn't quite enough content from the book. Then again, it's been a long time since I read it, so I could be wrong. Overall, a beautiful film, not quite as good as the 1995 film Sense and Sensibility with Kate Winslet and Emma Thompson, but worth watching for the detail that obviously took a lot of effort to get right. 8.5/10 Bethany Cox. The plot is a bit simple and the dialogues sometimes hard to understand, but they fit into the aristocratic world. Jane Austin's adaption of one of her finest works has truly been done justice through spectacular performances and awe-inspired scenery. Powered by its dramatically, emotionally, and artistically grounded love story in the history of cinema. Pride and Prejudice crafts the greatest romance film of all time. With the exception of Tom Hollander's absurdly silly Mr. Collins, the characterization of every character is flawless. And with the exception of the overly-fluffy and stuffy period pieces first act, Joe Wright captured the spirit of Jane Austen's classic novel astonishingly: Austen's biting sarcastic, yet delicate humour runs through the vein of this film.

What I love the most about Jane Austen is that she has a strong control over her characters: she develops them throughout the novel so exquisitely, and she can change the reader's perception of them so gracefully. And of course that was my biggest concern about this film: I doubted that such thing can be done on screen convincingly. I daresay Moggach's screenplay managed to pay justice to the characters, and their development, in a way I've never thought it would be possible.

Besides the aforementioned nitpicks, I have some other quibbles: I think Lydia's elopement is a turning point in the story and the film should've laid stress on it more, and I think the same should have been applied to Mr. Darcy's "revealing" letters to Lizzy.

Other than that, I think this is an astonishing adaptation, and a one that truly benefits from being condensed - for I think the novel gets a bit monotonous at some point. All the actors and actresses are perfect for their roles: I would've never thought I would say that about Rosamund Pike having seen Gone Girl first, but she is perfect as the most innocent and persuasively ideal character, Jane Bennet. Keira Knightley delievered her best performance in her career by far, and I think out of all the roles she played, this is the only one that trully shows her talent.

I would recommend this movie. My first "real" romance, directed with courage. Even if it’s a clunky, third-rate cliché, it’s grand in my eyes.241211 (3.0)I thoroughly enjoyed this film, as it was packed with parodies and genuine respect for the craft. The story follows Colt Seavers, the stuntman for Tom Ryder, who had a budding romance with a crew member, Jody. After a serious injury, Colt vanished for a year and a half, working in valet parking, only to return for Jody’s directorial debut: a "Space Action" film that mirrors their own history. When the lead star, Tom, becomes corrupted and goes missing, Colt has to track him **** supporting cast is great, from producer Gail Meyer to Colt's true friend and stunt coordinator, Dan Tucker. The film-within-a-film features Aliana, who loved the "Space Cowboy," and Nigel—which definitely felt like a calculated nod. Tom’s girlfriend, action actress Iggy Starr, also adds to the mix. It turns out Tom is a drug addict who sabotaged Colt’s back out of jealousy for his rising fame. He even killed another stuntman, Henry, at a drug party, then went into hiding with Gail’s help to frame Colt. The early mention of CGI and facial scanning was a perfect setup for the deepfake twist used for the **** climax is a blast—"Makes work worth doing!" indeed. Tom attempts his first and last real stunt, while the crew collaborates to record his confession. Colt, who had been hesitant after his accident, successfully pulls off a massive car jump, and Dan Tucker’s stunt squad takes down Gail’s gangsters. Even in a life-or-death situation, the pathetic Tom Ryder can't follow through, whining, "It was my best stunt ever!" Jody eventually succeeds with her debut *Metalstorm*, starring Jason Momoa under a different studio. The credits featuring the real "Fall Guys" were a joy, and the cameo by Lee Majors—the original lead of *The Fall Guy* TV series—arresting Gail and sighing "Actors, tsk" after Tom’s explosive failure was a hilarious touch. A fun celebration of movie stunts and people that perform them that’s further elevated by the performances of, and chemistry between, Ryan Gosling and Emily Blunt. The Fall Guy (2024), directed by David Leitch and starring Ryan Gosling and Emily Blunt, is a modern reimagining of the 1980s TV series about a Hollywood stuntman who moonlights as a bounty hunter. With its combination of high-octane action, humor, and a dash of nostalgia, the film is an entertaining ride, but not without its shortcomings.Pros: Ryan Gosling's Charismatic Performance: Gosling brings his trademark charm to the role of Colt Seavers, blending humor with action-hero grit. His comedic timing, especially in the more absurd stunt sequences, is spot on, and his chemistry with co-star Emily Blunt adds a layer of warmth to the film.David Leitch's Action Choreography: Known for his work on John Wick and Deadpool 2, Leitch excels in crafting visually dynamic action scenes. The stunts are explosive and well-executed, with a mix of practical effects and CGI that stays true to the spirit of the original show while updating it for a modern audience.Nostalgic Appeal: Fans of the original series will appreciate the nods to the 1980s show, from the iconic theme song to some of the classic stunts that have been recreated with a modern twist. The film balances nostalgia with contemporary elements, making it appealing to both older fans and new viewers.Cons: Thin Plot: While the film is packed with thrilling action sequences, the storyline feels somewhat underdeveloped. The plot revolves around Seavers being pulled back into the world of bounty hunting to find a missing actor, but it lacks depth and originality, serving mostly as a backdrop for the action.Underused Supporting Cast: Despite a strong supporting cast, including Emily Blunt and Aaron Taylor-Johnson, their characters feel underutilized. Blunt, in particular, is given little to do beyond being the romantic interest and comedic foil to Gosling's Seavers. The movie could have benefited from more dynamic character development.Pacing Issues: The film starts strong, with a good balance of humor and action, but the second act drags slightly. Some scenes feel stretched out, while others are rushed, leading to uneven pacing that occasionally disrupts the flow of the story.Conclusion: The Fall Guy (2024) is an enjoyable action-comedy with standout performances from Ryan Gosling and fun, inventive stunt work. However, its thin plot and underdeveloped supporting characters prevent it from being a truly memorable film. For fans of the original series and those looking for an entertaining, action-packed movie, it's worth watching, but it might not leave a lasting impression. 7/10. Adventure Action Thriller Martin Campbell Daniel Craig Eva Green Mads Mikkelsen Judi Dench Jeffrey Wright Giancarlo Giannini Caterina Murino Simon Abkarian Isaach de Bankolé Jesper Christensen Le Chiffre, a banker to the world's terrorists, is scheduled to participate in a high-stakes poker game in Montenegro, where he intends to use his winnings to establish his financial grip on the terrorist market. Daniel Craig sets the new standard for a character that has been portrayed by many, but perhaps never with this degree of authenticity to the written character (he is supposed to be less suave and more of a hammer). A thrilling, sexy, muscular entertainment masterpiece. Casino Royale is clearly an important reset for Bond, and I get why a lot of people love it. Daniel Craig brings a colder, more grounded energy that works well, and the movie definitely feels more serious than the older entries. The action is solid, and the stakes feel higher than usual.That said, it never fully pulled me in. Some parts felt longer than they needed to be, and while the tone shift is interesting, it also made the movie feel a bit heavy at times. I respected it more than I enjoyed it. Still a good film overall, just not one I personally connected with as much. A fair 6/10 for me. Son çıkan "Bond" serisinin en iyi filmi bence. The parkour and Texas Hold'em scenes in particular already feel out-of-touch, with both fads in the rear-view mirror, but that's hardly a new hurdle for this franchise.

Daniel Craig makes for a far better Bond than I'd anticipated, especially during the nail-biting action scenes or prerequisite mingles with the high-cultured elite. He isn't the quip-slinging lady killer that Connery or Brosnan were, at least not yet, but he's twice as convincing when it's time to flex a little muscle (or leap from one precariously-perched construction crane to another, as it were).

This isn't a perfect effort - the poker climax is recklessly telegraphed, and the final forty minutes feel like a weepy, long-winded epilogue - but it is an invigorating action joyride, stuffed with clever winks and nods at the character's past, and certainly one of the best Bonds ever made. The only James Bond Movie you ever need to see.This movie takes all the best of the previous Bond movies and combines them to make one SUPER Bond movie that will never be outdone. Casino Royale is probably the best Bond movie all around (at least at the time of this review). It relies more on your emotional investment in a smaller cast of characters while telling an extremely grounded story not often seen in Bond films. More or less, it’s a Bond origin story. The only real problem is it’s pacing at points, which after a quite few watches myself, can just be overlooked as it’s not overly offensive. Acting is solid, though this is unfortunately the first and last movie Daniel Craig even tries as this character. Eva Green as Vesper is a standout performance. Judi Dench’s M is always a treat, though she puts a bit of a spin on the character as Bond is somewhat ‘green’. Mads Mikkelsen does well considering how little he has to work with. Soundtrack and sound design really got a boost for this outing compared to the Brosnan era and Chris Cornell’s Bond song is in my top favorites. Special effects are practical for the most part and they look excellent, though I fully acknowledge the stylized CGI opening is amazing. At nearly 2 and a half hours with pacing issues, the film will stumble, but you’ll never be looking at your watch and wanting it to end. As a matter of fact, fans will be rewatching this one for a long time to come. There’s no such thing as a perfect movie and that’s even more true for a Bond film, but Casino Royale is the factual best entry to date in the series brought on by the Bourne series threatening to steal its audience. Casino Royale recognized Bond needed to be brought into the modern age without sacrificing its source material and I definitely recommend it. 324.title: The Creator

metadata.tagline: This is a fight for our very existence.

324.rich_text:
The Creator The Creator This is a fight for our very existence. Science Fiction Action Adventure Gareth Edwards John David Washington Madeleine Yuna Voyles Gemma Chan Allison Janney Ken Watanabe Sturgill Simpson Amar Chadha-Patel Marc Menchaca Robbie Tann Ralph Ineson Amid a future war between the human race and the forces of artificial intelligence, a hardened ex-special forces agent grieving the disappearance of his wife, is recruited to hunt down and kill the Creator, the elusive architect of advanced AI who has developed a mysterious weapon with the power to end the war—and mankind itself. One of the best Star Wars movies I've seen.

Oh wait, it wasn't Star Wars? I might have been deceived by -the entire movie-

Interesting plot, middling character development, with our protagonist having "given up" early-on, and later developments. The plot somewhat redeems itself later-on with a halfway decent twist.

We have Star Wars ships, Star Wars blasters and apparently, Star Wars deaths. Maybe the director/producer should have just stuck with Star Wars. I'm not going to say I hate that - Disney's best attempt at contiuing the series has left some room for improvement. It's nice to see similar concepts applied elsewhere, and this movie is worth a watch, if anything for the production, and getting to see the artificial-intelligence equivalent of The Avatar (not the James Cameron version). One of the best sci-fi movies I’ve seen. Great story, great special effects. Acting good enough for the story. Clearly has a general metaphor for the arrogance and ignorance of a seemingly all powerful nation, pitted against an integrated society of human and AI. Visually stunning, the sets and CGI are amazing! Ultimately though I didn't care about the robots at all, and was left with a feeling of unfulfillment. The acting is decent enough, and the character development is ok, but at the end of the day they're just robot machines!  I'd watch it again though! Good scienc-fiction movie. It can be better but its hard after all the similar movies and stories soif you watch it don't look for something completly knew and enjoy it as it is. Some stunning visuals, but the story lacks depth. Yes, there are some emotional moments, but they would hold everywhere due to the performances itself, yet when you see the final scene of the movie you get a "and that's it? that solves nothing on the bigger scale".
The whole point of the conflict and reason for further escalation gets like two sentences. Should've gotten more. Lots of ideas just slapped during the movie to the viewer, without going further.
In the end this movie is less than it could've been. I imagine this could potentially get much better if it had something of a Snyder-cut. But at this moment is just a flashy, shallow and somewhat chaotic experience. Overall it was ok, just some parts fell through boring letting the overall vibe down a bit, but the end part again got exciting and interesting. Jaw-dropping special effects and an original science-fiction plot about the powers of Artificial Intelligence remind us what it means to be human. Joshua (John David Washington) and especially Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles) quickly become characters that we care about. We also quickly develop a heart for the people and robots of ‘New Asia’ as they fight a war against Americans. Gareth Edwards establishes real stakes with massive explosions and high death tolls. We have no trouble understanding this is a real war. The value for human life - emphasized by the lack thereof - is dwarfed by the hatred of A.I. It’s all quite… scary, how real this is or can be in our world.

The combination of original visual effects and real-world locations in Southeast Asia are visuals that are rare in American film. It’s exciting to see a new part of the world in a movie. The Creator heavily relies on VFX, but you don’t realize it. Everything created is so seamlessly integrated into the rest of the environment. 

My favorite element of this film is the typography. Title card and even the credits, but the film is also divided into four sections: The Creator, The Child, The Friend, and The Mother. At the beginning of each section, there is a new title card. The typeface is an excellent choice, strong presence in all caps, but sophisticated with classic serifs. Each instance is matched with this Southeast Asian language. I’m not sure which one exactly, or if it was created for the film, but it places you in that part of the world with those visual cues. It’s a perfect design choice for the film. The use of typography in film is so underrated!

The film’s visual effects and sound design go hand-in-hand. Every new piece of tech has to make a sound! Everything is textured and touchable. Edwards brings realism to the alternate future of The Creator, and each scene is believable. 

There are a few plot holes, but nothing too massive to disrupt the flow of the film. What keeps you engaged is Joshua’s character arc from selfish depression to sacrificial love. The themes of family, innocence, goodness, love, and even heaven are all presented through this story about a war between humans and robots. Sometimes, the robots are “more human than human”... a reminder that we cannot forget what makes us human. As a young actor and filmmaker movie was good. Story (even tho little confusing) was good. Plot was predictable (that's my subjective opinion). Cinematography and CGI were definitely the best part of the movie. On the other hand directing was bad. In one scene Joshua didn't had a hand and in second cut it appeard out of ****'s small mistake, but too big for 2x Oscars nominee movie. Actors are really good and believable. Only extras could been more coordinated. Soundtracks and music was matching with atmosphere on scene. For my final rating is well deserved 6 mostly cause of a lot of mistakes (in details also). I think it don't deserve higher rating than this. An interesting sci-fi movie. Great visuals, but the main story/plot could be more interesting. You should give this a try if you like sci-fi movies. The Creator is very simple and dull as nothing really excites me one bit as I felt it had mixtures of inspirational scenes.

325.title: Gladiator II

metadata.tagline: Prepare to be entertained.

325.rich_text:
Gladiator II Gladiator II Prepare to be entertained. Action Adventure Drama Ridley Scott Paul Mescal Denzel Washington Pedro Pascal Connie Nielsen Joseph Quinn Fred Hechinger Lior Raz Derek Jacobi Peter Mensah Matt Lucas Years after witnessing the death of the revered hero Maximus at the hands of his uncle, Lucius is forced to enter the Colosseum after his home is conquered by the tyrannical Emperors who now lead Rome with an iron fist. With rage in his heart and the future of the Empire at stake, Lucius must look to his past to find strength and honor to return the glory of Rome to its people. The film is perfectly in line with the first installment in terms of setting, tone, narrative style, and composition, making it a successful sequel that is in keeping with the saga and doesn't attempt to overhaul anything. The plot is enjoyable from start to finish, even if it's rather simple and at times banal, almost as if it's trying to avoid taking risks, but it stops at the homework. It doesn't offer any great thrills, it doesn't add anything new, the story is quite similar to the previous installment, but it's a good diversion. This is a somewhat worthy successor to the original film; however, it falls a bit short. The main issue is that it tries to do too much, and in the end, it feels rushed and forced. Despite that, I had a lot of fun watching it. The casting is great, and so are the characters. It’s packed with action, and there are many different fight scenes. Something that stood out to me is that, after so many years since the original, the visual effects somehow feel cheaper. It should be the other way around. This film feels like a poor imitation of HBO's Rome, compressed into a single, illogical movie. Denzel Washington's performance, while strong, can't salvage the chaotic plot. Pretty much the same as Gladiator I. Of course nice story (even a bit complexer one), good fights, some good dialogues. But in in end most of that is already known from the first part, which by the way, have a (small) connection to the second part. Also the plot "lost son found - became the hero" like in star wars and so many other movies is a bit shabby. “Gladiador II” retoma a mitologia de Roma mais de duas décadas depois do original, centrando-se em Lucius (Paul Mescal), agora adulto, forçado a entrar na arena enquanto lida com a opressão dos novos detentores do poder. Ridley Scott entrega um épico de legado: visualmente impressionante, com sequências de ação grandiosas e momentos de intensidade emocional, mas que luta para atingir a mesma profundidade temática e ressonância moral do primeiro filme. Paul Mescal carrega o papel com uma mistura de raiva contida e vulnerabilidade, e Denzel Washington surge como um sopro de energia e carisma que eleva partes do filme. Pedro Pascal e Connie Nielsen acrescentam camadas, embora alguns personagens sofram por desenvolvimento desigual. O roteiro, por vezes, soa repetitivo ou excessivamente reverente ao original, fazendo da sequência mais uma “celebração” do que uma reinvenção; ainda assim, funciona como entretenimento épico com momentos memoráveis. Podríamos renombrar la película como Gladiator II: Tiburones en Roma. 
Aburrida a mas no poder, el protagonista mezcla acento británico con acento irlandés para un personaje africano con una actuación terrible como si estuviera en escuela de teatro.
Da la sensación de que el guión hubiera sido escrito por estadounidenses, en el peor sentido de la palabra. Historia y argumento superficial, vacío, aburrido, incongruente, sin respetar la historia original y que intenta suplir todas las carencias con CGI, tiburones y fuegos artificiales. Spoiler: no funciona “Gladiator II” arrives nearly two decades after the groundbreaking original, reigniting the saga of power, betrayal, and the quest for honor within the brutal arena of ancient Rome. As a sequel, it faces the colossal challenge of living up to its predecessor while carving out its own identity. The film adopts a more expansive narrative, featuring returning characters alongside newcomers who all add depth to the story’s intricate **** performances in "Gladiator II" are a standout feature, showcasing a rich tapestry of emotional depth that amplifies the film's dramatic stakes. The cast, bolstered by stellar performances from both established actors and rising stars, navigates the intricate relationships and moral dilemmas faced by their characters. The lead performance captures the essence of a man torn between revenge and redemption, adeptly conveying inner conflict with a nuanced portrayal. The emotional gravitas is palpable, drawing us viewers into the internal and external struggles of the characters. In comparison, the original "Gladiator" was marked by Russell Crowe’s iconic portrayal of Maximus, which combined stoicism with raw emotional power. While Crowe's performance remains unmatched, the sequel reflects a willingness to explore different facets of heroism and villainy, shedding light on the complexity of motives driving characters in a politically charged era. The contrast here lies in the sequel’s focus on ensemble performance, showcasing various emotional arcs, whereas the original was heavily centered on Maximus’s solitary journey. The film draws from a blend of historical events and creative liberties, weaving a narrative that resonates with contemporary themes while revisiting ancient Rome's brutal political landscape. The film sacrifices historical accuracy for the sake of drama, but we can appreciate the allegorical connections to modern-day issues like power dynamics and the fight for justice. In historical context, the film's setting features anachronistic elements that stir debate about its fidelity to ancient Roman culture. Unlike the original, which maintained a stronger adherence to historical figures and events, "Gladiator II" takes greater artistic freedoms. Nonetheless, the film's portrayal of gladiatorial combat and political intrigue is woven into a narrative that, while not strictly accurate, serves to provoke thought about the cyclical nature of power and vengeance. In my conclusion, "Gladiator II" emerges as a complex tapestry of performance, historical narrative, and thematic depth. The film's portrayal of gladiatorial combat and political intrigue is woven into a narrative that, while not strictly accurate, serves to provoke thought about the cyclical nature of power and vengeance. Its emotional core resonates with contemporary concerns about morality and justice. I recommend this film to mature audiences who seek cinematic graphic richness and a thought-provoking taste for morality in modern times. Awful pacing. Genuinely this movie could have been an hour shorter. Any scene with Ravi can be cut. CGI animals are not good and their behavior doesn’t make any sense. Acting was subpar. Film soundtrack was lack luster. Hanno’s character arch fell short. Overall disappointing. Gladiator II is entirely built of empty clichés. Take any theme you’ve ever heard about power, revenge, corruption, honor, and Gladiator II will have pages of dialogue trying to encapsulate it in a neat little line. The gladiator 2 was good. I wasn’t disappointed with the sequel. I really enjoyed the fighting scenes and the acting was great. Denzel did a great job minus the Roman accent. Nonetheless, phenomenal job by the cast. I would recommend this for a watch.

Grant Christopher Lee Michael Gough In a 19th-century European village, a young man about to be married is whisked away to the underworld and wed to a mysterious corpse bride, while his real bride waits bereft in the land of the living. Corpse Bride (2005)

Wonderful Love Story

 (11,950 –29 Sep 2025 – by Claudio Carvalho)

Victor Van Dort will marry Victoria Everglot in a wedding of interest of their families: his family believes that will climb to the aristocracy, while her family is completely bankrupt and expecting the wealth of the new-rich groom's family. Viktor and Victoria fall in love with each other in the first sight, but during their wedding rehearsal in the eve, Viktor messes up his vows and the priest asks him to practice. The shy and clumsy groom goes to the woods to recite his vows, and accidentally proposes to Emily, a Corpse Bride that was murdered before her marriage and is waiting for her true love. She claims that Viktor is her husband and brings him to the world of the dead. Viktor unsuccessfully tries to return to the arms of Victoria.  

What a wonderful love story "Corpse Bride" (2005) is! The fantastic Tim Burton presents a delightful animation, with romance, comedy, fantasy and musical using characters the slightly recalls "The Nightmare before Christmas" (!993), which is better, but in a totally different story. I am rewatching his filmography from 1988 on, and it is awesome, since all his movies are at least good. My Blog: ****/ Really weird movie timber and definitely has a corpse Bride somewhere in his house I like the creepiness to it define deserves the hype that it's got Don't know how My parents let me watch this when I was a little. Uma obra que sinceramente,se tornou uma das minhas favoritas,com uma ótima história, personagens que você se apega, atmosfera envolvente e que trás conforto para mim,se tornou um dos meus filmes favoritos e sempre que eu puder verei esse filme,lindo filme. This film wraps you in a moody, shadowy atmosphere that fits perfectly with Tim Burton’s signature style. The story is engaging, the characters are memorable, and the stop motion animation is stunning, especially with the fluid camera work that feels more impressive than many computer animated **** songs don’t leave much of an impression, and the overall runtime feels a bit too brief. Still, the charm, craft, and creativity shine through. You enjoyed it and would recommend it This is not my favourite Tim Burton movie by a long shot, but I did find myself enjoying it. The animation is absolutely amazing with the dark bold colours and inspired visual ideas. The music is good too, it adds very well to the atmosphere. The four songs are pretty decent, if nothing special. Remains of the Day was the one I liked best. The script is witty and deliciously dark in places, while the story is clever and fairly original, even if it drags slightly occasionally. The characters are wonderfully quirky and the voice work from the likes of Johnny Depp and Helena Bonham Carter is top notch. All in all, a beautifully crafted film, if not quite Burton's finest hour. 8/10 Bethany Cox A nearly forgotten stop motion movie. It is directed by Tim Burton, has its his style and tells a unique story. It is set in the Victorian era Britain and follows Victor Van Dort who comes from a nouveau rich family and has to deal with an arrange marriage with Victoria Everglot who is the daughter of an aristocratic family who lost a lot of their fortune / money. It is the standard arrangement that give one side wealth and the other side an upgrade in social standing. Luckily they fell in love with each other but a clumsy accident sets fantastic events in motion. I cant continue with more as it would be spoilers. It is an interesting story, with great ideas, full of fantasy and a lot of motives to enjoy and / or analyze. The title while fitting may be a bit misleading. The idea to use stop motion gives this a unique style. I did neither like nor hate it a first but it has grown on me since back then. Also it is a lot of work to create a movie this way. The time consumption is incredible and 1 day of work can only produce seconds of the movie. So I praise the efforts anyway as it is a lot of hard and dedicated work. Another strength are the voice actors. We got Johnny Depp as Victor Van Dort, Emily Watson as Victoria Everglot and Helena Bonhan Carter as Emily for the main cast. For the support we have Tracey Ullman, Richard E. Grant, Albert Finney and Johanna Lumley. All in all a great cast of voice actors. Then I must mention director Tim Burton who is famous for his unique movies. He does a really fine job here and I say this is one of his underappreciated movies. This is a fitting transition to the soundtrack. It is written by Danny Elfman and John August and full of good tracks. Overall I say this is a hidden gem. May not be of the highest order but still worth watching. Be warned a bit as some dislike Tim Burtons style. By far my favourite film since I was a child. If you had seen this film where you were a child I recommend you to do it again, maybe you'll understand it in another way. Its kinda hard when you truly understand what Emily has been trought (before and after meeting Victor). Just an amaizing film, music and animation. Timeless dark classic that breaks traditions only to create new ones. The voice cast is stellar with ampt comedic timing . The animation is top tier. В детстве смотрел, особо не понимал смысла. А сейчас пересмотрел и все стало понятно! Что мультик то не плохой, на 7 из 10. Corpse Bride was pretty good, not exactly something I would go back to today, but the animation was well done. I didn't really like the musical numbers that well though, but I do remember hating musical's as a kid so maybe I'm a little biased that way. 327.title: Stranger Than Fiction

metadata.tagline: Harold Crick isn't ready to go. Period.

327.rich_text:
Stranger Than Fiction Stranger Than Fiction Harold Crick isn't ready to go. Period. Drama Comedy Romance Fantasy Marc Forster Will Ferrell Maggie Gyllenhaal Dustin Hoffman Emma Thompson Queen Latifah Tony Hale Tom Hulce Linda Hunt Kristin Chenoweth John M. Watson Sr. Harold Crick is a lonely IRS agent whose mundane existence is transformed when he hears a mysterious voice narrating his life. A surprising movie. Knew nothing about it when I watched it, wanted more comedy, but it's an interesting movie. Kind of a weird movie, still ok. A woman is writing a novel, but Will Ferrell can hear everything she's writing about in his head. Also whatever the woman writes about him happens to him for real. Vacuous, boring, and morbid.
Although I don’t dislike Ferrell, absolutely every film he makes is awful and unfunny - yes, people seem unaware, but this film’s meant to be a comedy.
Ferrell is like the opposite of Jack Black, who seems very irritating and talentless, yet his films are often funny and good. This movie is very touching, and brilliantly thought out, with good laughs too, but not in the traditional Will Ferell fashion. One of my top 10 favorite movies of all time. Writer Karen Eiffel is suffering from writers block and starting to think she will never finish her latest novel. She only has to find a way to kill her main character, Harold Crick, but is unaware that Crick is actually real and that his life has started to be narrated by the author. Suddenly realising he is about to die Crick goes in search of the author in hope of changing her mind about killing him off.

Will Ferrell gives a subdued but humorous performance in the lead role; his reaction to hearing the narration for the first time is priceless. The movie itself is both heart-warming and intelligent as we see Crick going about his life in awkward fashion and the scenes with potential love interest Ana are a joy to watch.

The way in which the films finale mirrors the final chapters of Eiffel's novel is also cleverly done making Stranger Than Fiction a joy to watch from start to finish. A clever script and a good love story keep this one going. Its mildly funny at times. The soundtrack is great. I personally thought the ending was disappointing. This movie is great, which is why I'm so frustrated that the meta story, the novel, is such a terrible story. Anthropomorphizing the watch and assigning causal significance to it is a pretty cheap premise. This novelist being acclaimed in any way takes a suspension of disbelief that's much harder than accepting that a protagonist could hear the voice of the novelist who's writing about him, and suffer from the adventures which she devises for him.

That said, this movie one that I keep wanting to watch over and over again. Cute love story. Great cast. Pretty charming overall. Will Ferrell amuses in one of his best roles: a literary character who tries to change his final destiny. In the middle act the plot becomes weak and slow but recovers soon. Remarkable Hoffman and Thompson. An at times funny, but thoroughly sincere and authentic film. Starring Will Ferrell in a career-best performance, Stranger Than Fiction also features good performances from a stellar cast that includes Maggie Gyllenhaal, Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson, and Queen Latifah. Together, they help to bring to life a unique premise with a very non-unique core that explores the age old question, "What would you do if you knew you were about to die?" A very unique execution of this simple question, Stranger Than Fiction is an incredibly heartfelt film with a very human center that explores humanity and our greatest fear; death. With smart writing and good direction, Stranger Than Fiction quirkiness never gets out of hand and instead delivers on being a smart film that takes its characters seriously and though there is a certain lightness to the film, it can be incredibly dark as it explores death, fear, and the boundaries of our own world. Overall, Stranger Than Fiction is a clever film that showcases Will Ferrell's acting talent. A perplexing yet ultimately satisfying fantastical dramedy, featuring Will Ferrell's most deep and thoughtful, being his only real dramatic role. The script is what prevails; it is such a fresh and innovative and fun idea that I believed took years to develop, and came out beautifully.
