Everything about this is quite something but never very anything. Forgettable but enjoyable enough action fantasy. I did like the camerawork though; it had some cool moves and angles. They tried to be stylish and a bit noir. I don’t think that it worked. It’s like a below average Stigmata (1999). Greetings from Lithuania.
"Constantine" (2005) never got a sequel due to its lukewarm box office receive back in 2005. This film is entertaining and original enough that kept me mostly involved the few times i have seen it during years. Performances by all involved were uniformly good. There are a a lot of exposition scenes here as they were setting this world, and there is a lot to understand here. Directing by Francis Lawrence was solid - this film does looks great as it has some good visuals, and set design was also good. There isn't much action here, and third act of this movie is a bit uneven and was starting to drag. Overall, while being far from a great film, "Constantin" is original enough to keep one entertained for 1 h 50 min. It is uneven film in its pacing and third act wasn't very good at least for me, still this is a pretty good movie. Good, however not great. If you are bored with not much else to watch, this will definitely light up some memory cells (if you're old enough) and make you realize how much they tried to experiment with the formula for "super hero" type films. This was before the first Iron Man, and even before Superman Returns. Although Keanu's character is not a typical Avengers or Justice League costumed hero, they've tried to mash up Blade (1998) with some Matrix flavors, and then cook in some mystery/thriller elements. It is fun to watch a lot of those scenes that hold up fairly well, and then also fun to watch scenes that leave you wondering, "Did I actually enjoy this type of thing?" For example, in a "preparing to kill vampires" cliche scene, where Keanu puts the pieces together for a cross shaped shotgun / flamethrower combo (seriously, and it's made of gold), we get several minutes of exposition where the film maker's decided they needed to tell the audience what is going on instead of showing them. "What are you doing?" etc. In another cliche trope, it is great to know that as far back as 2005, bad writers were falling victim to the guilt of white mansplaining, and really needing the audience to feel it, too. So after the super powered Keanu tells the very human and vulnerable Rachel character to "stay in the car" and even gives her a super duper powered amulet that he says is a "get out of jail free card" to protect her from vampires, she of course becomes impatient, and decides to go and find him (he had already won his boss fight). She gets out of the car, defiantly says "Men!" and throws her ladies suit coat in the front seat- complete with somehow including the super duper powered amulet which also somehow came from around her neck to being thrown down with a button up front coat (not removed over the head in other words). Men! Always giving powered amulets and I'm not just staying in the car! A few minutes later both characters are in a hallway... more exposition to explain to the audience what is going on, and Keanu asks, "Wait. Where is the amulet?!" "Oh. I must have left it..." Cue the cliche "OMG" look on her face as she is about to be in trouble now. Again, for 2005, it is about a 7, so that's what rating I'll go with, although after many DC and Marvel and other super powered movies have been made since then, it would be about a 5.5 now. Still can't get over.... "Men!" as she defiantly decides not to wait in the car. Well, you can laugh at those scenes and enjoy Keanu's performance! Just good film. Interesting, well told story, good acting (Keanu Reeves, Djimon Hounsou, Tilda Swinton, Peter Stormare - they were just great!), high quality CGI (aged very well). Very high rewatch factor. As an on-again, off-again follower of the long-running comic book this film is based upon, I was all geared up to hate it mightily before it even spun up in the DVD player. With that said, it fares somewhat better than expected. It isn't a raging success story, but it's not a tragic insult to the rich, extensive source material either.

Keanu Reeves is a horrible choice for the lead, no doubt about that. Where the Constantine of print is a complex, witty, bitterly charismatic subculture hero, Keanu's interpretation is as nuanced as a bag of bricks. I don't know how much I can fault the actor for that - after all, he'd been playing dress-up with the same role for two decades by this point - but no matter where the blame lies, he lacks the unspoken authenticity the role needs to grow wings and fly.

Fortunately, that blow is softened by a dynamic introductory sequence that may as well have been ripped straight from the pages of the comic and a decent, if indulgent, primary storyline. With a full-blown war between heaven and hell in store, it would've been very easy to let this film's scope get carried away, but it wisely maintains a short focal range and that keeps everything grounded. Constantine won't be finding a home on anyone's top ten list, and it's not easy to look past Keanu being Keanu (with Shia freaking Labeouf crammed in as a throwaway sidekick), but the tone is right and the special effects work is an unbridled success.

Not nearly what it could've been, but also not what I feared it would become. I don’t know why, but I can watch this movie again and again and again. Whatever the criticism this is a 10/10 to me. Early 2000s superhero movies have a certain charm to them that allow even mediocre movies to be very memorable.  Constantine rises above a lot of 2000s superhero movies by having a very good cast of actors and a very engaging script for them to play with.  This being my first introduction to the character definitely makes me more excited to see more of him. Not more at least. The city is good journey. The segment show about prerequire before be good as it should be. And then come Islam for freeing the good deeds Decent movie. Has some pretty crazy possessions going on. The movie does tend to drag on a lot though. Hard to keep interested till the end. ironically this is the best dc movie and the most underrated modern classic to date its ironic best dc express no interest to the reimagining of Constantine that's still infinitely better than the failure of DCEU since its inception in 2013. u would think warner bros would be smart enough to green lit the sequel for a future crossover with this universe into their garbage dceu universe for a possible live action justice league dark movie. according to keanu reeves at Constantine: 15th Anniversary Reunion | Comic-Con@Home 2020 they discussed the ideas of the sequel and they never followed through and had no interest on continuing it. so for me keanu reeves is my favorite version of Constantine and he was the one who even introduced me to this character

329.title: Warfare

metadata.tagline: Everything is based on memory.

329.rich_text:
Warfare Warfare Everything is based on memory. War Action Ray Mendoza, Alex Garland D'Pharaoh Woon-A-Tai Will Poulter Cosmo Jarvis Kit Connor Finn Bennett Taylor John Smith Michael Gandolfini Adain Bradley Noah Centineo Evan Holtzman A platoon of Navy SEALs embarks on a dangerous mission in Ramadi, Iraq, with the chaos and brotherhood of war retold through their memories of the event. A highly accurate portrayal of modern warfare that counters Hollywood depictions through its mundanity, humanity and suffering. Warfare is immersive, because of the incredible acting, sound design and effects.

The writing isn't too deep or too character-focused, but it absolutely works. I've seen many films that are based on true events, but never one that's 100% based on the memory of the survivors. It doesn't promote war, but everything is presented through a pretty objective **** directing is great, the tension is always high especially during the happier moments. The cinematography and the pacing are good too. The sound design and the visual effects carry this film though. Alongside the acting, they create immersion. The cast is great and as I said the acting performances feel incredibly real.

Warfare isn't among the best films of 2025, but it's a very special one for many reasons. This film is told in real time, as a platoon of Navy SEALs embarks on a mission in Iraq. It’s also based on a real event remembered by the men who were there. It begins with the logistical prep, as they get ready for an attack on their building. Even when the firestorm begins, the “action moments” are tempered by the methodical procedures they undergo, including constant communication with the base. Since almost all of this takes place in the same location, it’s not the typical war movie. It’s more about the processes and procedures they follow, even when some of them get severely injured. Alex Garland & Ray Mendoza are co-writer/directors and Garland’s “Civil War” was an equally potent conflict film, albeit fictional  (my review). The determination, discipline and brotherhood of these men pushes thru the continuous intensity and chaos to show the horrors of war on a more intimate level. BTW, there are images of the real soldiers that play during the credits. One of the best war movies I ever seen. The level of  realism are top notch. Feels like first movie that shown military are not as nice as seen. 2025 has been a pretty bad year for movies in general, but this was one of the better ones, if not the best movie of the year if you got to see it in theaters. The movie was very 'intense', very, very intense. Greetings from Lithuania.
"Warfare" (2025) is a war film that is as authentic as it gets. This is a very tense, brutal and totally down to earth account of a warfare conflict. This film like no other in recent years for me was a brutal reminder that wars are fought by real people. And that is what is film shows. Overall, "Warfare" is a highly authentic was film. It nearly literally takes viewer to a war situation. It superbly made and acted film. Just might be Alex Garlands best yet. I appreciate what it is trying to go for, but I think it struggles to get there. Despite the short runtime, there is a lot of padding in this movie. You could easily cut 15-20 minutes out of it without missing a beat. This drags down the pacing and makes it difficult to stay interested throughout the film. Хороший фильм. Дикаприо как всегда шикарен. Да есть некоторые странные моменты. А так фильм советую.   (Привечяние: смотрел в IMAX) Warfare is not a movie that idolizes war, and tries to be as unbiased as possible. Although, it is from the perspective of the American soldiers in the middle of the war in Afghanistan. There is really no music in this film, but the sound design is so incredible to really puts you into the middle of the skirmish of war these soldiers are on. It is visceral, intense, boring, brutal, eerie, and heartbreaking all at the same time. (Mauro Lanari) 
A semi-documentary and hyperrealist autobiopic, strangely directed by Garland and less surprisingly distributed by A24, a movie that's anything but "war horror" (Francesco Parrino) or "a shocking audiovisual experience" (Andrea Chimento). "Final judgment belongs to the body: you leave shaken, perhaps irritated, perhaps admired" (Marco Tedesco). Perhaps, above all, indifferent. Alternatively, you can always just turn on a news channel.

330.title: Mr. & Mrs. Smith

330.rich_text:
Mr. & Mrs. Smith Mr. & Mrs. Smith 'Til death do us part. Action Comedy Drama Thriller Doug Liman Brad Pitt Angelina Jolie Vince Vaughn Adam Brody Kerry Washington Keith David Chris Weitz Rachael Huntley Michelle Monaghan Stephanie March A husband and wife struggle to keep their marriage alive until they realize they are both secretly working as assassins. Now, their respective assignments require them to kill each other. Mr. & Mrs. Smith can only work for some people because of its leads.

It's pretty intriguing until it gets stupid and ridiculous and that point is relatively early in the film. The story is predictable and can't be taken seriously at all, not even as a comedy. The dialogues are mixed, the lines are often unnatural. The characters are simple, but the lead actors make them fun to watch.

The direction is weird. I love Doug Liman, but I think he couldn't decide whether to make this a comedy or a drama. Weirdly I enjoyed the drama elements more. The soundtrack felt so out of place. The cinematography and editing are mixed. The casting is perfect though. The leads make it work and they are supported by unexpectedly famous people. The Brangelina chemistry is unmatched and their looks aren't bad either, I'm sad how their real relationship turned out.

Mr. & Mrs. Smith is a fun watch if you want a movie star energy kind of film, but it doesn't offer anything else. Esta buena pero muy predecible el final. Si que me gusto el giro de que ambos se enfrenten a muerte. Basica, buena para ver a la **** de un sabado, pero hay mejores.
Muchos actores conocidos de los que uno esperaria mas, pero actuaron mjy bien Years before there was the manga-anime Spy X Family, there was this film about a pretend marriage of professional assassins. Apart from the titular couple, its appeal lies in the action sequences, which live up to expectations. For a weekend. Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie just seemed to be having great fun making this action comedy and that fun is certainly infectious. Une odieuse bouffonnerie qui ne dit pas son nom dans laquelle s’enlisent deux stars hollywoodiennes dont le talent n’est pas confirmé (et ne le sera sans doute jamais). 

Tout est surjoué et volontiers un peu trop débile sur les bords (et au milieu aussi). Le merdier est également filmé n’importe comment, rendant ainsi toute scène (improbable) d’action totalement illisible. 

Des stars qui font de la merde donc, avec un réalisateur qui fait de la merde. Rien de tellement étonnant en soi à dire vrai, c’est bien plus fréquent qu’on ne le pense et ces trois là en ont un rayon à leur actif. I rewatched this during a lazy afternoon and did Anyone notice Vince Vaughn wasn’t mentioned in the after credits? Remember how big of a deal this was back in the day. The movie was overall very disappointing. The leads are enjoyable but the last 45 minutes of this are in desperate need of a recognizable villain, just endless goon killing. ТАК НАХУЙ...я сука спустя день після їбаного просмотра цього калла вонючого, пишу свою рецензію.ФІльм така їбана хуйня це повний пездець, починаючи з самого начала.Хуйня обригана начинається з показу двух клоунів самих тупорили ролей,два їбаних агента не можуть блять догадатсья хто із них хто,це їбаний крінж,крінжово було з усього починаючи юмора,гра акторів,самої історії.Пред піт не витягує,Анжелку сіськи не показали,ЗА ШО ХВАЛИТЬ ФІЛЬМ НАХУЙ??? Fun action romance comedy. A bit to tonque in cheek at times. The dumb over the top finale didn't help. I enjoyed the journey more than the destination in this one for sure. Awesome movie, and lots of action. I love how they try to hide that their in the same occupation from each other. Until they both end going for the same person then things start to change.

332.title: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga

metadata.tagline: Fury is born.

332.rich_text:
Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga Fury is born. Action Science Fiction Adventure George Miller Anya Taylor-Joy Chris Hemsworth Tom Burke Alyla Browne George Shevtsov Lachy Hulme John Howard Angus Sampson Charlee Fraser Elsa Pataky As the world falls, young Furiosa is snatched from the Green Place of Many Mothers into the hands of a great biker horde led by the warlord Dementus. Sweeping through the wasteland, they encounter the citadel presided over by Immortan Joe. The two tyrants wage war for dominance, and Furiosa must survive many trials as she puts together the means to find her way home. Love this film. The story is wonderful, the acting is fabulous, the writing is witty and hilarious, and the sound/music is energizing and perfect.  The best thing for me is the picture quality and visuals. Gorgeous colours in the sandy deserts and contrasting blue skies.  This is the film to calibrate one’s TV if needed.  Only minus I believe is that half the film is focused on particularly young Furiosa, but rather perhaps should have had some screen time on telling some background about praetorian Jack and how he made his way, as he’s a key character. Otherwise, the film’s momentum never ceases and has such a joyful otherworldly vibe.  This is one of several films I’ve watched over and over, including T2 and Aliens. Amazing prequel to the Mad Max movie; Any-Taylor Joy plays furiosa incredibly well. The supporting cast are very well written and contain a large amount of dept 弗瑞奥萨的复仇之路，是尼采式“成为你自己”的暴力演绎：她切断手臂，如同切断被命运强加的身份，以残缺成就完满。影片拒绝悲情，将苦难锻造成权力意志——每一次轰鸣引擎，都是对“永恒轮回”的肯定：即使世界只剩尘土与血，人仍能在毁灭中创造新价值。反派狄门特斯则暴露末日后“上帝已死”的真空，他以狂欢填补意义匮乏，却沦为荒诞的祭品。老米勒用机油与火焰写就此篇反乌托邦寓言：当旧秩序崩解，人类终于直面最残酷的哲学命题——自由不是恩赐，而是必须不断重写的生存美学 Fui con bajas expectativas a cine; fue muy promocionada y por mas que intente no ver trailer, por todos lados había carteles y demasiada propaganda e imágenes por lo que personalmente el tono de los colores y la pantalla verde me parece que se notaban, además Anya Taylor-Joy no me parece creíble como furiosa tenía unos zapatos muy grandes que llenar; pero debo reconocer que salí del cine con una gran sonrisa, es efectivamente una historia sobre la venganza, es una película sobre la venganza y nada más, pero no se sale de su cauce, de por sí tiene un ritmo que en ningún momentos para igual que su predecesora, pero no se siente agotador al contrario, se siente una historia muy bien contada, con un ritmo rápido pero creíble, las actuaciones y el mundo tan desolador combinan perfectamente.  Chris Hemsworth como un villano anárquico le sale completamente natural, completamente desordenado y dominante sin ningún motivo pero completamente metido en su personaje con un carísima que se sale de la pantalla, Los otros personajes todos muy metidos en sus papeles, ninguno acuta mal, todos tienen muy claro su papel y más que eso la historia concuerda con la ficción que plantea este universo desértico, hay estrategia, hay giros completamente impredecibles, y te quitan la esperanza, no es una película definitivamente optimista, diría al contrario que es clara en su tesis: "de donde saliste???  del lugar de donde vienes solo te pudo haber sacado algo... el odio... una de las fuerzas más poderosas de la naturaleza", y se mantiene fiel a su planteamiento, no lo adorna, no le da miedo matar personajes sin tanta elocuencia,el desierto está para devorar a todos, y solo sobreviven los mas **** esperaba eso y me dieron una fuerte dosis de cruda ciencia ficción. De la que ya a las productoras les da pereza hacer y a la gente le disgusta ver, tal vez en el fondo saben que ese mundo no es tan distante del nuestro y esa película nos lo recuerda sin tapujos. Excelente por sus director y los actores que no tuvieron miedo en ser parte de una verdadera expresión artística en la pantalla grande. This was a great Mad Max movie. Mad props to the filmmakers and great job to all of the cast! I highly enjoyed this movie. I definitely will watch this again. Really surprised by the lack of violence in this movie.
To me watching a movie based on a wasteland kind of calls for some gore.
But the only thing remotely close to violence were some blood splatters on gunshots. Klar, das Setting ist wie in den ersten Teilen spitze. Die Wüste, die Stämme, die Fahrzeuge - alles cool. Jedoch machen die Kriege teilweise keinen Sinn, die Geschichte ist oft belanglos und im Grossen und Ganzen reine Repetition. Die Entscheidungen der Charaktere sind oft nicht nachvollziehbar. Und dazu viel zu fest in die Länge gezogen. I started without much hope and got hooked. I think that's one of the best things you can say about a commercial movie. Strong and convincing performances, a decent story not pushing too much for our suspension of desbelief. Overall a very entertaining popcorn movie that goes way beyond the usual standards on that type of genre. um filme desnecessário para franquia. Todo o investimento para esse filmes poderia ter sido para uma sequencia do estrada da fúria. Pretty good movie. Action scenes, dialogues and costumes are good. Feels like a typical Mad Max movie. Lead role actors did some good acting too. You should give it a try.

333.title: Jurassic World

metadata.tagline: The park is open.

333.rich_text:
Jurassic World Jurassic World The park is open. Action Adventure Science Fiction Thriller Colin Trevorrow Chris Pratt Bryce Dallas Howard Irrfan Khan Vincent D'Onofrio Ty Simpkins Nick Robinson Jake Johnson Omar Sy BD Wong Judy Greer Twenty-two years after the events of Jurassic Park, Isla Nublar now features a fully functioning dinosaur theme park, Jurassic World, as originally envisioned by John Hammond. Enjoyable film. The setting is a dinosaur park that is open and people visiting the attractions, where in the original Jurassic park it was never opened to the public because they weren't ready. In the new park we see what could happen if there ever was an accident when crowds of people were touring. Bryce Howard is a good choice for the park overseer. She is a professional on the job, and when her nephews come to the park and are in trouble, she shows true motherly instincts. Chris Pratt was perfect as the alpha dinosaur handler. He has good looks and a good personality. All the interactions with Chris Pratt and the raptors were intense. The best scene is the motorcycle chase scene in the jungle where the alpha male was hunting with his pack of raptors. Such ferocious and intense dinosaurs. This movie is awesome. I have been a Jurassic world super fan ever since like preschool and this is one of the best in the franchise. Just love the plot, the action, and especially the final battle. Awesome movie. So we didn't learn but we're going back to the island where all my dino-kid dreams came to life?!  I'm in!  Love this ride from start to finish.  It's nice to see it done well and give every note of respect to the original! Despite the failure of Jurassic Park 3, Spielberg remained eager to produce a fourth film, though the deaths of Stan Winston and Michael Crichton delayed the project for nearly fifteen years. When it finally emerged, Jurassic World managed to stand out: it delivered the long-awaited vision of a fully operating park while still bringing fresh ideas. The casting works—Chris Pratt proves an effective last-minute choice, and Omar Sy is a welcome presence. Flaws aside (yes, even the infamous high heels), the film is both thrilling and surprising, and with hindsight, it arguably comes close to surpassing the original. Of all the movies in this saga, this one ranks fifth for me, after Jurassic Park, The Lost World, JP III, and Jurassic World: Rebirth (2025). This movie was the one that started the catastrophe that all fans complain about nowadays, and that’s why Rebirth had to create an entirely new story after the first three Jurassic World films.When I saw this movie in 2015, I left the theater happy only because of the nostalgia, since I hadn’t gone to see anything from my favorite saga in theaters since 2001. But this movie has aged poorly; I can’t watch it religiously like the first three films or even the new Rebirth by Edwards. I don’t give it my approval, because this movie was the one that started all the problems we complain about today. overall, it’s a breath of fresh air for the saga...

i started the movie with zero expectations, but from the very first shot there’s a clear visual play that grabs attention immediately. the characteristic humor of the original trilogy is present from the start — something to appreciate — and lines like “...if something’s chasing you, run” stand out for their wit.

the introduction is well constructed: the dinosaurs are incorporated gradually, creating immersion without oversaturating too soon, like a “warm-up” for what’s to come. it also establishes from the beginning a direct connection to the trilogy.

the biggest issue is the recycled premise of reopening the park, a loop we already know. at least this time it’s acknowledged with a certain irony.

the characters are presented clearly; chris pratt provides the main charisma and there’s enough chemistry between them. performances are solid, though not particularly remarkable.

the direction is notable, linking scenes and dialogue fluidly and adapting the narrative rhythm to moments of tension or calm. however, the problem with opening so strongly is that when the pace slows in later scenes, there’s a risk of losing part of the audience’s attention.

technically, it’s a huge leap forward: more realistic dinosaurs and natural movements that achieve full immersion. there’s an interesting subtext about using nature as a weapon and the dilemma of risking life for work, though the film never abandons its family-friendly nature, avoiding explicit violence.

despite being predictable, the film holds interest — especially in its first half hour — and delivers a measured ending: coherent with the story and knowing exactly where to stop. there’s even room to play with secondary characters, like zara young (katie mcgrath), briefly breaking the usual protection of main characters.

overall, it’s a breath of fresh air for the saga: visually spectacular, aware of its flaws, and entertaining enough to stand on its own. personally, it may not surpass the first — an almost unbeatable, though not perfect, work — but i actually enjoyed this one even more. The definite selling out point of the Jurassic franchise. But also halfway to being the ideal sequel. Opens up the park to show an interesting juxtaposition between modern theme parks and dinosaurs. But more importantly, so even more innocent people can have their vacations ruined by the jaws of a dino.I spent years thinking The Lost World was better. Now I'm not sure. Orrivel as cenas de ação são patéticas com um potencial enorme mas jogado no lixo, isso é uma blasfêmia contra os outros filmes da franquia, depois desse filme nunca mais assisto um filme de jurassic world na minha vida Jurassic World came out in this weird mid 2010's era where studios were basically remaking old IP with soft reboots. (Force Awakens, anyone?) They would basically copy the original film but then update it with modern things. And for the most part, it does work here. 

After the someone disappointing third instalment, a new cast and crew are put on display with a bunch of new characters and a story that ties in nicely with the original. Again, it follows the JP3 trope of having one big bad dino villain and again there are some really dumb moments in this film, but for the most part it was nice to be back in this world. Possessing neither the industrial significance nor the inherent majesty of the Spielberg original, it was always going to be a tall order for this modern revival to stack up. Jurassic World is wise to do its own thing for the most part, though nudge-grin-wink references to the first film appear shamelessly (and, often, charmingly) around every corner. And while it's fun to point and smile at the familiar scraps of a 22-year-old film, at some point it feels like the new effort is too frightened of its own merits to cast them aside.

At root, this is a simple mindless summer disaster movie with the spice of CGI dinosaurs thrown in where the earthquakes/volcanoes/tidal waves would usually go. Measured against that standard, it's still an awfully dumb bucket of over-familiar plot churn, but it feels more understandable and appropriate.

Long gone are the delicate ruminations on nature, humanity and our impending role as technological gods, tossed away in favor of more sizzle and fresh dino gimmicks. For all the trailer's promises that the new big bad is meaner, faster and - most importantly - smarter, it really doesn't seem to do all that much beyond stomping around the park and killing everything in sight. The new cast, helmed by Chris Pratt and Bryce Dallas Howard (who, impressively, manages to dash through jungle and mountain in a pair of stylish heels), doesn't seem much brighter.

A fair enough way to kill a couple hours at the cinema, but be prepared for a healthy dose of eyeball-rolls and manufactured drama.

334.title: Mulan

metadata.tagline: The flower that blooms in adversity is the most rare and beautiful of all.

334.rich_text:
Mulan Mulan The flower that blooms in adversity is the most rare and beautiful of all. Animation Family Adventure Tony Bancroft, Barry Cook Ming-Na Wen Eddie Murphy BD Wong Miguel Ferrer Harvey Fierstein Freda Foh Shen June Foray James Hong Miriam Margolyes Pat Morita When Imperial China calls one man from every family to defend the empire from invading Huns, a young woman disguises herself as a soldier to take her ailing father’s place. Facing ruthless invaders, brutal training, and the risk of execution if discovered, she must decide who she truly is— and what she’s willing to fight for. The resonant echoes of a hidden reflection: A 5.0-star "visceral" awakening of identity.1999 (5.0)Watching "Mulan" in 1999 was a "sensational" turning point that defined my childhood relationship with cinema. Growing up as a fan of Disney, I was suddenly confronted with a character that offered a profound "revelation"—an Asian eldest daughter who felt the suffocating need to hide her true self just to survive. I was so "hororong" (captivated) by this narrative rhythm that I lost count of how many times I rewatched it. Even after seeing it multiple times, I would visit the video rental shop to borrow it again, keeping the tape for a week just to immerse myself in its "raw" emotional world. I vividly remember bringing a cassette player to the TV to record the songs, desperately trying to preserve that high-tension inspiration. Discovering the alternative version of "Reflection" by Lena Park (Park Jung-hyun) on my cousin’s album was another "visceral" shock that deepened my connection to the story. One of my favourite films of all time. One of the best Disney come backs of all time. The greatest Disney movie ever made, it not only inspired countless animation films to come, but it also perfected what Disney had been attempting to do in prior decades. No other animated movie has ever come close to surpassing it. The Lion King is one of those films that seems to hold mythical status in popular culture, but for me, it’s never quite reached the emotional or narrative heights that others claim it does. It’s beautifully animated, sure, and the voice work is solid. There’s clearly craftsmanship on display. But strip away the nostalgia, and what you’re left with is a fairly standard coming-of-age story, dressed up in talking animals and Shakespearean ****, the story borrows from Hamlet, but it never digs into those themes with any real depth. It’s clean, safe, and broadly appealing—by design. There’s nothing wrong with that, but it doesn’t leave much room for real emotional complexity. It flirts with darkness, then pulls back before things can get too heavy. It’s meant to be digestible for a mass audience, and it succeeds at that, but for some of us, it doesn’t linger after the credits ****, I do like Elton John’s music. “Can You Feel the Love Tonight” is a genuinely beautiful song—but let’s be honest, it barely makes it into the film itself. His best work is saved for the end credits, which feels like a missed opportunity. The rest of the soundtrack, while iconic, is more Disney spectacle than genuine emotional resonance.I get why people love The Lion King. It’s big, it’s polished, it’s dramatic. But for me, it’s always been more of a technical achievement than an emotional one. It’s good—but it’s not sacred. É um exemplo perfeito de como a animação pode ser usada para contar histórias profundas e universais, ressoando com crianças e **** clássico que merece todos os elogios que recebeu e que continuará sendo celebrado por gerações. Can you feel the love tonight? i surely can, but it's not just the love, it's the strength, the power, the raw emotion, the joy, the sorrow, the anger, and the sheer artistry that pours into every frame of this cinematic masterpiece, The Lion King is a timeless generational story that resonates deeply through its powerful storytelling, cleverly crafted characters, and beautifully written, unforgettable songs, It's a tale as simple as it is profound, weaving themes of loss, redemption, and the unbreakable circle of life, from Simba's heart-wrenching journey of self-discovery to Mufasa's guiding wisdom and Scar's cunning malevolence, every character is brought to life with such depth and vibrancy in just a short amount of time, these characters and their stories make a lasting impact, carving a place in the hearts of all who watch, The Lion King is more than just an animated movie, it's one of the greatest animated movie of all time, a roaring testament to the power of storytelling, Hakuma Matata. It's a very familiar story - basically Hamlet with singing animals - but the famous studio really makes it their own through charm, whimsey and simple, effective characterization. Musicals aren't usually my thing, though, and once or twice it felt like the tunes were being crammed into a scene when they really weren't necessary. Thor: The Dark World is a movie that loses it's focus by the end and there are stupid character decisions throughout, but I managed to enjoy it pretty much. Continuing the second phase of Marvel's cinematic onslaught, which started several months prior in Iron Man 3, Thor's encore solo performance is a markedly stronger, more focused effort than his first. Though Earth still factors into the mix, particularly in the clever, gripping climactic fight scene, there's no mistaking that this is Asgard's story and that clear emphasis, missing from the original, makes a big difference.

As a distinctly fantasy-laden epic, it also benefits from a fresh, authentic flavor that its stable-mates just can't match. There's more to see than smashed **** and flattened taxi cabs in Thor's world, and that brand of open possibility makes for a delightful experience.

As visual feasts go, this is at or near the top of the pile: it's gorgeous, innovative and generally unlike anything else in modern cinema, a stuffed bagful of sensory treats. The acting, too, has taken a big step up since our last walk over the rainbow bridge. Surprisingly, this time Natalie Portman comes across as a clunky third wheel: Chris Hemsworth and Tom Hiddleston provide The Dark World's real intrigue, hammering home Thor's complicated relationship with his conniving adopted brother, Loki.

"Jurassic World: Dominion" (2022) is not going to win any awards for screenplay, but actors might win for keeping their straight faces during its whole 2 h 15 min runtime. Throw action and suspense at me while there are dinosaurs around!  I'm game! The final chapter of the trilogy tries to wrap up all the storylines, but falls short in many areas. Pretty good movie, good plot, characters, soundtrack. Great addition Laura Dern, Jeff Goldblum and Sam Neill. The return of Sam Neill, Laura Dern, and Jeff Goldblum works well, even if it sometimes feels more like fan service than real character **** script plays it safe. Dust Bunny Dust Bunny Sometimes there really are monsters under your bed. Fantasy Action Thriller Bryan Fuller Mads Mikkelsen Sophie Sloan Sigourney Weaver David Dastmalchian Sheila Atim Caspar Phillipson Line Kruse Rebecca Henderson Nóra Trokán Narantsogt Tsogtsaikhan Ten-year-old Aurora asks her hitman neighbor to kill the monster under her bed that she claims ate her family. To protect her, he must battle an onslaught of assassins while accepting that some monsters are real. Dust Bunny lands somewhere in the realm of mild intrigue but never fully commits to its potential. In a landscape saturated with formulaic releases, the film at least attempts to carve out its own identity, even if the execution doesn’t always match the ambition. Sophie Solan delivers a commendable performance as Aurora, bringing a level of sincerity that occasionally elevates the material.That said, the film’s R rating feels largely unwarranted; with a more restrained approach, it could have easily functioned within a PG framework without sacrificing its core narrative. While it doesn’t quite leave a lasting impression, Dust Bunny serves as a passable, low-stakes watch—best suited for a casual viewing with family, provided there’s some parental discretion. What a wonderful movie!  Someone else mentioned it has a Roald Dahl feel to it and I wholeheartedly agree.

Not too often you are fully entertained by a show that handles; fantasy, comedy, drama, horror all wrapped around a cohesive story where you care about the main characters. 

Many threads in this that follow throughout the story - lines that are hilarious such as throughout Mads Milkensen's character (we are never given a name) continues to call the little girl "Erora" when her name is Aurora.  Never is a chance missed for this but what makes it work is Aurora is always immediately ready to correct him - as if expecting him to call her Erora... no question its a game they are playing.

We are given threads of Aurora's backstory as the show progresses and it comes together in a very satisfying way.  Likewise for Mads Milkensen's "Intriguing neighbor" who is a hitman whose humanity is awakened by Aurora... great relationship that just works.

Other than having to look at whatever it is was done to Sigourney Weaver's face - she is always good.

Just a great - entertaining and very very worthwhile watch! Amusing, both a whimsical, horror/comedy. Innovative and creative, with unusual elemnets in a very Wes Anderson setting and style. Amusing little film from Fuller is a change of pace for him, but still entertaining and well produced. Think of it as the Professional meets 'Alice in Wonderland' and you'll get what he is aiming at. Not really horror at all but closer to kids/YA fare; think Roald Dahl. For such a lean film, the plot was a little difficult to follow at times. But very enjoyable and has just the right amount of stylization to set the proceedings. This movie is a TRIP!!! Looking forward to whatver Bryan Fuller comes with next. The mesmerizing 3:1 aspect ratio was and absolute experience, as I happen to own an ultrawide monitor! Very interesting visuals and unconventional tone.
Think Terry Gilliams wide lens aesthetic and close-ups blended with Jean-Pierre Jeunet's brave color grading, and mix that with a touch (just a touch) of John Wick. "Dust Bunny" is a brilliant and lush kaleidoscope of color, bizarrely wonderful characters, and one giant killer bunny. Brian Fuller’s television career has spanned genres. He was the mastermind behind beloved shows like "Dead Like Me," "Pushing Daisies," "Heroes," and "Hannibal," and has finally made the leap to the silver screen with a genre-blending R-rated fantasy-horror-fairytale about a girl who hires a hitman to kill the monster under her bed, who’s eaten her parents. The hitman in question reunites Fuller with his Hannibal star, Mads Mikkelsen, and he rounds out the cast with newcomer Sophie Sloan as his would-be client, Aurora, and a stable of beloved icons and character actors, including Sigourney Weaver (Alien), David Dastmalchian (The Suicide Squad), Rebecca Ferguson (The Acolyte), and Sheila Atim (The Woman King).

The concept blends both a child’s worldview and adult themes, and that juxtaposition is part of what makes the film so special and so easily enjoyed across generations. Pair that with Fuller’s visual artistry, gobsmacking sets, and inventive action setpieces, and you have the makings of something we haven’t seen on screen in decades: a horror-fantasy film for children and adults alike, harkening back to their heyday in the 1980s when the likes of "Gremlins," "Return to Oz," and "Ghostbusters" thrived.

It’s Amélie meets The Professional, with a bit of Poltergeist thrown into the mix. “The nostalgia is massive,” agrees Dastmalchian, who stars as a rival (and scene-stealing) hitman in the film. “It reminds **** being transported to the worlds of the Lucases and the Spielbergs. But [it’s also] his own thing. You can't really quantify Bryan Fuller. You can't put him in a box, you can't say, oh, ‘he's the next this, or he's the heir apparent to that,’ because he's carved his own place, and he's done it diligently, consistently over many years, and now bringing it to the movies."

The film came from a very personal place for Fuller, who channeled his own challenges growing up into the character of Aurora, who may be unintentionally complicit in the fate that has befallen her parents—and with good reason. “I hope that people who might have had a tricky experience growing up will see themselves in Aurora in a way that they may not be able to articulate,” Fuller explains. Instead, she turns to help from a stranger who goes on to become her found family; again, something that Fuller pulled from his own lived experience. Bryan Fuller created the unique TV series “Pushing Daisies,” so his take on a thriller is also expectedly distinctive. He also created “Hannibal” so he’s comfortable in this genre. Sophie Sloan plays a girl who has a giant, lethal rabbit under her bed. She enlists the help of a hitman neighbor (Mads Mikkelsen) to help her eliminate it. This isn’t a typical horror film, as a matter of fact, it’s not one. It’s dark fantasy with a somber stylized look that's often beautiful. In some ways, it reminds me of Wes Anderson, in its formal approach and idiosyncratic flair. The extended dialogue scenes drag down the pace, but there are many scenes with no talking. Yes, there are some violent kills, but they're often off camera or so quickly staged that it's not horrofying. Ultimately, it’s a bit sweet and never scary. BTW, Sigourney Weaver seems to be enjoying her evil character. What a great movie. Nice and strange. Likable characters, a plot you can follow, fantastic set design, and some good, fun monster action. Skip the blockbuster you were gonna see, and see this instead.

However, even her star power can't fully elevate a film that struggles to find its **** film's premise, exploring the ethical implications of AI companions and the blurred lines between human and machine, holds promise. However, the narrative falls into predictable tropes, with the AI becoming self-aware and posing a threat to its human family. The plot lacks originality and fails to delve into the deeper philosophical questions it **** supporting cast delivers decent performances, but the characters are underdeveloped and lack depth. "Subservience" (Aug 2024, R, $250k w/w) Make no mistake, this is a showcase for Megan Fox who hasn't starred in a mainstream film since 2016's TMNT (- not that this is a mainstream film). VIOLENCE The stepsisters, not the leading lady, compete/bicker with each other, sometimes in a joking way (not directed to the lead Cinderella, although they do think she’s “mad” and a “half-wit”) to the point where they are threatening to “scratch your eyes out”, push each other into dangerous places, dash brains out. Brave Brave Change your fate. Animation Adventure Family Fantasy Brenda Chapman, Mark Andrews Kelly Macdonald Emma Thompson Billy Connolly Julie Walters Robbie Coltrane Kevin McKidd Craig Ferguson Peigi Barker Steve Purcell Patrick Doyle In the mystical Scottish Highlands, Merida is the princess of a kingdom ruled by King Fergus and Queen Elinor. An unruly daughter and an accomplished archer, Merida one day defies a sacred custom of the land and inadvertently brings turmoil to the kingdom. In an attempt to set things right, Merida seeks out an eccentric old Wise Woman and is granted an ill-fated wish. Also figuring into Merida's quest — and serving as comic relief — are the kingdom's three lords: the enormous Lord MacGuffin, the surly Lord Macintosh, and the disagreeable Lord Dingwall. Honestly, Brave is one of Pixar’s most blatantly feminist movies, and not in a subtle or balanced way. While it tries to sell itself as a story of freedom and independence, the film constantly undercuts male characters and portrays them as shallow, useless, or laughable.

Every single male in the movie is reduced to a stereotype:

King Fergus is portrayed as big, loving, but ultimately stupid.

The three lords’ sons, who are supposed to compete for Merida’s hand, are nothing but comedic props—dim-witted, awkward, and talentless.

Even Merida’s triplet brothers are mischievous thieves with no depth.

The only “serious” male presence is the bear, which represents violence and evil.

This all comes to a head in the archery scene. Merida enters the competition herself and effortlessly outperforms every single male suitor in their own skill, in front of the entire kingdom. The message is crystal clear: not only can she decide her own fate, but she’s also superior to every man around her. It’s not empowerment balanced with respect—it’s empowerment through belittling others.

The story also sends a problematic message: “If you have issues with your mother, just do something reckless and harmful, apologize later, and everything will magically work out in your favor.” The male characters don’t matter at all in this equation; they’re too dumb to even understand what’s happening.

As some IMDb reviewers pointed out (and I agree completely):

The film celebrates disobedience rather than responsibility.

It feels like two different stories clumsily taped together.

It reeks of feminist fantasy—modern ideals forced into a medieval Scottish setting, with no sense of historical or narrative consistency.

In the end, Brave isn’t just a coming-of-age Pixar film. It’s a heavy-handed feminist allegory that sacrifices character balance and coherent storytelling in favor of an agenda. Yoklukta izlemenizi tavsiye ederim. The great American melting pot story, reflected in a bustling metropolis of anthropomorphic elements. In a city already well-populated by walking, talking clouds, trees and puddles, a new race of simmering flames doesn’t immediately fit in. These new, fiery immigrants seek the same sense of belonging that their counterparts once claimed (and now celebrate) but their physical incompatibility makes them unwelcome; strangers in a strange land, they struggle to carve a niche without evaporating their neighbors and strive to convert an intrinsically dangerous land into a home. The first little family over the border had to fight for every inch, but they were able to make it work, establishing a homestead that grew into a cultural center for other such transplants. Now, a generation later, their daughter has grown into adulthood and seeks a broader perspective, against the wishes of her kindly, but prejudiced, aging father.

Even when their storytelling falls a little short, Pixar is great at making us feel the feels. Easy to let oneself go, to appreciate the world building, learn to love the cast and admire the one-of-a-kind art style. In those respects, Elemental is something to behold.

There’s something worth exploring in the story, too, a prodding of the American dream from the perspective of an ethnic group that wasn’t exactly welcomed by Lady Liberty. The imbalance of successful early immigrants who denied the same opportunities to later arrivals is a valid note, and one which fuels old man fire’s sense of distrust. They all continue their journey to get their gold back from the Dragon, Smaug. If I have to sum up my overall feelings on the second installment in the Hobbit trilogy, it would be: complicated. Since looking at the trilogy of movies that came out 10 years prior to the release of Hobbit movies, I've been a fan of them and the world and wanted to see how Jackson would tackle the Hobbit adaptation. And… here lies the complicated relationship I have with almost all adaptations of my beloved IPs (books and others). I can't claim to be a book purist (although I readily admit that 99% of the time, the book version of the story would be better in this case). I haven't even read the Hobbit books, but even then and watching the Desolation of Smaug for the first time, I knew Jackson took a lot of liberty with the source material and practically stretches the adaptation that should have been two movies into a trilogy. The blame is not completely on him though; by that time, the there were a lot of studio interference with the production of Hobbit and Warner Brothers actually wanted Jackson to make another trilogy like LOTR and included some creative decisions that in hindsight don’t seem all that good. But whatever the case, the result is added characters (Legolas) and invented characters that were never in the original story (Tauriel). Some of these changes I understand. After all, movie is a completely different format from the books and to properly tell a story and entertain the audience, some changes are necessary. But some decisions (such as a certain love triangle and forbidden romance), I think were unnecessary and didn't add much to the plot. And knowing some behind the scenes later, I found out that many of the decisions and inclusions were notes by the studio and their creative meddling in the film. But other than this, DOS is a well-crafted film, both visually and narratively. As expected of Jackson, his direction and storytelling at transitions smoothly from one thing to the other. And even in the quieter sections of the story, your attention is riveted to the screen. So despite its flaws, Desolation of Smaug was and is still a very enjoyable experience for me.

A lightweight fantasy trifle with an all-world effects budget and a seriously inflated sense of self-worth. There's a classic adventure formula stuffed snugly at the core of this letterbox behemoth, but it's so thoroughly entrenched in a world of fluff and fat that it can sometimes be difficult to keep in view.

A certain degree of self-indulgence for the sake of fan service and depth can be excused. In fact, The Hobbit's light moments of fancy are where it has the most fun, showing off the strange little touches and quirks that make Middle Earth the puzzling, appetizing realm it truly is. At some point it's time to cut to the chase, though, and like a drunken slacker on holiday, this picture often hasn't the willpower to heed that call. For a hundred-thirty minutes it lingers, drowning its audience with padding, and just as it's finally getting to the good stuff, we slam headfirst into a flat black wall entitled "to be continued."

The Desolation of Smaug has its strengths: the aforementioned visuals are a revelation, the cast is wildly varied and dazzlingly colorful, and the dragon at the center of it all is truly awe-inspiring, a sight well worth seeing. The weaknesses, however, are just as numerous: most of the action scenes are carried-away bits of unreal CGI madness, the plot is overloaded with cameos and redundant, over-acted nobodies, and the constant pacing issues are downright crippling.

359.title: Ghost in the Shell

359.rich_text:
Ghost in the Shell Ghost in the Shell There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost. Science Fiction Drama Action Rupert Sanders Scarlett Johansson Takeshi Kitano Pilou Asbæk Michael Pitt Chin Han Juliette Binoche Peter Ferdinando Rila Fukushima Daniel Henshall Yutaka Izumihara In the near future, Major is the first of her kind: a human saved from a terrible crash, then cyber-enhanced to be a perfect soldier devoted to stopping the world's most dangerous criminals. I think this is an absolutely fantastic science fiction movie that absolutely gets an undeservedly bad rep simply because it is "anime". This is similar to other great sci-fi books/movies in that it is really a philosophical work that explores what it means to be human, what constitutes consciousness, and what differentiates humans from machines. Deep dives into the nature of consciousness with a side platter of police action, gunplay and high-speed pursuit. At first glance, Ghost in the Shell may come off as stiff and impenetrable, but like the thematically-similar Blade Runner, it offers untold rewards to repeat viewers. The nature of our memories, how they define us, the dangers of nefarious interference upon them; these are some pretty heavy topics, and it should come as no surprise that they need some time to really sink in.

Reflective and immersive, the film spends a lot of time ruminating on the meaning of life, both in conversation and in the long, lingering glances of city still-life it indulges upon between bursts of action. In these scenes, Kenji Kawai's magnificent score really gets a chance to shine; haunting and alien, it's a strange beauty and a perfect pairing for the uneasy-in-your-own-skin themes explored by the film. The art direction is a similar brow-raiser, effectively bringing the residents and landscape of New Port City to life in a style that remains loyal to Masamune Shirow's original work while also carving out a bold, fresh identity of its own.

Sua combinação de humor, emoção e magia o torna uma obra-prima que merece ser revisitada repetidamente.Essa animação não apenas marcou a história do cinema, mas também conquistou um lugar especial no coração de todos que embarcaram no tapete mágico para explorar um "mundo ideal". Aladdin is certainly a diamond in the rough film as the storyline sends you through the cave of wonders with a beautiful vision and a lot of charismatic energy. Even more than The Lion King, this is everything I picture when I think about Disney’s early ‘90s renaissance. Following the lessons and experiences of The Little Mermaid and Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin finds each of the studio’s departments running at peak capacity. The artwork is picture-perfect, expertly exaggerated and densely detailed but also smooth and fluid in action. A catchy soundtrack suits the unique flavor of the Arabian culture; at once hearty, catchy and exotic without feeling manufactured or exploitative (neither of which were a given in Disney’s previous efforts). And, highlighted - but not always dominated - by a typically high-energy performance from Robin Williams, the voice acting is unanimously excellent. It’s an A+ production across the board, one with no weak points or hesitations.

What struck me in this viewing was the abundance of rich, vibrant colors. Whether setting a scene or enhancing a particularly important plot development, the palette does its job with aplomb. As a sun-drenched desert film, one would expect a flush of shimmering yellows and oranges, and those tones do appropriately dominate its many daylight scenes. At night, though, a deeper, cooler range settles in, to equally potent result. A set of overnight developments outside the Cave of Wonders are especially magical, due in large part to these color choices. That spooky, panther-themed cavern would’ve been gorgeous even without such a powerful set of blue and purple tints - a marvelous display of imagination - but the dense, confident color selections push it from just another cool movie visual into an unforgettable memory. Aladdin is well-stocked with such moments.

The plot is quintessential Disney, for all that entails. Light and effectively humorous, with a strong foil, a lovable lead and (a studio specialty) all manner of loud, colorful supporting players. That Aladdin himself is so pure and simple was a necessity. If his character had been any more complicated, his personal arc more involved than “get over yourself and tell the truth,” he’d have been lost in the wash. With Williams’s Genie running at roughly three punchlines per second, there’s just no room for that kind of competition. As it stands, even poor Gilbert Gottfried is outshined by Williams's light. Probably the first and last time he’s ever been the second-noisiest guy in a scene.

Thor: Love and Thunder can feel cheesy or too ridiculous, but I loved it. Fresh off saving the universe in the climax of that last Avengers movie (doesn't it seem like three lifetimes ago?), our mighty Thor is stricken by a heavy case of ennui. Granted, he's spent the past however-long running around the cosmos with his new friends in the Guardians of the Galaxy, righting wrongs and soaking up the adulation, so it's not like he's been completely inert. He just wonders if, maybe, there mightn't be more to life as a thunder god than cheap thrills and easy wins. That's where the villainous "God Butcher" Gorr comes into play. Having violently ended a great number of minor deities already, his vengeful blade now points squarely at New Asgard. Where, coincidentally, Thor's old flame Jane Foster has just taken up a form of godhood.

Following hot on the heels of 2017's Ragnarok, the '22 model brings the whole band back together again with a few additional boons. Stunning visual effects, epic fantasy landscapes, belly-quaking rock'n'roll tracks, an irreverent sense of humor (trademark of returning writer/director Taika Waititi) and a decidedly loose connection to the greater MCU... yeah, this wants to be a successor to Ragnarok, all right. Shame, then, that it's just a high-profile case study for the law of diminishing returns.

Without exception, every single component that so felt effortless and precise in the previous film is weaker and broader in Love and Thunder. Where the last entry was delightfully quirky and witty, this one feels forced and excessive. Where I was ready to stand up and cheer at the opening chords of Led Zeppelin's "Immigrant Song," the similarly climactic placement of "November Rain," either the third or fourth Guns n’ Roses tune on the soundtrack, made my eyes roll. The ambitious visuals have taken a step down, the cast has lost its edge, and the story, though excessively simple, still under-delivers. Christian Bale is completely wasted as Gorr, acting his heart out in portrayal of yet another villainous afterthought whose sporadic barks are far worse than his bite. Natalie Portman is awkward and flavorless as an ex-lover turned rival; Thor seems more upset about being ditched by his semi-sentient war hammer. Even MCU heavyweights Chris Pratt and Chris Hemsworth have had far better showings, mutually saddled by a bland script.

Love and Thunder has bits and pieces that work - a handful of laughs, a few visual nods to the source material - but those are light and fleeting enough to have fit into an ambitious short film. Everything else is either a well-intentioned whiff or a confirmed misfire. What in the world happened here? Gene gözlerimi doldurdu. ;) This is a timeless classic, the story of a hyper-gifted boy with avoidant attachment and unresolved traumas who meets his patron and an analyst who makes non-conventionality and authenticity his battle horses. The film teaches that being high-performing doesn’t make us superhuman, because humanity is a tremendously complex concept and it’s not just exceptional intelligence that can define its semantic scope. Potential is something given to those who never deem themselves worthy.

This is a highly relatable movie which deals with so many complex psychological methodologies of genius, the common human emotion, and the freedom of choice that binds will to grow.

Will really encompasses potential, the weight that is carried by every person on this planet, and shows that we are more than what meets the eye, if and only if we help each other to forgive, to love and be better, not just for our sakes, but for everyone else's.

9/10, this is almost perfect, if only we saw more of Will's consequences, but maybe that could be up to us to decide. Been so many years since I last saw this superb film. Robin Williams was a genius on screen. Listening to his words you believed his pain and perhaps it now takes on more poignancy given we know how that ended for him. The bar scene where Will confronts the arrogant Harvard students, Robin Williams describing the night he first met his wife are just two. A beautiful film and I now feel I need to rewatch Dead Poets Society as that’s been too long since I last saw that. Possibly my favourite film of all time. The levels of emotion in every character and brilliant quotable moments make for a truly heart wrenching, emotional experience Matt Damon and Ben Affleck broke out as overnight darlings with this challenging take on love, maturity, happiness and responsibility. While Affleck dwells in the background as his book-dumb/emotionally-intelligent blue collar pal, Damon tackles the tough focal role: Will Hunting, world-class math genius with a deeply troubled past. Will’s a confused kid, paralyzed by the choice between what he wants to do (fool around with his buddies, getting drunk and starting fights) and what he feels he must (use his gifts to make something of his life). He bristles when push comes to shove and he’s forced to make a decision, but an empathetic therapist pulls him back to reality, walks him through the haze and teaches him the important, worthwhile parts of being an adult.

When they finally hook up (roughly half an hour into the tailspin), Damon and Robin Williams brew intense magic as a turbulent doctor-patient combo. They trade hats repeatedly during a series of heavy conversations, pushing and challenging and even threatening one another en route to finally acknowledging their problems, both to themselves and to each other. These sessions are rich and powerful, both as an indirect route to healing and as the first steps of a charged friendship; entrancing enough that most of the scenes outside Williams’s little jam-packed office can feel like an extended waiting game. How long until we can get these two back together again? Damon’s tricky romance with Minnie Driver, a bright and attractive English girl who loves and accepts him, also emits sparks, but it’s the guys' relationship that fuels everything.

Good Will Hunting is a complex story about complex people, but it’s not smothering or sentimental. It knows when we need a break and it’s not afraid to take risks, showing the less-flattering side of many sympathetic characters in the name of honesty. Will’s no saint, nor is the professor who sponsors him or the psychologist who shows him the light. They’re each well-rounded individuals, with their own desires, hangups and shortcomings.  That’s an impressive feat for any film, but it’s incredible to see from first-time screenwriters. There’s such raw feeling and emotion to this script... no doubt, plenty of that was brought forward and enhanced by a very capable cast, but it’s not like the stars were improvising every line or setting their own stages.

Civil War (2024) is a bold and intense look at a near-future America torn apart by internal conflict. Directed by Alex Garland, the film blends political drama with dystopian science fiction, delivering a unique and chilling experience that stays with you long after the credits roll.Pros: Visually Striking: The film is a visual masterpiece. Garland's direction, combined with stunning cinematography, creates a bleak yet hauntingly beautiful world that mirrors the chaos of a nation divided. Every shot feels carefully crafted, pulling you deeper into the narrative.Strong Performances: The cast, led by Kirsten Dunst, brings an emotional weight to the story. Dunst's portrayal of a mother caught in the crossfire of civil unrest is particularly gripping. Her performance feels raw and authentic, adding a layer of humanity to the film's broader political themes.Relevant Themes: Civil War feels eerily timely, exploring themes of division, power, and resistance in a way that resonates with the current political climate. The film doesn't shy away from asking tough questions about morality, loyalty, and the cost of survival in a fractured society.Tense Atmosphere: The tension in Civil War is palpable from start to finish. Garland masterfully builds suspense, keeping you on edge as the characters navigate dangerous alliances and impossible choices. The sense of dread is constant, making it hard to look away.Cons: Pacing Issues: While the story is engaging, there are moments where the pacing slows down, particularly in the second act. Some scenes feel drawn out, which can make the middle of the film drag a bit before picking up again towards the climax.Complex Narrative: The film's plot can be a bit convoluted at times. Garland is known for creating layered stories, but Civil War occasionally risks losing the audience with its complex political dynamics and multiple character arcs. It demands close attention, which may not appeal to everyone.Conclusion: Civil War (2024) is a tense, visually stunning film that feels disturbingly relevant in today's world. Despite some pacing issues and a complex narrative, it's a thought-provoking and emotionally charged experience that delivers both on action and introspection. If you're a fan of dystopian thrillers with a political edge, this is definitely one to watch. 8/10. Alex Garland has always known how to make us uncomfortable, but Civil War takes that to another level. It’s not just a war film — it’s a sensory experience that shakes you from the very first frame. With a camera that seems to breathe alongside its characters, Garland turns every image into a warning, every silence into an echo of what could happen if hate and division finally consume us.Kirsten Dunst is outstanding as a war photographer — exhausted, lucid, and painfully aware — witnessing an America fractured beyond repair. Her eyes say everything Garland doesn’t need to explain: horror has no sides, and capturing it with a camera doesn’t make it any less devastating. The film avoids political speeches and opts instead for a raw neutrality that’s as fascinating as it is **** director delivers his most mature work yet — a perfect balance of tension, visual poetry, and brutal realism. Every sequence is shot with surgical precision, from urban shootouts to those still moments that seem to freeze time. There’s something hypnotic in the way Garland portrays destruction — without heroism, without comfort — just the certainty that humanity is always one step away from the abyss.Civil War is a journey into the heart of chaos, where journalism becomes the last moral refuge. Its slow rhythm and oppressive atmosphere might unsettle some, but that’s exactly its strength: it refuses to let you watch comfortably. Garland isn’t looking for answers — he’s reminding us that if we keep seeing each other as enemies, war will stop being ****’s cinema in its purest form — powerful, precise, and necessary. When it ends, it’s hard to speak. Not because there’s nothing to say, but because you’re still processing what you’ve just witnessed. Strange movie. The minimalist storytelling focuses on chaos, survival, and moral dilemmas rather than political exposition, allowing viewers to engage deeply with the emotional and societal repercussions of war. Stunning cinematography, subtle performances, and a visceral sound design heighten the tension. This thought-provoking, suspenseful film challenges viewers to confront the uncomfortable truths about conflict's effect on identity and community. Something that stood out to me almost immediately, and consistently throughout the film, was the impeccable sound design. Not only did it sound very crisp, there is an almost constant sound of reverberating gunfire and explosions. It was very immersive and definitely ramped up the tension during the film. The first film. "Reservoir Dogs" is Quentin Tarantino's debut film, which instantly became a cult classic. The plot revolves around a botched bank robbery and its consequences for a group of criminals, each with their own code and secrets. Tarantino masterfully uses non-linear narrative, allowing the viewer to gradually uncover the characters' personalities and motivations. The dialogue is witty and memorable, and the dark humor gives the film a unique charm. The musical accompaniment perfectly complements the atmosphere. "Reservoir Dogs" is not just a crime drama, but a profound study of betrayal and trust, leaving the viewer in suspense until the very end. Way back in 1992, this seedy, asymmetrical chatterbox of a thriller made an immediate impression, arguing that there’s a clear ethical divide between criminals and psychopaths and catapulting the career of first-time director Quentin Tarantino. Although many of the edges are rough and the production budget is thin (a sacrifice Tarantino was happy to make in exchange for creative control), the director’s voice is already fully realized and he pulls a number of powerful performances from his shockingly star-studded cast. Primary among these are Harvey Keitel as the guilt-ridden loyal soldier, Michael Madsen as his antithesis, a cold-blooded maniac, Tim Roth as the spark that ignites their fire and Steve Buscemi as the flabbergasted bystander who can’t believe it’s come to this. They’ve all got dirty hands, but their perspectives on the stickup business are worlds apart.

It’s easy to see this as a trial run for many of the ideas Tarantino would refine and revisit, two years later, in the much more potent, polished Pulp Fiction. The two share an affinity for dark humor, rich (if maybe a bit indulgent) dialogue, essentially seedy situations and fallible, humanized assassins, not to mention their mutually jumbled timelines. The thing is, Reservoir Dogs would be fascinating even without an all-timer as a follow-up. It’s morally challenging, wickedly entertaining, thoroughly unpredictable and completely unlike anything else that was on the scene in ’92. Too often, we toss around the label of “trailblazer,” but I can think of no better term for what QT was doing behind the lens in the early ‘90s. This guy was on the razor’s edge. Featuring an unforgettable cast of characters and a story with universal appeal, it's no wonder this film has become a modern classic.Pros: Lovable Main Character: Gru (voiced by Steve Carell) is one of the most memorable animated characters of the decade.                                                                                                  -CriticMovies This Illumination Entertainment production introduced us to Gru, the lovably despicable mastermind with a penchant for mischief. So, let's strap on our rocket boots and see if this film's charm outweighs its villainous tendencies.

Visual Aesthetics:
Let's start with the visuals. "Despicable Me" boasts a vibrant and colorful animation style, with a character design that's as distinctive as Gru's elongated nose. The world-building, from the sleek underground lair to the suburban neighborhood, is visually engaging. However, in the ever-evolving landscape of animation, "Despicable Me" doesn't quite stand out as a groundbreaking visual masterpiece. It's more like a well-animated playground that serves the film's comedic intentions.

Soundtrack:
Now, the soundtrack. Honestly, the musical score is forgettable at best. It's not terrible, but it doesn't add much to the film's identity. The soundtrack takes a backseat to the on-screen antics, and the absence of a standout musical theme leaves "Despicable Me" lacking the sonic resonance that often accompanies animated classics

Story and Characters
:Let's talk narrative and characters. "Despicable Me" follows Gru, voiced by the charismatic Steve Carell, as he plans to steal the moon to assert his villainous dominance. The film takes an interesting twist when Gru adopts three orphaned girls, the adorable trio of Margo, Edith, and Agnes. The juxtaposition of Gru's villainous ambitions with his unexpected role as a father figure creates a dynamic that's both amusing and heartwarming. The Minions, Gru's yellow, gibberish-speaking sidekicks, steal the show with their comedic antics and infectious charm.

Themes:
Now, the themes. "Despicable Me" touches on the redemptive power of love and the transformative impact of fatherhood. It's a familiar trope – the villain turned reluctant hero – but the film handles it with a light touch and a healthy dose of humor. The themes may not be groundbreaking, but they add depth to what could have been a one-dimensional narrative.

In the grand scheme of animated features, "Despicable Me" doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it does offer a fun, family-friendly ride. The film's charm lies in its humor, memorable characters, and the unexpected warmth that comes from Gru's journey from villainy to reluctant hero. It's a solid entry into the animated genre, even if it doesn't reach the emotional heights of some of its Pixar counterparts.

Don’t waste your time Snatch completely failed to engage me from start to finish, to the point where I did not even bother finishing it. What many consider peak Guy Ritchie feels to me like his style at its most irritating. The frantic editing, exaggerated characters, heavy reliance on accents, and constant stylistic showboating create an exhausting experience rather than an entertaining one. The characters feel like hollow stereotypes built around quirks instead of personalities, making it hard to care about anything that happens. Compared to The Gentlemen, which uses similar ideas with far more control, Snatch feels like an overindulgent version of the same approach, a case of style overwhelming substance. It plays like a director parodying himself, resulting in a film that is alienating, tiring, and thoroughly unenjoyable. Car en effet, sur l’échelle de pénibilité au visoinnage, le « Snatch » est très élevé !

Eh oui, c’est tellement débile et prétentieux, tellement à la masse ce truc là (Ritchie a ce point commun avec Tarantino, à savoir qu’il pète toujours plus haut que son cul) que ça ne fera rire (?!) que les bobos et les peigne-culs de chez Télérama et consorts (con-sorts, cons très bien assortis).

Alors qu’en vérité, ce ramassis de conneries ininterrompues peine à nous arracher le moindre sourire, à part des grimaces et des rictus d’ennui. On lève les yeux au plafond et on trouve le temps bien long, à croire que la bouse dure trois plombes entières !

Le film est aussi victime de ses clins d’oeil éculés et de son humour rosbif périmé, ce qui n’aide pas non plus, loin s’en faut, malgré une bonne distribution… mais les acteurs là-dedans en font des tonnes et des mégatonnes : cette comédie est tellement lourdingue qu’elle plie sous son propre poids et tombe dans la fosse à purin… (et ça lui va bien, pour une fois !). Certain films innately embody the spirit and flair of a particular point in time. In Snatch’s case, the essence of the late ’90s is laced into its DNA. From the groovy, thumping soundtrack to the flashy, in-your-face visual motifs, the grimy criminal subject matter to the extreme sports-inspired camerawork, it boasts an impressive collection of very specific, time-sensitive pop culture calling cards. Watching this now, almost a quarter-century later, is like cracking open a time capsule. Imagine Pulp Fiction as produced by MTV.

Motivated the ultimate MacGuffin, a diamond the size of a cueball, the plot follows a number of desperate London criminals as they conspire and connive to pull one over on their rivals and reap the riches. We’ve got high-profile mob bosses and blue collar boxing promoters, ex-KGB agents and common street thugs, each armed with their own peculiar bag of quirks and tics. Though most parties are unaware of the others, their paths constantly interlace and overlap, and the whole mess eventually falls together in a great dogpile during the final act’s frantic, crowded, hilarious payoff sequence.

Snatch is an essentially dark comedy, stuffed with all manner of eccentric lowlifes, violent surprises and grim, ironic punchlines. It is a Guy Ritchie / Matthew Vaughn joint, after all, and following hot on the heels of Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, their successful debut, it punches a number of the same buttons. Reuses many actors, too, with Jason Statham and Vinnie Jones the most recognizable of the bunch. It’s newcomer Brad Pitt who steals the show, though, in his spectacular turn as an unintelligible, tattooed, caravan-dwelling boxer. His whole community is a riot, in fact, a tight group of lawless drunkards who honor no self-appointed superiors. Their unpredictability is just the fuel this film needed to bump its fire from a small blaze into a lofty inferno. Is it dated? Sure. Is it still entertaining? Yeah, that too. Not content to watch the action from the sidelines, Lee and Carter form an unlikely partnership and investigate the case themselves. Rush Hour is one of my childhood favorite comedies. I remember watching this entire series so many times as a kid and could never get enough. In 2025, many of the jokes play off of racist tropes and may not click with a more modern audience. However, being a millennial, this movie is one of those movies that will always live on in glory and hilarity. Wasn't a great fan of the actual villains but other than that it was great. 7/10 Once again playing a kung-fu cop, Jackie Chan crosses the Pacific to tackle an international smuggling operation. Once settled in LA, he’s paired off with a bigmouth street detective (Chris Tucker), an arrangement the FBI hopes will keep both men out of their way while better-trusted agents tackle the bad guys. Chan and Tucker both prefer to work alone, at first going out of their way to ditch one another, but when a kidnapped young girl enters the crosshairs, they grudgingly agree to cooperate and are surprised to find a lot of personal common ground.

Most of Rush Hour looks and acts like one of Jackie’s Hong Kong classics. The formulaic plot, the papier-mache villains, the fight scene quotas... even a few familiar stunts and tricks are regurgitated from preceding Chan productions. It’s been polished on the way to American shores, with Tucker adding his own characteristic brand of comedic zest, but the lingering spirit remains, and it’s unmistakable. The two stars take some time to mesh, clumsily traipsing through some delicate racial material as they get to know each other, but once they hit their stride as a duo, they’re lights-out. There’s a real connection here, a functional chemistry that plays well despite the partial language barrier, and the marquee names aren’t above having a good time. Their verbal sparring over the lyrics to Edwin Starr’s anthemic “War (What is it Good For)” must’ve been half ad-libbed, but the smooth rapport makes it one of the film’s most memorable sequences. That’s the kind of thing you can get away with when expectations are low and talent is high, and it wasn’t as evident in the sequels.

As broad crossover comedies go, I’ve sat through much worse. Chan and Tucker’s sweet and sour act works well, especially once they find their balance, and there’s neither too much fluffy action nor too many shrill comic freak-outs. It’s a good mix; tight, fresh and rewarding, but probably didn’t merit another two features. The production design as I said is good and the locations are not what I would consider too cinematic, it still works nevertheless. And it being his first hit movie is evident when watching the movie too I think, but still a really great thriller. Prisoners is a gritty, incredibly well-acted, suspenseful, thought-provoking crime drama thriller.
