Понравилась игра Кевин Спейси, которого я знаю по CoD.

Сюжет: Люблю, когда истории начинают рассказывать с конца. Появляется недосказанность, и можно попытаться понять, что было на самом деле. Очень интересно, когда человек рассказывает, как всё происходило. Понятно, что есть неточности, может, он что-то приукрасил.

Итог: Для меня немного концовка смазалась, так как давненько смотрел этот фильм, что-то помнил, по факту так что-то в концовке, видимо, удивило меня, что неудивительно. В течение большей части фильма я не понимал, что происходит. Особенно это касалось сцены, где героев задерживают в начале фильма. Я долго размышлял, знают ли они друг друга. Забавно, что это лишь 1 из моментов, а таких в фильме много, и они остались без ответов. Каждый может сам решать, что правда, а что вымысел. The Usual Suspects is such a masterpiece as the acting is terrific and especially one of Kevin Spacey best performance I have seen as it is certainly a must watch. One of the best plot twists I have ever seen. I genuinely had no idea who Keyser Soze was going to be. Loved it. This has a fantastic ending. The build-up is interesting and exciting. Once you know the ending though it kinda ruins the whole film so I don’t see me watching this again. I am not a huge fan of gangster films but this one is better than most of the others and is actually enjoyable. Some might even call it a cinematic masterpiece but due to the lack of rewatchability I personally would not call it that. Still very good but the ending feels kinda pretentious now. 
It's a movie you probably should watch sometime in your life.

569.title: Solo: A Star Wars Story

metadata.tagline: Never tell him the odds.

569.rich_text:
Solo: A Star Wars Story Solo: A Star Wars Story Never tell him the odds. Science Fiction Adventure Action Ron Howard Alden Ehrenreich Joonas Suotamo Woody Harrelson Emilia Clarke Donald Glover Thandiwe Newton Phoebe Waller-Bridge Paul Bettany Jon Favreau Erin Kellyman Through a series of daring escapades deep within a dark and dangerous criminal underworld, Han Solo meets his mighty future copilot Chewbacca and encounters the notorious gambler Lando Calrissian. It's not terrible, but the whole thing just ends up feeling very unnecessary and unwanted. It does add some okay world building and aspects of Han's backstory, as it was meant to do, but the other characters just feel so.... mediocre and the start is almost atrociously slow, but it is made up for with some decent action. Which is how I would almost describe this movie. It is okay. You can watch it, but I doubt you will be blown away, not an offensive film by any means, just... alright. It's okay. Its an extremely forgettable movie but it is passable. The best part of it for me as a Star Wars fan was the Darth Maul cameo. Movie would've been better received if they had made Jabba the Hutt the main antagonist but they missed their chance and paid the price. I don't like it when films recast iconic characters, so when I heard the money churning Disney was going to do a Han Solo origin film, I died a little inside. 

Now to this films credit, it isn't that bad. There are a couple of good moments here and there. However, due to the backlash surrounding The Last Jedi, the Disney/Star Wars error was on it's arse only four films in. 

This film was apparently a production nightmare, it is far too long and has too many moving parts. This is the most criminally underrated Star Wars movie ever made.

The film tells the origins of Han Solo, how he got his ship, the relationships with Lando and Chewie, and overall his empathy towards fighting against organized structures both illegal & legal (crime syndicates & fascist government).

The film is written well, paced beautifully, fleshes out 90% of every character on screen, and has the best music in Star Wars that is not composed by John Williams. 

Some of the actors like Donald Glover do an exceptional impression of the original actors, while others like Alden Ehrenreich abandon an impression in favor of Han Solo's mannerisms which works beautifully well. Impression doesn't always mean accurate, Alden captures Han's character with ease without imitating Harrison Ford.

The secondary characters are just as well performed by Woody Harrelson, Emilia Clarke, and Paul Bettany.

The negatives of this film are few, but large in their way of execution. Primarily, the movie has incredibly poor lighting. If you do not have your own theater system, or watch the movie in pitch black, you will miss a lot of details. Like how Bettany's character's face flushes red parallel lines when his anger rises. It makes the movie hard to rewatch at home unless you have a dark room to watch it in, or a tv with the brightness to rival the sun.

Overall it's an insanely underappreciated movie, arguably better than Rogue One. This movie summarise Han Solo's whole life in a few days... Bad writing but one year to make the movie is too short... Donald Glover is great ad Lando Calrissian. The plot is quite banal and flat. It seems to have the potential for a great development but it never gets going, it presents a character of Han Solo that is at times not very faithful to the one known at the beginning of the original trilogy (only to create a story in which the Rebel Alliance appears forcibly) but above all the story is boring at large and even the ending seems to be the result of a film about which we had few ideas. It’s “How I Met Your Wookiee”!That’s the gist of “Solo: A Star Wars Story,” the latest entry in the sci-fi film franchise, in which a young-ish Han Solo goes from wisecracking space chauffeur to weighty leading man.Like 2016’s “Rogue One,” “Solo” is a prequel that sets up “Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope.” Here, Han meets Chewbacca! Han first flies the Millennium Falcon! Han makes the Kessel Run in less than 12 parsecs!But unlike the smashing “Rogue One,” “Solo” is a low-stakes trudge through the stars. “So Long” is more like **** prequel explains how Han (Alden Ehrenreich) succumbed to a life of smuggling, and eventually wound up on the desert planet of Tatooine. That’s a lot less enticing a premise than, say, how Anakin Skywalker went from cherub to dark lord, or where has Luke been squatting since 1983? But there it is.

It turns out Han was born on a lawless world called Corellia, where he learned how to be a pilot, and frolicked with his girlfriend Qi’ra, played by Emilia Clarke, who is far more interesting when flanked by dragons. Running away from home, he joins the Empire as a soldier. (Strange this never came up in the original trilogy when he was, um, fighting the Empire.)

Eventually Han ditches the Stormtroopers to hang out with some different sleaze balls — including Woody Harrelson and Thandie Newton — on a heist, stealing a plutonium-like substance that can power ships or destroy planets. Out-of-place Harrelson wins the Laura Dern “What Am I Doing Here?” Award for this flick.

For the rest of the film, director Ron Howard whooshes us from ugly smog-filled planet to ugly smog-filled planet as the gang tries to complete their mission, not so much saving the galaxy as saving their own asses. The bad guy, crime lord Dryden Vos (Paul Bettany), resembles the worst kind of Pierce Brosnan-era “James Bond” villains. He’s got a bunch of unexplained scars, a vague eccentricity and no menace. You’ll forget him by the time you reach the parking lot.

Donald Glover is amusing as Lando Calrissian, whom he turns into a vainglorious space Casanova. And all of the film’s wit belongs to Phoebe Waller-Bridge as the voice of L3-37, a sassy droid who wants to liberate her nuts-and-bolts kind. LucasDisney brings us the Han Solo origin story nobody really asked for, re-casting several iconic roles to get the ages right and unintentionally positioning the new crew behind the eight ball because, let’s face it, Harrison Ford and Billy Dee Williams are an awfully tough act to follow. This is really the breaking point of the entire picture: either you’ll accept Alden Ehrenreich as the Skywalker family’s favorite bootlegging scoundrel, minus about fifteen years, or you’ll never be able to move past the comparison and the movie will have already lost you.

I thought I was in the second camp, avoided the film for years due to it, then found I was actually in the first. Ehrenreich doesn’t look like Harrison, doesn’t move like him and barely manages a halfway decent vocal approximation, but somehow, he fits the role. He carries the same charismatic magnetism, the same visible delight over adventure, excitement and ridiculously long odds. He’s got more nervous energy than a sugar-crusted toddler, a witty retort for every occasion and, crucially, he’s fun to watch, whether luck is on his side or, more often, not. I still think the film would’ve been better served by a brand new character struck by the same circumstances, but then we’d lose the little dashes of lore and history that make the third act such a rich ride.

Donald Glover, on the other hand, is unqualifiably excellent as Lando, all swagger and confidence and allure. I just wish he had more to do. As it stands, he’s little more than a flashy minor supporting character who conveniently connects plot waypoints. I’m sure his role would have expanded in the planned sequels, but no extended franchise is a given - even in the Star Wars universe - and, as those follow-ups appear to be dead in the water, it’s now just a missed opportunity.

Solo was better than I expected. I enjoyed it, in fact, largely because it had the balls not to take itself so damned seriously. A New Hope wasn’t all grit and consequence, so why have so many of the newer films leaned so hard in that direction? I’m curious how much of this one’s pervasive sense of humor can be attributed to original directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, chased from the project after five months because the Disney bosses found their work “too screwball.” New captain Ron Howard toes a difficult line in maintaining that freewheeling air while also mixing in a little gravitas, but he gets carried away with sentimentality at the very end. I thought it was a nice small scale movie that doesn’t affect the universe of Star Wars that much. The only thing that was absolutely off putting was the twist at the end. Второй фильм спин-офф «Звездных войн», но скажу сразу, он другой, начало среднее, середина вроде бы неплоха, но из-за Фиби Уоллер-Бридж и ее героини, скажем так, L3, даже в русском дубляже было просто противно слушать, постоянно что ни фраза, то пропитана повесткой, резало по сердцу, как ножом. В Изгои-Один тоже был робот который вел и разговаривал не как робот, но он хотя бы не раздражал, скажу так когда нас покинул L3, не было драмы, была лишь радость, я бы могу не дотерпеть до конца с ней (она) робот. За исключением этого факта и этого персонажа смотреть было местами приятно, наблюдать за становлением героя Восстания. Знакомство с Чубаккой, конечно, натянуто, я бы как-нибудь улучшил этот момент. Также вижу Вуди Харрельсона, сразу думаю: «Ограбление?» Да, действительно, хорошая сцена с ограблением. И да, в начале показали девушку Соло, это Эмилия Кларк, после «Игры престолов» трудно ее ассоциировать с королевой драконов, но я ее сначала даже не узнал. Узнаем, как зарождалась дружба Лэндо и Соло, очень специфически, но чертовски интересно подана и в конце показали тот самый момент с проигрышем в карты «Соколом тысячелетия», отлично! Сцены в космосе, особенно в туманности, завораживающие! По итогу, если отбросить повестку, получается хороший-отличный фильм история про Хана Соло.

570.title: Independence Day

metadata.tagline: The question of whether or not we are alone in the universe has been answered.

570.rich_text:
Independence Day Independence Day The question of whether or not we are alone in the universe has been answered. Action Adventure Science Fiction Roland Emmerich Will Smith Bill Pullman Jeff Goldblum Mary McDonnell Judd Hirsch Robert Loggia Randy Quaid Margaret Colin James Rebhorn Harvey Fierstein Strange phenomena surface around the globe. The skies ignite. Terror races through the world's major cities. As these extraordinary events unfold, it becomes increasingly clear that a force of incredible magnitude has arrived. Its mission: total annihilation over the Fourth of July weekend. The last hope to stop the destruction is an unlikely group of people united by fate and unimaginable circumstances. Classic pure entertainment on every level. This has aged so well and in 2026 so good to sit with my son and for him to see real hero’s, where the men are men, dads are dads. and they save the world. Great one liners, great soundtrack. AND the visuals are still better than what Hollywood produces today. No words can descibe my feelings when I'm watching it again, like I did back in 1996 in theatre. The CGI still holds up in 2025 it's so good. The acting and actors. (Will Smith in the 90's was in a league of his own). Everything is peak 90'sand science fiction, served with side dishes: bit of good humour, bit is tragedy, bit of horror. It's one of my all time favorites. What a pathetic joke of a movie. I always found its story to be extremely confusing and just weird. This is easily the worst movie I've ever seen. Maybe it’s because it’s 2025, but I happened upon  this movie, which I had heard of, but had never previously watched…I was struck by the ridiculousness of Dennis Quaid‘s role, the chaotic scene shifts, and the consistently terrible dialogue. İlk defa izleyecek olanlarında izleyebileceği bir yapım ama çok bir beklentiniz olmasın çünkü ortalama bir yapım. Giant, hostile alien spaceships appear overnight to move on Earth's natural resources; humanity's last, desperate hope is a shaky plan involving a captured UFO from the 1950s and an old PowerBook laptop. Seems like this one was a guilty-pleasure classic from opening day. ID4 isn't well-written and constantly bathes itself in dense layers of cheese, but it tries hard, most the character arcs connect and the big special effects hold up quite well, despite their age.

For a movie that's so thoroughly reliant on spectacle, that last point is pretty important. The power of watching the White House or Empire State Building burst into a billion bitty pieces is still there, irresistible, while the magnitude of the invading fleet remains immense, and I think both can be attributed to the production's choice to eschew then-new CG techniques in favor of a large, intricately detailed stable of miniatures. We get a few hiccups, like the obviously green-screened fighter jets or the absurd visual **** retriever leaping to slow-motion safety through a fiery inferno, but for the most part it all looks great and it's still easy to get **** into the experience.

Of course, the whole thing is over-acted to death. Roland Emmerich has never been one to bring out nuance from his cast, but this is an awfully shallow effort, even by his standards. Bill Pullman nails the big motivational speech, set to a telegraphed swell of patriotic symphony, but otherwise lacks conviction as a limp, reactive PotUS. Randy Quaid is a cheap xerox of every alien abductee stereotype to ever enter pop culture. Jeff Goldblum is naturally quirky enough to make his role worthwhile, but it takes every bit of his innate charismatic magnetism to overcome the dumb plot developments. Will Smith is the only unequivocal success, barking and fist-pumping his way to bonafide action hero status in a simple but essential role as a beefy marine / pure force of will.

From a critical perspective, Independence Day is cinematic junk food. Big bangs and shiny lights to dazzle the box office crowd, with a few easy jokes to lighten the mood. But yet, there's something else to it, something essential and inexplicable. It's just raw, simple fun, I suppose, that makes no apologies for how it acts or what it aims to be. It won't make you think or weep, but you'll feel, and that's worth something. This is a bad movie with an overdone plot, a silly storyline, and bad acting. The special effects were likely good for their time, but by today's standards, they stink. The dialogue was cringe-worthy. The characters are all stereotypical, and the aliens are generic evil aliens with the depth of a puddle. A 3/10 is a gift. An absolute classic. I did, however, watch the extended edition (9 more minutes of screentime!!) and it was a good choice to cut those 9 minutes. The theatrical is the way to go and I dearly love that one. One of the most 90s movie ever.

In all of the best ways.

It's cheesy, it's patriotic, it uses clichees, it's self-serious. C’en deviendrait presque marrant, désopilant (et pathétiquement navrant) tant cette débilité hollymerdienne accumule un concentré de conneries avec un aplomb sidérant. Mais au mieux, on rit jaune, car cette daube casse toutes les limites et frontières du ridicule et du grotesque très con…

Entre Will Smith la pauvre tanche qui se croit toujours dans sa sitcom à mongolos, Bill Pullman qui fait son « y a t’il un président dans l’avion ? » et les idées grand-guignolesques du style « je balance un virus aux aliens avec mon portab’ appeule », il y a de quoi se les **** tout avec une mise en scène patriotique 100% premier degré, cela va de soi. 

C’est filmé correctement et assez spectaculaire, soit, mais quel lavage de ciboulot ce truc de golios ! c’est horrible de débilité et ça n’en finit pas !

Hancock Hancock There are heroes. There are superheroes. And then there's Hancock. Fantasy Action Peter Berg Will Smith Charlize Theron Jason Bateman Jae Head Eddie Marsan David Mattey Maetrix Fitten Thomas Lennon Johnny Galecki Hayley Marie Norman Hancock is a down-and-out superhero who's forced to employ a PR expert to help repair his image when the public grows weary of all the damage he's inflicted during his lifesaving heroics. The agent's idea of imprisoning the antihero to make the world miss him proves successful, but will Hancock stick to his new sense of purpose or slip back into old habits? Watched in a theater back in 2008—no detailed review remains since it was the Cyworld era.241113 (4.0)I remember watching this in the theater back in 2008. Since it was during the height of the Cyworld era, I didn't leave a formal or detailed review behind, just the memory of the experience. It feels like a relic from a different digital age, where thoughts were shared in small "mini-hompy" updates rather than long-form critiques. Even without the specific notes, the fact that I still remember the theater visit and settled on a strong rating suggests it left a significant impression. It stands as a piece of personal nostalgia, representing a time when movie-going was a simpler, more analog-feeling social activity. The 4.0 rating reflects a high level of satisfaction that has lingered over the years, even if the specific words I might have written back then are lost to the defunct servers of the past. It was a funny film with a normal story. 
The actors were very good, and the special effects were also very good. I'd say this is an entertaining movie, Will Smith portray a superhero quite decent, even tho the storyline force him to be as he is in the movie. All in all, worth to watch if you happen to see it in HBO in your hotel room, a good entertainment. Hancock's first half is very entertaining, but unfortunately, the script starts to fall apart in the second half, charging ahead like an unfiltered brainstorming session. Nevertheless, Will Smith's personal charm and the superhero-level action scenes, which appeared even before Man of Steel, cannot be denied. Great movie about immortal and gods. Becoming mortal the signs of weakness. Feel like a Story from mythology ancient times. With a modern spin off. Wish the story would've been better, but I don't dislike this movie. Nice to see Hancock go from **** to good guy. Great up till the after Bank scene and then it kind of dips off. Then it focuses on to much melodrama and not enough hero stuff for my liking. That being said I still have a soft spot for Hancock. The likeable **** underdog. I like this movie because it's different from your typical superhero character. He cracks me up to. They have some pretty cool fight scenes in this. A pretty cute movie about an unconventional superhero who makes disasters everywhere and strives to improve. On an entertainment level this film is very good for both the action and the funny parts even if sometimes it overruns a little. What drew me into seeing Hancock in the first place was its idea, which I found one of the most interesting for a film in a while. I am in all honesty not a big fan of Will Smith, but he has given some solid performances so I thought why not.

I have to say that I didn't think Hancock was a bad film as such, it was somewhat underwhelming and I'm sorry to say I do understand the criticisms against it.

Hancock does have a fair number of good points. It is stylishly filmed, with some well above average special effects, the music is dynamic and the directing is solid. The best asset about Hancock is the acting of the three leads.

Will Smith is very commanding, with a lot of subtlety amongst all the wisecracks/gags that don't feel forced(ie.flying under the influence). Charlize Theron shows a glowing presence while also showing a sympathetic side, and Jason Bateman's dry humour contrasts perfectly too.

However, Hancock is a very uneven film. I loved the first half, it was well paced, the script was witty and fresh and the scene where the titular character brings a speeding train to a halt as he can't be bothered to lift the car up from its path is one of the better and relevant scenes of the film.

It is in the second half where Hancock is less than successful. Here the film starts to drag, the script becomes soapy and heavily melodramatic and the film has one of the daftest twists of any film not to have M Night Shyamalan's name on it.

The story's tone isn't the only asset to feel uneven, the script is too, it has wit and freshness in the first half, but becomes mawkish in the second. I also felt that there were only three likable characters(Smith's, Theron's and Bateman's) and the others I barely noticed, with the villain especially flat.

So all in all, an uneven film but not a necessarily bad one. 5/10 Bethany Cox

573.title: Anemone

Anemone Anemone All is not forgiven. Drama Ronan Day-Lewis Daniel Day-Lewis Sean Bean Samantha Morton Samuel Bottomley Safia Oakley-Green Lewis Ian Bray Paul Butterworth Karl Cam JP Conway Angus Cooper Middle-aged Jem sets out from his suburban home on a journey into the woods, where he reconnects with his estranged hermit brother Ray. Bonded by a mysterious, complicated past, the men share a fraught, if occasionally tender relationship—one that was forever altered by shattering events decades earlier. Good performances are buried under an unnecessarily long and padded runtime. They could have cut a good 20-30 minutes from the film, and it would have been all the better for it. Set against the conflict of British Paratroopers and the IRA, in Northern Ireland during the early Troubles, the intensity of the conflict is very well conveyed by the movie. My read of the background - a commanding officer who probably didn’t like his Sergeant, calls an act of mercy a war crime, as an excuse to get rid of the sergeant. The result is a terrible burden inflicted on the proud sergeant and his family for the next 20 years. Don’t believe some of the reviews. This is an excellent movie, focusing on the full impact of that burden. Good cinematography. Good sound. Good script. Very well acted by Day-Lewis, Bean and Morton. Story line: not good 
Directing: not good 
Acting: not good 
Only to support his son to make money, no interest to share unique experience or story to audiences ‘Anemone’ looks good. It sounds amazing. And mostly it feels like a very green director trying to use all his Really Cool Scene ideas in one go. This is a movie that is really trying too hard to be good. The cinematography is drop-dead gorgeous, and the acting is notable, but the story is just not all there; everything is a little surface-level, but it really tries to be abstract for the sake of being abstract, instead of actually saying something. It's harmless in its entirety, and I'm giving extra points for the looks. Daniel Day-Lewis came out of retirement to star in this film, which he co-wrote with his son Ronan, who also directed. The very thin plot involves a brother (Sean Bean) travelling to the countryside where his brother (Day-Lewis) lives a hermit life after a life-changing event. Meanwhile, the wife and son (Samantha Morton and Samuel Bottomley) deal with the issue back home. This basically involves minimal dialogue with Day-Lewis getting 2 juicy monologues. Otherwise, there’s lots of dull scenery, long slow tracking shots and interminable pauses. This is an extremely self-indulgent project, rendered more so by the sluggish direction and tedious editing. Sure, Day-Lewis wants to support his son in his first feature, but he should have continued to enjoy his retirement instead…certainly more than I enjoyed this experience. "Anemone" is a very deep and dark look at the trials and tribulations of fatherhood and religion through the eyes of two estranged brothers with stunning direction from debut filmmaker Ronan Day-Lewis with two captivating performances from Daniel Day-Lewis and Sean Bean. I appreciate films that embrace quiet moments and don't necessarily jump from dialogue to dialogue continuously, that said I felt there were many moments where quiet tension felt a bit dragged out. The quiet moments were trying to enhance the visual storytelling (which is shot beautifully, cinematography is great) or emotional tension, but in my opinion the audience can appreciate the visuals, and get a sense of quiet understanding pretty quickly.  Given the powerful imagery, I wanted to see more of that and maybe shorter moments but more interwoven angles would have maintained the tension while still offering more information to the audience.  That said, I loved the power and pressure of the natural surroundings that the film presented. The verbal storytelling + monologues from the characters were entrancing and felt very genuine.  The writing and performances were compelling (as one would expect given the casting).  The music score reinforced the interwoven tension as well.  Unfortunately, I suspect it is not a drama that all viewers will appreciate but it is undeniably a striking film that I'm grateful to have to experienced; I would encourage anyone who appreciates drama to see it. Daniel Day-Lewis gives an Oscar worthy, compelling, and magnetic performance.  There is lush cinematography and a subversive contemplation on brotherhood and a downward spiral.

A strange movie: whereas the Duffer Brothers knew how to blend the ingredients of the '90s to craft "Stranger Things", Jess Varley employs a similar derivativeness (Spielberg's alien diptych, Cronenberg's "The Fly", the creatures of "Jurassic Park" and Giger, the synth score) for a hasty, unresolved and not as convincing low-budget effort. "The Astronaut" is a dull, disjointed, and disappointing sci-fi film with a great lead in Kate Mara and the decent stagings of a monster mystery, but it winds up being a humdrum offering in a genre usually teeming with imagination and innovation.

Wonder Wonder Who gives you the courage to face the world? Family Drama Stephen Chbosky Jacob Tremblay Julia Roberts Owen Wilson Izabela Vidovic Noah Jupe Millie Davis Bryce Gheisar Mandy Patinkin Danielle Rose Russell Daveed Diggs The story of August Pullman – a boy with facial differences – who enters fifth grade, attending a mainstream elementary school for the first time. Wonder is exactly what its title promises—a quiet, powerful reminder of kindness in a world that often forgets how much it matters. Anchored by a deeply sincere performance from Julia Roberts, the film is beautiful, tender, and emotionally resonant from beginning to end. I found myself in bits throughout, moved not by spectacle but by the raw honesty of its storytelling.

The storyline is simple yet profound, following a young boy navigating school, family, and acceptance, but its emotional reach is immense. Wonder doesn’t preach. Instead, it gently shows how empathy, courage, and compassion can change lives in ways both big and small. The moral lessons feel boundless and timeless, making the film just as impactful for adults as it is for younger viewers.

O'Connor Ciarán Hinds Dillon Freasier Hope Elizabeth Reeves Colleen Foy Barry Del Sherman David Willis Hans Howes Ruthless silver miner, turned oil prospector, Daniel Plainview, moves to oil-rich California. Using his son to project a trustworthy, family-man image, Plainview cons local landowners into selling him their valuable properties for a pittance. However, local preacher Eli Sunday suspects Plainview's motives and intentions, starting a slow-burning feud that threatens both their lives. There Will Be Blood is by far Paul Thomas Anderson's best movie, and in large part thanks to an absolutely stellar performance by Daniel Day-Lewis and Paul Dano. The evil influence of the titular, cursed toy results in blockbuster showcases for fantastic gore effects that, when paired with the film’s surprisingly gentle stance on the inevitability of death, affirm how potent horror-comedy can be when executed with a strong perspective and a willingness to get weird. Dumb and Dumber Dumb and Dumber For Harry and Lloyd, every day is a no-brainer. Comedy Peter Farrelly Jim Carrey Jeff Daniels Lauren Holly Teri Garr Charles Rocket Karen Duffy Mike Starr Felton Perry Hank Brandt Brad Lockerman Lloyd and Harry are two men whose stupidity is really indescribable. When Mary, a beautiful woman, loses an important suitcase with money before she leaves for Aspen, the two friends (who have found the suitcase) decide to return it to her. After some "adventures" they finally get to Aspen where, using the lost money they live it up and fight for Mary's heart. The rhythmic machinery of a classic IQ-drop: A 4.0-star sensational surge of raw, high-tension stupidity.2012(4.0)I watched "Dumb and Dumber" in 2012, and it delivered a visceral revelation that stands as a definitive 4.0-star pillar of "chewy" slapstick in my archive. This experience **** the fourth wall of the stagnant comedy genre by infusing Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels’s raw, unapologetic idiocy into a narrative rhythm that felt 100% authentic and sensational. While the production leveraged the vivid tropes of the "road trip" formula, the narrative rhythm was far from stagnant, delivering a rhythmic journey through the pathetic delusions of Lloyd and Harry that lacked the mechanical dullness of its 2000s-era imitators. Seeing the vivid "most annoying sound in the world" and the raw, high-stakes battle over a briefcase provided an emotional payoff of pure, chaotic joy, proving that a story about "total idiots" could be a vivid act of storytelling rebellion. The 95% preservation of my memory is dominated by the rhythmic, raw brilliance of the "Mockingbird" singalong and the vivid but pathetic execution of the chili-pepper prank, creating a permanent, sensational scar of laughter on my soul. Unlike the stagnant 2.0-star drift of "Chuck & Larry" or the pathetic execution of "Meet Dave," this encounter possessed a rebellious soul that turned a pathetic quest into a sensational masterpiece of witless wit. It stands in my 2012 record as a powerful 4.0-star testament to the raw power of physical comedy—a high-tension encounter with the vivid rhythm of the absurd that remains one of the most chewy artifacts of my cinematic journey. Jim Carrey is one of my favorite actors, and I first watched *Dumb and Dumber* as a kid. Since I didn’t remember much of it, I decided to rewatch it for nostalgia. Throughout the movie, I didn’t think about anything else—not even my problems—and I laughed at so many of the ridiculous lines from these two crazy characters. I wouldn’t say it’s the best comedy ever, especially since I haven’t seen many movies in this genre besides sitcoms, but overall, it’s a fun and enjoyable film. This is dumb humor at its best. The dynamic between Lloyd and Harry reminds me a lot of the dynamic between Harry and Marv in Home Alone. This is a dumb movie, but thanks to the lead performances of Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels, it's also very funny. The classic saga of two brain-dead numbskulls who undertake a cross country trek to return a "lost" ransom briefcase, having mindlessly intercepted it at the drop-off. En route, they blow through sleazy motels and truck stop bathrooms, swapping rides and crossing wires with all manner of similarly dim-witted, off-color characters.

Ah man, this is such a Farrelly Brothers movie. Thick-headed humor, as easy and superficial as it comes, with an unrelenting time capsule for a soundtrack and a pair of lead performances so good they lift the whole mess into something that almost transcends mere stupidity. Almost. No two ways about it: this is the Jim Carrey and Jeff Daniels show, start to finish. Who else could ad-lib "the most annoying sound in the world" into something that's still so funny after thirty years? I certainly can't imagine another duo pulling off those famously terrible peach-and-baby-blue tuxes. The whole film seems to exist as a vehicle for whatever the stars felt like doing or saying that day, with said Farrelly siblings more than happy to let the cameras roll, and we're all the richer for it. Even the throwaway quips are solid gold. Carrey was in the midst of an early career apex at the time, with Ace Ventura and The Mask having already topped the box office that same year, but Daniels is, unexpectedly, there with him every step of the way. It's a showcase of impressively loose, laugh-out-loud physical comedy from a guy who wasn't (and still isn't) known for that type of work.

A not-insignificant number of jokes have curdled over time (wow, I did not remember so much homophobia) and there's no escaping the numbing, jaw-dropping idiocy of it all, but the key scenes still stand tall, the sheer force of personality is strong and there's no denying the amount of fun everyone was obviously having on-set. Is it possible that I am a fan of one of the quirkiest chapters in the MCU?! A bog standard average film with some poor acting. The CGI was good, some of the action scenes were worth watching, but in the main, it's definitely a little kids film. The best bit of the whole film was the epilogue - go Thanos! I thought the antenna of Ant-Man and The Wasp is heavily disjointed but you still get the good comedic and magic shrink able entertainment. Yes, Paul Rudd is likable, but that simply isn't enough to carry the film. Yet another Marvel product that offers nothing new in terms of technical or directorial innovation, but is solidly made. It's essentially a typical average movie, but somehow I'm really tired of Marvel's lazy formula.A few additional thoughts:- Creepy CG Michael Douglas haunts my dreams.- “I’m ready, Daddy.”- Obvious continuity errors in the reaction shots.- Being locked up at home for a few years actually sounds pretty ideal.- Why does this movie remind me of a better one that I could be watching instead (INVASION OF THE BODY SNATCHERS)?- The jokes about the size differences are actually quite funny.- Creative action, but poorly executed (kicks and punches clearly miss).- Why is every sound effect so over-designed and loud? Ant-Man y la Avispa, dirigida por Peyton Reed, es una secuela que mantiene el espíritu ligero y divertido de su predecesora. Con un equilibrio entre la comedia, la acción y el desarrollo de personajes, la película logra entretener y ampliar el mundo de Ant-Man de manera satisfactoria.

Una de las fortalezas de Ant-Man y la Avispa es la química entre los protagonistas. Paul Rudd como Scott Lang / Ant-Man y Evangeline Lilly como Hope Van Dyne / la Avispa tienen una dinámica encantadora en pantalla, lo que añade un toque de romance y complicidad a la trama. Su trabajo en equipo en las escenas de acción es emocionante y visualmente atractivo, aprovechando las habilidades únicas de cada personaje.

La película también destaca por su sentido del humor. Los momentos cómicos están bien integrados en la narrativa y proporcionan alivio cómico en los momentos adecuados. El elenco secundario, como Michael Peña en el papel de Luis, añade un toque adicional de diversión y locura a la historia.

Ant-Man y la Avispa aprovecha la premisa única de la capacidad de cambiar de tamaño de los personajes para crear secuencias de acción creativas y sorprendentes. La dirección de Peyton Reed logra mantener la acción fresca y emocionante, presentando peleas en miniatura y persecuciones trepidantes que mantienen al espectador enganchado.

Sin embargo, la trama en Ant-Man y la Avispa puede sentirse un tanto predecible y convencional en comparación con otras películas del Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel. Aunque hay momentos de tensión y emoción, la historia no logra alcanzar las mismas alturas de impacto emocional que otras entregas de la franquicia. Además, algunos de los villanos carecen de una profundidad y motivación adecuadas, lo que puede restar fuerza al conflicto central.

A nivel visual, Ant-Man y la Avispa ofrece efectos especiales sólidos y una dirección de arte vibrante. El uso de los entornos en miniatura y los efectos visuales para representar las habilidades de los personajes es impresionante y se integra de manera orgánica en la historia.

En resumen, Ant-Man y la Avispa es una secuela ligera y entretenida que expande el mundo de Ant-Man de manera satisfactoria. Con su sentido del humor bien ejecutado, las escenas de acción creativas y la química entre los protagonistas, la película ofrece una experiencia agradable y divertida. Aunque la trama puede ser predecible en momentos y algunos personajes no se sienten completamente desarrollados, en general, la película cumple con su objetivo de entretener y ampliar la historia del héroe en miniatura. Ant-Man and The Wasp is a great film that while definitely not as good as the first movie, it's still worth a watch. The first thing I can say is that the fact the story continues on where the first movie while also taking place after the events of Captain America: Civil War is a great idea since it puts in stakes for the story while still allowing the story to take place and it's a good story for the most part. The pacing is while not quite as good as the first movie, is still great to ensure you aren't bored throughout the film. The writing is a great balance between utter comedy and serious matters to leave you invested onto your seat at all times even if some of the jokes are not. The CGI and action sequences remain phenomenal and keep you excited on how the fights go on, and no fight is distracting bad overall. The characters remain great and help elevate this film, and the actors on top of them are excellent in terms of acting. Now despite the fact I think this movie is pretty good, it's no better than the first film with some kinda big flaws. Like I said earlier, the jokes are not that funny and leave you annoyed, the villain is fine but in no ways a good Ant-Man villain and the fact that they chose not to let her die but not bring her back makes me question why she couldn't have just ended her time with the MCU right then and there, and one particular moment when I felt nervous on what was going to happen but then they succeeded without showing how they got past it and that felt totally dumb. Overall, while I definitely prefer the first movie over this one, I still enjoyed it overall and I recommend it if you enjoyed the first one and I can't wait to see how they end the trilogy with Quantamania.

The rhythmic machinery of a chaotic distortion: A 5.0-star sensational surge of parodic perfection.2011(5.0)I watched "Scary Movie 4" in 2011, and it delivered a visceral revelation that stands as a definitive 5.0-star pillar of high-tension absurdity in my archive. Seeing Anna Faris’s vivid commitment to the chaos provided an emotional payoff that felt both raw and authentic, proving that a fourth installment could be a vivid act of storytelling rebellion against franchise fatigue. The 95% preservation of my memory is dominated by the rhythmic, raw humor of the alien invasion and the vivid but pathetic struggle of the protagonists to survive their own stupidity, creating a permanent, sensational scar of pure joy on my soul. Unlike the stagnant 3.0-star drift of "Cats & Dogs" or the pathetic execution of "Return of the Noble Family," this encounter possessed a rebellious soul that turned a pathetic premise into a sensational masterpiece of wit. It stands in my 2011 record as a powerful 5.0-star testament to the raw power of visual comedy—a high-tension encounter with the vivid rhythm of the ridiculous that remains one of the most chewy artifacts of my cinematic journey. Watching it in that specific classroom setting made the experience even more intense. It didn't just portray brilliance; it exposed the raw, unsettling reality behind it. For my younger self, seeing a story that deconstructed the myth of the genius so powerfully was a true eye-opener. A solid 4.0 for a movie that challenged my perspective before I even knew what hit me. It’s one of those films that’s easy to watch and easy to remember, but that leaves a strange feeling once it’s over. That’s when the film breathes more freely and becomes more suggestive and less predictable. But whenever it seems ready to go deeper, it retreats back into a very familiar, almost textbook **** the end, it’s an honest and effective film, easy to watch and true to what it sets out to do. But it also prioritizes accessibility and controlled emotional impact over real complexity. Everything fits, everything flows, but it rarely surprises.A well-made, well-acted story that remains slightly cold at its core. 'jurassic park' is not just an adventure movie: it marks a turning point in film history. its release sparked a genuine cinematic revolution across multiple aspects, raising technical and narrative standards within the industry. while it wasn’t the first film to show dinosaurs on screen, it was the first to present them with such overwhelming realism that audiences truly felt they were witnessing living, tangible creatures for the first time.

the achievement lies in a flawless combination of elements: the meticulously crafted dinosaur designs; the sound work, with roars and ambient noises that create complete immersion; and, above all, the innovative use of special effects. spielberg blended life-sized animatronics with computer-generated imagery in a convincing balance that continues to impress even three decades later.

john williams’ score not only accompanies but amplifies the experience. its main theme has become a cultural icon, capable of evoking within just a few notes the sense of wonder and awe that defines the film. it is music that transcends the screen and embeds itself in collective memory.

narratively, 'jurassic park' balances thriller tension with moments of awe and reflection. the story raises ethical and scientific questions about the limits of genetic manipulation and human control over nature, while never losing pace or the ability to keep viewers glued to the screen.

even for those who are not fans of the genre or adventure films in general, it is hard to deny the magnitude of this production. 'jurassic park' not only redefined how cinema could portray prehistoric creatures but also left an indelible mark on popular culture and a whole generation of viewers.

although i don’t consider it the greatest masterpiece of cinema, i fully recognize its enormous impact on film history. 'jurassic park' is neither my favorite movie nor one i am personally fascinated by, but it would be unfair to dismiss the innovation it brought. its ability to break technical and narrative barriers makes it an essential reference, and that element of novelty means that even for a viewer who doesn’t hold it in high regard, the experience is more enjoyable. in the end, it is a well-crafted and visionary film that deserves its place in collective memory.

in short, more than just a dinosaur movie, 'jurassic park' is a masterclass in how creative vision, technical talent, and storytelling can come together to create a timeless spectacle. In fact, it’s hard to get into at first. Baz Luhrmann’s cinema is excessive by nature, and here he decides not to hold back at all: everything is big, shiny, loud, and fast. It can be disorienting, even tiring, but as the minutes go by, the film starts to impose its own rhythm and, surprisingly, it ends up working.This is not a classic adaptation, nor does it try to be. This isn’t pure Fitzgerald, but a Gatsby filtered through Luhrmann’s imagination, closer to a pop opera than a literary drama. At times it feels like the spectacle devours everything, but there are also moments when the film slows down just enough to let the characters breathe, and that’s when it begins to gain emotional weight.Leonardo DiCaprio is genuinely strong. His Gatsby is vulnerable, obsessive, and tragic without heavy-handed emphasis, and he manages to convey that mix of grandeur and fragility that defines the character. Joel Edgerton, meanwhile, brings solidity and restraint, acting as a necessary counterbalance amid so much visual excess. The Da Vinci Code The Da Vinci Code Seek the truth. Thriller Mystery Ron Howard Tom Hanks Audrey Tautou Ian McKellen Jean Reno Paul Bettany Alfred Molina Jürgen Prochnow Jean-Yves Berteloot Etienne Chicot Jean-Pierre Marielle A murder in Paris’ Louvre Museum and cryptic clues in some of Leonardo da Vinci’s most famous paintings lead to the discovery of a religious mystery. For 2,000 years a secret society closely guards information that — should it come to light — could rock the very foundations of Christianity. A big-budget, big-name, big-screen adaptation of one of the decade's biggest literary phenomenons. Given such gravitas, it shouldn't be surprising that The Da Vinci Code frequently threatens to buckle under the weight of its own expectations.

And threaten it does, in typical bloated, self-indulgent fashion, but like a Weeble it's able to sustain such wobbles intact. The intense, brainy series of puzzles and mysteries at its heart are largely to thank for that. Although the figurines dancing around their outskirts are persistently fake and irritating, there's something so deeply interesting about these riddles that they're able to power the film instead.

The plot comes and goes as it pleases. Ian McKellan gets to deliver all the sizzle, in a profoundly thought-provoking monologue on the roots of Christianity, then abruptly changes his tune in one of an endless series of stupid, unnecessary swerves. In that sense, it feels like a film that thinks it needs to do more than it does. Tom Hanks, thrust into an unfamiliar role as a thriller/action lead, never feels completely at-home, and Audrey Tautou (best known from her work in Amelie) is flat and unconvincing, a major disappointment as his co-star.

There's the sparkle of something powerful glimmering at the heart of The Da Vinci Code, but actually unearthing it amidst so much padding and space-filler is a task on par with one of the film's most difficult brain teasers. Beside what happened in the renaissance era, The Da Vinci code still being discussing in the 21century. Human still be the subject to be developed. But as Christmas approaches, Jack's rag-doll girlfriend, Sally, tries to foil his misguided plans. A fantastic technical achievement with it's fair share of memorable moments, but it doesn't quite come together to make a truly satisfying movie experience. This is the Christmas movie I watch pretty much every year. I think this is one of the best animated stop-motion movies ever made. I may be very biased due to this being a core movie from my childhood, though. "O Estranho Mundo de Jack" é muito mais do que um filme de animação. Ele combina visual, música e narrativa de forma harmoniosa, criando uma experiência cinematográfica completa. É uma celebração da criatividade e da imaginação, com uma mensagem poderosa sobre autodescoberta e aceitação.Mesmo após décadas de seu lançamento, o filme continua a encantar públicos de todas as idades, provando que obras-primas não envelhecem – elas apenas se tornam mais valiosas com o tempo. The character designs and animation quality are top-notch. Jack Skellington as the king of Halloween works well. My problems with the movie are that the story is all over the place, and it's so evenly split between Halloween and Christmas that it doesn't really feel like a Halloween movie or a Christmas movie. Tim Burton is one of a select few creatives capable of handling creepy, adult material in a way that's not just appropriate, but also downright appealing, for younger audiences. Beetlejuice, Pee-Wee's Big Adventure and Edward Scissorhands are all great examples of this trait, but of the lot I think this is his most timeless creation. Which is odd, since it's the only one he didn't direct.

Like the very best fairy tales, The Nightmare Before Christmas is adventurous and unusual, taking outlandish concepts for granted as a means of **** the audience into its own private corridor. The plot is predictable and natural, but also doesn't sacrifice its ability to throw the audience for a loop from time to time, and efficiently straddles two major holidays in a manner that never feels forced or exploitative.

Of course, the visuals are remarkable, a stop-motion showcase that constantly bubbles with charm and personality, but the soundtrack is really where it hangs its hat. Danny Elfman has never felt more at-home in the Burton universe, and considering the pair's long, storied history together, that's quite the achievement. The tunes are occasionally just a bit too catchy for their own good (I've been humming them for the better part of a day now) but that's a small price to pay for a modern fable this special. 10 of 100 star "Killers of the Flower Moon" is a gripping historical drama showcasing stellar performances and an evocative narrative. One of the standout elements is Leonardo DiCaprio's transformation, achieved through prosthetics that alter his appearance dramatically, giving him a permanent frown reminiscent of Orson Welles. DiCaprio's acting reaches its pinnacle in a heart-wrenching scene where he processes the death of his daughter, delivering a performance that feels raw and genuine.Lily Gladstone, however, emerges as the film's most captivating presence. Her expressive eyes communicate a profound depth, keeping the audience guessing whether her character is aware of the sinister plans around her. Gladstone's portrayal adds an air of mystery and emotional weight to the story. Robert De Niro, as expected, is masterful, bringing a duality to his role as a public figure and a Mafia boss, blending menace with charisma. Supporting performances from Jesse Plemons and Brendan Fraser are equally compelling, with Fraser's physicality adding an intimidating dynamic to the courtroom scenes.Martin Scorsese's direction is exemplary, blending his signature style with historical authenticity. The film seamlessly integrates archival photographs and dynamic sequences, such as a memorable scene mixing rock and Native American music during a discovery of oil. The period setting is brought to life through meticulous attention to detail, from vintage cars to cultural nuances, creating a vivid depiction of 1920s America. The narrative also highlights racial tensions and the early days of the FBI, offering a sobering reflection on the era's complexities.Despite its strengths, the film isn't without flaws. Some editing choices, such as continuity errors and a broken 180-degree rule in a conversation, stand out as distractions. DiCaprio's accent, while period-appropriate, feels slightly forced and occasionally pulls focus from the story. At three hours long, the pacing falters at times, particularly in the early sections, which may lose some viewers' engagement.Emotionally, the death of Gladstone's character’s mother fails to resonate as strongly as intended, which detracts from the film's otherwise powerful emotional core. Additionally, DiCaprio's morally corrupt character may surprise viewers expecting a more traditional hero, ultimately shifting the narrative's emotional center to **** conclusion, "Killers of the Flower Moon" is an ambitious film that succeeds in delivering a compelling story with remarkable performances and meticulous craftsmanship. While not without minor shortcomings, its powerful themes, exceptional acting, and Scorsese's visionary direction make it a memorable cinematic experience. This did not need to be a 3-hour movie. There's so much needless filler added in and glamour shots that don't do anything for the movie. They could have easily trimmed this down to a little over 2-hours. Having to sit through 3-hours of this was punishing, especially with how uneventful it could be at times. Brilliantly shot, directed and acted. Too bad this is (basically) a true story. Leo and Lily are phenomenal, with Lily (arguably) stealing the show. This is not a feel good movie, despite the modicum of justice served at the end. The film tells the story of the Osage, a Native American tribe that was nearly wiped out. The reason for this tragedy was the immense wealth the Osage gained from oil. The film impressively shows how boundless greed can collectively drive people and how easily one looks away, simply because the victims have a different skin color.

Masterfully performed by Leonardo DiCaprio, Lily Gladstone, and Robert De Niro. What I particularly liked was how Leo took a completely different approach with his character Ernest this time. His demeanor, facial expressions, and mannerisms are so different that from the beginning, I saw Ernest, not Leo.

It was certainly a fine line to write this script. On one hand, the drama must not fall short to avoid boring the audience. On the other hand, one wants to pay respect to the many, many dead and tell their story as honestly as possible. Scorsese masterfully succeeds in this. One should not expect a classic drama from the outset; rather, a down-to-earth approach is pursued. With this knowledge, I had a lot of fun and found the film very exciting—at least for the first two-thirds. In the last hour, the film falls apart somewhat and ends the storylines too abruptly. I found this unfortunate, as Scorsese had taken his time until then. With a runtime of almost 3.5 hours, I would have liked a more consistent tension curve.

All in all, I was very well entertained. The sets, costumes, and actors are all at the masterful level one expects from Scorsese. However, I would have liked a more rounded experience with the script. Distracting fake teeth, accents and other actor tools aside the casting is great with an interesting screenplay, cinematography, soundtrack and overall production value is very good. Sadly there wasn't anything to hook into beyond the superficial. We spend time with the characters but I never felt a human connection. Its a shame that the overlong runtime couldn't have been paces across a longer 6 episode season of TV instead of cramming it all into a 3hr 20 min window. As such entire time periods skip with little warning. Worth a watch if you have the time to spare!

Now THIS... is a reboot.

EXCITING - CREATIVE - PROVOCATIVE - COOL

I'm a huge fan of preqeuels, so this one definitely got me. The concept pulls you in, but the characters are what you stay for. Suddenly, you'll find yourself caring so much about and even identifying with a CGI ape... but that's what film is about, right?

The premise presents some thought-provoking questions about humanity, which is the whole purpose. The original series had plenty of these moments, and Rise folds in all of the same questions. A film becomes powerful when it makes you start thinking. 

Though not without its own flaws, Rise is a great establishment of the rebooted series, laying the groundwork for Dawn, which is where they always should have gone with the story... James Franco has shown more versatility in previous leading roles, but his character in Rise of the Planet of the Apes is intended to be about as straightforward and vanilla as it gets, so that's precisely what he delivers. The real focus is on the simians, anyway, with whom the picture treads lightly amidst some very tricky material. It often toes the line between excess and authenticity, but never fully gives in to temptation and emerges as a far better film for exercising the caution. The resonant echoes of a hidden reflection: A 5.0-star "visceral" awakening of identity.1999 (5.0)Watching "Mulan" in 1999 was a "sensational" turning point that defined my childhood relationship with cinema. Growing up as a fan of Disney, I was suddenly confronted with a character that offered a profound "revelation"—an Asian eldest daughter who felt the suffocating need to hide her true self just to survive. I was so "hororong" (captivated) by this narrative rhythm that I lost count of how many times I rewatched it. Even after seeing it multiple times, I would visit the video rental shop to borrow it again, keeping the tape for a week just to immerse myself in its "raw" emotional world. I vividly remember bringing a cassette player to the TV to record the songs, desperately trying to preserve that high-tension inspiration. Discovering the alternative version of "Reflection" by Lena Park (Park Jung-hyun) on my cousin’s album was another "visceral" shock that deepened my connection to the story. This film **** the fourth wall of typical fairy tales, offering a "chewy" and complex look at duty and identity that left a 95% preservation of pure nostalgia in my heart. It remains a perfect 5.0-star pillar in my archive, a testament to how a "pathetic" sense of invisibility can be transformed into a powerful and life-changing cinematic roar. The (mostly) true story of two passionate gear-heads and their tireless quest to unseat mighty Team Ferrari at the grueling 24-hour Le Mans endurance race. Armed, that is, with the financial backing (and all-too frequent corporate meddling) of Ford Motor Company. In that sense, Ford v Ferrari is a war on two fronts: these guys are playing catch-up against a more advanced opponent while also fending off the various obstacles and bad ideas tossed down from their own corporate brass.

Christian Bale and Matt Damon, somehow sharing the screen for the first time, provide all the personality this flick needs to maintain momentum, while the hair-raising cockpit scenes nail every hairpin turn. Bale plays the more fiery of the pair; a sparky, **** driver who comes out of near-retirement for this chance at immortality. Damon's man is full of piss and vinegar, too, but more amicable to the kind of machinations necessary for navigating a corporate American boardroom. From the first word, they're great together. It's not an easy relationship to define - blows are exchanged, often comically, more than once - but there's no arguing their kinship, even if both might brush it off as a mere working association. They both know the fine points of their job, and the slight quirks and deviations that make them essential to one another.

Several of the film's plot twists are telegraphed, even for those (like I) who didn't know the full story coming in, and it's guilty of occasionally dipping into the well of over-worn sports movie tropes, but otherwise it's an effective pulse-pounder.

The rhythmic machinery of a jungle rebellion: A 4.0-star sensational surge of raw, high-tension primal grit.2008(4.0)I watched Tarzan (1999) in 2008, and it remains a vivid 4.0-star pillar of shwi-shwi hand-drawn brilliance in my archive—a raw revelation of how a sensational animated classic can dismantle the stagnant safety of a traditional fairy tale. This experience **** the fourth wall of the adventure genre by infusing the raw, high-tension precision of Phil Collins’ rhythmic beats into a narrative rhythm that felt 100% sophisticated and chewy. The narrative rhythm was far from stagnant; instead, it offered a sensational acting power show where the raw, high-tension sliding through the trees and the bbo-jjak curiosity of Jane left me in a state of absolute awe at its visceral soul. Seeing the vivid, lush jungle and the raw, hororong power of the leopard battle provided an emotional payoff that felt both authentic and sensational, proving that a story about "belonging to two worlds" could be a vivid artifact of pure cinematic joy. It stands in my 2008 record as a powerful 4.0-star testament to the raw power of the Disney Renaissance—a high-tension encounter with the vivid rhythm of the deep jungle that remains one of the most chewy artifacts of my cinematic journey. Creed se un spin-off que nos cuenta la historia del hijo de Apollo Creed, Adonis Creed, en su sueño por convertirse en una leyenda del boxeo, esta cinte nos transmite el espíritu de la saga de Rocky a la época actual para que las nuevas generaciones conozcan a esta personaje, pero sin perder su esencia A perfect boxing film that intrigues you and shows boxing scenes that are very intense and makes you feel part of the movie. Apollo Creed was very important for Rocky and making a film of him training Apollo's son targeted emotions of boxing viewers that like Rocky. I really liked the movie, the environment, the scenes, and the actors performances. Envolvente, emocionante, inspirador, bem trabalhado e com grandes momentos de luta. Sem duvida um filme que se deve ver. The same story, new generation. "Dawn of the Planet of the Apes" (2014) is a hands down one of the best sequels ever made. This movie has everything to keep you entertained for 2 hours from start till finish. Good acting, superb storyline, great settings, amazing special effects - it's all there and it all clicks. The best moments in this movie are the one without action actually, it's when apes (especially Caesar) and people starts to communicate. Dawn of the Planet of the Apes is an excellent follow up to Rise of the the Planet of the Apes. This Thriller will keep you on the edge of your seat to see what happens next, and has you wanting for the next film. ... the perfection that exists during these minutes of film... this is PRIME Planet of the Apes...

ENTHRALLING - THOUGHT-PROVOKING - EMOTIONAL - DEEP

This is where the concept needed to be taken all along. A natural balance of characters; the multiple layers of conflict that Caesar navigates and faces; the focus on Caesar himself and the world that he's created; and all of these elements in harmony to tell the story... Set a full ten years after the events of its predecessor, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes sees humanity near extinction while Caesar and his ever-expanding family have established a functional utopia amidst the desolation. Most of the first act is a simple, enveloping visual treat, establishing the world as it now stands and savoring the unique visuals of San Francisco (and the surrounding area) in the aftermath of a near-total human annihilation event. Crumbling cityscapes, creeping plant life, reverberations of a lost civilization... the setting lends itself nicely to vivid, poignant splashes of scenery, and the effects team is more than up to that challenge.

In fact, moving on from that slow, thoughtful series of reflections is a feat the film struggles with. Though rich and layered in its own ways, the story plays second-fiddle to the mood at large, and often feels telegraphed by the events of the first film, not to mention the original series. It's a deep, thought provoking installment, with some lights-out physical acting from the entire motion-capture cast, but I couldn't shake the sense that it could have stretched itself much further than it did. When it came time for the parallel climactic face-offs amidst the fireworks of an inescapable human/ape conflict, I kept thinking to myself, "Is this really all there is?"

Firm, fiery and intelligent, but perhaps a bit too safe, too happy to fall back on a set of standard action movie routines. Beautifully dark, it's also a decided step back from the promise seen in Rise of the Planet of the Apes. Dawn of the Planet of the Apes showed remarkable excellence in story, character development, and visual effects. This movie smoothly elevated the POTA series from mid-budget sci-fi to the heights of epic science fiction. Possibly the best animal motion capture movie i've ever seen, with this i can say that the Planet Of The Apes movie was really something special, i am more than convince that the way i see Caesar and the rest of the Apes now as really something that are absolutely serious possibly more than the human, and it's crazy when you think about it, nothing has more personality input to these animal characters better than the Planet Of The Apes franchise, this big emotional weight for these characters, and Dawn Of The Planet Of The Apes is possibly the best one so far, it's frustrating, it's terrifying, the terror was somehow even worse and scarier compare to the previous one, props to not only Andy Serkis but Toby Kebbell as Koba, the supporting cast was great, and the CGI was way better than the previous one which is one of my problem with the previous one, Caesar was indeed slowly became more grown and as long as the human still exist he sometimes still give his respect to the good human and they still showing that in here in which i found great, overall Dawn Of The Planet Of The Apes delivers a better story, a better technical aspects than the previous one, and incredible sequel overall, an achievement for sure in terms of an animal motion capture film.

633.title: Captain America: The First Avenger

Captain America: The First Avenger Captain America: The First Avenger Action Adventure Science Fiction Joe Johnston Chris Evans Hayley Atwell Sebastian Stan Tommy Lee Jones Hugo Weaving Dominic Cooper Richard Armitage Stanley Tucci Samuel L. Jackson Toby Jones During World War II, Steve Rogers is a sickly man from Brooklyn who's transformed into super-soldier Captain America to aid in the war effort. Rogers must stop the Red Skull – Adolf Hitler's ruthless head of weaponry, and the leader of an organization that intends to use a mysterious device of untold powers for world domination. This movie was quite interesting, had a lot of really cool battle sequences. And Captain America is like my favorite Avenger. Although lots of the characters didn't reveal their signature looks towards the near end of the movie, besides that, good movie. A flag-waving spectacle of forced pride: A 3.0-star shield that couldn't block the cringe.110728 (3.0)I watched this in the theater in 2011. Back then, I used to run to the cinema for any Marvel release with pure excitement, but this one was a massive mismatch for my taste. The very reason it became such a huge hit in the US was exactly why I hated it: that blatant, unapologetic American exceptionalism. It felt too "shameless" and predictable, lacking the "chewy," complex tension I usually look for. While the production value was there, the "Captain America" bravado felt a bit too forced for me to fully embrace. A skeptical 3.0 for a hero who was a bit too "Star-Spangled" for my liking. Can we stop for a minute and appreciate how absolutely SPOT ON this movie is to the comics and the history of Cap?  I mean if this is where we are starting - how high are we going?!  Great start to the MCU! Captain America: The First Avenger delivers exactly what it needs to: a clean, straightforward origin story with a likeable lead and a nostalgic World War II backdrop. Chris Evans fits the role surprisingly well, giving Steve Rogers an earnestness that never feels forced. The film doesn’t try to be overly complex and benefits from that simplicity, moving from skinny Steve’s determination to the creation of Captain America in a way that feels smooth and **** action is fine, the pacing is steady, and the retro atmosphere gives it a unique identity compared to other Marvel entries. Red Skull is a bit underused, but the movie still manages to set up Cap’s personality and values without dragging things out. Overall, it’s a solid, engaging introduction that does exactly what an origin story should, without unnecessary twists or complications. No spoilers. Captain America: The First Avenger is a really enjoyable action film that adds to and deepens the beginnings of the MCU. I really love the backstory that Captain America has, and how he became the super hero we know him as. Hugo Weaving as Red Skull is a huge bonus as well.

This is an Action Epic set in the past of where the MCU usually takes place.

Captain America has to travel across the globe in this Adventure Epic to save the world.

The threat that Red Skull puts on in this Epic tale is beyond evil the world currently knows at that point.

As a superhero, Captain America is a One-Person Army Action hero that needs no one else for this tale.

The way he obtains his powers and some of the technology in this Sci-Fi Epic is very interesting.

Watch the story of how Captain America became the Superhero we know him as now.

There are plenty of location to behold the Urban Adventure.

There is a lot of Action throughout the movie, even before Steve Rogers become Captain America.

This is Adventure through time, but mostly set in the past.

The world changes permanently in this Sci-Fi film. Fantastic origin movie for one of the greatest superheroes. 

This movie nails Caps origin story, and although there are so many world war movies, it still keeps the setting fresh and enjoyable. The main characters are memorable, the action sequences are entertaining, and each scene carries weight. The standard hero tropes are in full effect with Marvels golden child, but you still feel compelled to walk away a better person. I don't really know why, but I really like this Captain America film. I like the characters, the 1940s setting and the story. If I think about it, not much happens, but at least what's on offer is good. This is really the film where I think Steve Rogers could show his personality and thoughts. Captain America: The First Avenger is a well-crafted superhero origin story that sets up Steve Rogers' journey with a strong narrative foundation. The plot is engaging, blending a classic underdog story with a war-time adventure that feels both grounded and larger than life. The pacing is solid, moving through Steve's transformation and early missions without dragging, though some action sequences are presented in montage form, which makes them feel a bit rushed. The script does a great job of keeping the dialogue natural, mixing heartfelt moments with humor and sincerity, making Steve an instantly likable character.

Joe Johnston’s direction leans heavily into a 1940s aesthetic, capturing the era’s charm while delivering the high-energy action expected from a Marvel film. The cinematography enhances this old-school feel with warm tones and well-framed action shots that keep everything clear and visually engaging. Some sequences feel a little stylized in a way that makes them stand out from the rest of the MCU, but that actually works in the film’s favor, giving it a unique identity. The balance between practical effects and CGI is well-handled, making the world feel lived-in rather than overly polished.

Chris Evans absolutely nails the role, bringing depth to Steve Rogers beyond just being a strong, noble hero. His performance is supported by a great cast, with standout moments from Hayley Atwell and Tommy Lee Jones. The score, composed by Alan Silvestri, adds to the film’s grand yet sentimental tone, making key moments hit harder. Overall, this is one of the stronger solo MCU entries, delivering a mix of action, heart, and a well-paced origin story that sets the stage for one of Marvel’s most iconic characters. This movie was an amazing origin film for Captain America. Based on his comic origins, the movie kept to many of the comics' origin and kept it as close to the source material. As the movie follows Steve Rogers through his early army days, fans can't help but root for Steve Rogers' kind heart and his acts of heroism and compassion, ultimately making him our Captain America. Film with a classic plot for its genre but well done, especially in the characterization and evolution of its protagonist. The historical context gives something more to the plot of the film, with more realistic tones than many other films of its genre

636.title: Anna

metadata.tagline: Never make the weapon the target

636.rich_text:
Anna Anna Never make the weapon the target Action Adventure Thriller Luc Besson Sasha Luss Helen Mirren Luke Evans Cillian Murphy Lera Abova Alexander Petrov Nikita Pavlenko Anna Krippa Aleksey Maslodudov Éric Godon Beneath Anna Poliatova's striking beauty lies a secret that will unleash her indelible strength and skill to become one of the world's most feared government assassins. As a story focusing on the characters, their relationships, and the shifting sense of distrust they have for each other as well as their own perceptions, Anna works very well. The actors pull off the subtle clues of their personalities, and the whole sense of trust and distrust really is milked to full effect.

But when the plot actually cashes in its suspense in the form of plot twists, it becomes almost enragingly stupid. For mild spoilers: Someone falls into a trap, which is a theme of the whole movie. But they fall into the extremely convoluted trap with the perfectly-coordinated illogic of a slasher-movie bimbo. And then a police investigation comes to the perfectly exact wrong conclusion, using some logical deductions that make utterly no sense to the audience as they're coming out of their mouths, and even less sense when they actually think about it.

This is a movie that spends its entire run selling itself as smart, and succeeding. And then it concludes by using the summer-blockbuster technique of "Throw around lots of details that deliberately don't make any sense, and hope that it confuses people enough to make it look intricate and clever." Which doesn't work even in less cerebral movies, or when you're using it to save the day, and not to betray people's delicate trust in justice. Mindscape has a solid premise, it opens with assertive scenes and good production for suspense. The two main leads, Mark Strong and Taissa Farmiga, are effective for drawing the audience's sympathy, they are strangely involved in a confining situation originally as therapist and patient. It escalates into darker territory as they uncover secrets and danger alike, but unfortunately the movie reaches the conclusion without the same confidence it starts, leaving a dry stale taste as it weakly draws to a close.

Story follows John Washington (Mark Strong), a psychic with the rare skill of accessing another people's memories. He is tasked to help Anna Greene (Taissa Farmiga), a smart young girl with troubled past. Washington has suffered from a botched session before and currently struggling with his own issues while Anna is an enigmatic girl who distinctly represents a caged bird. The unique thing about their relationship is Washington serves as a therapist but at the same time a sort of detective investigating her deep rooted anxiety.

This brings so much potential as it dabbles with the idea of abuse or manipulation. Washington grows increasingly protective of Anna, there's also a hint of sensuality beneath the adoration but none too blatant to overshadow their unique bond. It has the luxury of both mystery ambiance as well as a bit of sci-fi tone. Its cinematography works in intriguing manner as it portrays the world in noir theme yet it also has the liberty to present a more modern cityscape. Coupled with good script, the movie is a surefire hit for mystery fans.

However, it seems to lost its momentum half way through, rehearsing the same material with little thrill. The mix between supernatural and futuristic world have a few decent set-ups for more development, but none pays off satisfyingly. Chemistry between the leads is nice, although the curiosity produced by their interaction doesn't hold until the last arc. Furthermore, some of the crucial intricacies are skimped over, leaving a few plot holes as it wobbles towards the climax.

For a thriller with such promising start, it's even more disappointing when it ends so blandly. Unlike most of its genre, where many reach dynamic conclusions, Anna's finale is anticlimactically resembled mediocre dramas’. Summary: Mindscape is a decent thriller that delivers some twists and surprises. 70/100 [B-]

A man with the ability to enter peoples' memories takes on the case of a brilliant, troubled sixteen-year-old girl to determine whether she is a sociopath or a victim of trauma. I saw some of the trailers and they were very interesting to me, however in spite of its boring trailers, I saw the movie and I really liked it. It may be predictable for some people but not to me. The premise is interesting and the cast did an awesome job during the whole film.

The entire cast is so damn talented, Taissa Farmiga (American Horror Story) and Mark Strong (Kick-Ass) did an amazing job here. Moving on, the concept is awesome and original to me but I have some issues with the script, because some of the dialog was predictable and the film becomes somewhat silly in its third act. Anyway, the most interesting elements in Mindscape are all the "visions" that the film shows us, some of them are very disturbing and strange.

The movie cares about its characters and their previous story. In addition, all of these characters are very well developed. I actually felt sorry for Anna's character, her story is quite sad; also, Taissa Farmiga does an excellent job performing Anna's role. Moving on, the film keeps you guessing the whole time and I liked that; you don't trust in some of these characters and you don't know if Anna is crazy or she's just an innocent girl.

It is entertaining and it makes sense. Another thing that I like about it is the ending, Mindscape ended up being entertaining, interesting, different, well filmed and superbly acted; in spite of some weak dialog and a messy final act. Its final act has its ups and downs, but the last 5 minutes are quite good, the ending is perfect and well done. I also loved the art design of the end credits. I think that it deserves at least a 7/10 rating, it's a very underrated flick. [B-] Excelente filme com um final fraco meresse uma continuação explicando o final , exelentes atores como Taissa Farmiga que foi otima em seu papel e mereceu o destaque que teve Rainha teen né, amore.
É linda.
Aclamada.
Ovacionada.
Requisitada.
Amada.
Odiada (qnt maior o alvo, maior o recalque né).
