The Bourne character is used as a launch to what  is ultimately happening on the geopolitical stage —controlling outcome and the operatives used. 
I thoroughly enjoyed every installment. If Bourne’s character has found peace and has decided to move on, Cross’s character is a glimpse into a perrenial conflict and the latest technology used to overcome it My least favorite of the series. Didn't really have anything to do with the actual series. It was an ok movie, but it's like a different movie in itself. It would be nice if it wasn't a movie from the “Bourne” franchise.

After three good films, the “Bourne” franchise seems to be laid on solid foundations, and the success of the following films seems assured. In fact, franchises like that turn into money-making machines for the studios… but what I found in this film is something capable of disappointing the most ardent fan of the franchise: it's a “Bourne” movie without Jason Bourne.

In fact, the script focuses entirely on Aaron Cross, a completely new and unknown character to us, whose journey as a CIA operative seems to start with "Outcome", another top secret agency program specializing in the modification of psychology and behaviors through certain drugs. When the program is discontinued by higher order and everyone involved is murdered, Cross does what he can to escape and save his life.

The movie isn't really that bad, if we forget about the previous movies and their extremely far-fetched connection to the Bourne franchise. It starts very slowly, more than any of those that preceded it, and there are many points where the story sounds confused and disjointed. Even so, it untangled itself and the ending worked relatively effectively. Tony Gilroy's direction proved to be far less interesting and original than that of his predecessor, with whom he collaborated directly, and the script, which he also assures, is good enough, but far from the quality achieved previously. There are also some editing issues and scenes that seem to be there just to take up time.

Without Matt Damon and the franchise's title character, the film feels constantly out of place. Say what you like… if a movie is so closely associated with a character it becomes difficult to conceive of a sequel or prequel in which she doesn't appear in some way, even if she is younger or older… Jeremy Renner does what he can for us trying to make this absence forget, but he can't, despite being a talented actor and doing a good job here. In the cast, he is undoubtedly the one who manages to stand out and shine the most. Rachel Weisz is not so good: the actress works as she can, but the material she receives is bad and the character never develops properly. Edward Norton is uninteresting and seems to be uncomfortable with the character. It is, without a doubt, the worst work by this actor, at least with regard to everything I've seen so far.

Technically, it's an intense film and one where there are many redeeming qualities: the cinematography is elegant and well constructed, making the most of the filming locations. The editing, as I said, leaves something to be desired, as does the pace of the film, but this is balanced by a good selection of special effects, visual and sound, and a judicious and well thought-out use of CGI. The action scenes aren't as impactful as what we've seen in previous movies, and the chases look a lot like what we've seen in previous “Bourne” movies. The biggest strenght of the original Bourne movies is that they were fast, they were short, and they didn't waste time. They went straigh to the point

This movie is long, slow and wastes a lot of time.

It wastes time showing Jeremy Renner doing random stuff and hanging out with Oscar Isaac in Aalaska. It wastes time setting up a shootout for what feels like an eternity. It wastes time with a lot of talking and very little action.

Also, what's all this super soldier, genetic enhancement **** Wasn't it enough just having very skilled assassins?

The ending feels very abrupt. When "Extreme Ways" by Moby started playing I geniunely thought to myself: "wait, really? It's over already?". The film is very long and yet it still feels incomplete. Maybe they were hoping for some sequels.
Also, Rachel Weisz is really bad here.

There's some cool moments and I appreciate that it actually attempts to be different, but it would be easier to appreciate it if the name "Bourne" wasn't in the title. This could've been a fine standalone film. Finally! Legacy will be the pinnacle of the Borne movies. A mature actor with a mature plot. Renner takes Damon's attempt at an action hero and does it 10x better. You don't need to suspend belief to imagine Renner as a gruff operative which makes a fresh change from Damon as the "Deer in the Headlights" we've seen in the previous films.
The story was full of intrigue and the slow boil which was the first act was a much need change from the Damon lead cartoons we've had before. Solid action flick but not nearly as good as the Damon Bourne films. Probably should not have been made. When the actions of Jason Bourne spark a fire that threatens to burn down decades of research across a number of secret intelligence agencies, Eric Byer (Edward Norton), the man who built the programs, decides he must sacrifice one of them: Outcome. Aaron Cross (Jeremy Renner), one of Outcome's six agents, and research scientist Marta Shearing (Rachel Weisz) go on the run when Byer targets them for termination. But Cross proves to be a far deadlier target than Byer realizes. It isn't quite as compelling as the earlier trilogy, but The Bourne Legacy proves the franchise has stories left to tell -- and benefits from Jeremy Renner's magnetic work in the starring role. I'll give The Bourne Legacy a B-.

Train Dreams Train Dreams The extraordinary story of an ordinary life. Drama Clint Bentley Joel Edgerton Felicity Jones Nathaniel Arcand Clifton Collins Jr. John Diehl Paul Schneider Kerry Condon William H. Macy Will Patton Alfred Hsing A logger leads a life of quiet grace as he experiences love and loss during an era of monumental change in early 20th-century America. Such a beautiful movie. Every frame a painting. The music transcending. It felt like going through an old photo album of a lost family member. 7.5/10

I just wish i connected more with the characters and the film emotional weight, despite its absolutely stunning visuals, great performances, and solid storytelling, Robert's simple yet fascinating life, along with the environment around him and the time period the story takes place in is genuinely interesting to watch and experience, Felicity Jones delivers a heartfelt and lovely performance, while William H. Macy brings a quirky presence as the philosophical old logger, and Kerry Condon with her brief but thoughtful performance, all of them contribute nicely to the film's world.

Still, for some reason, i never quite felt the emotional connection i was hoping for, i'm not sure if it comes down to the execution or if the film simply doesn't push that aspect far enough, it's still a well made film that plays decently overall, but i wasn't completely in love with Train Dreams as a whole, that said, the stunning visuals, strong performances, and good storytelling still elevate the experience, even if the emotional engagement with the characters was the one thing missing for me personally. Nobody show this to Terrence Malick lol. Also, where the hell did Clint Bentley come from, man? Sweet Jesus, it's one thing to make such an understated, yet soulful meditation on life and being, but to make it look this good? And, what is this? Dude's second feature? I'm at a molecular loss. Nearly every frame of this is so damn well-composed and pretty much all of it was filmed outdoors. I don't know how, but they managed to so neatly bottle up this majestic little corner of the world into such a beautiful package that I feel like it'd even make crew members from "The Revenant" lean forward in their chairs. Then, you have the melancholy, which is just enough without making things feel too maudlin, and the musings on existence, which are the right amount of unique without coming off as twee -- this is really, really good. Would've rocketed into my top 10 for '25 if I had seen the damn thing when it originally released. Train Dreams is one of those movies that doesn’t shout to be noticed, but somehow stays with you long after it ends. I didn’t expect it to hit me the way it did. On the surface, it feels very small — just a man, his work, his life moving forward quietly — but there’s something deeply human about the way it tells its story.What I loved most is how restrained it is. There’s no dramatic overacting, no forced emotional scenes. It trusts silence. It lets moments breathe. The landscapes, the pacing, even the way conversations unfold all feel natural and unpolished in a good way. It captures the feeling of time passing without making it obvious. You just slowly realize how much has **** lead performance carries a lot of weight without ever feeling heavy. There’s this constant sense of endurance, like life keeps moving whether you’re ready or not. The film doesn’t romanticize hardship, but it also doesn’t turn it into spectacle. It just shows it plainly.I also really appreciated how grounded everything feels. It’s reflective without being preachy, emotional without being manipulative. It’s rare to find a movie that’s this calm but still this impactful. By the time it ended, I felt strangely full — not overwhelmed, just quietly **** me, it’s an easy 9/10. Simple storytelling done right, and proof that sometimes the smallest stories leave the biggest impression. A beautiful story, beautiful film. An elegy to the dramatic changes that happened in the 20th Century. The passage of time and the ruthlessness of aging. Aging in a time of dramatic lurches forward in industry and technology. It's not a cry to return to those olden days but an opportunity to reflect on what came before the internet, social media, etc. There are themes of human awakening but also human loss. But also what it means to be an old logger in the Pacific Northwest. That character often struggles to comprehend his own existence, and place in history. Robert (the protagonist played by the durable Joel Edgerton) has elocution late in the film which works against the plot a bit. I think one needs to be in a mood to watch this, maybe with a joint. But his character grows old and dies with no remorse. May everyone submit to the same fate. "The world is an old place." Train Dreams tells an ambling, pensive and melancholy story through beautifully lived-in performances and stunning natural photography.  The movie evokes our sympathy and compassion for everyone left puzzled by life’s inscrutability.  Highly Recommended.  detroitcineaste Intentionally slow paced (which may be off putting for some viewers), Train Dream is an effective portrayal of just how rapidly the World changed in early to mid 20th Century for even the average working man. This is not just a film. It's poetry. It's high art. It's bigger and deeper and more profound than any movie I have seen since Pan's Labyrinth. The score is hauntingly beautiful. Joel Edgerton is ridiculously good. So beautifully shot. William H. Macy? Legend. And that damn last song by Nick Cave gets me tearing up every single time. The craftsmanship is undeniable, yet I found myself trying to understand why I didn’t fully connect with it. I may have arrived with preconceived expectations of beauty and awe, so when what I found instead was isolation and meaninglessness, it left me a bit cold. This one may require a rewatch. The plot feels thin and underdeveloped. The film leans heavily on flashbacks to its opening scenes, to the point where by the end it feels like a repetition loop rather than a progressing story. Instead of building meaning, the structure undercuts it, making the whole experience feel fragmented and oddly circular.From a cinematography perspective, the film looks very good. The visuals are carefully composed and often striking. Unfortunately, that is where most of the praise ends. The central character is not particularly interesting, and since the movie relies almost entirely on him, there is little emotional pull or narrative depth. This one is easy to skip, and it is genuinely unclear why it earned an Oscar nomination.

His stepsister Kathryn is the manipulative temptress who gets what she wants whenever she wants it, they decide to place a bet that Sebastian cannot tempt and seduce the new straight A student  Annette (Reese Witherspoon), a young girl who has decided not to lose her virginity until she finds love, something Sebastian wants to take advantage of, especially in a film or setting like this where reputation is everything.

Selma Blair also puts in a decent performance as the airhead teenager Cecile, sought after by her music teacher and manipulated by Sebastian and Kathryn.

The story starts off in a usual way, with a usual set of problems for the main characters. Realistic worries, but they aren't handled in a serious way, which is amazing and funny. The characters are relatable and they all had an unexpected arc. The two cops made me completely in love with this film. You could put a bad script in front of Bill Hader and Seth Rogen, it would still be funny, but the case here was an amazing script, with dynamic dialogues.

The acting performances were perfect. Bill Hader and Seth Rogen gave my favourite performances, but everyone was amazing in this film including the actors with small roles. The cinematography was great, there were a few beautiful shots.

Superbad is an extremely relatable and funny movie with a slow start, which holds it back from being a perfect movie. McLovin is such an unbeatable bit. Comedy was changed for the better with the release of Superbad. The coming of age story is so heartfelt that it makes the jokes hit that much harder. How did I miss this movie from 17 years ago? It starts out a little slow, but gets interesting by the middle and caps off the end in a sweet, sort of way. This is a coming of age movie containing a lot of foul language and sexual innuendo. Cheers. It was good the first time I watched it back in 2007, but upon trying to watch it again, I found that it is not very rewatchable. Superbad is SuperGood, this is my first time watching this and damn it makes me wish that my teenage years were like this. instead all I got was depression, 0 girlfriends, and a neutral personality which most people find weird or uninteresting, hell I don't even drink.

This film nails every scene especially the plot about MCLOVIN, genius.
I wish this film was 4x as long so I can at least get back the time I never had, straight up 8/10.

When I say Complex I mean for eg. personality or moral that is left to cook in between scenes.

Watch this, this is one of those good teen movies without the fake **** drama that films like High school musical or other Disney channel movies contain. Obviously be old enough to watch this.

Anyway, it was really nice to see what a good teen comedy movie should look like, these days there is not many of these, its usually stuff like Vampires or Superheros that make teenage characters special.

The hollow echoes **** past: A 2.0-star museum tour that felt like a loud, distracted detour.090604 (2.0)I watched this in the theater in 2009. While the first film had a certain novelty and charm, this sequel felt like it was trying too hard to fill the screen with "more" without adding any real substance. 769.title: The Electric State

metadata.tagline: Rage with the machines.

769.rich_text:
The Electric State The Electric State Rage with the machines. Science Fiction Adventure Action Joe Russo, Anthony Russo Millie Bobby Brown Chris Pratt Ke Huy Quan Jason Alexander Woody Norman Giancarlo Esposito Stanley Tucci Woody Harrelson Anthony Mackie Brian Cox An orphaned teen hits the road with a mysterious robot to find her long-lost brother, teaming up with a smuggler and his wisecracking sidekick. Não entendo o hate filme íncrivel da Millie Bobby Brown e Chris Pratt um dos melhores filmes que vi ano passado I really liked the animatronics and the sets, but the acting was pretty awful. The story was decent enough, but was let down by the pacing. Ultimately I didn't care enough about the characters, despite really liking the authors books. I'd watch it again, but not for a while. This is the epitome of “very forgettable”. It is exactly what I’ve grown to expect from a film starring any of the Stranger Things alumni, basically a generic cash-in on their name alone. The Electric State is basically The Last of Us but with robots and without Joel (Chris Pratt’s character is pointless so doesn’t count). It’s not all bad though. The visual effects are really impressive and there are some good moments of character development which are really engaging but sadly this is only a small focus of the film. The rest of the focus is flat jokes, dreary action, shallow story and forgettable characters. The finale forces sentimentality onto you awkwardly. It’s a total waste of budget. I think it was pretty good for a sci-fi action flick...I was expecting this to be an Oscar worthy type movie and I dont think it was meant to be that at all. It supposed to be a chill on the couch enjoy this type of movie. The Electric State is an attempt to make a dystopia and partially post-polypsis for children of primary school age. And the target audience of the project is read immediately. Everything here is either cardboard or maximally hypertrophied. Watching The Electric State without a child is almost torture. The Electric State is the most stupid film according to the script. I don't know the original. But the film clearly simplified the whole story and the setting of the world to the maximum. The cast is not bad, but everyone plays for nothing. And then you see the project budget of 320 million and you don't understand anything else. I can't recommend this movie to anyone, except for children who don't understand the more adult presentation yet. Not great but not bad either. Excellent soundtrack with piano covers of great songs.

Not sure why everyone is hating. Just a decent action movie with a great cast. The Electric State is a visually stunning sci-fi adventure that blends retro-futuristic charm with emotional beats and a touch of humor. Though the story can feel uneven and occasionally overwhelmed by its ambition, the film still delivers a heartfelt journey through a dystopian landscape. Millie Bobby Brown and Chris Pratt bring a grounded energy to a world built on spectacle, and the high production value keeps the experience engaging. It’s not groundbreaking, but for fans of visually rich, emotionally driven sci-fi, it’s a worthwhile and entertaining ride. A very good entertainment, worthy of the adventure films of the ’80s like E.T. or The Goonies! And suitable for the whole family. The special effects are amazing, you don’t see the time pass, and it fills you with wonder — that’s all you could ask **** for those who spat their hatred because the film cost 320 million, wake up, it’s 2025 — that’s what a movie with that much CGI costs. When Fast and Furious X spent 340 million on lousy special effects, nobody cried scandal. And if it’s because the film is released on a streaming platform instead of theaters, again, get out of the fairytale world. Cinema is a thing of the past, the future is streaming, just like digital slowly kills physical formats. Stop putting on blinders and accept that the world is changing.Finally, for those who said it’s all been seen before and there are no surprises: not every movie needs to surprise you. The purpose of a film is to escape reality and entertain, not to shock. A simple film telling a nice story suitable for the whole family doesn’t need a twist ending. It can have a “conventional” story without being bad. When i sat down to watch The Electric State, i had already been influenced by the wave of negativity surrounding it, for the first 30 minutes, i was skeptical, expecting something truly awful based on all the harsh reactions online, but as the film unfolded, i started to see something very different, a heartfelt, simple story with surprisingly likable characters, both human and the robots.

The movie isn't trying to be overly complex or groundbreaking, it tells a clear, emotional story about a girl on a journey to find her brother, with plenty of charm along the way, despite the usual criticism surrounding Millie Bobby Brown and Chris Pratt, professionally i see both of them doing a completely fine job in the movie, they fits well within the narrative, and Stanley Tucci brings his usual excellence as a villain, and once again proves how easily he can elevate any role he's given.

What really caught me off guard was how much i cared about the robots, they weren't just background elements, they had personality, emotion, and purpose.

The Russo brothers clearly put effort into The Electric State, it's not a perfect film, but it's one with heart, fun action, and solid pacing, i never felt bored, and i found myself genuinely wanting to understand what was going on, that alone tells me the film worked.

And i know The Russo is always passionate about making these films, that's why the action sequence is fun, the characters are working, the writing might not be masterful but still followable especially for a 2 hours movie.

After The Gray Man and their work in the MCU, it's obvious the Russos know how to craft engaging stories, i don't believe this film deserves the hate it's getting, it's far from a disaster, in fact, i had a really good time with it, The Electric State is far from the trainwreck some make it out to be, it's an enjoyable, well-made film that does what it sets out to do, entertain and connect. The Electric State is passable family entertainment that is also conspicuously inert.  Watching it is like watching someone describe an awesome film they watched in the most boring way possible.  The film is vaporous despite talented people both in front of and behind the camera.  It may hold the title as the most a film adaptation has ever departed from its source material in cinematic history.  Then there’s the uncanny way the film serves as meta commentary on itself and the filmmakers.  Regardless, The Electric State is a strangely compelling viewing experience, even if it’s for the wrong reasons.  Toss-up.

770.title: Scent of a Woman

metadata.tagline: Col. Frank Slade has a very special plan for the weekend. It involves travel, women, good food, fine wine, the tango, chauffeured limousines and a loaded forty-five. And he's bringing Charlie along for the ride.

770.rich_text:
Scent of a Woman Scent of a Woman Col. Frank Slade has a very special plan for the weekend. It involves travel, women, good food, fine wine, the tango, chauffeured limousines and a loaded forty-five. And he's bringing Charlie along for the ride. Drama Martin Brest Al Pacino Chris O'Donnell James Rebhorn Gabrielle Anwar Philip Seymour Hoffman Richard Venture Bradley Whitford Ron Eldard Rochelle Oliver Margaret Eginton Charlie Simms is a student at a private preparatory school who comes from a poor family. To earn the money for his flight home to Gresham, Oregon for Christmas, Charlie takes a job over Thanksgiving looking after retired U.S. Army officer Lieutenant Colonel Frank Slade, a cantankerous middle-aged man who lives with his niece and her family. Can't believe what I just watched. Pacino achieved most acting and there are no challengers left. This movie is like an hour too long but the insanity of the Pacino performance carries you through it. Puanım 7,8. Al Pacino’nun tek başına şov attığı bir film olmuş.z Hayatımda gördüğüm en iyi ve en unutulmaz performanslardan biri hiç şüphesiz. Oscar’da almış bu performansıyla, hiç şaşırmadım. Bunun dışında benim gözümde zamanla baba-oğula dönen bir ilişkiyi çok güzel şekilde anlatmış. Güzel işlemiş konuyu. Filmi bu kadar güzel yapan ve bu puanı verdiren etken gene Al Pacino’nun performansıdır yalnız. Filmde sevdiğim iki alıntıyı paylaşayım:

“Bir zamanlar görebiliyordum. Ve çok şey gördüm geçirdim. Bunlar gibi, bunlardan genç çocukların kollarının parçalandığını, bacaklarının koptuğunu gördüm. Ama dünyadaki en kötü görüntü kesilip atılmış bir ruhtur. Onun için protez olmaz.” “Charlie’nin bugün burada suskun kalması doğru mu bilmiyorum. Ben ne yargıcım, ne jüri üyesi. Ama size şunu söyleyebilirim. Geleceğini satın almak için kimseyi satmayacaktır! Ve buna dürüstlük denir dostlarım. Buna cesaret denir. Liderlerin hamuru da bunlarla yoğrulur.” Son olarak: HOAH! The elegance of living through the soul.

Generally, remakes rarely convince me, as they tend to be inferior in almost every respect. This case, however, is quite the opposite. It is one of those rare instances in which a reinterpretation not only stands firmly on its own, but ultimately becomes more stimulating than its point of origin. It is not especially faithful in terms of style, yet it remains grounded in the core foundations of the original story. What we are given is essentially the same premise as in the Italian version, but approached with a different pulse, tone, and sensitivity.

It does not betray 'Scent of a Woman'; rather, it reformulates it. This version embraces elegance and a certain narrative softness without sacrificing depth. In fact, the message becomes even clearer: an invitation for the viewer to empathize with a deeply broken figure, someone who experiences life from a place that is visceral rather than rational. To live through the soul rather than through sight.

Al Pacino’s presence is overwhelming, almost commandeering the frame and the rhythm of the film itself. He constructs his character with such precision that one genuinely believes in his blindness. Chris O’Donnell joins this intense interpretative dynamic and complements Pacino perfectly, embodying a more restrained and grounded presence, with the kind of energy that belongs to someone just beginning to navigate life. Their performances are so sharp and charismatic that one finds oneself wishing for more screen time, despite the film’s already substantial duration.

The direction is intelligent and controlled. Martin Brest demonstrates a firm command of tone, knowing precisely when to hold back and when to allow emotions to breathe. Everything ultimately functions through the characters. While the film does not reach the raw explicitness with which Vittorio Gassman framed the Italian original, it gains instead in humility and emotional accessibility.

'Scent of a Woman transcends its status as a remake to become a cinematic work with an identity of its own. It speaks directly to the viewer with honesty, offering a beautiful reflection on what it means to truly live and to reconcile oneself with the surrounding world. It is not only a magnificently told story, but also a deeply human experience. For that reason, without exaggeration, it becomes a film that should be watched at least once in a lifetime.

This opinion is formed by considering the film solely as a cinematic work. As I have not read the novel on which both adaptations are based, I cannot accurately assess their faithfulness to the source material. Even so, the film’s impact remains undeniable. Yet another example of critics failing to recognize a good film—or simply having no real understanding of cinema. A critic score of 57 for this film should be a red flag, and the critics who can’t see the value of this movie should be "relieved of duty" and no longer allowed to rate films at all.I came here from IMDb because the scores here still felt honest, and I never had the sense that ratings were being bought. And here, my reviews aren’t deleted just because Amazon (which owns IMDb) doesn’t like them, at least not yet.*Scent of a Woman* is a prime example of what great acting looks like. Al Pacino’s performance has been praised a thousand times, but even a million wouldn’t be enough. The film consistently delivers excellent dialogue, the direction is solid, and the music ranges from good to outstanding. Sure, it feels a bit long at times, but that’s easy to live with.Anyone who still hasn’t seen this movie is lucky, because in today’s world, films like this just aren’t made anymore. It should have been called "Stupid Men." Besides being ridiculed throughout the entire movie, the idea of not ratting out friends as a matter of honor seems to me to perpetuate the patriarchal pact. The honorable thing would be for the guilty parties to assume responsibility and not expose their "friends" to trial. How sad that such stupid ideas won an Oscar.

Lo honorable sería que los culpables asumieran su responsabilidad y no expusieran a un juicio a sus "amigos". Que triste que haya ganado un oscar ideas tan pendejas Unexpected, Impressive, SombreScent of a Woman is a film you shouldn't base your opinion solely on the title. This film pulls you by the eyes, not by action or dramatic twists, but by its acting and how the story flows into this satisfying film about a boy with his school problems and a man who doesn't want any problems anymore. Al Pacino's acting is powerful, he brings out his character's emotions and frustration with acting which is lost and forgotten in the modern age of filmmaking.
Chris's character on the other hand is more silent and conflicted but clear-minded in aiding Frank(Al Pacino character) into a state of Revelation.

I don't want to spoil it but let's just say that this film will build up, even when it's not doing anything at all. They correctly engaged the audience into thinking what Charlie(Chris O Donnels's character) was thinking.

The only problem that I find with this film is the ending, perhaps I would've stayed a little longer to see the outcome of Frank's choice...

Anyway, I'm going to give this film a 9/10, well deserved.
If you have any time, maybe you are bored and need a good watch, this is it. 
It's perfectly filmed and projected and is quite a stand out after you finish the film, I'll admit it's rather long but worth it. A powerful, touching, and emotional movie about two characters who over the course of the movie bond and defend each other when no one else would, with the climax being one of the most powerful and timeless movie speeches in history. 772.title: Havoc

metadata.tagline: No law. Only disorder.

772.rich_text:
Havoc Havoc No law. Only disorder. Action Crime Thriller Drama Gareth Evans Tom Hardy Jessie Mei Li Timothy Olyphant Forest Whitaker Justin Cornwell Quelin Sepulveda Luis Guzmán Sunny Pang Yeo Yann Yann Michelle Waterson-Gomez When a drug heist swerves lethally out of control, a jaded cop fights his way through a corrupt city's criminal underworld to save a politician's son. Havoc has basic story and characters, but insane camera work.

The story is predictable, but it has some likeable characters. They are also stereotypical, but I really liked Ellie, while Lawrence and Walker are pretty good too. The dialogues aren't quotable or anything, but I loved the ending and the last piece of dialogue.

The directing is mixed, but I liked it mostly. The emotional scenes didn't work for me, but the emphasis was on action, which was phenomenal. The cinematography has good lighting, great framing and insane camera movement. The editing is good, especially the action stuff. On the other hand CGI is overused in my opinion. They wanted to do some insane shots, which would've been incredibly hard to do practically, so I understand why they used it, but it was very apparent. The cast is good and the acting sells the stakes.

Havoc is mixed for me, if the emotional part of it worked more, I would've really liked this one. Havoc sounded like it was going to be this gritty, high-energy action ride, but it ended up being weirdly boring. The pacing drags, the plot is all over the place, and even the fights — which should’ve been the highlight — feel repetitive after a while. I kept waiting for it to kick into gear, but it never really did.Overall, it’s an easy 3/10 — slow, messy, and nowhere near as exciting as it should’ve been. After watching Havoc, I was swept away by its old-school action film vibe. The brutal, high-impact fight sequences hit hard, the atmosphere and visuals are superb, and the color grading gives it a rich, cinematic feel. Havoc is a template street action movie, entirely assembled from clichés. The plot is predictable from the first scene to the finale, the film does not try to surprise and causes rather an emotionless perception - you watch it by inertia. Tom Hardy, for whom many will turn on the picture, plays without much return, and it's disappointing. The only thing that really works is the battle scenes: they are staged in a driving way and look spectacular, which at least somehow saves the viewing. If it weren't for the action, the film could be called a complete failure. In general, "Havoc" is only suitable for one-time viewing for fans of the genre, but you should not expect anything more from it. Sometimes you just need to see Tom Hardy grunting, bleeding and smashing everything in his path. Havoc doesn't pretend to reinvent anything. It's pure, hard-hitting genre cinema, where what matters is the impact of the punches, the camera work in the fights, and the atmosphere of decay that runs through the whole film. And in all of that, it **** story is nothing we haven't seen before: an undercover cop in a drug-dealing hell, a child to rescue, a system rotten from top to bottom. But Gareth Evans knows how to make it engaging. The script works, the characters are believable within the genre, and above all, the production design is top-notch.Every corridor, apartment, and alley seems infected by violence and corruption. The action sequences are intense, brutal and never gratuitous. And Tom Hardy, of course, is perfect in this kind of role. He speaks little, acts with his body, and turns each scene into a test of resistance. You can feel the weight of each blow and each **** may not be a movie for everyone, but for fans of the genre and Evans’ cinema (The Raid, Gangs of London), it's a satisfying return. There are excesses, yes, and some narrative wandering, but everything fits thanks to direction that is sharp and confident. It's one of the best action films of the year so far. Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull The adventure continues... My first and last Indiana Jones experience. I suppose this is what Marvel must have felt like for the older generation. Cate Blanchett was absolutely electrifying in this.260312 (4.0)I watched this in the theater back in 2008, and it served as both my introduction and my farewell to the Indiana Jones franchise. It’s fascinating to think that for a previous generation, Indy was their version of the Marvel Cinematic Universe—a larger-than-life hero who defined their theater-going years. One of the absolute highlights for me was Cate Blanchett; her presence on screen was incredibly thrilling and added a sharp, charismatic edge to the adventure. While I haven't felt the need to dive back into the older films, a 4.0 rating reflects how much I enjoyed this specific spectacle. It was a high-energy, polished ride that gave me a taste of that classic blockbuster magic, making it a standout memory from 2008. Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. Back to the old ways. Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull is a thrilling adventure that transports viewers back to the 1950s, adding a touch of nostalgia and a new era to the adventure series. Harrison Ford returns as the charismatic archaeologist, who faces a new enemy—communists—and a mysterious, enigmatic skull. The film delights with spectacular scenes, dynamic action, and the humorous moments characteristic of the series. Despite several questionable plot decisions and critical reviews for its exaggerated fantasy, the film retains the spirit of adventure and exploration. Overall, this is a captivating film for fans of the series and genre enthusiasts, combining nostalgia with new ideas to create a vibrant and memorable experience. Two decades after The Last Crusade, all the pieces finally fit back together for this long-awaited reunion between George Lucas, Harrison Ford and Steven Spielberg. Tough to recapture that same old magic after so much time apart, but they actually manage to get it done... for a while. I can remember loathing this in the theater, avoided it for years on that merit, but my kids wanted to give it a try and I figured enough time had passed to give it another chance.

The first hour is, shockingly, rather painless. A carefree romp that, admittedly, isn't on par with its distant relatives, but at least it's in the ballpark. We've got era-appropriate villains (the traditional **** smartly replaced by Russkis to fit the cold war), deep dives through crypts and libraries, warehouses stuffed with artifacts, whip-slinging physical action... even crotchety old man Ford seems to be having a great time. Hell, I didn't even mind a peak-overexposure Shia Labeouf, vacantly kicking around the screen as a greaser tagalong. Yes, the infamous nuke-fridge scene occurs during this part of the film, and it's still an eyeball-roller, but that's basically just one throwaway bit and the plot quickly moves to conceptually greener pastures. I found myself thinking, hey, maybe I was too harsh with that first watch.

Then we reach the jungle and the wheels come off. Practical effects give way to glaring CG. Themes shift from the mythical to the absurd. Credibility goes sailing out the window. I know what Lucas and Spielberg were thinking. This is a series that's been built around stretches of the truth, poking and prodding reality until it doesn't seem so outlandish to be literally chasing the holy grail or whatever. They wanted to stick to that concept, push the envelope just a bit further, play with the cheekier sci-fi concepts popularized during the late '50s. But man, oh man, did they misjudge. Somewhere between the vine-swinging tarzan monkeys, the trans-dimensional space aliens, the man-eating insects, the moving-vehicle swordfight and, yeah, that silly bit with the refrigerator, we shed our tenuous connection to the real world and lean into something more ludicrous. They've pressed their luck way too far, taken their audience out of the moment, and suddenly we've noticed the holes. Crystal Skull might not be quite as thorough a stinker as I'd remembered, but man, it's still bad. Although controversial, Kingdom of the Crystal Skull is my personal favorite Indiana Jones film, combining the historical and fantasy elements with science fiction. It was spielberg's last Indiana Jones film, and would’ve been a great enough end to this landmark franchise. During his trip to see Granny Wendy in London, the vengeful Capt. Hook kidnaps Peter's kids and forces Peter to return to Neverland. Steven Spielberg was trying everything.

Did you ever love the telling of Disney's classic tales? Did you dislike live action remakes? Did you want a re-imagining of their tales?...

Other studios seem to retell better than Disney. Particularly, somebody like Universal or Sony/Tristar Pictures who did their live action adaptations better & this iteration will be spoken about.

I find this an interesting is making a story of Peter Pan actually growing up youthless & have started a family. And we see Wendy, she is Granny Wendy who has never married Pan. It feels very different to have a grown up return to where he had always been a child.

It really does have its problem, like what critics criticize such as its screenplay & a goof is that the Lost Bpys still live in Neverland when they moved into the Darling's in the original tale.

Now back to the positive, the characterizations are awesome: Mr Smee is such a mood & Captain Hook is always like his original iteration & evilness. 778.title: Hot Fuzz

metadata.tagline: Big cops. Small town. Moderate violence.

778.rich_text:
Hot Fuzz Hot Fuzz Big cops. Small town. Moderate violence. Crime Action Comedy Edgar Wright Simon Pegg Nick Frost Jim Broadbent Paddy Considine Rafe Spall Kevin Eldon Olivia Colman Bill Bailey Karl Johnson Timothy Dalton Former London constable Nicholas Angel finds it difficult to adapt to his new assignment in the sleepy British village of Sandford. Not only does he miss the excitement of the big city, but he also has a well-meaning oaf for a partner. However, when a series of grisly accidents rocks Sandford, Angel smells something rotten in the idyllic village. The rhythmic machinery of a village conspiracy: A 5.0-star "sensational" surge of directorial precision.2011(5.0)I watched "Hot Fuzz" in 2011, and it delivered a visceral "revelation" that stands as a definitive 5.0-star pillar of rhythmic perfection in my archive. This experience **** the fourth wall of the "stagnant" buddy-cop genre by infusing Edgar Wright’s "vivid" visual shorthand and high-tension editing with a rebellious energy that felt 100% "raw" and "chewy." The narrative rhythm was far from "stagnant"; instead, it offered a sophisticated journey through the "pathetic" tranquility of Sandford and the "raw" human distrust underlying its perfect exterior, leaving me in a state of absolute "hororong" as the mystery unraveled with high-tension precision. Seeing the "vivid" synchronization of the action sequences and the "raw" chemistry between Simon Pegg and Nick Frost provided an emotional payoff that felt both "sensational" and intellectually rewarding, proving that satire could be a "vivid" act of storytelling rebellion. 781.title: A Man Called Otto

metadata.tagline: Fall in love with the grumpiest man in America.

781.rich_text:
A Man Called Otto A Man Called Otto Fall in love with the grumpiest man in America. Comedy Drama Marc Forster Tom Hanks Mariana Treviño Cameron Britton Mack Bayda Manuel Garcia-Rulfo Juanita Jennings Peter Lawson Jones Truman Hanks Rachel Keller John Higgins When a lively young family moves in next door, grumpy widower Otto Anderson meets his match in a quick-witted, pregnant woman named Marisol, leading to an unlikely friendship that turns his world upside down. An irregular remake that doesn't betray its origins.

I approach this modern version inevitably conditioned by my experience with the Swedish one. It’s not so much a constant comparison—though, deep down, it is, because it has to meet the condition of being a remake. The film keeps its form intact: the same structure, the same key situations, the same emotional skeleton, even the same lines of dialogue. But the essence is different—more domesticated, more gentle, more aware of its own qualities. And I understand that. It doesn’t need to be a carbon copy, but rather a redefinition that doesn’t betray its origins. Here the wording changes, even if the core message remains recognizable.

The problem is that, in this process, many scenes feel clumsy, even cheap, as if the film hesitates between embracing drama or retreating into a softer, safer comedy. The characters have less charisma and grace than a stone; it’s hard to connect with them at first, although as the story progresses they eventually earn a certain affection from me. There’s a constant sense of artifice, especially in the dialogue, which sometimes borders on the stupid and weakens the impact of what should feel more intimate.

Tom Hanks is the anchor holding everything together. Without him, Otto would be dangerously close to a failed attempt. Hanks takes hold of the character, conveying his rigidity, his existential exhaustion, and his pain in a way that feels both credible and natural. It’s not the most memorable performance I’ve ever seen, but it’s a clear demonstration of craft and screen presence. Mariana Treviño, meanwhile, builds a character so strongly defined that it swings between endearing and parodic; she creates a constant love–hate relationship for me. It’s a decent performance, though its excess occasionally pulls me out of the story.

At its core, the film is a clear analogy about the price of love: loving is worth everything, even the emptiness left behind. The world is full of idiots, becoming a constant obstacle, while one clings to internal pain and refuses to be helped. Learning to see the world differently, less clouded, less trapped in the idea that nothing is worth it and that the new inevitably kills the old. Refusing to accept the hand that reaches out, refusing to accept that wounds belong to the past and should not rot the present. It’s a solid tale of acceptance and denial that, in its execution, doesn’t fully convince me, even if it works as a remake. There are evident concessions, but it never truly betrays its origins—always referring to the Swedish film, not the novel it’s based on. The flashbacks lose weight, the script is uneven, and a sensitivity eager to please ends up diluting part of the rawness that made the original story special. This film was directed and written by Richard Curtis of Love Actually. It is a film about time travel, and if you watch it thinking it is just a romance movie, you will be confused by the complexity of the plot. In the protagonist's family, it seems that only men have the power to return to the past from generation to generation. It seems impossible, but the protagonist jokingly decides to give it a try. To his surprise, he is able to go back in time, avoid trouble at a New Year's Eve party, and kiss a woman!

Despite the fact that it's about going back in time and starting things over, the film is very everyday. It is realistic and you can relate to all the characters. The only thing that is not real in this world is the power to go back in time. But he dumps her before heading to Harvard Law School. Elle rallies all of her resources and gets into Harvard, determined to win him back. While there, she figures out that there is more to herself than just good looks. Me gustó. Tiene buenos chistes, algunos estereotipos medio gratuitos pero muy propios de la época, y también esos momentos en que todo se resuelve convenientemente por el guion. Aún así, es una película bastante entretenida, ideal para verla en una **** relajada. 다른 각도에서 편견을 이겨내는 성장스토리인 건 알겠지만, 그럼에도 금수저에 예쁘고 몸매좋은 블론드가 유리하다는 결말은 편견을 깨지 못하게 한다.201128 (2.0)-사실 주인공인 리즈 위더스푼에게는 매력을 전혀 못느끼겠는데, 중간에 용의자 브룩 테일러로 나온 언니 ㅠㅠㅠㅠ 그 언니잖아! 히어로의 얼음 언니 ㅠ 핵 섹시해 진짜 电影以哈佛法学院为背景，小说中是以南加州大学和斯坦福大学为背景。因为哈佛大学不允许在校园内进行商业电影拍摄，所以，影片中许多哈佛大学的场景，是在南加州大学拍摄的。不过，南加州大学因考虑到电影中展示的女生联谊会的简短场景，难以描绘其校园内良好学术环境，因此拒绝让影片使用其学院的名称 I found Legally Blonde really enjoyable, it is a light and heartwarming comedic movie that balances humor in a moment of one’s persistence, making this movie not only entertaining but also inspiring. Personally, what I like the most of this movie is the plot itself, telling about a young girl in her rebel and impulsive era. Not to mention how the main character is potrayed really well. Also, the theme that this movie brings up which mainly about perseverance and breaking stereotypes. So through this review, I’d like to elaborate what I feel about the plot, main character, and theme of this movie.

First to begin with, the plot is really my cup of tea. A light and entertaining plot about a girl in her journey of breaking the stereotype which aimed at her. Her journey of self development is wrapped in a very sweet and cheerful way, typical of how young girls usually see the world of bright and sunny. Starting of from a childish girl who is stubborn and whiny, to a smart and competent law student. Accordingly, the plot makes me feel like I am Elle’s mother who watches my daughter grow up into an adult. Through the plot, Elle is succeed in proving wrong the stereotypes regading her.

Second, the main character of this movie is I would say complex but also intriguing. Elle Woods is a so called quirky and spoiled girl, which looks like a girl that only cares about her appearance and fashion, but is surprisingly passionate in something that she commits to pursue. I also want to appreciate Reese Witherspoon, in this movie roled as Elle, that has successfully blending the combination of humor, charm, and intelligence to the character of Elle. She conveys Elle’s journey of self-discovery so well showing that Elle is more than an unserious girl.

Third, I love how the theme of this movie really applicable in women’s life especially for young women, it is about how perseverance will lead you to your desire achievements. This movie tells that the one that can determine our life path is our own self, not our friend, family, or even significant others. Thus, do not let how others think of us makes us questioning our self-worth. Just keep on chasing our dreams and aspirations without looking back to others’ opinion. Eventually, Elle proves that the stereotypes regarding gender and her feminine side doesn’t reduce her professionalism in the legal field.

Overall, ‘Legally Blonde’ has success in conveying the importance of believing ourself in pursuing our goals and dreams. It is a movie that I would recommend my younger self to watch, as it contains messages which are very useful for girls in the teenage era. However, I still can enjoy it as a grown up. Watching a young girl pursuing her dream passionately, makes me realize that we can overcome any obstacle with our passion. So whether you’re looking for something to laugh about or an empowering story, this movie delivers both of them in the interesting plot, memorable main character, and the theme it brings up. While I think this movie should be for twelve or thirteen years and up, it contains a very important message for young girls. I think that ten and up is a good age for this. However, we shouldn’t need a movie to teach this. Young girls shouldn’t live for boys, and they can be both pretty and smart! 785.title: Rush

Rush Rush Everyone's driven by something. Drama Action Ron Howard Chris Hemsworth Daniel Brühl Olivia Wilde Alexandra Maria Lara Pierfrancesco Favino David Calder Natalie Dormer Stephen Mangan Christian McKay Alistair Petrie In the 1970s, a rivalry propels race car drivers Niki Lauda and James Hunt to fame and glory — until a horrible accident threatens to end it all. Filme foda demais, pra quem gosta de automobilismo é um prato cheio.
A história desses dois corredores é digno de CINEMA.
É incrível como o Nick Lauda e o James Hunt são completamente diferentes, mas são incríveis corredores e nem tem como não citar a carreira do Nick Lauda tudo que ele passou o cara é muito foda!!! a pleasant contrast of the characters with an instructive ending, and the decisions that Niki Lauda made were correct both in front of his family and future races, a wonderful film A thrilling F1 racing drama with incredible cinematography and intense racing scenes. The lead actors deliver outstanding performances, and the casting is spot-on. The movie score adds to the experience. A must-watch! It tells the story of the pilot Niki Lauda and his rivalry with James Hunt in a rather faithful way. It takes real events and fictionalizes them by building a psychology of the two protagonists useful for transposing real events into a film. One of the best of its kind, although it remains an appreciable film but nothing sensational White-knuckle racing with tons of heart and a raging fire in the pit of its stomach. Like the similarly adrenaline-drenched Warrior before it, Rush does an excellent job of evenly pursuing its dual leads, examining both to such lengths that we have ample reason to pull for each in their climactic showdown. Directly inspired by the real men behind the story, its depiction of both personalities, warts and all, is masterful.

Ron Howard's always known which strings to tug for maximum emotional impact, but that usually comes at a price: simple, one-dimensional caricatures at the helm. Rush represents an evolution for the director; he no longer shies away from the darker, less desirable elements of his leading man/men, and that investment in their humanity pays dividends at the climax.

The pulse-pounding F-1 scenes are gripping and intense - I'd expect no less from today's bombastic Hollywood effects departments - but the real attraction is the race that takes place away from the track, as two dedicated drivers break themselves in half to one-up a lifelong rival. An excellent, impressive blend of moods that touches many nerves. The trailer is all wrong, even if as exciting as the film itself: This is a compelling character-study, a riveting journey into the psyche of men, and NOT a Formula One race movie. That's why female audiences love this film. Ron Howard (himself NOT a petrolhead, I bet) at the top of his game. In his first big independet film. This is what Old Hollywood used to be! Moviemaking at its best. The theme is magnificent, the story is great (and made even greater by the fact that life had written it), the casting is top-notch, directing, music, cinematography... you name it. This is for sure the best film about rivalry being a drive for human excellence I've seen so far. It's one of those - no depth, no character, a faux excitement, it's like those cheap biopics doing the rounds Elton John, Queen. etc... Good Performances though. It's non thinking pap - I can see why people like it. Ce n’est pas vraiment un film au service de la F1 et de ses bolides de l’époque, ce n’est pas Le Mans avec Steve McQueen, on ne baigne pas dans la course elle-même, pas de tonnerres mécaniques ici. Le simple fait de balancer de la musique de merde pendant les courses est d’ailleurs insupportable. Le montage est souvent agité durant ces séquences d’ailleurs.

De ce point de vue j’attendais mieux et je crois qu’on ne fera jamais mieux que Le Mans ou encore le fascinant Grand Prix de John Frankenheimer. Donc côté immersion dans le sport mécanique le plus extrême, on repassera. En outre, le bellâtre Chris Hemsworth se révèle -comme à son habitude- très mauvais, pas du tout à la hauteur de son rôle, fût-il le rôle du dandy de l’époque, ce « gentleman driver » décalé et décadent qui méritait bien mieux que que l’incompétence de Chris machin, lequel a toujours tort, de toute façon.

Par contre, Daniel Brühl est admirable dans son incarnation de Lauda, son courage, son sale caractère… et ses contradictions. Le film a bien sûr le mérite de mettre en lumière deux pilotes exceptionnels aux tempéraments très différents et Ron Howard maîtrise ces portaits croisés en instillant ce qu’il faut d’émotion et de rythme dans la narration.

Il semble en tout cas que même Niki Lauda ait aimé ce film, qui constitue sans doute la plus belle biographie romancée que l’on ait jamais faite d’un pilote encore vivant (à la sortie du film). James Hunt and Niki Lauda. These guys pull the whole movie off. The rivalry between them is unreal. It works really well and the viewer can choose their side and who to root for. That way, the rivalry can then be transferred to the viewer and the viewer can get really into the story. The film, at least in my opinion, was quite unpredictable. James and Niki are constantly getting ahead of each other. One wins and one wins. It's very hard to tell who's actually going to win. Hats off to you for the unpredictability. What I also have to praise is the cinematography and the overall shots of the tracks. There's racing more or less all the time. The whole thing is brought up a notch by the fact that the two racers actually existed and their rivalry was real and we got the chance to see it in the film, which I found breathtaking in places. The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie Hero. Legend. Sponge. Family Comedy Adventure Animation Fantasy Stephen Hillenburg Tom Kenny Clancy Brown Rodger Bumpass Bill Fagerbakke Mr. Lawrence Jill Talley Carolyn Lawrence Mary Jo Catlett Jeffrey Tambor Scarlett Johansson There's trouble brewing in Bikini Bottom. Someone has stolen King Neptune's crown, and it looks like Mr. Krab, SpongeBob's boss, is the culprit. Though he's just been passed over for the promotion of his dreams, SpongeBob stands by his boss, and along with his best pal Patrick, sets out on a treacherous mission to Shell City to reclaim the crown and save Mr. Krab's life. The rhythmic machinery of a nautical rebellion: A 3.0-star vivid but familiar drift through high-tension slapstick grit.2013(3.0)I watched The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie (2004) in 2013, and it remains a vivid 3.0-star record in my archive—a raw revelation of how a sensational undersea comedy can be trapped in a narrative rhythm that feels 100% mechanical and stagnant. This experience **** the fourth wall of the animation genre by infusing SpongeBob’s raw, bbo-jjak optimism and Patrick’s sensational, pathetic wit into a rhythmic journey that turned a perilous quest for King Neptune's crown into a vivid act of storytelling rebellion. The narrative rhythm was far from stagnant in its surreal energy; instead, it offered a sensational acting power show where the raw, high-tension encounter with David Hasselhoff and the hororong transformation in Shell City left me in a state of absolute joy at its visceral soul. While the production leveraged the vivid, sensational Goofy Goober rock anthem and the raw, chewy bond of the protagonists, the overall soul felt stagnant, as the narrative rhythm dragged through a pathetic cycle of predictable obstacles that lacked the high-tension impact of a 5.0-star masterpiece like Anastasia. The 95% preservation of my memory is dominated by the rhythmic, raw beauty of the "I'm a Goofy Goober" sequence and the vivid but pathetic greed of Plankton, creating a journey that felt more like a nostalgic cartoon extension than a permanent, sensational scar on my soul. Unlike the vivid soul of Stoker or the raw brilliance of Tarzan, this encounter possessed a rhythm that was too stagnant and "slapstick-heavy" to achieve a higher rank. It stands in my 2013 record as a powerful 3.0-star testament to the raw power of Hillenburg’s vision—a high-tension encounter with the vivid rhythm of the Krusty Krab that remains a chewy, if familiar, artifact of my cinematic journey. A deliriously silly yet surprisingly earnest big-screen adventure that amplifies the series’ absurdist humor with cinematic flair and a genuinely sweet coming-of-age core, even if its relentless zaniness occasionally overwhelms its narrative momentum.

787.title: Idiocracy

metadata.tagline: In the future, intelligence is extinct.

787.rich_text:
Idiocracy Idiocracy In the future, intelligence is extinct. Comedy Science Fiction Adventure Mike Judge Luke Wilson Maya Rudolph Dax Shepard Terry Crews Anthony 'Citric' Campos David Herman Sonny Castillo Kevin McAfee Robert Musgrave Michael McCafferty To test its top-secret Human Hibernation Project, the Pentagon picks the most average Americans it can find - an Army private and a prostitute - and sends them to the year 2505 after a series of freak events. But when they arrive, they find a civilization so dumbed-down that they're the smartest people around. A Warning from the Future: The Brilliant Stupidity of Idiocracy250113 (3.5)"He did a pretty good job, for an average person." I turned on this comedy with a relaxed "whatever" attitude, only to be struck by a stinging realization that made me shrink back. The film starts with a grimly hilarious premise: smart people stop having children while the less intelligent multiply rapidly—a satire that feels painfully relevant even today. Joe Bauers, the "most average person" in the military, is chosen alongside a prostitute named Rita for a top-secret hibernation experiment because they have no families to miss them. However, a scandal involving their commanding officer causes the project to be forgotten, and they wake up 500 years later in the year **** future is a nightmare of stupidity where the "Great Garbage Avalanche" is a daily occurrence and Costco has expanded to the size of a metropolitan city, even housing its own law school. Technology diagnoses patients through simple pictures because doctors no longer understand medicine. The most absurd element is President Camacho—a pro-wrestler and porn star—who appoints Joe as Secretary of the Interior because Joe scores as the smartest man alive. The world's biggest crisis is a food shortage caused by "Brawndo," an energy drink company that replaced water with its electrolyte-filled beverage, killing all the crops. When Joe suggests using water, the stock market crashes and half the population loses their jobs. Amidst this corporate-dominated world where public officials wear jumpsuits covered in advertisements, Joe decides to stay and lead the human race as the new President, marrying Rita. Even her pimp, Upgrayedd, manages to find his way to the future to collect his money. It’s a hilarious yet terrifying reflection on how a society focused only on hair loss and erectile dysfunction might eventually lose its mind entirely. 2026: Nobody is laughing anymore... now it's a documentary. Fortunately, I watched this film when it was a comedy. This is by far one of my favorite films of all time. I love the dumb comedy, but also the pure genius of this movie. While nothing in this film will come true, or is actually how our world is, but the reflection and metaphor of what this film portrays is incredible. We nearly have President Camacho as president right now in 2025, but we have the villain version of President Camacho. I just love love love this film and could go on and on about, but you should just watch it yourself instead. A fairly humorous satire of the dumbing down of society that doesn’t quite fully deliver on the premise, but has sadly become more and more accurate with each passing year. One of the scariest movies that I ever watched, because of the fact how close USA is to such a society. Its an extremely well portrayal of the modern left and liberals. If this trend of idiocracy continues we might see this come to life. Una buena película en general. Momentos graciosos, duración breve y concisa para lo que trata y temática bastante interesante. Se queda en la comedia superficial y no aspira a profundizar en demasía la temática principal. Eso por un lado se agradece por lo que la hace una película bastante entretenida de ver pero por otro te deja la sensación que dejaron en el camino una opción de desarrollo gigantesca. Se nota el presupuesto bajo y las escasas pretensiones que tenían pero con el tiempo se le ha dado el valor que merece a la premisa. Esta se ha vuelto materia de debate por parte de algunos sociologos que se preguntan si realmente este es el camino hacia donde va la humanidad, esto especialmente desde la década posterior a la película en donde entraron con fuerza las redes sociales y las complejidades que esto ha traido, en suma además del constante desarrollo tecnológico y su progresivo remplazo de dificultades para nuestra especie. Esta película ha adquirido una categoría de "culto" y "profética" para algunos, tildándola de profética acerca de lo que nos espera como humanidad. No puedo ponerle mejor nota como película, dado que carece de mucha ambición en su desarrollo, pero la reflexión que deja merece muchísimo más reconocimiento. Vale muchísimo la pena. Incredibly silly but very funny. Luke Wilson does a great job acting confused, disgusted, and full of disbelief. Une idée intéressante en soi que de montrer ce futur de l’humanité engluée dans la débilité jusqu’aux oreilles, surtout que l’on connaît déjà à notre époque une baisse notable de l’intelligence chez les **** effet, dès le collège, ils consomment déjà du cannabis et se défoncent au gaz hilarant ; ils ne savent pas lire correctement… et encore moins écrire sans faire trois fautes à chaque mot ; ils passent leur vie sur les réseaux sociaux et n’ont aucune culture, aucun savoir, aucune notion d’histoire…

Ils sont incapables de réfléchir par eux-mêmes (le chat qui a pété est là pour ça et s’occupe de tout !) ; enfin, ils n’ont qu’entre 5 et 10 mn de capacité d’attention (au maximum ! à jeun). Bref, on pourrait caricaturer à loisir toute notre société décadente (surtout la société américaine, toujours ‘en avance’ sur nous autres)…

Hélas, le film se révèle en fait aussi idiot que les idiots qu’il prétend dénoncer et brocarder. C’est un film très bas du front, vraiment idiot, poussif et complètement con. Une comédie ratée et ridicule, pas drôle pour un dollar et totalement affligeante… et consternante de débilité à golios et de putains ****. Un simple film de merde super con et inutile ! Seven years after Office Space, writer/director Mike Judge trades cubicles and fluorescent lights for a dark dose of cynical sci-fi. With a premise loosely borrowed from Futurama, Judge cryogenically freezes a pair of nobodies, then defrosts them in a dumbed-down version of America that’s embraced its laziest self-indulgent traits. In the intervening years, it seems, the conscientious intellectuals hemmed and hawed about having children while the low IQ crew kept plugging along, flooding the voting ranks with an army of dimwits. Now, in the year 25xx, a pro wrestler serves as president, capital punishment is a depraved spectator sport and brain cells have become an endangered species. By comparison, the statistically average slacker (Luke Wilson) and cranky prostitute (Maya Rudolph) who’ve just arrived from the before times seem downright galaxy-brained.

In the years of real-world social and political development since 2006, it’s become a hand-wringing refrain that we’re gradually slipping into an Idiocracy of our own. This speaks to both the film’s status as a long-lived cult hit and its unfortunate prescience. Where preceding science fiction yarns dreamed about dazzling future advancements, intellectual and technological, Judge’s horoscope sees only fatal regression. An infantile population that spends its days **** down energy drinks and slobbering on the shoulders of giants.

Maybe this joke’s too real to be funny any more. Maybe it wasn’t much more than a harsh, but apt, idea in the first place. Whatever the reason, Idiocracy doesn’t make for a great night’s entertainment in the year 2024. Its story feels lean; simplistic and over-stretched, even at a light hour and twenty minutes. The humor is good in small doses, but too one-note for a feature length. Everything boils down to a riff on how incredibly stupid and gullible our ancestors have become. *Everything*. Even Dumb and Dumber has more versatile tools in its belt. In a way, this makes Idiocracy an ironic example of all the trends and behaviors it warns us about, a sort of meta-rehabilitation effort; thick-headed comedy as a last resort. That’s disappointing, because while the aforementioned Office Space has grown dated, an ode to the working gripes of a previous generation, its story beats are still effective, its punchlines bring the goods and its plot actually goes somewhere. Idiocracy, on the other hand, leans entirely on its heavy-handed premise. And now that reality’s beaten it to that punch, eclipsing many of its sillier prophecies in a vibrant example of stranger-than-fiction, there’s nothing left to talk about. Except, perhaps, Terry Crews in a gaudy American flag outfit and a bad weave.

Idiocracy has moments, but not enough to make it worth revisiting. It was much better in my frazzled and beleaguered memory banks.

The stylish symphony of vivid carnage: A 5.0-star "sensational" subversion of cliches.2011 (5.0)I watched this film in the theater in 2011, and it was a "sensational" experience that completely overwhelmed my senses. It took every imaginable genre cliché and mixed them together so masterfully that I found myself lost in the "chewy" and rhythmic chaos of it all. The "vivid" and stylish depictions of slaughter were so sophisticated that I actually questioned if it was okay to be this entertained by such carnage. It felt like a "revelation" in cinematic flair, **** the fourth wall of typical horror or thriller tropes to deliver a "raw" and high-tension immersion that kept me on the edge of my seat. Unlike the "1.0-star traumas" of the same year that felt stagnant and hollow, this movie was 100% immersive, blending its "sensational" visual violence with a razor-sharp narrative pace. The 95% preservation of my excitement stems from how the film turned familiar elements into something entirely fresh and "visceral," proving that even a story built on cliches can become a perfect 5.0-star masterpiece when executed with such "raw" and daring sophistication. It remains in my archive as one of the most stylishly brutal and unforgettable theatrical encounters of 2011. This is by far one of my most favorite horror movies of all time. What makes this film unique is how it uses the tropes for its narrative purpose. I personally, would move or remove some of the scenes in the first act to give the movie a sense of mystery. Apart from that, I find this to be a throughly enjoyable film! An ingenious vehicle for poking and prodding the clichés inherent in every horror movie made over the last thirty years. Part self-referential tongue-in-cheek a'la the first Scream and part identity crisis horr-edy in the same ballpark as Shaun of the Dead, The Cabin in the Woods adds a bevy of original salts and spices and emerges as something completely different. I was told to avoid spoilers like the plague, and I'd strongly advise you to do the same: this is not a premise that translates well to explanation, and half the fun lies in the viewer's slow internal realization of where it's headed.

Brilliantly paced, unrelentingly funny, thoroughly unpredictable and boldly written (with an ending so ballsy and appropriate, I wanted to stand up and cheer), this is one of the brightest, most daring, original efforts I've seen in years. Great fun that may be directed particularly at hardcore fans of the genre, it's just transparent enough for casual viewers to have a ball, too. The twist is meaty and has surprising endurance - works well even if you know going in what to expect.  The stunt casting of Bradley Whitford and Richard Jenkins goes a long way.  The future stars that comprise a chunk of the cabin victims are fun also, and it's always nice to see Amy Acker.  Goddard is great, but the Whedon-esque nature of this thing can be grating at times.  I wouldn't look for the deeper meaning this movie claims to have at times.  Just sit back and enjoy the ride.  It is very exciting, and quite funny to boot. La Cabaña en el Bosque es una película de terror que se atreve a desafiar las convenciones del género. A pesar de tener algunos momentos impactantes y un enfoque novedoso, su fusión de humor y horror puede resultar un tanto desigual. La trama, aunque intrigante, puede volverse confusa en momentos clave. Aun así, la película se destaca por su originalidad y la manera en que subvierte las expectativas del público. El elenco entrega actuaciones competentes, y las sorpresas argumentales mantienen el interés. En general, es una experiencia de terror inusual que, aunque no es perfecta, es digna de verse. A wonderfully creative and funny horror film from Drew Goddard. While it has clear influences from classic horror/comedy such as the Evil Dead series, it puts its own unique spin on it that is both silly and genius. The concept alone might not be enough to hold its entire runtime, but with a great cast and some innovative gory set pieces, it still manages to be bloody good entertainment throughout.

But as Cam's training accelerates, Isaiah's charisma begins to curdle into something darker. Him is a weird mix of horror and fiction, using professional football as a compelling metaphor of modern life. Visually polished and disturbing, the storyline focus around ambition, showing the path to success as a way to madness. A satire somehow of virility and fame, brilliant indeed, but clumsy at the same time. Let me start this off with saying I had zero hope for this movie, I saw the reviews, I read the blurbs and I had no intention of watching this movie at all.  But I got bored and it was free on peacock so I figured why the heck not. 

I didn't just like this movie, I didn't just think it was okay, I was absolutely enthralled by it, I loved it.
The weird dreamlike set pieces, the contrasting visuals, the progressively more absurd story that is so absurd its just genuinely fascinating and then that ending that let's you know the creators, yeah they were in on the joke just brings it all home. 

This movie is a dark, violent, absurd exercise in extremism with a sports twist and I don't even like sports, but I loved it all the same. 

I recommend giving it a shot because its one of those movies that you will either absolutely love or absolutely hate and its worth the risk to see which camp you fall into.

Him (2025), dirigida por Justin Tipping y producida por Jordan Peele, es como ver un partido donde cada touchdown cuesta sangre y cada ovación te hace dudar de quién realmente está celebrando. La historia sigue a Cameron “Cam” Cade, un joven jugador de fútbol americano que ve una gran oportunidad de mentoría con Isaiah White, un legendario quarterback retirado. Pero lo que empieza como entrenamiento prometedor se convierte en algo tétrico: hay cultos, rituales, sacrificios psicológicos, y algo que definitivamente no es solo físico. Wikipedia+2Roger Ebert+2Lo que funciona muy bien:La atmósfera: la película sabe generar tensión, no solo con sustos baratos, sino con el ambiente del lugar aislado, el mentor carismático que empieza a oler a podrido, y el cuerpo de Cam que parece volverse terreno de sacrificio físico y psicológico. Roger Ebert+1Las ideas: ambición, fama, sacrificio extremo, el precio de la excelencia y hasta cuestionamientos de identidad. Roger EbertAlgunos personajes secundarios no tienen arco definido; el mentor Isaiah tiene momentos excelentes, pero otros quedan medio **** balance horror-deporte sufre: cuando no está en modo terror o siniestro, baja mucho la intensidad. Es como si estuvieras viendo dos películas distintas pegadas con **** resumen, Him es una película que recomiendo si te atrae el horror psicológico con metáforas deportivas, lo grotesco, lo simbólico; no tanto si buscas algo limpio, directo o con todos los hilos bien atados. Te deja con buen sabor si entras al juego, pero también con ganas de que algunas ideas hubieran sido mejor pulidas. This could have been a criticism of toxic masculinity, money, brianwashed sports mom/dad ruining their children's lives for THEIR failed dreams, cheating with drugs, unhealthy media pressure on athletes, escaping anxiety in drugs and sex, **** no Jordan Peele had to be extra artsy-fartsy and on-the-nose and ruin any potential subject with an over-the-top, dumb, cryptic "horror" movie... 'HIM'  has an appealing concept that combines sports, horror, and social commentary, but its execution relies solely on style. Jordan Peele produces with his own touch, to the point of seeming like a parody of his work. Exploring issues like racial capitalism and the collateral damage of sacrifice in a superficial manner, the film fails miserably in its attempt to blend 'The Neon Demon' with 'Whiplash.'
