No entanto, optou por multiplicar símbolos, metáforas e explicações, em vez de construir uma narrativa sólida. O resultado é um filme que não assusta como terror, não emociona como drama e não provoca como crítica social. É um híbrido que nunca encontra identidade própria.

791.title: The Aviator

metadata.tagline: Some men dream the future. He built it.

791.rich_text:
The Aviator The Aviator Some men dream the future. He built it. Drama Martin Scorsese Leonardo DiCaprio Cate Blanchett Kate Beckinsale John C. Reilly Alec Baldwin Alan Alda Ian Holm Danny Huston Gwen Stefani Jude Law A biopic depicting the life of filmmaker and aviation pioneer Howard Hughes from 1927 to 1947, during which time he became a successful film producer and an aviation magnate, while simultaneously growing more unstable due to severe obsessive-compulsive disorder. Just not a huge fan of the production design here. Leo is solid but the movie does lose a lot when Blanchett's Hepburn fades to the background in the 2nd half of the movie. Great acting and people, especially the way he fought his fears and stood up for his rights, and despite the fact that he was a womanizer, his relationships with the women close to him were interesting and not flat. With a 3-hour run time, The Aviator feels a little too long, but DiCaprio is excellent in the lead role and it provides an interesting look at one of US history’s most unique characters. This on-the-surface look at the life and times of one of America's most notorious recluses delivers plenty of dirt, if not much introspection. The mysterious Howard Hughes is certainly a tricky subject to nail down, with much of his daring decision-making and eventual descent into madness left officially undocumented, but I still can't shake the sense that there's still a lot of untouched meat to this story.

Cate Blanchett is enveloping as Katharine Hepburn, for which she deservedly won an Oscar, but the rest of the cast feels too careful and uncertain, particularly Leonardo DiCaprio's turn as Hughes himself. Leo's eyes don't seem bright enough to concoct the miracles he's performing, while his smirk lacks the **** authenticity that would make the most powerful men in the country shudder. Director Martin Scorsese seems similarly lost amidst such complicated material, which comes as a real surprise. Scorsese hammers his audience over the head with the outward symptoms that made Hughes such a curious individual in his later years, but fails to examine the reasonable, humanizing concerns that led to such paralyzing compulsions.

As an adventurous history lesson, one could do far worse, but for such a long run time and so colorful a subject to deliver so few answers is a big disappointment. This was just a bad movie. Boring and strange. The worst part was Cate Blanchett's rendering of Katherine Hepburn. Poor Kate must be rolling over in her grave. The accent was way over the top exaggerated and the over-acting was an absolute embarrassment. Scorsese should've straightened her out and told her to fix it. Someone should've told him to straighten it out if he didn't see the problem with her performance. Her performance was one of the worst things I've ever seen in a movie. I saw it a few years ago but it has still stuck with me. ‘Vis ma vie de mégalo cinglé’ mais ce n’est pas très intéressant, cette vie de mégalomaniaque névrosé obsessionnel toqué même si Di Carpaccio ne ménage pas ses efforts. La faute bien évidemment à des longueurs terribles, terrifiantes d’ennui et de blablas stériles.

Et contrairement au ‘Loup de Wall street’ (par exemple), Scorsese n’a pas l’humour ni un détestable cynisme auquel se raccrocher. J’ignore si son film a la moindre valeur historique mais tel qu’il est, ii n’évoque et n’induit aucun sentiment particulier chez le spectateur à l’égard de cet Howard machinchose et personnellement je m’en contrefousde ce blaireau qui se mouche avec des bifetons.

La seule chose dont je me fous pas, c’est que la fin de ce film interminable (inter-minable ?) advienne enfin… et arrive ! et quel sentiment de libération quand évzntuellement… elle arrive. Enfin. Bref, ça reste visuellement beau, mis en scène avec soin mais putain, je me suis emmerdé pendant les deux derniers tiers du film. ou les trois quarts, je ne sais plus. Dommage pour le début qui partait bien. Mais au début seulement. From the talented Martin Scorsesse comes an admittedly ambitious but compelling and visually stirring biopic on legendary rebel billionaire Howard Hughes. Although it is nearly three hours, I don't think the film dragged that much and I was gripped for the whole duration. My problem is to do with the secondary characters though. The Aviator is one of those films where a lot of detail goes into making the protagonist and a few more key characters convincing and relateable, but the secondary characters aren't given as much attention as well. This is not the first film to have this problem though, Kinsey which was still very good had it too, as did Chaplin. Back on target, actors like Willem Dafoe and Ian Holm are not given that much to do, they do fine with what they have, but their characters have the sense of appearing there one minute and disappearing the next. Another problem was that occasionally the drama was lacking, the story was well constructed and paced, and the themes here are very ambitious, but other than well staged plane scenes parts of the more dramatic parts felt somewhat lukewarm.

Complaints aside, this is still a very good film. First of all, it is amazing to look at, the scenery is gorgeous and the costumes are sumptuous. The music is also a delight, beautiful and poignant, dramatic and haunting in others. I loved the small clips of Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor, orchestrated here and it works(it was originally written for organ you see), and Tchaikovsky's 5th and 6th Symphonies, the latter of which has a final movement that is so heart-rending as it always reminds me of death, don't ask why though. The Aviator is brilliantly directed by Scorcesse, and the script does have moments of meaningful power. And the acting is pretty exceptional. Leonardo DiCaprio gives one of his better post-Titanic performances here, he proves he is more than a person that is all looks no talent, for he really is brilliant as Howard Hughes. Cate Blanchett is wonderful as well as Katherine Hepburn, and Kate Beckinsale surprised me. Like DiCaprio, she too proves that she is more than a pretty face by giving a really good account of herself as Ava Gardner while looking absolutely amazing in the process. In a smaller role, Alec Baldwin was also enjoyable.

Overall, not absolutely outstanding, but The Aviator is a very striking, ambitious and compelling biopic. 8/10 Bethany Cox Dicaprio is Howard Hughes in this biopic and Cate Blanchett is Katherine Hepburn. Both are great in this ordinary and mediocre movie that has nothing to do with Scorsese great qualities as a director. Surely it's not his best film. For a Scorsese movie this is rather dull.
It's production values are high and with help of the era it's set in is extremely stylistic, but it comes across as a rather paint by numbers biopic.
Blanchett as usual is superb. The Aviator is a entertaining biopic which paints a picture of the life of Howard Hughes, the  aviation pioneer who dealt with various physical and mental health issues during his lifetime. Though the movie is nearly three hours long, there's hardly a dull moment. Viewers watch the highs and lows which Hughes had over the course of a 20 year period (1927-1947). The storytelling is excellent and will keep you hooked throughout the movie's duration. In addition to the compelling storyline, the production design and cinematography are amazing. The movie wouldn't be as good as it was, though, without DiCaprio's stellar performance as Hughes. DiCaprio's performance alone makes this movie worth watching. Overall, The Aviator is an interesting biopic about the interesting character that was Howard Hughes, and it's definitely worth a watch.

Crank Crank There are a thousand ways to raise your adrenaline. Today, Chev Chelios will need every single one. Action Thriller Crime Brian Taylor, Mark Neveldine Jason Statham Amy Smart Jose Pablo Cantillo Efren Ramirez Dwight Yoakam Carlos Sanz Reno Wilson Edi Gathegi Glenn Howerton Jay Xcala Chev Chelios, a hit man wanting to go straight, lets his latest target slip away. Then he awakes the next morning to a phone call that informs him he has been poisoned and has only an hour to live unless he keeps adrenaline coursing through his body while he searches for an antidote. The ultimate rhythmic assault: A 4.0-star heart-pounding sprint that never looks back.130605 (4.0)I watched this in 2013, and it was a revelation of pure, unadulterated energy. The premise—having to keep your adrenaline pumping to stay alive—created the most literal "chewy" tension I've ever experienced. It was sharp, chaotic, and relentlessly rhythmic, moving at a pace that made even "Source Code" feel slow. While it lacked the emotional weight of "The Chaser," its commitment to its own insane logic was brilliant. A high-voltage 4.0 for a film that understood exactly how to keep my pulse as high as the protagonist's. From start to finish 'Crank' is a huge and messy joke that could have been told by a disruptive teenager to his closest troubled friends. Writing a structured critic about such a poor movie is a total prowess. I could not resist to make a list of its numerous flaws...

Filming process and camera angles are twisted and drafty, colours (in addition to lighting, calibration and contrasts) are more than ugly, dialogues are dull and predictable, characters are not developped at all, fight scenes are terrible, 'bastard' is the closest word I found to describe the overall pace of this film, all characters must share a small group of neurons between them, the plot is based on adrenaline and the scenarists don't know anything about this hormone, Statham beats each and every characters without any difficulty, his body still works after all the crap he does and takes (including bullets), driving scenes can actually cause vomiting (and there are a lot of those), the editing is disgusting, every woman present in 'Crank' was hired to showcase her body, blood scenes are awful, the movie doesn't hide at all its marketing principles (and therefore shows a lot of advertising especially when the 'hero' enters shops), we can clearly see the use of green screens in many shots, bad guys are boring, overall acting is hardly decent, some scenes are iconic by their infinite stupidity, and it is a true miracle Statham's carrier didn't stop right after that release. Crank at its best is a guilty pleasure that ALMOST becomes the classic action film it wants to be but just misses the bar by a few inches. A pretty interesting movie, but a little strange                                                                                                     . Chev Chelios is arguably Jason Statham's best known character and Crank is arguably his best known film, but it is far from his best film. Chev Chelios (Statham) is a gun for hire, who will work for anyone who can pay him. One day he wakes up in a daze and finds a video in which a former employer tells him, that he poisoned him with a rare adrenaline inhibitor, which will kill him in a few hours. Chelios goes out seeking revenge, but must keep his adrenaline pumping, in order to slow the poison down. It's a strange story, but as usual, Statham is terrific, playing his most extreme character. Chelios is a crazy man who goes to extremes, however that's all this film has to offer. Non-stop action can sometimes be fun, but when it's the same thing repeating over and over again for 90 minutes, even the biggest action fan gets tired of it. Statham is paired with Amy Smart who starred in my favorite movie of all-time, The Butterfly Effect, and surprisingly she was terrible! She plays Chelios's girlfriend, a girl who is as dumb as dirt and who follows this crazy man blindly through the city on his hunt for revenge. Crank has some humor and a terrific leading man, but unfortunately, there isn't much of story. Besides Statham's well known one-liners and his ridiculous moves, there is really nothing to see here. Crank is one of those films that starts out strong and then just never goes anywhere. Having seen a lot of Statham's movies lately, I was hoping his best known film would be his most exciting, but it wasn't. It's the same scene repeated many times over, and I was tired of it after a half hour. From the beginning to the end, Crank is like a 90 minutes trip on something. Neither does it deliver complex characters nor a deep plot but it is very entertaining and fun to watch.

796.title: Heretic

metadata.tagline: Question everything.

796.rich_text:
Heretic Heretic Question everything. Thriller Horror Scott Beck, Bryan Woods Hugh Grant Sophie Thatcher Chloe East Topher Grace Elle Young Julie Lynn-Mortensen Haylie Hansen Elle McKinnon Hanna Huffman Anesha Bailey Two young missionaries are forced to prove their faith when they knock on the wrong door and are greeted by a diabolical Mr. Reed, becoming ensnared in his deadly game of cat-and-mouse. Not many surprises but a decent movie nevertheless, with good acting, tense moments, and a solid plot. Hugh Grant transitions a little too smoothly from the nice old guy next door to a memorable monster and the protagonists work well, without being the usual cannon fodder you find in horror movies. Only just recently saw this, and have to say was I very impressed. The story seemed like it was going to be fairly generic, but a combination of the great character writing and performances elevated the whole thing beyond a seemingly basic premise. Hugh Grants performance deserves all the praise it has been getting, he was truly great in this role. I think this film is really interesting and has some very good acting. I also liked the details like the references to literary works, philosophers, etc. Personally, I can't strictly consider it a horror film, but on the other hand, as a mystery and thriller, I think it's an excellent film. It has become one of my favorites in the genre and I recommend it without hesitation. It's Hugh Grant, so what can you say? From beginning to end, the film is filled with tons of questionable topics—albeit sensitive in nature—that truly push the audience to the edge of their seats. The tone and dialogue sprinkled throughout each cinematic scene proposes an entirely new angle to not only view a highly religious topic in an alternate light, but to also bring your early childhood beliefs and their initial influences into question. The lighthearted portrayal of two churchgoing women trying to bring awareness of God with pamphlets is played very well by Sophie Thatcher and Chloe East. Both are brilliant actors whom, despite their robust sense of actor-maturity, display the subtle nuances of innocence and blind trust so eloquently to the degree of infatuation—a level of infatuation that the audience can see building within Hugh Grant's character. This build-up of infatuation then turns into intrigue and then into borderline obsession strictly to prove several points even he himself cannot quite differentiate between. The film is a maddening maze that feels eerily similar to that of a smaller version of Alice In Wonderland that truly presses down on your core beliefs. The confined area of the film caused a shocking feeling of heightened claustrophobia that I've never felt before. However, the film's ending left me desiring more of a climactic expression of closure since its synopsis brought such deeply opinionated stances on very racy subjects that would otherwise bring forth a fiery debate for those interested. It’s a great film and worth the watch. After finishing Heretic I was left a little lack luster and almost disappointed in what this could have been. However, the more I reminisced with it, and talked about it with friends who watched it, the feelings I had for it really grew on me. It is an impressive thought experiment with thrill and horror thrown into the mix. It actually makes good light of all points of view it is trying to express within the themes of this film. It never depicts any point of view as truly right or wrong, and is honestly respectful to the religion it is trying to dissect. Although it takes a stab at dissecting religion as a whole. This movie is absolutely worth the watch whether you are a believer in a religion or not. Some films manage to unsettle you without ever raising their voice. Heretic does just that from the very first frame. It’s a tense, slow-burning thriller where every pause feels deliberate, every line carefully chosen. Almost everything takes place in a single location, but the atmosphere it builds is dense and claustrophobic. And at the center of it all: Hugh **** performance is mesmerizing. He doesn’t force the fear—he suggests it. The way he looks, smiles, speaks just a bit too slowly—it’s all deeply disturbing. I haven’t seen him this sharp in years, and here he’s far from the charming romantic type people usually associate with him. This time, he’s something else: charisma turned into **** script plays with religious themes without preaching. There are clever lines, uncomfortable questions, and moments where you don’t know whether to laugh or tense up. It often feels like a chamber play, where everything rests on the actors and their subtle choices—and all three leads are outstanding.Visually, it’s not flashy, but it uses darkness and confined spaces to trap you with the characters. It’s small-scale filmmaking that dares to tackle big themes: faith, guilt, manipulation, power. Not everything lands—perhaps the ending lacks the punch of the opening—but the ride is worth it.Heretic doesn’t reinvent horror, but it twists it in clever ways. It’s elegant, uncomfortable, and full of shadows. And above all, it reminds us that true horror doesn’t always scream—it whispers. Heretic is a smart and chilling psychological horror that crafts fear through words, silence, and atmosphere instead of gore or jump scares. It takes place mostly in a single house, where a seemingly polite and composed figure gradually exposes his darker intentions. The film explores themes of control, religious manipulation, and blind faith, offering a slow-burn tension that creeps under the skin. With sharp dialogue and eerie stillness, it keeps the audience on edge from start to finish. There's a layer of dark humor beneath the dread, and the questions it raises linger long after it ends. It's a tight, unsettling thriller that shows true horror doesn't need spectacle-it just needs conviction. Heretic è uno dei miei film preferiti.
Non è un horror commerciale, ma un film che va capito.
La storia mi è piaciuta molto, immersiva e ben scritta, la regia di Scott Beck e Bryan Woods l'ho trovata eccezionale e la fotografia stupenda.
Attrici bravissime e bellissime nel loro ruolo, assolutamente carismatiche.
Se questo film non è un 10 è per il finale, che onestamente ho trovato un pochino forzato e inverosimile.
Nonostante questo film stupendo, dategli assolutamente un'occhiata Heretic is a slow-burning psychological thriller that challenges its audience with weighty themes of faith, manipulation, and belief. While the film stumbles in its final act and risks alienating viewers with its ambiguous resolution, it thrives on tension-filled dialogue and a hauntingly brilliant performance from Hugh Grant. Directors Scott Beck and Bryan Woods craft a claustrophobic, talk-heavy horror experience that’s more about mental warfare than traditional scares. Heretic may not be for everyone, but its bold approach and philosophical edge make it a provocative entry in A24’s growing horror catalog. A24 productions really are consistently high-quality. I wasn’t expecting much from this film (even though seeing Hugh Grant in such a role was intriguing), and yet it managed to surprise me with its constant shifts in direction. It starts off as a standard hostage thriller, then halfway through takes a supernatural turn, then veers into something almost Matrix-like, before finally circling back to something truly twisted. It keeps you hooked from start to finish, and even if the ending is slightly weaker than the rest, it’s still a very solid thriller.

Wonder Woman 1984 Wonder Woman 1984 A new era of wonder begins. Action Adventure Fantasy Patty Jenkins Gal Gadot Chris Pine Kristen Wiig Pedro Pascal Robin Wright Connie Nielsen Lilly Aspell Amr Waked Kristoffer Polaha Natasha Rothwell A botched store robbery places Wonder Woman in a global battle against a powerful and mysterious ancient force that puts her powers in jeopardy. Wonder Woman 1984 was fun and entertaining entry to the DC and Gal Gadot continues to prove that she is the perfect Diana Prince/Wonder Woman and delivers another terrific performance and Chris Pine as well but both Pedro Pascal & Kristen Wiig gave stellar performances as the villains and Hans Zimmer's score is solid and Jenkins direction is good again and I wished the writing was a little stronger but I loved the plot. The second Wonder Woman film may not be perfect, but it has something that makes it special—especially for those who still believe in heroes that inspire through kindness. Patty Jenkins once again offers a bright, hopeful vision of the character, and Gal Gadot is flawless: calm, charismatic, and profoundly **** movie dares to mix tones: from colorful, light comedy to the drama of difficult choices. And while that sometimes creates ups and downs, there are unforgettable sequences—like the opening in Themyscira or the flight through fireworks—that carry the epic soul of the best superhero cinema.Kristen Wiig and Pedro Pascal bring an interesting duality as antagonists, even if their arcs could have been more developed. Still, both are fully committed, and it's refreshing to see a story that allows room for nuance and evolution.This isn’t your typical action blockbuster, and that may throw off some viewers. But that's exactly its strength: Wonder Woman 1984 isn't just about fights or flashy effects—it's about values like truth, sacrifice, and longing. A rare gem in a genre that often favors spectacle over emotion.There may not be a third installment, but for many—my daughter included, who adores her—Diana will always be the symbol that makes us dream. A superhero who proves her strength through compassion, not brute force. Film with a more classic and banal plot than the previous film, resulting rather flat and without a great evolution from beginning to end but appearing as a film equal to many others of its kind, which seems forced and boring at some point during its development End s up being pointless. There's no direction to the film. No real big bad and no real epic fights. It has a long runtime but it somehow feels much longer than it actually is. I think this was the first film that made me realise how bad an actress Gal Godot really is. They managed to cover it up in the first wonder woman but it feels like they just didn't try in this film. This movie is a disappointing sequel with a slow pacing and slow reveal for many of the villains. The final act is stale and ultimately too little too late. This leads to fans already having lost interest and patience in this movie before the finale. The best part of this film is wonder woman's final suit, however, she does not wear the armour for long during the film and is used poorly and could have been used more to fuel viewers' excitement for the film. Happy 4 year anniversary merry Christmas to one of my favorite movies Wonder Woman 1984 this is better than Wonder Woman because I love storyline all the characters are relatable shows teach you about yourself and what you want in your life but also teach you about your attachment style how that relates on what you truly want and wish for and how it relates to your self and relationship you have with your self and with other people Barbra have anxious attachment style max have avoided attachment style Diana have a secure attachment style she got super comfortable with Steve very fast but also wants to find out what is the consequences to having Steve back and what does that mean for her and for a lot of people I love roles switch from Steve learning about 1984 works Diana was helping him to fit in In 1984 her wish to bring Steve back she lost her powers and gave it to Barbara even though Diana can’t feel physically pain but she can still get physical sick how she loooks but can’t feel physically look part but can’t feel the part but she renounce her wish and I love how she was happy to get her powers back and being control of them and save the day I love Linda carter cameo asteria I love it I love all the action fight scenes there were fun entertaining dc at the house 5 star 10 out 10 star 100 out 100 star Wonder Woman 1984 has some interesting artefacts as it still delivers strong solid chemistry between Gal Gadot and Chris Pine but I felt the storyline was very questionable as it was really all over the place. It's been seventy years since her introduction to the world of men, and though she's grown more capable and active in that time, Wonder Woman still carries a torch for the short-term romance that violently ended in a WWI fireball. It seems unhealthy that she hasn't accepted the loss in all that time, still dining alone and sad-eying all the happy couples at adjacent tables, but it's convenient for the story (and for viewers) that her heart hasn't moved on, so here we are. Of course, that lost love does eventually, improbably, return from the grave, thanks to the influence of a mystical wishing stone, but (as always) there's a steep price.

While it lasts, Diana and Steve's reunion is an enjoyable reversal of roles. Now it's the **** soldier who plays the naïve fish out of water, goggling and gaping at the fashions and conveniences of modern luxury in 1980s America, while the worldly Amazonian princess smirks and explains. The weird throwback/leap forward aspect is shallow, but it works. I felt that the first film suffered for its close tonal relationship to other films in the DC Universe, all grim and bleak, and the vibrant, colorful air of these early scenes serves as a sorely-needed dramatic departure. It's fun to watch, easy but functional, and the dominance of a "me" generation serves the broader theme of human greed as a divisive force.

As the plot drags out, though, those simpler pleasures lose their zing and the various threads wrapped around the wishing stone grow unwieldy. It all culminates in a completely nonsensical climax that momentarily throws the entire world into upheaval before the headliner shows up in a new outfit, swings a few punches, lobs some lofty philosophical mumbo-jumbo and literally rides off into the sunset. I didn't buy the evil plot, nor the heroic resolution, and was left unfulfilled.

The effects work hasn't improved from Diana's first outing, either. Most times, the direction is smart enough to mask such shortcomings behind abrupt camera shifts and motion blur, but any time we get a clear shot of the heroine running full-speed (and this happens more than once), it's a hilariously bad look. We're talking made-for-TV special effects here. Absolutely astonishing that a major studio could release something so shoddy and second-grade, especially after so many unexpected release delays.

Ultimately, WW84 is a story of one step forward and two steps back. It conquers the issues of individual identity that plagued the first film, gives us another chance to enjoy the chemistry between costars Gal Gadot and Chris Pine, but also struggles to tell a cohesive story, rambles on for ages (there's at least thirty minutes of fat on this steak) and whiffs on the ending. Plus, the effects. Oh, those effects. A good concept, established with loads of creative energy, that loses its way and peters out after the first hour. It’s clear that it isn’t a film that is at the height of the previous one, it doesn’t  contribute anything to the plot, it’s understood that it is another Wonder Woman story, but it doesn’t really contribute anything. On the other hand, I understand that it is difficult to bring Wonder Woman's powers to the big screen, but they are still not entirely convincing. This is a terrible movie on all fronts. The story, conflict, and characters are superficial and extremely dull. The story and writing are outright bad. Compared to Wonder Woman, this movie offers an illogical story, and the writing makes it cringe-worthy. If you decide to watch this, only do so for the action sequences and Gal Gadot; otherwise, I'd recommend you skip it and watch something else.

798.title: The Others

The Others The Others Sooner or later they’ll find you. Horror Mystery Thriller Alejandro Amenábar Nicole Kidman Fionnula Flanagan Christopher Eccleston Alakina Mann James Bentley Eric Sykes Elaine Cassidy Keith Allen Renée Asherson Michelle Fairley Grace is a religious woman who lives in an old house kept dark because her two children, Anne and Nicholas, have a rare sensitivity to light. I watched this movie for the second time. The first time I saw it was when I was a child and I was very scared. This time it was very interesting and the ending was unexpected, although I remembered the plot a little. Ahh the others,un film che non ti aspetti.
Parte con delle premesse davvero interessanti, facendoti formulare delle ipotesi che verranno smentite al 100 per cento nell'assurdo finale.
Film in generale di una grandissima qualità, a volte lento , ma lento nel modo giusto.
Regia solida e buone musiche.
Performance grandiosa di tutti gli attori, ma soprattutto della grandissima Nicole Kidman, con una recitazione che io definirei ipnotica.
Non un normale film horror, ma un esperienza.
Da vedere assolutamente The Others lives up to the unpredictability hype, you can't guess what's happening.

The characters are incredibly well-written. Their decisions, the plot makes sense until everything gets a new meaning. This movie is famous for its plot twist, so I guess it's no spoiler that there's a huge one here. I could not guess it and from the characters' perspective it gives a new meaning to their life as well.

It's well-directed, while the cinematography is great and the editing is efficient. The sound design is outstanding as it is the key to horror. The casting is good enough. There's not a lot of fame, but everyone is well-cast. The acting performances are overall really good, but Nicole Kidman's is stunning.

The Others is not the typical film I would watch, but it does amazingly at what it aims for. Um filme que me mostrou o que é plot twist.
Suspense na medida, atuações incriveis, imagem, som, atmosféria impecavel e uma história boa, sem duvidas é um filme que marcou, mas tem seus detalhes, como um certo arrastar em determinados momentos, fora isso é um daqueles filmes para ver a 1° vez que se surpreender e para ver a 2° para pegar todos os detalhes e ficar aidna mais facinado. Has pacing issues and some charactes make little to no difference. But overall a good one time watch. This film is really nicely shot with solid sound design. I really can’t complain but I will by saying that it is a little drab with lots of dark grey and dark brown. The film is very much along the lines of The Sixth Sense (1999) but with a different angle (although it does also have a familiar twist). It is not quite as good on all levels though. There are some really creepy moments and some excellent scares but this isn’t enough to make it stand-out. It is worth watching for the creepiness but sadly it is not as scary as proper horror and not as good as the similar The Sixth Sense (1999). It’s worth noting that I just prefer things set in modern times. Overall it’s entertaining but nothing outstanding at all. Dark (literally). I first saw the creepy, infuriating Others when I was still figuring out what made a good movie and what made a bad movie. Even then, when I thought New Year's Eve and even Catwoman were funny, it was obvious to me that the film was a waste of time, relying on acting ability. Some time later, I saw this movie on TV, and my opinion was not only unchanged, it was solidified by the "movie power" I had developed by watching many movies.

The film is dark from beginning to end. I don't mean the style, but the brightness. The main character Grace's (Nicole Kidman) two children die when exposed to sunlight. Therefore, there is no electricity in the room, and it is boring from beginning to end. Honestly, why did they set it up this way? It's boring, boring, boring. Boring to death.

You want to know when the real horror comes into the movie? It's about an hour into the movie. Until then, Nicole Kidman makes a scene and leaves a creepy remark about her kid seeing a kid named Victor. It's creepy, and yet nothing is going on. There is a heavy air that something is going to happen, and yet nothing happens for an hour after the movie starts.

Those who like this movie will say that the great performances of the cast members are not to be missed. Well, sure. Great performances, especially from Nicole Kidman. She played the character of Grace, a frightened, yelling, and screaming woman, beautifully. However, that may have been rather counterproductive. This Grace character yelled at the children and seemed to me to be a character who constantly shifted blame. It is a mystery horror film, so it is predictable that something spiritual will come out. I am annoyed by the characters who self-centeredly deny it. You can tell it's counterproductive to the cast members who play these characters well.

As you can see, there is not much to this film. It is not particularly scary, and even the acting is wasted. Well, I could forgive it if the ending was better, but it's a rip-off of The Sixth Sense, and that's all I can say. Was the entire script made for this ending? When I think so, hatred rises from the bottom of my heart. The Others wants to feel like a horror movie, but it's nothing more than a psychological thriller. Moreover, the thriller is quite average, suspense is not sustained throughout the film. The first half of the film is very tight, all the main action takes place in the last 20 minutes. The main twist is not surprising at all. And as a result, you don't understand why everyone liked The Others so much. For me, this is a completely passing thriller The quiet thriller mood, Nicole Kidman's outstanding performance, and the ending will propel The Others to a climax similar to The Sixth Sense. I thought it was a good movie. It did feel pretty spooky and atmospheric and the story was intriguing enough to keep me interested to watch it right through until the end.

It was a good length and didn't seem to lag at any particular point. It had good acting, I felt that Nicole Kidman and the two child actor/actresses were particularly good, giving very realistic and believable performances and all in all it felt like a pretty high quality production, so it is worth seeing, although its not a particularly fast paced movie but rather more of a spooky slow burner, I suppose.

I'm not usually interested in period dramas but I do like a good supernatural movie, or ghost story, so this fit that well.

The main downsides to it, if any, is that it doesn't feature any amazing special effects, so don't watch it if thats what your looking for, its more a modern 1940s movie I suppose and it may be possible for others to guess some of whats going on before its revealed, though there is an extra twist at the end, which will probably surprise most. I thought that the end was pretty good but I suppose if you've seen many similar movies then it may be possible to figure it out.

All in all, it struck me as being a good, quality production. The story was interesting enough to keep me interested and there are some twists towards the end, although we, as viewers, are kept somewhat in the dark (har har) for most of the movie, its worth it to wait until the end when all is spookily revealed.

I thought that the story was pretty good in general and I would say that its worth watching, for the performances alone almost. It did seem a pretty traditional ghost story made for the screen and it did work, all in all, pretty well, so I would recommend it.

We're the Millers We're the Millers If anyone asks. Comedy Crime Rawson Marshall Thurber Jennifer Aniston Jason Sudeikis Emma Roberts Will Poulter Ed Helms Nick Offerman Kathryn Hahn Molly C. Ich wollte diesen Film schon vor langer Zeit sehen. Ehrlich gesagt wollte ich ihn schon immer sehen. Jason Sudeikis plays a sad-sack drug dealer in the early stages of a mid-life crisis who, in trying to land a big score, convinces a ragtag group of loose acquaintances to pose as his sticky sweet All-American family. Outside of a few decadent striptease spots from Jennifer Aniston, who seems to know how cheap a gimmick they really are, We're the Millers is formulaic to the bone. Which is a shame, because there's some quality comic talent wasted in this cast.

With a cookie cutter sense of humor and no knack for improv, it's not particularly silly, nor witty, nor even all that funny - it just shows its hand bafflingly early, than follows the charted course all the way home to a stagnant, peachy-keen, groan-inducing finish. I found more laughs in the two-minute blooper reel than I did in the preceding hundred-ten, and may have been actively rooting for the cast to fail spectacularly during the third act, if just for want of a curveball. Amusing at best, it's terribly tame considering the rich, risqué subject matter. The movie is very long, and a small scene of the movie that I felt went on for too long as well, really made feel a little tired. However, it does have an uplifting story and a great cast, although the parts I said in the beginning are hard to ignore for me. Well-balanced movie, laughed more than i should. Sometimes gets frisky too which is nice. Miss movies like these before woke hollywood This was a really enjoyable watch during some downtime, it's a funny feel good story that'll keep you laughing. Great situational comedy! The movie We're the Millers was surprisingly entertaining and humorous. Jason Sudeikis plays a small-time pot dealer who is cheated out of the money he owes to his source. In order to settle the bill, the zany and eccentric supplier sends him on a large-scale drug smuggling operation into Mexico. In order to create the Miller family, the uber-American family, Sudeikis persuades stripper and neighbour Rose (Jennifer Aniston) to act as his wife, runaway Casey (Emma Roberts) as their daughter, and teenage neighbour Kenny (Will Poulter) as their son. Nope Nope What’s a bad miracle? Nope was an excellent film. I appreciated how Jordan Peele highlighted the existence of Black cowboys, a reality that often seems overlooked or forgotten. The movie blended suspenseful jump scares with well-timed comedic moments, which made it engaging and enjoyable.Daniel Kaluuya, Keke Palmer, Steven Yeun, and the rest of the cast delivered outstanding performances. Honestly, one star is already too generous — and for me, it’s a definite Nope. Isn’t it odd that we’ve never managed to capture definitive visual proof of extraterrestrial life? Especially now, with a decade of portable, internet-connected, high-resolution personal cameras under our belt? The romance of a UFO chase is still very much alive - no shortage of seekers out there with their eyes on the sky - but still the photographic evidence remains elusive. That’s the conceit behind Jordan Peele’s latest, Nope, which aims to outline the circumstances that might allow the dream of first contact to coexist with the reality of such a closely-observed world.

Set in the vast desert isolation just beyond Los Angeles, Nope draws great dramatic tension from the smothering, lonely stillness of the ranch. Alongside a small cast, we witness strange, recurring phenomena and feel the hair on our arms rise. At its best when toying with the same brand of subtle eeriness found in Signs and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, it leaves plenty to the imagination while still showing us more than we might have expected. There’s some loose meta commentary here, too - I’d expect as much from Peele - but it’s less overt and essential than it was in Get Out. That shift may have been a mistake. Though the 2022 model boasts potent ambiance and a knack for well-timed suspense, I found the meat of the story to be rather lean. It’s creepy, it’s moody, it’s visually powerful. That’s really where it all begins and ends. Not your standard cookie cutter movie. An interesting premise that fails to stick the landing. Runs a bit to long. Jordan Peele is, amongst other things, a master of delivering haunting and curious images. For that aspect alone, Nope is his visual opus, even if it doesn't have the spark and cohesive satire of Get Out, it exceeds far beyond the messy, rushed and confused sophomore entry Us.

Peele's films have other strengths; they're exceedingly human and nuanced; they have great dialogue and they unfold neatly and layers upon layers reveal and coalesce. The disparate elements don't always gel, but it's cinema at its best when they do.Kaluuya and Palmer are a perfect duo and there's a decent chunk of comedy and black comedy in their performances. Nope is slow, haunting, surprising with clever use of music, character backgrounds and costume and design work.

Pretty paint-by-numbers stuff until the villain abruptly succeeds in offing his nemesis, surprising even himself, and the whole world turns on its ear. Unprepared for the responsibility and scrutiny of rule, Megamind immediately yearns for simpler times, concocts a new heroic foil and drastically worsens the situation.

In that it’s a CG family film, centered around superheroes, from a villainous perspective, it’s only natural that Megamind should borrow from / compete with The Incredibles and Despicable Me. And, while it doesn’t benefit from those comparisons - lacking the energy of the former and the heart of the latter - it still finds room to surprise and do its own thing. The plot’s main thrust is an inspired take, a sort of “What If” tale about Lex Luthor finally tackling Superman, facing some difficult realities and ultimately growing as an individual. It acknowledges and corrupts a number of recurring tropes from the genre, twisting overplayed scenarios in fresh and interesting new ways. Puis, des éléments dramatiques s’invitent dans le décor et tranchent radicalement avec le reste : les maladresses s’enchaînent alors les unes après les autres sans que l’on ressente pour autant la moindre émotion ici ou là… Mais c’est à dire vrai le film entier qui fait pschiiit et s’évapore lamentablement malgré la gravité du sujet… et si l’on continue le visionnage, ce n’est que pour voir à quel point, jusqu’où le film va s’enfoncer dans la connerie et l’ignorance ainsi que le manque de respect évident d’un bout à l’autre, le respect de toutes les victimes (y compris allemandes) du régime **** et de son endoctrinement effarant (et le gamin en est un exemple frappant, bien évidemment). Dommage bien sûr pour les comédiens qui s’en sortent bien (Sam Rockwell impérial comme d’habitude), mais également Scarlett Johansson étonnamment convaincante dans le rôle de la maman, je dois dire. Mais bon, hélas, il s’agit surtout d’un film raté et prétentieux qui a décidément loupé le coche ! Jojo Rabbit is a movie that mixes funny and sad parts in a bold way. The story follows Jojo, a young boy in **** Germany, who has an imaginary friend - a comical version of Adolf ****. The idea is odd but Taika Waititi makes it real with his silly mocking style. He uses humor to show the dangers of following leaders without **** movie blends dark humor with touching moments. Roman Griffin Davis, who plays Jojo, shows a child’s innocence and confusion as the brutal facts of war break his simple view of the world. Scarlett Johansson, who plays Jojo’s mother, gives comfort and strength to her role providing warmth amid chaos. The tone shifts sharply, from funny to dark ideas, which may disturb some viewers yet holds your attention. Jojo Rabbit gives a new look at World War II using humor to look at strong themes of hate, love as well as human connection. It is not perfect but it gives feelings that stay with you. I give it a 9 out of 10. Alternating between bitter poignancy and flippant hilarity, Jojo Rabbit thrives as an emotional roller coaster. Gravely serious situations are often cut with a well-timed, stress-melting laugh. Light moments of childish infatuation take a sudden swerve into existential turmoil. That's a hallmark of director Taika Waititi, who explored similarly polarizing contrasts in 2016's Hunt for the Wilderpeople, and, as it turns out, it also suits the essence of childhood during wartime.

Here we spend time with a ten-year-old German boy (passionately interested in the fading Third Reich), his troubled but deeply caring mother, the comically inept **** left to supervise their small town, and the sarcastic Jewish girl secreted away in their attic. Largely due to circumstance, the kids deal with some very adult subjects, trying everything to convince their peers to take them seriously. It doesn't work, of course, and that leads to some of the richest comedy, but they redouble their efforts. It's only in the very last scene, with the shadow of impending invasion finally past, that the specter of assumed adulthood is released and we finally catch a glimpse of these children acting their age. I wasn't sure the film would actually come together until that perfect moment, but what rich rewards for a thoroughly up-and-down journey.

Whimsical but honest, colorful but draining, it's both wonderful and terrible, often at the same time. My spine was shivering as it cut to the credits. Simply wonderful, Jojo Rabbit is an easily endearing mix of comedy and drama with a heartfelt story centered around otherwise uncomfortable subject matter. It never once disrespects or makes light of the history it's portraying, while managing to pull off humor that would feel right at home in a Monty Python sketch or Mel Brooks feature. The cast is superb all around, held together mostly by terrific child actors; however, Thomasin McKenzie may be the film's number one breakout star. I consider the film to be absolutely incredible! From start to finish, it had me captivated with its compelling storyline, impressive visuals, and outstanding performances. The direction and cinematography were masterful, creating a visually stunning and immersive experience. The Atlantic said if perfectly: ""Jojo Rabbit’s script isn’t emotionally complex enough to address the cruel realism of its world, and as the bleakness continues, the jokes fall flatter and flatter."

The movie is a well made terribly told story with no direction. The movie either doesn't know what it's trying to say or doesn't know how to say it effectively. From Rozy sudden and frankly lackluster death to jojo's characterization (which I can't blame the actor for,he was great). Taika unfortunately got lost in his strengths,tge slapstick comedy that usually works so well for him feels immature here. This should've been better. An offensive mess. Truly awful. 806.title: The Zone of Interest
806.rich_text:
The Zone of Interest The Zone of Interest Drama History Jonathan Glazer Christian Friedel Sandra Hüller Johann Karthaus Luis Noah Witte Nele Ahrensmeier Lilli Falk Anastazja Drobniak Cecylia Pekala Kalman Wilson Medusa Knopf The commandant of Auschwitz, Rudolf Höss, and his wife Hedwig, strive to build a dream life for their family in a house and garden next to the camp. A Chillingly Peaceful Atrocity: The Beautifully Grotesque "Zone of Interest"250211 (4.2)How could a film be so warmly and peacefully cruel? This drama, which portrays the **** atrocities from the perspective of the perpetrators, is remarkably unique. Director Jonathan Glazer, known for "Under the Skin," brings a vibrant yet eerie aesthetic that fits the subject matter perfectly. Throughout the film, the cheerful sounds of domestic life juxtaposed with the distant, horrifying noises of the camp create a truly profound sense of dread. Now that I know this is based on real people, a second viewing would likely reveal even more layers of metaphor and hypocrisy. The story centers on the Hoss family: Rudolf Hoss, the commandant of Auschwitz, and his wife Hedwig. They live a life of upper-class luxury, supported by a staff of servants, right next to the camp walls. While smoke billows and screams echo nearby, the family shamelessly enjoys boating, tea parties, and spa days as if nothing is **** family's indifference is staggering. Rudolf discusses the efficient construction of crematoriums as if they were simple infrastructure projects, while Hedwig treats the stolen furs and jewelry of Jewish prisoners as spoils of war. The only ones who seem to register the horror are the family dog and the youngest daughter, who struggles to sleep. Rudolf himself is a master of duplicity—a "doting" father who oversees mass murder during the day and forces a female prisoner into sexual slavery at night via a secret tunnel. Even the grandmother, who visits briefly, eventually flees the house after witnessing the stench and glow of the crematoriums at night, though she initially spoke of "Bolshevism" with the same callousness as the rest. The film brilliantly uses sound and hidden details, like human remains flowing down the river where the children swim, to emphasize the absolute banality of evil. Rudolf Hoss, the inspiration for the father in "The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas," is depicted here as a man obsessed with the logistics of death, eventually spearheading the deportation of Hungarian Jews. It is a terrifying portrait of how humans can compartmentalize unimaginable cruelty behind a veneer of domestic bliss. This could be the most boring movie to you, but there is no denying how horrifying and eerie this movie is throughout the entire runtime. While most of the focus on the film is just everyday life of a family, it is a family that gets their nice life off the blood, death, and torture of the horrifying sounds you hear in the background the entire movie. Probably a must watch. Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how easy! You just have to look away, and then the evil is simply not there. As long as your own little microcosm fills you with a feel-good atmosphere, the world is a good place. Jonathan Glazer exposes them all: the Hoess family, the neighbors, the fellow travelers, and the Germans in the Third Reich. He doesn't need the usual scenes of horror and terror from the **** criminal database. Rather, the stark contrast between the family idyll on the one hand and mass murder on the other side of a wall perverts the crime to the point of unbearableness. The stylistic device of making the horror a reality only through sounds and smoking chimneys is clever and consistent. A significant, an important film. Es una maravilla. Desearía que hubiera más películas así. No necesita de escenas explícitas para transmitir la criticidad de lo que está pasando que es gravísimo! logra ponerte los pelos de punta a través de los díalogos, la música y las excelentes actuaciones. Realmente la recomiendo! Jonathan Glazer’s masterful direction in *The Zone of Interest* contrasts the mundane life of the Höss family with unseen horrors through static frames and chilling sound design. The haunting background noises and eerie score intensify the emotional weight, forcing viewers to imagine the atrocities. While its slow pace and minimal dialogue may not suit all, the film’s deliberate approach makes it deeply impactful, offering a chilling meditation on evil and human indifference. The Zone of Interest is the inversion of every Holocaust film you’ve seen. All we see of Auschwitz are the front gates and the roofs of the buildings from over the wall that separates the camp from the Höss’ property. A sprawling garden, beautiful flowers and paths, a gazebo, a pool, and a greenhouse all lie in the shadow of ignored horrors unfolding merely feet away. As Hedwig (Rudolf’s wife) says, “The vines will grow and cover it all.” The horror of the film is what lies just out of sight the whole time. CONTINUE READING ON LETTERBOXD: ****/603YtV I got what they wanted to show here, but for me I would've still preferred it more with either a story or at showing even darker scenes - yes the idea is to show how **** family lived like it is all normal there, but still I have loved Jonathan Glazer for some time, I appreciated Under The Skin, absolutely adored Sexy Beast and even enjoyed Birth very much, but here, finally, he has found his material.

His crisp and clear photography just simply plants you with these people, with the sights and more potently, the unavoidable sounds. You are like the black dog, contextless, moving in and out of places, sometimes watching, sometimes being ushered away.

Glazer's attention to pacing, shot length and editing is exquisite; he crafts a listless ordinary film as tightly as a coiled spring and as tense as a trebuchet. It is not artless, however, and still trades in some avant-garde and strange techniques that never feel out of place.

It wasn't the very clever way of breathing new relevancy into the holocaust genre that resonated most with me, it wasn't the haunting ending credits music that says: stay in your seat and endure or walk outside and discuss, but you won't be talking about this film here, now. What resonated most was the ending collection of scenes on the mundanity and gently servile nature of keeping even things as horrifying as the holocaust alive. It was a powerfully moving and contextualising coda that I rarely see in film. (Mauro Lanari) 
From the particular to the universal: the inductive process is reputed an essential conquest of human thought, but Glazer is the first author to apply it to Auschwitz-Birkenau, no one else before him had dared to use or exploit the Holocaust/Shoah as a pretext to denounce something vaster, more general and generic: anthropic indifference, cognitive scotomization, attentive neglect as a defense and survival mechanism, a very effective adaptation strategy to ensure a quiet existence. "Bourgeois criticism": why? It is not a characteristic aspect of a specific socioeconomic subgroup. A worn-out theme? I would say yes. A mandatory topic for any self-styled intellectual even if no one has been able to suggest a shred of a remedy. Furthermore, if the attack is sterile, the only reaction it provokes is rejection and one ends up squashed by a hammer blow like the Talking Cricket in the 4th chapter of Collodi's book. Our director knows this very well, so he tries to avoid such fate by hiding himself and concealing his "j'accuse" under the surface, covered by the cumbersome history of the Höß family, object of an unconditional cathartic condemnation. The Nàzis are always the others. The result is an unbearably ambiguous and intellectually dishonest film, the little villa rebuilt by set designer Chris Oddy is indistinguishable from a current house with vintage or retro taste, behind the garden, beyond the wall, reemerging from the waters of the river there could be any random nefariousness or obscenity, external and extraneous to the "comfort zone" of the "Interessengebiet", relegated to the "zone of disinterest" of our (un)consciousness. Rightly or wrongly, the Jews consider their genocide a historical unicum, it was impossible for them not to be indignant when Glazer, in his acceptance speech for the Academy Award he received, admitted that he made no distinction with the massacre in Gaza. The hypocritical banality of a filmmaker and his marketing. 
Ps: it didn't take much to be provocative with a bit more originality. "Are we dust and will we return to dust" (Gn 3:19)? Crematoria are an accelerated version of it. I don't know how the standards have changed so that a movie like this gets universal acclaim. I thought it was absolutely dreadful. Once again, a director is trying to make "great cinema" in a form that the little man in the movie business obviously imagines these days. But there's nothing great here, except perhaps boredom. The story is literally non-existent, there's not even much plot. The sets are horribly sterile and artificial. This may be intentional, but it destroys any immersion. The camera work is completely inorganic, almost irritatingly uniform in the outdoor scenes. It gives the impression that this was deliberately chosen in order to be able to insert the CGI backdrop with as little position calculation as possible. The entire film - including the exterior scenes - looks as if it was shot in a studio. In my opinion, the highly praised sound design is a joke. A few screams, gunshots, muffled rumbling and in the few false color scenes (is that supposed to be infrared?) an obscene, artificially deep pitched burp - I can't describe it any other way. And then - completely without warning - the movie simply ends. At an absolutely inappropriate point, in the middle of the "plot". Before that, a few scenes from the present have been cut in, showing the cleaning ladies sweeping and vacuuming the present-day museum. What is that supposed to tell us? I don't understand it. And to be honest, I'm not interested either. I'd rather watch Schindler's List again.

É um daqueles raros filmes que conseguem ser tão impactantes para adultos quanto para crianças.Veredito: Lilo & Stitch não é apenas um dos melhores filmes da Disney, mas uma das melhores animações já feitas. 100/100 – Obra-prima. Lilo & Stitch is one that certainly has a ton of heart with the essence meaning of family as out of all the Disney films I have ever seen this by far the most creative one you will ever see. Disney steps outside its comfort zone with this mashup of Hawaiian culture and alien invasions. Like the toothy, sharp little blue furball at the center of all the drama, the film is loud and impulsive, recklessly chasing stray plot threads and then abruptly abandoning them for another distraction.

It’s far less careful and composed than the studio's usual feature work, which serves as both a positive and a negative. On one hand, it's fresh and different; a necessary (and welcome) new direction for a company that had been making movies for six-plus decades at the time. On the other, well, it often feels like something produced by the competition. Lilo & Stitch lacks that certain bit of polish, that magical sense of balance. Stitch, the aforementioned extraterrestrial beast, is a far cry from the standard Disney archetype, even in extreme circumstances. His audacious, violent nature lends itself to some impressive action scenes and a few laughs, but damages the character's sudden, climactic transition into a concerned, invested member of the family. He effectively flips a switch and wakes up, and that's not much of an arc. The human characters fare a bit better - their story has more emotional heft - but they, too, leave a lot on the table.

Still, despite all that, I enjoyed myself. This film's got personality and heart, its unique locale plays an important thematic role and factors directly into the climax, the action bits work very well and the visuals are stylish and interesting (I like the trend toward minimalism). Consider it a lighter entry in the catalog. This was absolutely incredible. I am not lying when I say that this shot up into the top ten Disney films of all time for me. They did not hold anything back and that makes this excellent.

811.title: Watchmen

metadata.tagline: Justice is coming to all of us. No matter what we do.

811.rich_text:
Watchmen Watchmen Justice is coming to all of us. No matter what we do. Mystery Action Science Fiction Zack Snyder Malin Åkerman Patrick Wilson Billy Crudup Matthew Goode Jackie Earle Haley Jeffrey Dean Morgan Carla Gugino Laura Mennell Matt Frewer Stephen McHattie In a gritty and alternate 1985, the glory days of costumed vigilantes have been brought to a close by a government crackdown. But after one of the masked veterans is brutally murdered, an investigation into the killer is initiated. The reunited heroes set out to prevent their own destruction, but in doing so they uncover a sinister plot that puts all of humanity in grave danger. 以“超级英雄”之名，拆解英雄神话。曼哈顿博士窥见原子与宿命，却问不出“为何”：能力愈大，意义愈远，揭示工具理性将世界拆碎后，价值理性已无处安放。笑匠把荒诞当护身符，在废墟中嬉笑，折射后现代对宏大叙事的犬儒。法老王的“完美谋杀”用功利演算换和平，把康德“人即目的”碾作一张资产负债表。而罗夏以绝对律令对抗结果，用血写下“不”，守护残存的自由意志。影片让每位“守望者”成为现代性隐喻：科学、权力、资本、道德，在废墟上角力，无人能全视黑夜。最终，守望之塔空悬，世界继续滑向偶然；问题留给观众——当神性退场，人是否敢承担自身的罪与责？这是后英雄时代最冷的讽喻。 Zack Snyder’s Watchmen: The Ultimate Cut is the definitive cinematic interpretation of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ genre-defying graphic novel — a bold, uncompromising vision that pushes the superhero film into operatic, philosophical territory.

Running nearly four hours, this version restores the Tales of the Black Freighter animated segments and the pseudo-documentary Under the Hood, weaving them into the main narrative. The result is a richer, more faithful adaptation that deepens character arcs and thematic complexity, particularly the existential weight carried by figures like Dr. Manhattan and Rorschach.

Visually, Snyder captures the look and feel of the source material with obsessive precision. From the iconic slow-motion brutality to the saturated color palette, every frame feels ripped from the page — stylized, haunting, and loaded with symbolism.

Narratively, The Ultimate Cut excels where many adaptations fail: it doesn't shy away from the moral ambiguity or bleak cynicism that defines Watchmen. Instead, it embraces it. The film asks hard questions about power, surveillance, and the cost of peace, offering no easy answers. In a cinematic landscape crowded with formulaic heroes, this version dares to challenge the entire concept of heroism itself.

While its extended runtime may test casual viewers, those familiar with the source material or craving a more intellectual, stylized take on the superhero genre will find this to be a near-masterpiece. It's dense, demanding, and at times overwhelming — but it’s also one of the most ambitious and faithful comic book adaptations ever made.

Watchmen: The Ultimate Cut is a haunting, stylish, and uncompromising triumph — not just a superhero film, but a dark mirror held up to the genre itself. Truly one of the most underrated, and fantastic superhero movies ever created. Zach Snyder's magnum opus, a true masterwork of style and storytelling 
Overall: 10/10 J’aime pas (trop) les films de supers héros : c’est toujours lobotomisé du ciboulot, rien que du divertissement à la macgerbale calibré pour la masse du troupeau bêlant… mais rien de tel ici grâce à un scénario remarquablement intelligent qui évite les clichés.

Pas de stars -c’est pas plus mal- car tout est passé dans les effets spéciaux (superbes) et le filmage est à la hauteur, ce qu’il faut de tape-à-l’oeil mais toujours maîtrisé. Je ne suis pas fan pour autant de ces supers héros là : l’ersatz de batmou et sa boîte de ravioli, Miss latex (sans commentaire), le monsieur et sa tronche de serpillère, le Musclor transparent qui pérore la bite à l’air… mais tout est présenté de telle façon qu’on ne fait plus attention à leur look de clowns.

Plus de deux plombes et demi et on ne voit pas le temps passer en tout cas. Dommage, ces musiques, je veux dire, ces chansons de merde ici et là (Simon et Garfunkel au secouuuurs putaaaainnn… sans compter ce foutu braillard à l’intro et sa guitare de crevard !) 

Y avait plus de pognon pour terminer la musique ou quoi ? et placer aussi un extrait du Requiem de Mozart m’a choqué… un peu de modestie, Môssieur Snyder, ce n’est pas de l’art que vous faites, c’est un honnête divertissement et… c’est déjà pas mal… mais sans plus ! cinematic wise it was really good but it was sooo long and boring it made me go to sleep in fact I enjoyed the comic story within the movie (Black Freighter) more than I enjoyed the movie Um dos melhores filmes que já vi na minha vida. Um filme com a pegada mais séria, diferente desse humor barato que vemos em outros filmes do gênero. This may be the most literal adaptation **** novel we'll ever see, but that doesn't mean it's as successful as it could've been. Way back in the year 2009, when the MCU was still in its infancy, this film represented a sort of holy grail for comic book fanatics. It was almost a religious experience, seeing these themes, characters and visuals represented so respectfully on the big screen. As with the preceding 300, Zac Snyder absolutely nailed the look and feel of the comics, but beneath that dazzling superficial showcase is a troubling lack of soul, conviction and character.

With the exception of Jackie Earl Haley, who is absolutely magnificent as the mentally teetering vigilante Rorschach, Watchmen spotlights a large collection of miscast characters which never really seem to buy into what they're saying or doing. The words are right, ripped line-for-line from the bubbles and narrative boxes of the comics, and of course everything looks great, but bland inflections, bad interpretations and a hectic, compressed timeline strip away the power of the plot's weightiest bits. In a way it's TOO loyal, as the one major moment that skirts the source material - a significant tweak to the story's conclusion - works better than all the rest.

Snyder was ambitious to tackle such a booby-trapped property, and to do so with so much admiration for its roots is admirable, but there's a reason this was dubbed unfilmable for so many years. There's so much going on at any given moment that even the most familiar reader runs the risk of being bucked, and even at three hours, a large portion of the story resides on the cutting room floor. For Watchmen, those seemingly dispensable character moments are just as important as the heaviest plot developments. A valiant effort, but ultimately a failed one. One-of-a-kind superhero movie! Probably the best one I have seen. Interesting story, excellent strong visuals, great sets, mix of the best film styles... The acting is excellent, the dialogues thoughtful. It's been a long time since any movie gave me so much food for thought. I always watch this movie in one breath and am delighted. Watching this movie will steal you the joy of reading the original opera. The movie misses completely some of the key concepts of the original (e.g: the important talk of two characters in a very far place).
You could either watch a decent action movie or read one of the greatest comics ever written. Think about it. While it isn't his worst film, never has Zack Snyder's penchant for perfectly adapting a source material aesthetically while completely missing its point thematically been so apparent than with his adaptation of Alan Moore's classic Watchmen. Snyder clearly idolizes these characters, whom Moore wrote intentionally as selfish, arrogant, cynical, hypocritical, cowardly, and downright terrible people.

812.title: The Rule of Jenny Pen
812.rich_text:
The Rule of Jenny Pen The Rule of Jenny Pen Horror Thriller James Ashcroft John Lithgow Geoffrey Rush Nathaniel Lees Maaka Pohatu Thomas Sainsbury Ian Mune Ginette McDonald Holly Shanahan Bruce Phillips Yvette Parsons Confined to a secluded rest home and trapped within his stroke-ridden body, a former Judge must stop an elderly psychopath who employs a child's puppet to abuse the home's residents with deadly consequences. (Mauro Lanari) 
A strand of austral cinema disregards the need for a logical screenplay, invoking a presumed mysterious and hostile nature of its land. From "Picnic at Hanging Rock" to certain works by Jane Campion and George Miller, up to the "Wolf Creek" diptych, things happen due to a malevolent genius loci. You watch Ashcroft's film hoping that the events will clarify as the minutes pass; instead, the opposite happens. A morbid atmosphere that kicks off with the most striking idea, the involuntary bonze, and then explores the meanders of a nursing home as if it were the delirium of the Overlook Hotel. Some come out satisfied, others with a headache. Worst nursing home - EVER!

Rush and Lithgow are great in this movie as adversaries. Lithgow is especially delightful as a sociopath who decides to terrorize the residents of an English nursing home. Rush is a new resident who has been afflicted by a stroke.

There's a great set-up here, but there is a big problem. The staff of the nursing home is criminally negligent. They are never around when Lithgow is rampaging through the nursing home. This gets so out of hand, it stretches credibility. The Rule of Jenny Pen is good enough if you are in the mood to watch a good horror and thriller movie. I watched a man lick doll's  bootie for an hour and a half 10/10. Very bad. Very bad. Very bad. Very bad. Very bad. Fewer moviegoing experiences are more frustrating than watching a film in which the creators have no clear vision for what they’re trying to say. Regrettably, such is the case with this second feature offering from writer-director James Ashcroft. When a revered judge (Geoffrey Rush) suffers a stroke, he’s moved to what has to be the most ineptly run convalescent home in New Zealand to undergo rehabilitation. While there, however, he – like many of the facility’s other residents – becomes the target of taunting and abuse by another patient (John Lithgow), a manic dementia case who menaces them with a macabre hand-held puppet he calls Jenny Pen, the one who he contends rules over everyone housed at the home. When the judge protests, though, he’s summarily ignored and called delusional by the utterly clueless staff, an aspect of the narrative that’s wholly implausible and undermines the credibility of whatever the story is supposed to represent. That’s made worse by a meandering story that seems to vacillate between presenting a straightforward tale of elder abuse and floating the possibility that the judge may indeed be suffering from his own internal delusions now that he’s trapped in his own stroke-afflicted body. That kind of purposeful ambiguity might have worked better if it had been employed more skillfully, but, as it stands, that uncertainty is never properly developed. And, as the film plays out, it grows progressively more unbelievable and disjointed, leaving viewers wondering what’s truly supposed to be going on. What’s more, this offering is laughingly billed as a horror flick, but there’s virtually nothing the least bit scary about it; it instead languishes in the realm of a modest (though largely unfocused and unengaging) psychological thriller. To its credit, the film incorporates some searing comic relief in the form of witty, pointed one-liners (mostly delivered by Rush), and the two leads struggle mightily to elevate this cinematic mess into something more respectable. But even their considerable talents – no doubt a casting choice aimed at providing a touch of class to a production unworthy of it – are not enough to salvage this woefully undercooked project. Please, do yourself a favor and don’t waste your time or money on this one. The Rule of Jenny Pen is a savagely funny little horror movie.  Although you’ll need to suspend your disbelief on more than one occasion, the film’s merits more than make up for its lapses.  The gripping performances by Geoffrey Rush and John Lithgow alone make it worth watching.  Recommended.  detroitcineaste Jenny Pen is the name of the hand puppet that John Lithgow’s character wears, as he terrorizes the residents in his assisted living community. Geoffry Rush plays a judge who suffers a stroke that sends him to the same facility. Thus begins the conflict between the bully and the partially paralyzed witness to the evil. Rush gives a stolid, serious performance, while Lithgow relishes in his creepy villainy. New Zealand director James Ashcroft effectively created the somewhat unpleasant environment with numerous patients in horrible, sometime helpless conditions. He’s also thrown in some dumb “dream sequences” and, as one of the writers, chosen to ignore reality with so many absurd situations (the caregivers never seem to be around when things go bad, even in groups). Lithgow and Rush are both Executive Producers on this film, which explains another reason they might want to be involved. There was potential to make a thriller, but Ashcroft chose to exploit discomfort without minimal tension to create this dreary drama.

813.title: Big Fish

metadata.tagline: An adventure as big as life itself.

813.rich_text:
Big Fish Big Fish An adventure as big as life itself. Adventure Fantasy Drama Tim Burton Ewan McGregor Albert Finney Billy Crudup Jessica Lange Helena Bonham Carter Alison Lohman Robert Guillaume Marion Cotillard Matthew McGrory David Denman Throughout his life Edward Bloom has always been a man of big appetites, enormous passions and tall tales. In his later years, he remains a huge mystery to his son, William. Now, to get to know the real man, Will begins piecing together a true picture of his father from flashbacks of his amazing adventures. Big Fish has just got such a larger portrait of life as the vision is just wonderful in every surface. I will admit I like Tim Burton, and have enjoyed a vast majority of his films, Edward Scissorhands, Beetle Juice, Batman and Ed Wood. Big Fish is I think one of Burton's better movies in my personal opinion, maybe not his very best, but it is a very sweet, imaginative and moving film. Here Burton delves into familiar territory, a strange place between reality and fantasy, dream and nightmare. The story is really sweet, and while slow at times, does have a poignant ending. The visuals as pretty much always in a Tim Burton film are gorgeous, not Gothic here like in Sleepy Hollow and Edward Scissorhands but evergreen and picturesque. The scenery was beautiful and so was the cinematography, and Danny Elfman's score is stunning. His score for Edward Scissorhands blew me away, but the lyrical, sensitive and hypnotic themes used here make it a score that is truly special. The screenplay is well crafted, and has a bittersweet feel to it. Sentimental yes, but also bittersweet. The acting is remarkably good, with Ewan McGregor making for a handsome yet somewhat charming young Edward Bloom, and the wonderful Albert Finney a revelation as his older self. Billy Crudup is excellent as the son who is intent on exposing his father, and sets out to learn the truth, and Danny DeVito is great as the shape-changing circus ringmaster. Jessica Lange is beautiful and alluring as Sandra and Helena Bonham Carter is almost unrecognisable as the Witch. Then there is Alison Lohman, Marion Cottilard, Robert Guillaume and Matthew McGory(as Karl the Giant) and they are very good as well. Overall, I loved this film, it is moving and very imaginative. 9.5/10 Bethany Cox A nice fairy tale that mixes fiction and reality. Some of the fantasy episodes are even great and lovely, a strength by Tim Burton. This is a movie about story telling.  How they are created, their importance, how they connect us.

Secondary its about how sons and father's connect.  Some beautiful visuals as well.This isn't a great movie but when it works its a great accomplishment. Melancholic adventure with its story told through narration, packed to the brim with visual effects and over the top sequences. Sadly the pacing is off and we never spend long enough with any of the characters to form any meaningful connection between them. Whats clearly meant to serve as a metaphor for paternal discourse ends up as a flat and meaningless whimsey. Es una obra de arte, no entiendo a los que trabajan para las revistas y puntuan con malas notas. Debes verla y al final es imposible no llorar A heartwarming, whimsical tale of the relationship between father & son.
This movie shows there is more in the kit bag of Tim Burton than being the master of gothic storytelling. This movie is sad, but it's also happy.
It's hertwarming, but also heartbreaking.
It's mature, but also childish.

It's amazing, and it makes me tear up everytime. This is why Tim Burton does Fantasy. Fantasy isn't something about lies, it is more about adding hope and dream to the truth. Big Fish is Tim Burton's masterpiece. It's one of my favorite movies, and it makes me cry every time I watch it. It's beautiful, it's unique, its heartwarming, its moving, and it nails the aesthetic of an American Tall Tale. You will never forget this movie. Go watch it!

The King's Man The King's Man Witness the bloody origin. Action Adventure Thriller Matthew Vaughn Ralph Fiennes Gemma Arterton Rhys Ifans Matthew Goode Tom Hollander Harris Dickinson Daniel Brühl Djimon Hounsou Charles Dance Shaun McKee As a collection of history's worst tyrants and criminal masterminds gather to plot a war to wipe out millions, one man must race against time to stop them. It’s a really good film. It’s almost completely unrelated to the first 2 Kingsmen films and is much better than the second one, which I know put some people off the franchise. And Ralph Fiennes is just too good in everything not to be enjoyed here. I hated the sequel. It was pure garbage. I like to think Channing Tatum was to blame, because if I never saw him again in a movie it would be too soon, but with him or without him the movie **** third, the prequel, was a serious movie, and a history lesson. It was compelling and well done, and as usual Ralph Fiennes was ****, we have the original, a comical action packed spy thriller. The sequel, a complete mess with terrible casting, and embarrassing directing. And, the prequel, a well acted history lesson in HD. I liked **** you can learn to separate them into three different categories of movies, and not try and find the "original" in the prequel, you may discover that it's a pretty good film. Still, it has a lot of good stuff. Gut visualisierte Schauplätze. Sogar die Geschichte ist interessant: Eine Alienrasse lässt die Menschen auf der Erde gedeihen bis es genug sind um sie zu "ernten". The premise would not be so bad, but along the development the film gets worse and worse, the story is banal and at times senseless ending up boring more and more. Besides the basic idea of ​​the story it is not clear what film it wants to be, ending up being neither funny, nor with a good story, nor exciting, nor an action film There's something sincere about how fantastical and wacky this is. It's like the Fifth Element if it was really bad, or like a Marvel movie with no charismatic characters. Colorfull and action paced nothingburger...
